speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A plain review of the President’s speech and the 21 addenda issued by the respective Ministries and Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) since, reveals much more than that.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The plans go well beyond the remainder of the current term of this Government’s office.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These plans are not just incremental in nature.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are aimed at delivering decisive advantages to Singaporeans of the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They are not at all easy to achieve.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To materialise these plans, we require the strong support of fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also need highly competent and dedicated leaders at all levels of government, including the political leadership, to execute these plans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the defining characteristic of this People’s Action Party (PAP) Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It sees as its responsibility not just to take care of the current generation of Singaporeans for the near term.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All our present-day advantages, hard won on the back of generations past are not considered, I quote, “a pinnacle of achievement, but as a base from which to scale new heights.” It sees as its bounden duty to lay strong foundations for future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Indeed, this principle of steward leadership is specifically embedded in the concluding paragraph of the President’s speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She urges us to, I quote, "keep faith with future generations yet unborn and build a Singapore that thrives and endures for many years to come.” The approach taken by the Government gives us in this House a unique opportunity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is my hope that hon Members who will be speaking during this debate will nail their colours to the mast and unequivocally state where they stand on the Government’s ambitious plans to build an enduring and thriving Singapore for now and years to come.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By doing so, we will be able to explore building a consensus on these plans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will include an agreement on funding the projects involved in the plans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We will also be able to avoid the polarising effect of these long-term plans becoming political “footballs” of populist politicians.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What we cannot afford to do as a small country with no natural resources is to adopt a “stop/start” or “feast and famine” approach in funding these important plans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such an approach will quickly deplete our precious resources and will almost certainly spell doom for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Importantly, as I will be alluding to shortly in my speech, it is my belief that building consensus in this House on such key plans will help us retain trust and unity which the President has identified to be essential for the future of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The President stated in her speech that as we emerged from the pandemic, trust in the Government has strengthened.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The President also emphasised that trust and unity are key to dealing with our priorities that includes securing our place in the world, growing our economy and refreshing our social compact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But we are not among the top three.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, we should not behave as though we have arrived.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The results of the survey are consistent with anecdotal experience.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We also know, though, that the trust built today can be easily lost tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the impermanent nature of this “being”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Trust cannot be assumed; it has to be conscientiously built and nurtured.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The question I raise is how do we ensure that this strategic resource in the form of the reservoir of trust between our people and Government can be retained and even deepened as our nation navigates through an even more challenging socioeconomic environment?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to draw focus on three areas: (a) the work of our Public Service officers; (b) the work of our political leaders in this House; and at the end of my speech (c) the Forward Singapore exercise conducted by our 4G Team.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Public Service plays a vital role in the maintenance of trust between our people and the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It will continue to play an important role in future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my respectful view, the strong trust relationship that we enjoy today is attributable in a significant part to the blood, sweat and tears of our officers in discharging their solemn duties.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To underscore this point, Sir, please allow me to share that, not infrequently, I receive detailed email replies from public officers, especially from the Housing and Development Board (HDB), to my queries on behalf of my constituents in the wee hours of morning!

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I cannot help feeling bad for them as they obviously sacrificed their personal time with their families to deal with official work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These officers have a strong sense of duty.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We owe them a huge debt of gratitude.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What I feel distinguishes our Public Service from others is that in both design and implementation, our officers have foremost in their minds the ordinary Singapore Citizen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In their roles, they serve to strike a balance between achieving policy objectives, exemplifying values such as compassion and fairness, accountability for the use of national resources and the desire to do justice in each and every case.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This turns out to be a significant ground of appeal.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By being flexible and not mechanically applying the timeline, we managed to achieve a better balance between the policy intent and the legitimate expectation of the ordinary citizen.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My reward was that I got a photo of Baby Qi Yue who happened to lift her head for the first time on the day that the Government allowed Mdm Zhu’s appeal!

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Budget 2023, an announcement was made on the GST Voucher - Cash (Seniors’ Bonus).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The policy intent was to help lower-income senior Singapore Citizens aged 55 and above cope with the cost of living.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To gauge the financial circumstances of the senior, the Government uses the income earned in 2021 as a proxy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I had a situation where my resident earned more than $34,000 in 2021 but had a significant drop in income in 2022 owing to personal circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, having regard to the policy intent of the bonus, the Ministry of Finance (MOF), in its reply to the petition issued by me on behalf of my resident, was prepared to be flexible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It sought documents supporting my resident’s claim that his income dropped significantly in 2022 before assessing whether it is prepared to provide him with the bonus on a discretionary basis.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Again, this is an enlightened approach and there is much to commend the Public Service for exercising flexibility to ensure that the policy intent is met.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What I am drawing attention to is the process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our citizens must feel that they were listened to, their views considered seriously and they received proper explanations in a respectful manner on the outcomes even if they may disagree with them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This approach will, in my view, deepen this strategic resource of trust between our people and the Government as an institution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Trust is the red thread running through the three points that the President made in her speech which made an impression on me.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, the President highlighted the need for us, as a little red dot, to close ranks and stay united against global forces which will continue to try even harder to influence our domestic public opinion, so as to uphold Singapore’s vital interests.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hon Members may recall the debate in this House on the Foreign Interference (Countermeasures) Bill that was passed in 2021 to deal with hostile information campaigns by foreign powers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What I thought significant then was the united view expressed by hon Members on both sides of the aisle that Singapore politics is for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As responsible politicians, we must continue to close ranks and hold the line on core issues of national importance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, the President highlighted that this unity as a nation will be important as we aim to secure economic opportunities amid a global economic slowdown to strengthen our position as a trusted and reliable business hub adding value to the world.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On this, it may be useful to emphasise one important takeaway from this year’s Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The raison d’etre behind our economic objectives was never economic growth for its own sake.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Rather, growth is a means to achieve our broader objectives of advancing the well-being of every Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This affects our prospects for growth this year with inflation still running high.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It seems to me what the President advocated in her speech about making sure Singapore is united in the context of a global economic slowdown has become all the more important now.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Third, the President emphasised the need to strengthen our social compact through programmes aimed at uplifting the disadvantaged and vulnerable and to keep us as one united people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The President identified this effort as a priority of the 4G team which is engaging Singaporeans through the Forward Singapore exercise to renew and update our social compact.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I will talk more on the Forward Singapore exercise later in my speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The President also laid down the Government’s four key priorities to strengthen our social compact: (a) expanding opportunities for all, (b) strengthening social safety nets, (c) building a smart and liveable city and (d) deepening Singaporean’s sense of shared identity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, the President stated that the Government will look into ensuring that advantages and privileges that may come with meritocracy does not become entrenched such that it weakens our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This point about the need to re-examine meritocracy was probably the most quoted point by my residents about the President’s speech whom I engaged with before drafting this speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All of them expressed wholehearted agreement with the President.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They agreed with the Government’s call to devote more resources to our children who start out with less.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The support, however, is not just a question of fact, but a matter of degree too in order that we can make a tangible difference for these children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One other area of potential support that the Government should consider is to address the housing environment of children living in overcrowded flats.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a point that I have raised several times; the last being at the Ministry of National Development (MND)'s Committee of Supply (COS) 2023 debate during my speech on strengthening inclusivity in housing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I said “each child is precious, and we must do our utmost to ensure that they grow up in more conducive housing environment”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To be fair, based on statistics provided by HDB, there are not many such cases, but I have come across a few.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One possible way that can be considered is to provide for Social Service Agencies to run study centres for these children near rental flats that are open after school.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this way, our children will be able to study in a more conducive environment after school.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Tava even provides study support and mentoring for these children.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, the President emphasised the need for a stronger network of stakeholders to help provide opportunities for all, participate in nation building and build unity.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I agree and I believe that all hon Members feel the same way too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The question is how can we achieve this?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I said then that we need to do something more fundamental to move this needle.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I suggested that successful organisations and individuals must feel more invested in the lives of the less fortunate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They must know that we are bound together in one common destiny.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is clearly not an easy ask but we must quite clearly put in as much effort as possible to realise this objective.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One area where stakeholders can help is to level the playing field when it comes to giving our children sporting experiences which are perceived to be within the exclusive domain of the well-to-do.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am not a golfer, but I have certainly read about the amazing story of Mr Mardan Mahmat, who was Singapore’s number one golfer for more than 10 years.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He dropped out of primary school at the age of 12.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A year later, he became a caddie at Jurong Country Club.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a teenager, Mardan frequently snuck into the club’s golf course when no one was looking and, by himself, learned how to play the game.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He obviously had loads of talent because he managed to hone it by himself.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Long story short, he became Singapore’s number one golfer.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do think though that something can be done through stakeholders with the appropriate resources to organise efforts to reach out to interested children, give them the sporting experience, suss out from among them the next Mardan Mahmat whom they can help to nurture to be a Singapore golf champion.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am aware that many of these stakeholders already do wonderful charity work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do hope though that they can consider this as a worthwhile extension of their efforts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The idea here is to provide children with the requisite talent and drive, regardless of their background, with opportunities to pursue their sporting dreams and become national athletes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to the work of political leaders in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The President stated in her speech that the trust between the political leadership and the people is a key strength that we must continue to nurture.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The President gave important guidance in this regard.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She advised that our interactions as politicians be anchored on mutual respect and the shared goal of advancing the larger public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should work through our differences, enlarge our common ground and draw strength from our diverse perspectives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We, politicians, are at our best when we present our arguments in a measured way, recognise the inherent trade-offs in each of the policy suggestions that we make and present cogent arguments as to why we feel the balance should be struck one way or another.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: What the President stated brought to my mind the speech that I made during the opening of the 14th Parliament when I advocated several proposals for Parliamentary reform of our evolving democracy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I said then that building consensus in this House is an important outcome of our work here.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I described consensus as a process of contestation, persuasion and resolution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Equally important is that such engagement will enable Singaporeans outside this House to have a better opportunity to understand the points of agreement, points of disagreement raised by their elected representatives and, through that, they will be able to better appreciate how these points impact on the ordinary lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore has always preferred an undramatic approach to problem solving.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is our political heritage from the first generation of our political pioneers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some of you may have recognised that I quoted a line from Dr Goh Keng Swee at the start of my speech – that we must consider our starting today merely as a base to build tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Dr Goh was one of our deepest policy thinkers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He said, and I quote, “Deciding on policy and determining a line of action is different from engaging in a debate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Cabinet government is not a debating society or an academic seminar.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Views are aired and, if done with style and elegance, the participants go home happy.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In Government, you have to live with the consequences of your decision.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If you make a mistake, the results are painful.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In political life, there is no alibi for failure.” I feel that we, in Parliament, should bear this in mind.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When we deal with the real issues in this House, we know that they often matter to millions of lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When we say that we are not “ideological” about something, it means that we are not wedded to whether the idea is from the left or the right, from the PAP or the Opposition, we are not wedded to repeating yesterday’s solutions tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We should be disinterested in merely sounding good.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On their own, they do not serve the interests of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is against this background that I argue the need for constructive politics in Parliamentary proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before the Second Reading of the Bill in this Parliament, there were concerns within certain quarters about the broad language of the Bill and perceived lack of judicial oversight.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My hon friends across the aisle proposed amendments to the Bill to address, among others, these points.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, even before the hon Minister for Home Affairs delivered his Second Reading speech, lines were already drawn.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This led to the hon Minister making a plea in this House to hon Members not to use Parliament as a forum to read out prepared speeches based on lines that were already drawn before he rendered his speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: When I rose to speak on the Bill, I highlighted that whilst there were important differences between the views of the hon Members from both sides of the aisle, they were few, compared to the substantive areas of agreement between them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I do not remember a single journalist covering this point in his or her article.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech on building consensus in Parliament, I said that, and I quote “agreement, collegiality, friendliness, all these make for poor headlines”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For these reasons, I advocate an introspection within each of us in this House to build the common ground that the President referred to in her speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Parliamentary proceedings should not be turned into arenas for “entertainment” that we regularly see in other countries.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will erode our people’s trust and confidence in their elected representatives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These engagements are aimed at identifying the values, priorities and policies needed to strengthen our social compact and to build a better and brighter Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wish to make two points on the Forward Singapore Exercise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, as we look forward, we should not forget the values that allowed us to make progress as a nation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I, therefore, feel that the President’s reminder that we should hold dear to our core values as Singaporeans is a timely one.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is the enduring legacy of our founding generation of leaders led by our founding Prime Minister, Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time – and this my second point – I feel that it is important for the Forward Singapore Exercise to adequately capture the idealism of our youths so that they will be able to identify with and support our vision for the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: After all, they have the biggest stake in our plans for the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A few weeks ago, during a house visit, I met my resident, Mr Sherman Chua, aged 21.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He is working with a Silicon Valley company in the artificial intelligence (AI) space.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As we all know, this space is simply “exploding” at the moment with the advent of ChatGPT and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He told me that as a result of his exposure to this space, he is convinced that life as we know it will change a lot through imminent and rapid adoption of AI.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: He expressed to me his concern that Singapore is not investing enough resources to get ahead in this area.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In his view, if nothing is done in this space within the next five years, Singapore may be passed over and runs the risk of becoming a laggard.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I invited him to drop me an email containing his views and I will link him up with the relevant pillar leads in the Forward Singapore Exercise.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am sure there are other young people like Sherman in our communities.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If we are to consider Singapore as a base to scale and not a pinnacle on which we rest, we must recognise that the nature of the electorate is changing.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It has been changing since World War Two ended – a generation that has never known war, communalism, death by gunshot or violence, days of hunger, or nights of terror.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Today, a new generation is emerging, standing taller and brighter than the ones before.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a result, we have, today, a generation that has never experienced hardship to the same degree and scale of the past.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: From the start of their working life, they understand that they can ask for work-life balance and mental wellness days, not as entitlements but as a fact of Singaporean life.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These are the natural fruits of 60 years of careful tending.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Our people today would naturally have different responses to Government policies than those of the past.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This word “lived experience” is used quite a lot today.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some may feel uncomfortable at how it elevates subjective experience to a policy truth on which we often build an edifice of rights and allocations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The fact remains that people’s psyche will change and, as they do, their government must change and to a degree and at a speed unprecedented.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We cannot be an analogue government in a digital world, if we are to keep faith with our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All this is not to say that Singaporeans are less tough today than we were in the past or that we rise any slower to a challenge.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are a people new to pandemics and the world has not seen the scale and intensity of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: History is a good teacher but, like PSLE mathematics, we do not need to have worked out the same sum before to get the right answer in a new one.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are a different people today and require a new style and substance in our policies.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Two things which guided our leaders after the war must not change.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The President’s speech, like those of almost all Presidents before her, speaks of the need to ensure that Singapore “endures for many years to come”.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: No large country suffers from this same paranoia.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But this is the nature of small states – to be short-lived.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We must, therefore, trust one another, trust our leaders and trust our shared identity so as to build a brighter future together.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, it has become fashionable to hammer this word "meritocracy", as if those of us who use it do not know it was originally coined as criticism.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Michael Young, the British sociologist, in 1958, argued that a system that rewarded merit defined as "IQ plus effort" is as flawed as that one rewarding accidents of birth, because having cognitive ability is as much a matter of genetic lottery.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is true, except we may prefer to adopt this system, compensate for its shortcomings rather than adopt the alternatives which are random assignment, other criteria such as money, power or birth.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In 1971, then-Prime Minister Mr Lee Kuan Yew gave a famous speech about 300 people in a jumbo jet.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Most of us remember that speech for the graphic image of the jet crashing and a country bereft of leadership.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But the main idea for me is this, how did these people get on the plane?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Lee said at the time, and I quote, "The main burden of present planning and implementation rests on the shoulders of some 300 key persons." He goes on to say, "Outstanding men in civil service, the Police, the armed forces, chairmen of statutory boards and their top administrators." And then, he goes on to say, "These people come from poor and middle-class homes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And these men have risen to the top by their own merit, hard work and high performance.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Together they are a closely knit and co-ordinated hard core.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If all the 300 were to crash in one jumbo jet, then Singapore will disintegrate.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: That shows how small the base is for our leadership." This idea that a man comes into leadership, or indeed, into any position of opportunity, by what he can do, how hard he has worked, the stuff he himself is made of, not who his father was, who his friends are, or how much money he has.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This idea that one looks at a man and not his pedigree is as old as Plato's Republic and the Chinese Imperial Examinations.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, this must remain the only way to get on that jet.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The fly in this ointment, of course, is that the two are not unrelated.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How much a man is, determines how many advantages his son or daughter has, who this son marries, and in turn, the kinds of privilege he confers on his own offsprings.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, there are people who are born into HDB rental blocks that their parents live in, as well as those who inherit good class bungalows (GCBs) that their parents may themselves inherit.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The Government can make sure that both have a roof over their heads, they have vaccinations in the clinics, that the sons of the rich serve alongside those of the poor in National Service, but there is no way that the first can afford everything that the second does.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We talk often of income inequality and that is indeed an issue.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But what I want today to speak about is wealth, because that is an even more glaring offence to the meritocratic ideal.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The billionaires should compete among themselves so as not to allow the state to benefit from their preferences for luxury goods.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The same goes for the tax for GCBs, country club transfer fees and so on.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Net worth is not net income, and it is the first which may be a stronger force for fracture.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My second point on inherited wealth is to ask for some data.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The data on the Gini coefficient is clear.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is a sign that Government transfers are a good way to reduce income inequalities.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But the Gini coefficient includes only wage income.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I am not asking for a segregation of the super-rich in terms of everyday life, merely in tax regimes, as a matter of fairness.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: They are, of course, still free to enjoy $4 or $5 wanton mee at one of my coffeeshops at Serangoon Central.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to keep common spaces open because these are, after all, financed by tax dollars.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The second piece of the puzzle is, therefore, the redistributive function of the state.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In order to keep us from fracturing along the lines of inherited wealth, we must also level the playing field for those who are not unto the manner born.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In health, education and housing, as well as some elements of transport and financial planning, we must create a minimum standard of living for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The budget of our top two universities here run to billions of dollars a year, with high resources inside the classrooms, the best labs, professors; and outside: with overseas travel, mental health and wellness and a close network of mentors.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: What about the rest of the other 60%?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Can we think of some educational spending or resourcing for the 60%?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Whether in terms of skills, continuous training, micro-credentials, or even the sort of non-academic opportunities, including sports, which Mr Murali has talked about, that Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) affords to their students?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This latter could include opportunities in the arts, sports as well as access to community service and overseas exposure.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore would then truly be a home which provides higher and lifelong education for all.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This aggressive redistribution, which is a hallmark of Singapore's socialism, must become even stronger and not just in fiscal policy, but in public censure of any pretence to social class.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In this, I refer to the most recent incident where the resident of a condominium mocked, humiliated and ridiculed a security guard for clamping the wheels of his car.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: His utterance – flaunting his wealth, his contempt for the guard is abhorrent and has no place in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are some things that money cannot buy and in Singapore, this includes the price of insult and derogation of any man doing an honest job.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We have in 60 years indeed, gone from mudflats to metropolis and may now have a different level of wealth and income but we must not stand for those who think money buys access to a different class.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In our schools, in our army camps, in this House of Parliament, we stand or fall as one.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Our jumbo jet may be a lot bigger today, but entry is still by merit and there is still just one class.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, as in 1971, we are still flying the same flag, with the same five stars: democracy, progress, peace, justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, the success of Singapore lies not within the few in a jet, but in the multitude of ideas in many people who live and work on this island.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In 1971, Mr Lee was speaking of unity and the need for all Singaporeans to feel that we are, at the root of our identity, one people.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At that time, his fight was to avoid being torn under and along racial lines.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At that time, a Malay newspaper had been advocating "bumiputera" policies.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One Chinese newspaper, on the other hand, has been playing up pro-Chinese Communist news.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The English press at the time had been pushing for "more permissiveness in sex and drugs and worked up a campaign against National Service." In 1971, the way towards unity was to build common ground in a common language and culture, and a stake in a prospering country.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Today, we may all speak a common language, our schools all teach in English and the power of different language newspapers may have weakened.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But we still face provocations, falsehoods, dissension sown and manufactured, and we still face a world who has no interest in the success of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Aside from the fault lines I spoke of earlier, there are other challenges: foreign and other malign influences through social media, the rise of a victimhood culture where each special group stand on its rights and sees "micro aggressions", where subjective feeling and "lived experiences" take priority over objective truths and rational discourse.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And as Singapore ages, the demands for state resources for older Singaporeans will rise, we can expect rising resentment among the young.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, this is a serious issue which we must tackle.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The challenges today are as numerous as ever.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It seems it is the fate of a small nation, to always strive lest we fall.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This can exhaust and frighten, or it can inspire and energise.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The choice is ours, all of us who have chosen to fly this jet together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Imagine for a moment, if you will, being a teenager again.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The awkward parties, the search for self, the facial breakouts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But one of the feelings that many of us will find inextricably linked to our adolescent years is one of exclusion.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Now imagine the same feeling, only that you are now supposed to be a fully functioning, fully participating adult in society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: By some measures, we are among the richest countries in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: When adjusted for actual purchasing power, we climb even higher; to third, just behind Ireland and Luxembourg, two European countries often used as tax shelters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But amid this wealth, we also see sharply dissonant scenes of the elderly picking up cardboard, selling tissue packs, or clearing plates at hawker centers, of an underclass of workers who live in dingy, overcrowded rental flats and rely on food handouts, of people who quip that in Singapore, you can be poor, or you can be sick, or you can die, but you cannot stop working.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In her address last week, Mdm Halimah urged us to improve our social compact and strengthen our social safety net, emphasising how, I quote, "the fruits of progress must be shared fairly." I support the President's sentiment and the Motion, but in this speech, I will speak more about the apparent economic success declared by the headline numbers versus the economic precarity felt by a large group of Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I will go on to discuss hard living in Singapore, especially after the pandemic, before concluding with proposals that can help us hopefully improve the circumstances of those who are struggling the most.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The market price of a 4-room HDB flat – all 970 square feet of it – ranges from $460,000 in Jurong East to a whopping $860,000 in Queenstown.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Sengkang, the district I represent, recently saw a flat change hands for close to $1 million dollars.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And island wide, close to a dozen 4-room flats sold for more than $1 million-dollar mark in the first quarter.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The cost of a new Japanese sedan, like the Honda Civic that I drive, is $180,000, around five times the price of what it goes for in other advanced economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Put another way, buying a car would cost close to three years' salary of a typical middle-income individual here, compared to around 14 months in the US.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our decades-old aspiration toward Swiss standards of living has, alas, also brought with it Swiss-style prices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Reports routinely place Singapore, tied with New York, as the most expensive city to live in in the world.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this Government has argued that such metrics do not reflect the typical experience of a Singaporean household who consume different things and have access to taxpayer-funded grants and subsidies for big-ticket items like purchasing an HDB flat, the sting is that many of these things the rest of the world deem affordable is, for us, not.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: That said, by some measures, Singapore is eminently affordable, at least when compared to other advanced economies.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Delicious hawker meals, which we rightly celebrate as a part of our natural, intangible heritage, can be had for a few dollars, plus a dollar more if you happen to live in Sengkang.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Our public transportation system is excellent and many of us commute on it on a day-to-day basis by paying relatively affordable, albeit rising, fares.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Most of us are able to send our kids to school without the need to resort to expensive private schooling that would break the bank.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It stems from the fact that for those among us that do not own or have access to capital, life is exceedingly hard.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is one of working long hours but barely getting by, of living out each day with little hope for the future, of seeing the enormous prosperity that our country has achieved but feeling that, somehow, this has mostly passed you by.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But for those of us who own assets like stocks and bonds, who run or inherited a business, or were fortunate enough to get on the housing ladder early on, it is possible to enjoy the fruits of this wealth and rely on high-asset prices to cushion the effects of high prices of goods and services.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, the challenges of the poor would likely have been compounded by the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Across the globe, economically vulnerable households have tended to fare poorly as a result of the COVID-19 shock.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Detailed surveys from economies, both Western and Eastern, suggest lower-income groups experienced greater job market losses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This may seem especially unfair, since the less well-off were often our essential workers and had to continue on in the frontlines, even as the rest of us sheltered comfortably at home.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Unfortunately, the poor did not find much relief after the pandemic.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While this has come down, inflation, in excess of 6%, continues to eat away at incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even by the Government's own statistics, household real wages decreased in 2020 and 2021, and the small increase last year does not fully make up for the losses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, there are those of us who have been lucky enough to have sufficient savings to invest and, in some cases, have been able to tap on higher interest rates offered by the market to shore up our finances.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But such discrepancies only serve to further exacerbate the discrepancy between the wealthy and the rest.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Researchers who have devoted their lives to studying poverty tend to believe that its causes may be broadly defined into two groups.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The first argues that low incomes constrain the ability of the poor to save, eat well and pursue educational opportunities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Since poverty causes poverty, the solution is to offer one-off transfers that help the poor extricate themselves from their plight.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A second group believes that the poor are limited by their God-given abilities, talents or motivation, and they will always be among us and the solution is to provide small, but repeated, income support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I believe that there is merit to both these perspectives on poverty.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Inasmuch as we want to offer opportunities for those of us to escape the poverty trap, the basis of most of the Government's anti-poverty policies, there are those that happen to be endowed with less potential, stricken by physical or mental disability, or who face persistent discrimination, and hence, require the support of society-at-large.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And in a rich, advanced economy, I believe that doing so is the correct and compassionate thing to do.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We take pride in ourselves as people who are quantitatively sophisticated and highly efficient; we make and meet KPIs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Targeting the poor is impossible, or at least, imperfect, without an official, transparent benchmark.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We have, instead, a confusing mishmash of thresholds that have been applied by different agencies at different times.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We sometimes see reports for the lowest quartile, or quintile, being treated as the poor, or simply the halving of median household incomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Other unofficial lines, based on ensuring social inclusion or allowing for relative, not just absolute, poverty would suggest higher amounts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: These range from $2,500, to as much as $6,400.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: One may quibble with these numbers and this Government has certainly done so, by arguing that the high-end estimates overstate what are needs versus wants in the household.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A poverty line is defined as the lowest income level that would be deemed adequate in a given country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This leaves a tremendous amount of latitude in terms of what is "adequate".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: What may be regarded as an absolute minimum necessary to purchase goods and services for basic needs in a poor country may be shockingly low, when set against expectations of needs in a rich country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, there is clear evidence that as countries get richer, the value of what is conventionally regarded as a basic need changes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And the fact is, we are no longer a developing country.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The sort of things that we need to be as a full participant in Singaporean society has changed.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Smartphones may seem like an unnecessary perk to some, but without one, many basic Government services become increasingly difficult to access.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A holiday may strike others as a luxury, but for large families cooped up in tiny apartments, a brief getaway to Malaysia offers an important respite that can ensure the mental health of parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And money spent on "ang pows" and gifts and celebrations are not just frivolous spending; they represent rites of passage and acts of reciprocity that speak to a moral economy and societal norm, which cannot be reduced to dollars and cents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is, in my view, an insult to suggest to a family that the supplemental tuition that their struggling kids need to stay afloat in our overcrowded classrooms is not sufficiently "basic." Or that spending on deodorant in our hot and humid climate, particularly before an interview or a big date, is truly "discretionary".

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Part of the problem is a disconnect between what this Government has claimed to be basic, versus what Singaporeans themselves perceive as necessary for human flourishing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But if we can all agree that a good life includes opportunities to education and decent healthcare, employment with work-life balance and a sense of inclusion when one participates in social, cultural and religious activities, then why do we not extend these to the most economically vulnerable in our midst?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This line should be established based on components that go beyond just the crude, "basic" needs of housing, food and clothing.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Set up a committee, with representatives, from not just MSF, but also leaders from civil society and experts from academia, to figure out what this should be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Then, peg all thresholds for Government assistance, especially ComCare, to this line or higher, but never lower.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Local Qualifying Salary, effectively our minimum wage for Singaporeans should likewise be tied to this line.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even after we have established a new threshold for ComCare, we need to recognise that the system can stand to be refined.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While I agree with the general principle of being responsible with public monies, we should not become overzealous in the opposite direction.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It is tempting to design a public welfare system that attempts to sieve out only those that we deem "worthy" of support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: So-called "welfare kings or queens" should be excluded as such individuals undeniably exist.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We may even have some "regulars" in our Meet-the-People Sessions, but they are few and far between.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Most of my residents possess a lot of self respect and feel uncomfortable seeking help from the state, even when they are going through a tough situation not of their own making.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: A system that is stingy about financial assistance to the eight or nine folks that just want a little bit of support in a particularly trying time, just to deny the one or two abusers, strikes me as excessive and especially since all that effort translates only to a modest payout.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: With precious few exceptions, how can someone's lot improve in just three months?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Even when we make appeals and reappeals to agencies, such as the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA), we are often told that we should wait for six months before trying again, since life circumstances are unlikely to change much in the interim.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And even if they did, providing some additional months of support would help those who are in need partially fill up the hole that they find themselves in.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: As my hon friend Mr Leon Perera has argued in this House, poverty imposes a non-trivial "bandwidth tax": the cognitive burden of poverty, in and of itself.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Being in dire financial straits not only imposes mental stress as one searches for job opportunities; it can affect our handling of all-important job interviews, or our performance in a job during the probation period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It steals mental resources that are better spent on improving our situation or providing care for our dependants.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: It even reduces the little pleasure we receive from what we are able to consume.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Think back on the last time when you had a tight budget before your next paycheck came in and how you had to worry about whether you could make the rent or the mortgage, pay for your meals next week or clear bills that would keep the lights on.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Play out that exercise every single day and week, and you will sense what it is like to be poor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Layer on that, the need to "prove" that you are indeed poor every few months to a Social Service Office (SSO) officer, who has the power to snatch away the fragile lifeline that you have.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can reduce the need for such burdensome and intrusive pre-approval scrutiny by obtaining many documents directly from our public and semi-public agencies, such as rental or utilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We can deploy conditional cash transfers (CCTs) in exchange for desired behaviour, such as supplementary educational expenses or preventative healthcare spending, and use the fulfilment of the condition as sufficient evidence to qualify for support.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: We could set the default that automatically qualifies all Singaporeans in rental flats for an extended period in the Fresh Start home ownership programme, as recently suggested by a local social sector leader.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The Government might argue that beyond ComCare, there is the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS), our other key anti-poverty programme, that is also aligned with incentives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But, as I suggested before, not everyone who is poor is able to work and even when they can, circumstances might constrain how much they can.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The WIS is based on an earned income tax credit (EITC) which, in turn, is a refinement of the negative income tax.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Without going into technical details, it is sufficient to note that our scheme tends to be viewed more as a grudgingly offered financial supplement, conditional on one putting in sufficient work hours, rather than a genuine anti-poverty tool aimed at helping provide additional support to our low-income earners.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: This is in part because the amounts offered by the WIS are paltry, majority of which is not even accessible for meeting daily needs, since most of it goes straight to the Central Provident Fund (CPF).

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: In contrast, the maximum income for the US programme is closer to twice that.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The $500 minimum monthly income requirement introduced last year may also inadvertently exclude workers who are most in need of the flexibility afforded by our part-time employment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: While the ostensible reason for the requirement is to exclude some of the more well-off families from benefiting from the programme, it seems like the more tried and tested tool – total household or spousal income or the annual value (AV) of one's residential property – would be sufficient to rule out the non-poor.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, while we are reassured that those who are already on ComCare would automatically receive Workfare, I am sure that we are aware of many poor families, who for various reasons, are not on ComCare – perhaps because of the onerous documentary criteria I mentioned earlier or if they happen to have an estranged child who is also a high-income earner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Workfare also seems to be blind to the differential needs of parents with children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: Why would the youthful poor necessarily need less money than the elderly?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Lim, you have half a minute left.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That was also the period that saw the birth of the United Nations (UN), the International Monetary Fund (IMF), the World Bank (WB) and, in later years, the World Trade Organization (WTO).

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These organisations formed the backbone of the modern multilateral world we live in.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Common values recognised in international law included the recognition of the sovereignty of nations and the prohibition against the use of force except in self defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: With the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) and the WTO, trade among nations grew and the world became more interconnected.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was a backdrop that was conducive to Singapore’s growth as a small nation since the rule of law is especially important for protecting the small and the vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The last few years have seen an unprecedented retreat from multilateralism.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, Russia, through its predecessor state, the USSR, is also a charter member of the UN with a veto in the security council.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Two of the biggest beneficiaries of the liberalisation of trade following GATT and the WTO are the US and China.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They are now the two biggest economies in the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Other countries are also taking their cue from the superpowers, and we see increasing calls for protectionism from different countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the long run, this is likely to create more silos and a divided world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The multilateral system is not dead, but I think it is important for those that believe in its importance to continue to speak up for it and help bring in those who are sceptical.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The source of the scepticism is that free trade has sometimes exaggerated the differences between the rich and the poor in different countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As jobs and roles move to different countries, there will inevitably be winners and losers at home.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those who believe in multilateralism, I think it is important for us to acknowledge some of these side effects and then have domestic policies that correct for this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think the multilateral system has benefits for everyone, not least of which is greater security.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And in this testing time, we need to win back as many of the sceptics as we can.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore itself has not been immune to some of these effects and this leads me to the second area I wish to address in my speech.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The President’s Address acknowledged the importance of Singapore continuing to grow, but that these opportunities must be shared equitably.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I believe this is fundamental to preserving our society where everyone has opportunities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Singapore’s growth over the years has been remarkable and, as we moved from third world to first, the living standards of almost all our people improved dramatically.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, now that we are a developed country and our GDP per capita is among the highest in the world, continuing to be a growing high-income country is more difficult.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We need to find better, higher-paying jobs for our citizens.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, with higher incomes all round, the cost of living is generally higher as higher incomes for citizens translates into higher costs for wages for businesses and higher rentals as people pay more and compete for the real estate.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, global inflationary pressures and higher interest rates also add to pressures in the cost of living for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Against this backdrop, I think the measures in the President’s Address to ensure that Singaporeans continue to have opportunities to train and get employment throughout their working lives is vital.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would also suggest that this be coupled with income support while people undergo training.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This should be enough to tide them over temporary rough patches.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Going to an earlier stage, I think it is important for our schools to remain the great leveller for education.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the past, children would attend school and learn things like the alphabet from there.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I recall entering Primary 1 without any knowledge of how to read or write Tamil, but it was still possible to learn from scratch.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now, with most children having preschool education, the entry benchmark has risen and basic literacy and numeracy is required for children attending Primary 1, failing which, more may fall behind.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The next matter, which I think has been alluded to by some of the earlier speakers, is the proliferation of tuition, even after children attend school.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Parents across all income groups try their best to supplement what their children learn in school with tuition.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In HDB heartland malls, an increasingly larger footprint is being used for such services.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While such services are helpful for children, there is a concern by parents who cannot afford such services that their children may lose out.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have some parents who come to MPS to seek assistance when they are going through a rough patch and they often indicate their children’s tuition expenses are part of their normal monthly expenditures.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Education in our schools is highly affordable and of a very high quality.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is important that parents believe such education is adequate for their children and that children who are unable to attend or afford tuition and enrichment classes do not get left behind.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This is an important part of keeping our playing field open for children of all backgrounds to thrive.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This year there are 42 events being organised by a range of different organisations.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This event receives strong but quiet support from the Government, which through the Tamil Language Council, provides grants for the organisation of events at this festival.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am grateful to the Government for its strong support for the Tamil language in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Tamil speaking community makes up around 5% of our population and it is one of Singapore’s official languages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Government supports the language in many ways.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Tamil Language Council supports the Tamil Language Festival.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another committee, the Tamil Language Learning and Promotion Committee, otherwise known as TLLPC – which I have chaired for several years – offers support for the learning of Tamil outside of classrooms.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The TLLPC team organises events and supports activities throughout the year to make the use and learning of Tamil language fun.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Grants are also given for the production of local Tamil content by the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) under its Public Service Broadcast Programme and this allows for the creation of good quality local content, which is monitored by the Indian Programme Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This support is commendable and has helped the Tamil language remain a vibrant language in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Tamil is now also widely offered across more schools.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When I was in preschool in the 1980s, it would have been very difficult to find preschools offering Tamil as a second language.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When my father was in primary school in the 1950s, he started studying Tamil in Primary 1, but had to drop it in Primary 3 when his teacher passed away and no replacement could be found.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: He then had to switch to the Malay language.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We have come a long way from those days, with Tamil now available across many preschools and government schools.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As the number of Tamil students are small, there are fewer Tamil teachers than for other Mother Tongue languages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, even though the number of children is small, the Tamil children in schools still have a variety of different needs, including children across different age groups and with different subject-based banding.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It will be helpful to know if the Ministry of Education (MOE) has any plans to deal with this issue.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This may include plans on how we may develop a larger pipeline of Tamil teachers for our Government schools and preschools.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The learning of Tamil in Singapore has come a long way, with quiet support from the Government going a long way.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I am grateful for this support and hope it will continue.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, even with these changes, one major feature of our education system remains central – examinations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: As a parent of two children who have gone through PSLE and are now in secondary school, I am rather familiar with both the joy and – more often – the frustration that parents go through when helping their children through major national examinations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Tutoring my own children has also provided me insights into the academic curriculum and its continued focus on examinations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I remember spending an inordinate amount of time working with my children through assessment books and past examination papers.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would often have to peek at the answer sheets behind, so I could teach them how to answer science questions with just the right number of points while putting up with taunts from my own offspring, which went along the lines of, “See, you also don’t know!”  I would also have to repeatedly drill my children on mathematics problem sums.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: To get a good pass in Singapore’s examinations, students need to not only answer questions correctly, but also quickly, or risk the “horror” of having many unanswered questions at the end of the paper, due to examination time limits.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Many mid-year examinations have been done away with, but these have been replaced with weighted assessments which occur throughout the school year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The major national examinations like the PSLE, "N", "O" and "A" levels always loom just around the corner.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Perform poorly in any of these examinations and the students will find their future educational options narrowed down or delayed – a prospect that many students and parents fear, no matter what the Government says about the many pathways to success.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They can incentivise teachers to cover their subjects more thoroughly, a skill which our local educators excel in.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Examinations motivate students to work harder to gain a sense of accomplishment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, there are also negative effects of examinations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: They can motivate students to aim for test mastery instead of subject mastery.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Tests encourage teachers to narrow the curriculum and lose instructional time, which could lead to “teaching to the test”.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Examinations, typically, assess only certain aspects of a learner's knowledge, potentially overlooking other aspects of their education.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Examination outcomes may not be definitive since they are solely based on a student's performance on the examination day.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If a student is unwell or performs poorly under stress, it could adversely affect their examination results and their scores may not be an accurate reflection of their grasp of the subject matter.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: If the student fails to achieve their desired examination results, they will have to settle for courses of study in secondary schools or tertiary institutions that they may not be so inclined towards.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: National examinations induce tremendous amounts of stress on students, as they determine their future educational pathways and, consequently, their future careers and earning potential.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While it can be argued that it is good for young people to learn to cope with stress, when stress becomes toxic, it can have negative effects on learning and knowledge retention and, in extreme situations, could become chronic.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: By channelling their energies into preparing for examinations, students may forgo opportunities to experience the joy of learning and achieving mastery in what really is important for life.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The streaming approach puts students through a standardised test like the PSLE, sorted them into good, average and weak students, and put them on different education streams in secondary schools with different subject combinations based on their test scores.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The new Subject-based Banding approach also sorts students into good, average and weak students for each subject, and channels them into subject combinations based on their assessed ability in each subject.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: While subject-based banding is less rigid than streaming, it is still based on the same principle.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: A student has to meet a specific test score in order to study the subjects they are interested in.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The ostensible reason for implementing this sorting mechanism is to provide some assurance that the student can cope with the rigours of that subject or subject level before being allowed to take it.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: This is probably why through-train programmes are currently available mainly to an elite few students who qualify for the Integrated Programme by virtue of their stellar performance in the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There is little risk that these students will become early dropouts of school.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: The 10-year through-train programme will pair up existing primary and secondary schools and complement, not replace, the non-through-train tracks in these schools.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: My hon friend, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, elaborated on this proposal in detail during the COS debate earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: We need to make our education system less of a sorting mechanism for identifying students’ abilities and more of a launchpad for students to discover their strengths and interests and develop deep skills in their areas of interest.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Students should not be channelled away from their interests just because they did not obtain a certain cut-off point in their examinations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: There might be concerns that some so-called “kiasu parents” will push their children to take subjects that are far beyond their abilities.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, I believe that most Singaporean students and their parents are keenly aware of their own limitations and will not bite off more than they can chew.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: After all, if a student takes a subject at too challenging a level, they will have difficulty scoring the much coveted "A1"s in national examinations.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I would now like to move on to another aspect of education which needs more focus in Singapore – financial literacy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Singapore is a major financial hub, with numerous global, regional and local institutional investors and high-net-worth family offices based here.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Billions of investment funds are raised and managed in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Yet, Singaporeans generally lack the financial know-how and confidence to manage their own personal finances and plan for their future.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: In the two decades since it was started, it has launched various programmes and provided resources to help Singaporeans better manage their finances.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: However, the programmes seem to be mostly ad hoc and campaign-driven.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Various surveys have been conducted on financial literacy among Singaporeans since its launch, but it is not clear how much the financial literacy of Singaporeans has improved over the last two decades, as these surveys do not seem to have followed the same scope or framework.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Based on the results of the recent surveys, it appears that a lot more needs to be done to enhance Singaporeans’ financial capacity and literacy.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: And instead of doing more, it appears that some co-funding of financial literacy workshops for schools under MoneySENSE has been discontinued.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: For a developed country, with such high educational, wealth and income levels, and an established status as a leading international financial hub, the survey results show worrying statistics about the financial literacy rate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
