text: Securing our economic competitiveness will become more, not less, important in the next phase of Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: This is incumbent upon all of us, and upon my team: we will create good jobs and a good future for all Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Underlining our governing approach is the core ethic of individual effort and personal and family responsibility.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want Government actions to reinforce, not negate, individual and collective responsibility.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We want Government actions to catalyse more involvement by other members of society – employers, unions, community groups and non-governmental organisations (NGOs).

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Then we can all chip in and do our part collectively, to tackle inequality, rekindle social mobility and move forward together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: They want us to do more in certain areas, as we have heard from the speeches today and I am sure in the coming days, but there is general support for the moves that we have proposed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The Opposition has offered some revenue alternatives, but their sums do not add up.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: In this debate and over the course of the remaining term of Government, I look forward to hearing concrete alternatives from the Opposition – not just opportunistic or populist ideas to chip away, bit by bit, at the trust in Government, but a serious alternative agenda for an alternative government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is how politics in a first-world Parliament should work.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I have said this before: I do not assume that the PAP will win the next General Election or that I will inevitably take over as Prime Minister.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Every General Election from now on will be about who forms the Government; not just what percentage of the votes the PAP receives and how many seats the Opposition wins.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: As we develop into a mature democracy, we must have not just a serious Government, but also a serious Opposition that thinks carefully about what it will do as government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Where the Opposition have good ideas, or where they can make a contribution to the ideas for improving our country, we welcome them.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But we ask that you be upfront about the realities and trade-offs we face as a country, and be honest about your plans, policies and intentions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Forward Singapore is a bold agenda, and it depends on all of us to realise.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Though we will not see change overnight, we can each start to embrace the new social compact today.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: If we all do this, we can be assured that we, too, will benefit when others feel a deeper sense of responsibility towards us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We can then sustain a virtuous circle of uplift, progress and confidence, and thus strengthen our solidarity and trust as a nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: The more we put into this new social compact, the more we will receive in return.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And society as a whole, Singapore, will grow stronger and fairer; more just and more united.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Actually, I only have one more paragraph left.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But it is the most important paragraph because it is my final message to everyone.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nations globally are only realising now the true impact the crisis has left on social fabrics.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In America, the erosion of authentic relationships between people has been dubbed the "friendship recession".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In China, economic slowdown as a result of the pandemic has driven youths to "lie flat" or 躺平; and indeed, in Singapore, as we build a "new social compact" as a nation, many in our communities and in our neighbourhoods are picking up fragments left from the pandemic, to rebuild lives and livelihoods and to make sense of the post pandemic world.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Have we considered the invisible implications of COVID-19 on the social fabric of our nation?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I propose, Mr Speaker, that these invisible impacts are most felt by those driven further invisible in our post-pandemic society.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, domestic and caregiving norms at home which have been in place for generations, have not caught up with these great strides in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Women in their dual roles, often in equal parts of working and of caregiving, are taken for granted and go unnoticed and underappreciated.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a result of the pandemic, the lines between these women's professional lives and domestic responsibilities have become even more blended.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Work from Home or in the COVID-19-era slang – WFH – was a word that was both celebrated and feared by our women workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At NTUC, our sisters and unions have been pushing workplace norms to embrace flexible work arrangements (FWAs) of which WFH is an example of, for decades.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: COVID-19 created the opportunity for FWAs to be adopted widely, but it also brought into better focus, the challenges women workers and companies need to overcome for FWAs to continue to be adopted both widely as well as wisely.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The realities are that FWAs or otherwise, will not shift the burdens of caregiving from the shoulders of mothers, wives and daughters, should women still be	culturally expected to be the sole or main caregivers at home while balancing their careers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A wider scope for caregiving leave can also be considered, for our workers to be able to share caregiving duties outside of the typical parent, grandparent and child familial sets, to include family members such as uncles and aunts, nephews and nieces.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Keep the number of caregiving leave days but allow for flexibility on who a worker can give care to.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Now that normalcy has been restored to most of the workforce, more workers are called back to serve their nine-to-fives in offices.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us not lose the momentum we have made in the progress for FWAs in the past three years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: FWAs are a critical workplace philosophy to help our women workers balance their dual duties.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Labour Movement on our part, will continue to support and push for companies to redesign jobs and to ensure FWAs are win-win and sustainable for businesses and workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Another group of workers who have seen much changes since the onset of the pandemic are our freelancers and, in particular, platform workers who are the lifeblood of Singapore's gig economy.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Having transformed the way we eat, shop and move and especially so in the thick of the pandemic, our freelance gig economy has grown in the past three years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Yet, as a community, they still bear invisible risks we do not fathom as a nation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These include risks to their physical safety in transit when delivering food or other logistical requirements, but also concerns over the adequacy of their retirement savings, health safety nets and housing.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While the Government will continue to work with these platforms to ensure equitable outcomes for platform workers, Singaporeans should also bear in mind these invisible risks borne by platform workers the next time they tap into their services.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a progressive Labour Movement, the NTUC and our associations – National Taxi Association (NTA), National Private Hire Vehicles Association (NPHVA), and National Delivery Champions Association (NDCA) have been engaging our ever growing freelance and self-employed community and garnering support to address their concerns with our Tripartite Partners – the ride hail platforms, delivery platforms, taxi companies, the Ministry of Manpower (MOM), the Land Transport Authority (LTA), the CPF Board, and the list goes on.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The move from pandemic to endemic has certainly brought further light to the precariousness of our riders and drivers' livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As business models shift and adjust with the gradual opening of our economy and borders, this should not be done without due consideration that these moves have on the livelihoods of our platform workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A poorly executed app update resulting in a few hours of glitching will impact earnings and even the safety of our riders and drivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is an important move and draws visibility and, more importantly, public awareness and discourse to the issues that this evolving and growing group of workers face on a daily basis to their livelihoods and safety.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our drivers and riders are a proud, independent group of Singaporean workers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I call on all Singaporeans to work with the Labour Movement and Tripartite Partnership on defining a fair, dignified livelihood for our platform workers in the new normal.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On dignified lives, this brings me to the last group and arguably, the most vulnerable group of adult Singaporeans living among us.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For those among us who are parents, do you remember the looks shot at you as you might have brought your wailing infant to a crowded mall, or worse, a fully occupied plane?

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: You may have, on some occasions, muttered to yourself, "Just a few more months of this to get through".

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For some parents out there with children with special needs, they never really find solace from public scrutiny, even as their children reach adulthood.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On my block visits in Punggol Shore, I encounter a good number of cases of adults with special needs – some of them undiagnosed, cooped up at home, rarely stepping into the outside world having fostered no real sense of independence.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When I speak with their parents or siblings, I am often met with worries about how their ward might continue to upkeep a standard of living and quality of life should they pass on.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Sure, state-centric solutions might exist, but all parents would wish upon their children a life of safety, choice and protection, at least one that goes beyond the confines of an institution.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I met with Mr Y when he contacted my office and asked me to visit him at home as he was too sick to leave his home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I remember Mr Y laying on his sofa when I saw him in his flat; he was very ill, and his stomach was painfully distended.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Even though he was relieved to see me and smiled a lot, he looked like he was in the jaws of death.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Y had last stage cancer and his doctor told him that he only had weeks to live.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Y told me that he was in pain and the only reason why he was still holding on was because he did not know what to do to ensure that his son and his wife continued to enjoy a good standard of living after he passes on.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He was worried as his son has no language skills and his wife is a foreigner; and while she is a full-time caregiver to his son, after his passing, he wished for her to find work.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He was also adamant that his son would be able to live and age in place in the flat that he owned and not to be confined to a home or institution.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Y was estranged from his family and there were no additional supporting networks for him.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He had no will, no Lasting Power of Attorney; he did not even have a "Plan B" on how to ferry his son should the bus fail to turn up that day to bring his son to daycare.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After listening to him, we knew we were running against time.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We even arranged for job interviews for his wife and paid attention to his final funeral wishes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: More importantly, we knew we had to set up the necessary safety nets for his son, while Mr Y was still of sound mind.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That was two weeks after our initial meet-up at his sofa in his home.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Y left a very long-lasting impression on me.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: His story is not unique among caregivers and guardians of special needs adults.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Mr Y envisaged a warm model of care for his son and this was about his son living in the community he grew up well into his later years.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is, well, a care model around a village more than it is around an institution.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What this means is that our adults with special needs would be able to live in a safe and dignified manner, fulfilled lives in their communities with the support of other members of the community.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I believe that Singaporeans have what it takes to be that village for adults with special needs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: No institution can give this great an assurance to families of our special needs adults than the community itself.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Together, this need not be true for the invisible slices of Singaporeans we have formed a blind spot, as a result of the pandemic.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Strengthening the social compact begins with kindness and kindness begins with putting ourselves in the shoes of others.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As I continue to tell the stories of those I champion, I will call on the Government to effect change and renew the kindness of Singaporeans to effect lasting change.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we all know, the COVID-19 pandemic has brought unprecedented challenges to our nation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The rising costs of living, coupled with the economic impacts on the pandemic, have added further strain to many Singaporean households.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Despite these challenges, I firmly believe that as a nation, we have the strength and resilience to overcome them.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is now more important than ever that we come together as a society and work together, towards a shared vision for the future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: I will focus on three key areas that I believe are critical: one, the importance of Mother Tongue languages; two, strengthening the role of the M3's Focus Area Four (FA4) in supporting vulnerable groups in the Malay/Muslim community; and thirdly, building trust and prospects for our workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By embracing our cultural diversity, supporting vulnerable communities and investing in our workforce, we can build a society that is both resilient and prosperous.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Allow me to touch on each point in greater detail in Malay.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In Malay):   Mr Speaker, Mother Tongue languages are a cornerstone of Singapore's multiracial and multicultural society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: They provide a vital link to our diverse heritage and cultural identity.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In Singapore, each ethnic group has its own Mother Tongue language, such as Mandarin for the Chinese community, Tamil for the Indian community and Malay language for the Malay community.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This data demonstrates the significant level of proficiency and emphasises the importance of these languages in our society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In addition to serving as a communication tool within our respective ethnic communities, Mother Tongue languages have played a critical role in building social cohesion and national unity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: They have helped to foster a sense of belonging and shared identity among Singaporeans of different ethnicities, contributing to the country's success in maintaining social harmony.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Beyond their cultural significance, research has shown that being bilingual or multilingual offers cognitive benefits such as enhanced memory, cognitive flexibility and decision-making skills.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: For example, a study by the University of California found that bilingual individuals performed better in cognitive tests than monolingual individuals, highlighting the cognitive advantages of being bilingual.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Thus, the cognitive benefits of being bilingual or multilingual are numerous, making it a valuable skill to have in today's globalized world.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As a Malay Singaporean, I can personally attest to the significance of the Malay language in my daily life.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is not only the language I use to communicate with my family members, but it also allows me to actively participate in the wider Malay community.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: For example, when attending cultural events such as Hari Raya Aidilfitri or weddings, the ability to converse in Malay allows me to connect with my fellow Malay Singaporeans on a deeper level and better appreciate our shared cultural heritage.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Given their cultural and cognitive benefits, it is crucial for the Government to continue investing in the preservation and promotion of Mother Tongue languages in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This includes ensuring that Mother Tongue language education is accessible to all and providing resources to support its learning.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By recognising the value and significance of Mother Tongue languages, we can continue to build a society that embraces diversity, promotes social cohesion and values our shared cultural heritage together.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This includes initiatives to support marginalised groups in the community amid economic recovery and transformation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: One such example is Focus Area (FA) Workgroup within the ambit of M3.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: FA4 is an important framework that seeks to provide support and assistance to Malay/Muslim workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: FA4 is especially significant in today's context as the country continues to grapple with the economic and social impact of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is because the pandemic has disproportionately affected certain groups, including those in low-wage jobs, gig workers and mature workers, among others.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: FA4 plays a crucial role in ensuring that these vulnerable groups in the Malay/Muslim community have access to the necessary support and resources to navigate these difficult times.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As the Malay proverb goes; if you do not ask, you will get lost; if you do not row, your boat will drift aimlessly.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: FA4 is an important framework that seeks to provide support and assistance to vulnerable groups in the Malay/Muslim community, especially in today's challenging economic and social climate.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By addressing the unique challenges faced by vulnerable groups such as platform workers, women, mature workers and youth, FA4 can help create a more inclusive and equitable society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is important in the social compact of Singapore as it seeks to build a more resilient and cohesive community for the future.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we look towards the future, it is evident that trust will continue to be a crucial component in shaping the workforce landscape.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is especially true at the tripartite level, where our ability to work together has enabled us to make significant progress on the national economic agenda.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: As we move forward, we need to maintain this trust and continue to collaborate to support workers and ensure that they are equipped with the necessary skills to succeed in the ever-evolving job market.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Building trust with the workforce is a crucial factor in the success of any organisation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: A high level of trust at the workplace fosters a positive work environment where everyone feels valued and supported, and this leads to a more engaged and productive workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: At the national level, trust is strengthened by working together to create good opportunities for our workers and investing in training to ensure that workers build up resilience in their careers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Over the years, the tripartite partners in Singapore have made significant efforts to support the workforce, especially those who were badly affected during crises.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Through these conversations, the Labour Movement hopes to build a stronger connection with workers and better understand their perspectives.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Such feedback will also contribute towards charting our longer-term strategies in the road ahead.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Looking to the future, the Labour Movement recognises the need to “future-proof” our workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Building trust with the workforce is critical and the tripartite partners in Singapore have made significant efforts in the past to support workers during challenging times.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Presently, the Labour Movement's #EveryWorkerMatters Conversations campaign has sought to listen to the voices of workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Looking to the future, the Labour Movement recognises the importance of helping workers build resilience in their careers as well as a skilled and adaptable workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: To do so, we plan to form more CTCs.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, more needs to be done to support vulnerable workers and youth and it is a call to action for tripartite partners to continue this trust-building effort with workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By working together, we can create a workforce that is skilled, adaptable and resilient in the face of challenges.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: (In English): To conclude, as Secretary-General Mr Ng Chee Meng of NTUC, said, and I quote, "As the voice of workers, we at NTUC want to forge a new workers' compact, one defined collectively by the working people in Singapore." This quote encapsulates the theme of today's speech, which is the importance of recognising and valuing diverse perspectives and building collaborative partnerships in achieving progress and success as a nation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The importance of Mother Tongue languages, the role of M3's FA4 alongside PWM in supporting vulnerable groups in society and the other existing initiatives are all critical components of a cohesive and resilient society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: By recognising the value and significance of our diverse cultural heritage, investing in the support and resources of our vulnerable groups and building trust with our workforce, we can continue to progress and thrive as a nation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Let us continue to work together to build a Singapore that embraces diversity, promotes social cohesion and values the well-being and success of all its citizens.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The global workforce has come under considerable strain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: These strains are caused by increased international competition, outsourcing of business functions, generational transitions in the workforce and the speed of technological advancement.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: COVID-19 has also vastly changed the way we work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many jobs are created while many are lost.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As uncertainty becomes more pervasive, we need to restore confidence by addressing underlying structural causes of such an anxiety.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As President Halimah said, we will strengthen social safety nets so that in every stage of life, Singaporeans can better cope with uncertainties and look forward with confidence.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is impossible to shield Singaporeans from all such vagaries if we are to keep our economy open.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: An open economy is our livelihood after all.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we can certainly enable Singaporeans by pushing for training and reskilling and ensuring that all our workers are well-equipped to rebound and capture opportunities in the brighter areas of the economy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And if they do fall, they can bounce back quickly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The economic outlook globally is more volatile and uncertain.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Companies are racing to incorporate such capabilities into their work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It also heralds the acceleration of the loss of certain jobs, such as lower-level analysts and research jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Those slowest to react to such changes stand to lose the most.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And out of these affected individuals, some segments of our workforce are in greater danger.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They will be in their late-40s and 50s now; some of them are even in their 60s.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This segment of individuals joined the workforce when Singapore was still in early stages of economic development.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of them sacrificed their education to support their families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They have tended to work in one company, industry or function.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some have not upgraded their skills since entering the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many of them have risen through the ranks over the years in technical and managerial jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When faced with the need to switch jobs, they tended to see a sharp drop in income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Another group of vulnerable individuals comprise our self-employed persons (SEPs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have seen the disproportionate impact COVID-19 had on SEPs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Through NTUC’s assistance in administering the Self-Employed Income Relief Scheme (SIRS), we are fully aware of the imperative to strengthen financial and career resilience for SEPs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Because of irregular contributions to CPF, it was also difficult to dispense loss of income support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They not only face difficulties in landing new jobs but they also find it more difficult to acquire new skillsets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They also face the perennial and perhaps trickiest issue of workforce ageism, which requires addressing of mindsets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As President Halimah also rightly highlighted, it is important for us to concentrate our efforts to improve social safety nets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: At this point, I was pondering about Assoc Prof Jamus Lim's observations and suggestions on support to our needy Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It can have an unintended cliff effect where those below the line get the support but those above do not.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The line also misses out on other issues that needy families face, for example, trying family circumstances, ill health and job readiness.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It casts undue intention on just the financial circumstances of needy families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Experience from other countries has also shown that it is hard to simplify to just one figure and there is a tendency for people to want to stay below that figure; not too many of them, but certainly, there are.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I fully agree that our poor need extra help, and we can do better, and we must do better.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, our policies are shaped to give more to those who have less.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, we have many assistance schemes with different ways of helping for different outcomes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And there is also some sense to have separate criteria for different schemes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For example, ComCare is for poverty alleviation, supporting them in their needs versus Workfare, which is to help workers level up, tackling some inequality.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In my work as the Mayor of Northeast Community Development Council (CDC), I have often hoped to simplify the 60 schemes that the Northeast CDC run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But the more that we walk the ground, the more we realise that targeted solutions will work best and we cannot shine away from assessments.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Not only does it reflect our prudence of responsibilities to public resources, it allows us to size the assistance to the needy appropriately.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, an approach of providing support based on the varied needs of Singaporeans and their families might work better in a singular poverty line.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is rigorous in its assessment and flexible to the needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I agree that documentation can be a burden.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I struggle with that in my work in CDC too.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And we must continue to make applications simpler.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is good for both Social Service Office (SSO) staff and applicants.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With greater digitisation in the Government, we can already see the benefits of streamlining and we will, and I think, can do more on that front.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we have different schemes with different criteria, what is most important is to make sure that while we streamline the application process, that the schemes are also effective.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our SSO officers work hard on the ground to do this, and I do feel, maybe I thought it incorrectly, but the way that Assoc Prof Jamus Lim characterised what they do might not be entirely fair.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They seek not to take away the lifelines of the residents they serve.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our SSO officers work hard to help our needy residents.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I am extremely proud of them and knew a lot of them through the work in ComLink.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In fact, many of them take on duties beyond what I required of them because of the multifaceted issues facing lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I certainly know my Tampines and Sengkang SSO officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They built strong relationships with our ComLink families, testimony to the dedication and good work.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But I acknowledge there will always be gaps in our schemes with the families or residents who need help in the Northeast District which includes Sengkang, I will do my best to help them as Mayor of Northeast CDC.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must not also forget that helping more, which we must do, also requires that we earn more to pay for it.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It is easy to say to do more, but it is much harder to pay more.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Good growth, good jobs and good wages are clearly important to helping needy residents better and more sustainably.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In our new social compact and strategy, we hope to mobilise more support from all of community: corporates, charities, volunteers and philanthropists.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have seen how donors, corporate donors, went from just pure financial support to volunteering personally to solve ground problems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Our Northeast CDC WeCare programme supports thousands of families, above the ComCare financial qualifying lines.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It was funded by donations from religious organisations, temples, churches and mosques and funds from CDC.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Only when we own the problems and solutions can we do more and build a stronger Singapore.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, I would like to suggest a couple of areas of focus to help Singaporeans to be able to rebound from tough times in two distinct phases: pre-loss of jobs and post-loss of jobs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: However, such a tight labour market also creates an environment whereby future-proofing opportunities may be put in the backseat.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In this volatile economy, the key is to reskill to remain relevant in the workforce and to keep abreast of the changes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The first suggestion I have is that we can help employers to allow workers to reskill while being gainfully employed.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This will allow companies to send workers for training while being subsidised for such costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The costs of hiring temporary staff or replacement staff are increasing.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The related costs of hiring and onboarding staff are also not insignificant.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Hence, we can consider increasing absentee payroll funding support based on the age of employees, with older workers receiving greater support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers in vulnerable and sunset sectors can also be considered for enhanced absentee payroll support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We should increase this cap, considering the increase in overall business costs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Companies sending a larger number of mature workers for training should also qualify for a higher cap.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Companies will be incentivised to hire mature workers and our mature workers will be incentivised to train.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, on improving the post-loss of job support.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This support can be linked to training and job search to preserve the work ethos of the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This builds on the principles behind our Workfare and COVID-19 Recovery Grant.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must not forget that the longer one stays out of the workforce, the poorer employment outcomes will be.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Thus, our system of unemployment support should taper off with time to ensure that individuals remain incentivised to re-enter the workforce.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Next, we can also enhance the Career Conversion Programmes (CCPs).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can increase allowance and income support during the conversion process as workers will still need to care for their families.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can also extend the enhanced CCPs to our SEPs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Many SEPs in the profession are in there because of their need for more discretionary income.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some of them do want to go on to other careers, hopefully, more permanent ones.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The next move is to extend career trials to SEPs as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Currently, SEPs will not be eligible for career trials under the existing eligibility requirements.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Could the Government look into expanding the eligibility and for those considering a job switch to undertake formal employment?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While training and reskilling is an important feature of the nation's work ethos, it may be demoralising for workers to continually train but unable to secure employment.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is especially so for older workers whose runway is much shorter.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While we cannot completely remove such risks, we can moderate the risk by having more Place-and-Train programmes.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can do so starting from the Public Service ecosystem, including the suppliers to the Public Service.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: More outreach efforts to potential host companies could be undertaken to increase the scope of such programmes and the Labour Movement stands ready to assist.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   The working environment today is very different from what it used to be.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The pace of economic transformation will be accelerated as geopolitical risks become more volatile.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can promote and strengthen training programmes to ensure that Singaporeans have the skills that they need and capture job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Workers and businesses that are relatively slow to respond to changes will be hardest hit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Therefore, we have to prepare for the work environment before and after job loss so that Singaporeans can bounce back quickly from the tough times and seize job opportunities.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Job opportunities remain key to improving the quality of life for the people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The Government and the unions will do their best to help Singaporeans achieve this to ensure that all Singaporeans will not be left behind.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Let us work together to create a better future.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, over the years, we have continued to strengthen our social safety nets.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With an increasingly volatile global economy, we must help Singaporeans cope with the uncertainties and enable us to have the confidence to forge ahead.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The first is the Member, Mr Desmond Choo, had pointed out that there is a cliff effect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But if I am not wrong, this applies to all lines already in place.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And I wonder if the Member is suggesting that we should therefore encourage the Government, by the same token, to remove all thresholds that they currently have because of the same cliff effects?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: The Member also suggested that there were many schemes for many outcomes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: And, of course, I agree with this specific tailoring.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But still, it does not strike me as precluding a clear benchmark for which we can tag all these idiosyncratic needs to a clear benchmark line.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: Just a third point, Mr Speaker, is that he mentioned that SSO officers have worked hard to support residents, including in Sengkang and, of course, I should clarify that I agree with this.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: But it is clear that they are constrained by the system.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: If the Member may clarify, how having an official poverty line makes it harder to provide tailored solutions?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim
text: It is like saying that just because you seek this, you set a passing mark of 50%, but we cannot help a student to actually score higher than that —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Assoc Prof Lim, you can keep it more compact, please.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I think what he meant, if I get him correctly, when he asked for a singular poverty line, that there is a line cutting across all schemes by which different schemes will be benchmarked too.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: If not, then why would he be asking for a one singular poverty line rather than the current system that we have that will have different lines or different qualifying criteria for different purposes?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: And I think that, in our position, it is still better to adjust and be flexible to the needs of the ground, making sure that we size support appropriately for different schemes and not have a "one-size-fits-all" scheme.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: I do agree with him that even if you have a singular line, it is not mutually exclusive.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: And I am glad that he agrees with that; regardless of whether you have a single line or not, you still must understand that the needs of the grounds are complex and you do need to have targeted schemes for targeted problems.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: That is one part that, first, I wish to clarify.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: And the second one is whether they are constrained by the general policies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo
text: But what I can speak on behalf is the schemes that CDC run.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I totally agree that this is very important and we have to pay particular attention to low-income families, especially those with young children.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: There is no adjustment to the qualifying criteria despite a high inflation rate over the last two years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We understand that MSF has allocated about $601 million in its 2023 Budget to administer long-term and short-term financial assistance to vulnerable Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: But the question is whether this amount is sufficient?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To have a better comparison, we can look at how other advanced countries are providing cash benefits to assist vulnerable families.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: The Organization for Economic and Cooperation Development (OECD) countries spent about an average of 7% of their GDP on cash benefits.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: As Singapore is not a welfare state, it may not be fair to compare us with most of the OECD countries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Perhaps, we can look at those closer to home, such as South Korea.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: South Korea spent about 3% of its GDP on public social expenditure in cash benefits and how is it compared to Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Now, 0.1% of GDP appears small, compared to 3% of GDP South Korea spent on cash benefits for public social expenditure.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: I am not advocating that we have to increase the ComCare expenditure by 30 times to match South Korea's.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: However, it is important that our support for low-income families keep pace with inflation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Singaporeans have been very much affected by the 14-year high inflation rate.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We feel it every day as we buy our food, coffee, and groceries and pay our bills.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: According to an August 2022 study last year, it is the low-income households earning less than $2,500 a month which are the hardest hit, as they spend almost all their income every month.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Given the high inflation rate for the past two years and the expected slow economic growth this year, there is scope to help families cope by easing the qualifying criteria for help schemes across the board.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Likewise, HDB rental flat qualifying criteria can also be eased by 10% so that applicants with less than $1,650 monthly income can apply.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has indicated that it is “almost a certainty” that inflation will be higher and longer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: That is, high inflation will be the norm for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: To better help the low-income families, I would like to suggest that all the Government assistance schemes could incorporate an inflation component so that both the qualifying criteria and the quantum of assistance rendered could be adjusted annually in tandem with inflation.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (West Coast)
text: We do not want inflation to add another layer of uncertainty for the lower-income families.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Deputy Chair of the Government Parliamentary Committees (GPCs) for Education, and Culture, Community and Youth, I will be focusing my speech on these areas as covered in the President’s Address.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would also like to declare my interest as CEO of an educational organisation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Education can unlock potential; it can allow a child to transcend his or her humble beginnings to achieve success; it can inspire a mid-career switch from discouragement to determination; and it can empower a generation to believe that there is nothing that they cannot do, on account of their gender or ethnicity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Education, however, is more than just what is taught or learnt in formal, institutionalised settings.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, as the writer Mark Twain once said, “Never let school interfere with your education.” For true education to be effective, we need to look at it from across all the multiple stakeholders in our society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Families, employers, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), Voluntary Welfare Organisations (VWOs), social groups and communities all have their part to play, be it via advice and guidance you would give to your child or a policy that you would implement in your organisation.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I would argue, as we move forward into this post-COVID-19 era, an era that is probably as uncertain and unsure as any before it, that it will be the education of our society that will be crucial to Singapore’s next phase of development and that this education will not be a whole-of-Government, but rather a whole-of-community effort.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We live in an era where we are bombarded with information constantly and consistently.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, unless we have a way to process this information, it remains purely that – “information” that does not serve much use.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Education used to be about helping to turn that information into knowledge.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, if information was just random facts, education helped transform it into knowledge, that is, the information now made some sense and it was something that we could use.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the assumption then was that just because you knew something, you could put that knowledge to good use and actually do something.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, now it was not so much about what you knew but what you could do.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: So, I believe, indeed, that one of the key objectives of education should focus on what we can do rather than on what you know.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is no point amassing degrees and certificates if you ultimately cannot perform in terms of the skills that you need to deliver.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, Mr Speaker, I would like to suggest that we should also aim to go beyond skills and to strive for the attainment of competencies as the ultimate end-goal of education.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If skills are what you can do, then competencies are how you do it.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And these are competencies that we should emphasise to ensure that our students, workers and people stay relevant for the future.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Creating new value focuses on innovation and creative dynamism of thinking on how one can apply methods, processes and techniques in real-world and practical settings to either solve existing or emerging challenges, while working towards the betterment of community and society.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our system has had a long history of taking a fairly safe and established route to attain the results that we have been judged on.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, the obsession in the past with 10-year series and sample examination papers to see how we would perform in terms of being able to attain a particular set of results.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Students and learners who aim to create new value have got to be courageously curious and regularly push the boundaries and challenge the status quo.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that we can take steps in this direction by not just encouraging our students, but also our educators and even our employers, to be courageously curious as well so that they can create new value for their students, learners and employees.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The ability to reconcile tensions and dilemmas sees students and learners being able to apply themselves in real-life scenarios by taking into account seemingly contradictory viewpoints and opinions and opposing concepts in formulating potential solutions to situations in the real world.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Real life is messy; real life is uncertain; real life requires you to work in the grey.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And let us have the courage to apply this to that mother of all examinations, the PSLE.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have made this point before at the previous Motion of Thanks to the President in 2020.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This combination of coursework and examination is already practised in many other programmes, such as the International Baccalaureate (IB), and I believe that we can apply a similar concept to the final Primary 6 students’ grade instead of making it purely about a high-stakes one-shot examination.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, the competency of taking responsibility is a powerful lifelong concept that encourages students and learners to connect it to the ability to reflect on and evaluate their own actions in light of their individual experiences and also in their collective exposure to the world around them.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Taking responsibility means that students and learners are proactive and focused in dealing with societal and environmental challenges and issues that present themselves, and the emphasis is not on waiting for “the Government” or “someone else” to do it, but to show initiative, be accountable and take responsibility in dealing with the matter at hand.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The MOE Addendum to the President’s Address presented by Minister Chan Chun Sing talks about a “collective responsibility”, and I could not agree more with the Minister.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just as all of us have a part to play in shaping and strengthening our social compact, every stakeholder – the Government, educators, students, parents, employers – all need to work together also to ensure that we contribute to the development of students and learners who have the competencies to take on the challenges of the next phase of our nation’s development.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Before I move on to the next part of my speech, Mr Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to also thank all of our educators – from our preschool educators to our primary and secondary school teachers, our polytechnic lecturers, our university academics, our trainers, those who work in continuing education – for the great work that they are doing and that they continue to do in the growth and development of our people.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would now like to move on to the second part of my speech, Mr Speaker, that talks about the trifecta of diversity, equity and inclusion, and why I feel that they are critical to Singapore moving forward.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: By its composition, Singapore is remarkable for its diversity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have four major ethnic groups and Singapore’s inter-religious organisation (IRO) oversees 10 religions in our country.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When you further divide the ethnic groups into sub-groups, such as the Teochews, Hokkiens, Cantonese and so on for the Chinese; or Tamils, Malayalees, Punjabis and so on for the Indians, then we truly have a rich palette of cultures not just co-existing but thriving together in peace and harmony.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is truly something unique and special and is due, in large part, to the many policies that, while not perfect, were critical and crucial in ensuring that the diverse groups in Singapore learnt to live together in one common community, especially in Singapore’s early days.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, a look around this august Chamber would be a wonderful reflection of the diversity that I am referring to.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In terms of age, gender, ethnicity, religion and other demographics, I would argue that we have a good representation of different Singaporeans here.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Again, while the Group Representation Constituency (GRC) policy might be criticised, I would argue that the diversity in this Chamber is a positive result of that.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The one area I feel that we could do better would be to see how we can work on a greater diversity and representation in the Public Service leadership.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that some progress has been made over the years in terms of increased gender diversity.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, it would seem that we could do better in terms of greater ethnic diversity in Public Service leadership, especially at the senior levels.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I sincerely hope that this is something that the Government can look into when formulating its Public Service leadership strategy.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, it is mentioned in our nation’s pledge that we believe that our society should be a democratic one based on “justice and equality”.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this regard, equality is important and crucial, but we must also take this in a particular context because equality is about being equal in status, rights and opportunities and making sure that individuals or groups are given the same resources or rights to other opportunities.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I think that we should also seek to embed equity as something that guides us in our journey forward as a progressive and caring community.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If equality is about everyone getting the same thing, then equity is recognising that not everyone has got the same means and resources.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And for us to progress as a community, we have to see how different groups and individuals are provided with what they need rather than be given the same thing as everybody else.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I would encourage not just the Government to continue with this approach but also for our fellow Singaporeans and members of our community to develop and lead their own initiatives in this area as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is something that I strongly believe in and it is my hope that even as equality remains a core pillar of our democratic society, the concept of equity will become embedded not just into the core of our community, but into our consciousness as well.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the inclusion strategist Verna Miles once said, "Diversity is being invited to the party, inclusion is being asked to dance." It is not just about celebrating diversity in our community, institutions and organisations.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We should also continuously endeavour to be inclusive by involving all those diverse groups and individuals in many ways and at multiple levels in genuine and open engagement.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, in schools and institutions – I shift the focus back to education once again	– let us actively promote inclusion by involving students from different backgrounds and with different capabilities too, so that they can learn how to learn and how to work together.

speaker: Mr Darryl David (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, I end my speech in support of the Motion of Thanks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some of these changes are once in a generation, some might say once in a century.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Not just the relationships between the great powers, the US and China, but the relationship between humans and technology, between humanity and artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just one year ago, if someone had suggested you could log into a server online, have a conversation with a software application, have it write a detailed essay that might be indistinguishable from some journals, you might have been told that was a bit speculative.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just one year ago, if you said you had an AI which could outperform many humans at advanced placement exams in the US, you might have been told that was a stretch goal.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Now, imagine that technology developing five, 10, or 15 years from now.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In short, the genie is out of the bottle.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What has been invented cannot be un-invented, whether it is the light bulb, the computer, the smartphone, cloud computing or AI in its current form.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is the world we live in – a brave new world for Singapore and Singaporeans in the generation ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This means the world of SG100 will be very different from the world of SG50 just a few years ago.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some might say the world of SG100 will be as different from SG50, as SG50 was from the early days of our Independence in 1965.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Just as today, we look back and reflect on what the founding generation of Singaporeans and leaders did, the choices they made, the directions we took, in SG100, there will be another generation looking back at what we decide today and in the next few years.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And they will know whether we chose well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is incumbent on us to make those decisions soon, given how quickly the world is changing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have to move very quickly and very decisively.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I will speak first on togetherness in our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There is an old saying from Mr Lee Kuan Yew to the effect that "all other policies would 'bend at the knees' for our water survival." We still face existential challenges and dangers as a small country, whether it is water security, our ability to defend ourselves in an ever more hazardous world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But there can be no policy stability, no policy continuity, no ruggedness of policies to bend at the knee for other issues if as a society, we are fragmented, divided and splintered.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We will be less than a dot if we are splintered.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There can be no consensus on redistribution or a social compact, regardless of what view is put forward on any side of the House or in our society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There can be no consensus without that basic idea of togetherness – a togetherness that each of us sees fellow Singaporeans as our brothers and sisters.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Before we can be our brother's keeper, we have to see that fellow citizen as our brother or our sister, as the case may be.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, I would suggest that in this new era, every policy in the Government must have one eye on the impact of governance and policy, on our cohesion and our social togetherness as a nation and as a people.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens when any photo or video can be a deepfake?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens when people can no longer trust what they see online, whether on a broadcast video, a WhatsApp message, a social media platform or something that is circulating around?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: What happens when people feel they cannot trust what they see and hear?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That is the world we are going to have to deal with.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This means every policy has to keep social togetherness and social cohesion – one eye on it, sometimes both eyes, but always mindful.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In a world of unnatural AI, where the unnatural AI is the new natural, we have to assume that the natural workings of society are going to be very, very different.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I use the word "togetherness" with some consideration.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: You can have different views, come from different backgrounds, have different ideas, different perspectives, but that togetherness is what allows us to pull together and move forward as one people, especially in times of difficulty.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This means we need to double down on how people meet, face to face, in the community.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When HDB estates are designed, do the shape of blocks and neighbourhoods make it harder for people to come together when going out for work, to play, or to school?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Or does the shape of estate designs make it easier for people to interact spontaneously or serendipitously?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My Clementi residents tell me that the older blocks with void decks are not quite the same as the newer blocks, which do not have void decks and therefore have fewer shared spaces for organic interaction in the same way as before.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: My residents feel that about the newer blocks.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Do our policies bring Singaporeans of different backgrounds and different journeys together throughout life, especially from young – children who have come from different starting points and different stories, but who all can learn from mixing with one another?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: When people connect, engage, come together, and learn from one another, that sharing and exchange of social capital lifts up a society.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It deepens our closeness and identity as Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: And the beauty of social capital is that unlike fiscal capital, which when redistributed is a case of addition and subtraction.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But when we have social capital, exchanging and sharing, it multiplies, makes our society richer, more interesting, more unique, deepens our identity as Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We need to make sure that mixing, that face-to-face interaction happens all the more so in an era of AI.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We also need to equip our students to compete in a world of AI.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Even if tomorrow, as some jurisdictions have talked about, we legislated against the use of ChatGPT and other technologies, that would not protect our students or our people – not when a competitor or another firm halfway around the world might be making use of AI.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We have to recognise these new and challenging realities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: So, each new technology, even as it brings new challenges, also brings opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In the new world of technology, there will still be these opportunities, moving ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: For example, AI content creation will change as more computing power becomes available.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today, it takes time – if you key in an instruction into Stable Diffusion, DALL.E or Midjourney 5 – to create that image, that one frame.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: But as computing power increases, imagine if those images can be created 30 times a second.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That means you now create a complete AI-generated video.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Imagine now, if you add in dialogue, sound and movement, you are basically making your own movies, your own content without Hollywood, potentially cinema-quality as well.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The next step, of course, then is monetising, marketing and creating opportunities out of that content.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Because if you have a very marketable AI content that you have designed, you can sell it to the rest of the world.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Generate revenue in the same way that content is generated today on social media platforms.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There will be these opportunities both in the content as well as in the backend – the AI programming, the infrastructure, the data centres, the engineering.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There will be opportunities for Singapore as well, but we need to move quickly before others get there before us.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We also need to continue nurturing and deepening the life skills and human skills which AI cannot replicate.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: That includes in the digital world, helping our students get better at building friendships, face-to-face interactions, communicating with fellow human beings, persuading, building networks, growing social circles.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I debated this in Parliament some time back with Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong when he was Education Minister in a Parliamentary Question.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: These life skills are more important than ever today.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Today we already have computers studying us and what catches our attention.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Whether it is Facebook, Instagram, or TikTok, there are algorithms which look at what catches the eye, what draws your attention, what makes you more likely to click or move your mouse or manipulate the computer screen.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: The software is already watching us even as we watch the screen.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: E-commerce platforms do this; the social media platforms do this too.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: They use it to make money, shape consumer behaviour, and study what we want.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In a world of AI, we can also leverage this to transform the education process.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We already know that different students learn differently.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Some students learn better by listening, speaking; they learn better through a verbal way.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are some students who prefer to learn by reading and absorbing.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: There are many students who learn best by doing things with their hands – building, creating, coming up with something with their hands and handiwork and craftwork.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Instead, it means teachers can be freed up to focus on human skills, life skills, and helping prepare students for life.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Life skills such as how to work as a team, how to connect with your peers, or how to grow as a person.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These were points highlighted by President Halimah in her speech at the Opening of the Second Session of this 14th Parliament.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But she reminded us that "we are far from powerless".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our history and what we have achieved as a nation today has shown that our strength has and continues to be our people and our will as one people, Government, businesses and citizens "working together to make the improbable, possible".

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are many important aspects that President Halimah has covered in her speech and plans that the Ministries have also outlined in the various addenda to her speech.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In my speech today, I will touch on two areas which I feel are important for Singapore and Singaporeans to be ready and more importantly, confident for the changes we are facing and to remain relevant now and in the future.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They are: one, education and continual learning – to equip Singaporeans and expand opportunities throughout life for all; and two, a society that values and support families.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For our young: with the fast pace of change and rapid digitalisation across many aspects of work and life, what we teach, how we teach and when learning happens has changed and will need to continue to transform.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In schools, we are preparing our young for work and careers that do not exist today.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For our young, building strong foundational knowledge and skills, including science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM), is crucial.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With rapid digitalisation, technology skills need to be part of core curriculum.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With how technologies are evolving and the potential benefits and risks they pose, technology skills are essential not only to enable use and leverage of these technologies and tools.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Equally important, is the understanding of the pros and cons to enable discernment and appropriate use.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For example, the benefits of ChatGPT, which everyone has been talking about.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: ChatGPT gives the ease of use with human-like conversations, extensive applications to produce text, images, music and code – to just name a few.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But just last week, an article in The Straits Times highlighted what seemed realistic artificial intelligence- (AI) generated images that surfaced in recent months and the difficulty to differentiate a fake photo from the real one.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There are both benefits and risks as AI and new technologies continue to play a bigger role in our work and lives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With increasing use of technologies, there are rising concerns around privacy, biases and discrimination.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Policies are needed to protect, but with a balance so as not to impede the benefits to be derived from these technologies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is an area that the Government will need to continue to monitor and manage.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In a fast-changing landscape and with disruptions, we will need to be agile and adapt quickly.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Adapting is not just about being flexible and making changes rapidly, but making the right changes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The irony is that in order to deal with changes and to be confident in making the right changes, it will require effort to understand and discern.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The need to analyse data and information, to ask questions and understand in order to use and build on the knowledge is essential.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To be adaptable, our students will need to build their problem-solving skills and creativity.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the pace of change and the complexity of the changing landscape, to prepare our students for success, we must also develop them to collaborate well with others and to communicate confidently to articulate their ideas and thoughts.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As outlined in the MOE addendum, how teaching is done in our schools has evolved.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To support our students to be able to collaborate and communicate effectively, schools will also need to continue to provide ample opportunity for students to do team-based learning around projects and problem solving.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: These skills will train our students to collaborate with diverse groups and also require them to communicate effectively.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will prepare our students and give them life skills and the confidence for opportunities in Singapore and overseas, both in school and in the future.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With people living longer and healthier, our workforce is multi-generational.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The needs and experience of workers differ between generations in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
