text: With change, people of all ages in the workforce will need to acquire knowledge at each stage of their careers and lives.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Apart from work, workers have to manage their different obligations and life stages, hence, learning has to be organised and accessible both online and hybrid-enabled access to learning to fit the learning needs and the different obligations, life stages and schedules of our workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: COVID-19 has also brought fundamental changes and shown us the possibilities of how work can be organised and where work can be done.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: President Halimah touched on the need for broader and a more open meritocracy to allow every Singaporean to have the opportunity to take on meaningful work that tap on their strengths and to be rewarded fairly for it.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I feel that our schools, institutes of higher learning (IHLs) and our SkillsFuture programmes, have and do provide pathways for learning, training, certification and credentials to recognise the skills acquired for our students and those in the workforce.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What we need, is for businesses and society to recognise skills, competencies and experiences of workers of all ages and qualifications, and not just academic levels of attainment for job opportunities and qualification.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The family plays an important and central role in our society.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The family provides our sense of belonging in society and are our first line of support and care.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With an ageing population and people living longer, families are multi-generational and caregiving needs will increase.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With smaller families, some families need to care for both the young and seniors.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For example, a middle-income household living in a private property taking care of aged parents or siblings may not qualify for any relief or subsidy for eldercare services because of housing type.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Our resident, Mdm Lee – not her real name – shared with me her worries on the long-term care needs for her brother.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: They live in a terrace house with her brother, aged 65 years old, her sister who is in her 50s and an aged mother in her early 90s.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In fact, during the COVID-19 period, it was really quite trying for this family in terms of caregiving needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As her husband, herself and her siblings are either retired or nearing retirement, she is worried about affordability for her brother's long-term care when his condition gets worse and he needs to stay in a nursing home.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am not saying that we discount means-testing, I think that is required.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But we need to think about the flexibility and also, the circumstances.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: And sometimes, we do it on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As our population is ageing, we will have more and more of such scenarios.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In this complex and rapidly changing world, while the Government has to do more, our businesses, citizens and society, too, have to do our part.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Working as one people, we have been able to weather challenges and emerge stronger.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am confident that as one people, we will move forward together to address challenges and seize opportunities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the one hand, we are young enough to use many forms of social media, but not young enough to use youth slang like "OOTD", outfit of the day; and "IYKYK", if you know, you know.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are old enough to remember the feverish days of the Malaysia Cup; but are a little too old to banter about the latest K-drama heartthrobs – though to be fair, I can name one or two.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, placed between seniors and the young, I wish to focus my speech today on these two demographic profiles that bookend society at the opposite ends.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wish to ask how we could give greater confidence to seniors and the young, to assure them that they are indispensable parts of our social fabric.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Put another way, how do we build a country for all ages?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One attitude that will erode solidarity across generations is the tendency towards ageism.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Ageisim can be directed against both older people and the young as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Ageism manifests itself in our minds, when we stereotype people based on age; it manifests in our feelings, when we harbour prejudice; and finally, it manifests in our actions, when we discriminate against people.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: WHO notes that ageism can exist at three levels.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, at the institutional level, when laws, policies and social norms restrict or disadvantage individuals based on age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, ageism exists at the interpersonal level, in interactions between two or more individuals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One of my residents, who is 97 and in excellent health, likes to go around asking anyone she meets in Teochew: "I am 97 years old this year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Are you afraid of me?" When we hear of someone so senior, some of us would, with good intentions, overprotect the person or assume that the person needs help without stopping to think that everyone ages differently.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We have also come across single elderly people who need to rent rooms to stay, due to disagreements with their family, but are rejected by landlords in view of their advanced age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Think also, of the millions of dollars spent on hair dyes and anti-ageing products, so as to present a younger image of ourselves, for fear that we might otherwise not be taken seriously.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is also a sexist element to this, where professional men with grey hair are respected, but women with grey hair doubted; but that deserves a more detailed discussion on another day.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Ageist attitudes are also familiar in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How often do we hear of middle-aged jobseekers who report that once their age is revealed to the prospective employer, they would receive a polite response to wait for a follow-up call, which does not come?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The recent global COVID-19 pandemic, too, saw ageism rear its ugly head.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A United Nations independent expert, Dr Claudia Mahler, noted that the pandemic restrictions and lockdowns had resulted in a wave of ageist comments and hate speech; older persons were blamed as the reasons for lockdowns and labelled as vulnerable and burdens to societies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To combat ageism, the WHO highlights three strategies: first, through laws and policies; second, through public education; and third, by increasing inter-generational contacts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At the official or policy level, there are positives in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We see many health-related initiatives toward active ageing, including the latest Healthier SG initiative.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government is also looking into more options for seniors to age-in-place instead of in an institution and for assisted-living accommodation that preserves the individual's autonomy to make decisions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such preservation of an individual's autonomy is a precious tenet that we can also see in legislation, such as the Mental Capacity Act (MCA).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under the MCA, donees and deputies must give weight to the preferences of the incapacitated person, as far as possible.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the employment front, there are policies to incentivise employers to hire older workers through wage offset schemes, such as the Senior Employment Credit.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Apart from laws and policies, the other two strategies that are likely to have more impact are public education and increasing inter-generational contacts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As far as public education is concerned, what more can be done?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For our students, we could review our education curriculum from primary to tertiary, to remove any ageist stereotypes and dispel any misconceptions about certain age groups.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On employment, I note the efforts of MOM to encourage our employers to hire older employees and embrace multi-generational teams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Another aspect is to watch our public discourse, including debates in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Ministers and Members of Parliament should avoid making statements that may inadvertently perpetuate ageism, such as: "By the year 2030, we will face a silver tsunami", which evokes all the wrong images.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This provides opportunities for cross-generation neighbourly activities, such as gardening, games and mutual care.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Research has shown that the benefits of such inter-generational contacts go beyond reducing ageist attitudes; they also benefit older people in improved health and psychosocial well-being, reducing distress and loneliness.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We should continue to promote more inter-generational contacts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From older people, I next move on to the young.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the President's Address, the President highlighted that youths showed a strong interest to take action and initiate change on issues they cared about.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She affirmed that the Government would engage the ideas, dynamism and energy of young Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth's (MCCY's) addendum to the President's Address, it was further stated that the Government would encourage more youths to engage in constructive civic discourse, through platforms, such as the Youth Circles and the Youth Action Challenge.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MCCY said it would continue to create new platforms to give youths the opportunity to shape Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, in a TODAY media report the next day, some young people expressed cynicism about existing forms of engagement.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Several interviewees argued that the engagement had to go beyond just talking, but should enable young people to have direct participation in governance and policy formulation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: One person doubted that the views of young people would be accepted unless those views aligned with the Government's own ideals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Whatever the views expressed, there was common ground that any engagement should foster in young people a sense of responsibility.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe it is worthwhile to distil what the priorities of our young citizens actually are.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What are the issues young people care about?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the President highlighted mental health and sustainability, it would be wrong to interpret this as meaning that young people only care about "woke" issues, such as climate change or discrimination.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my past work as a polytechnic lecturer, I could see in my students' concern about their parents, making ends meet and how to improve themselves and their families' station in life.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In an article published in the Workers' Party (WP) Hammer last year, WP Youth Wing President Nicole Seah also shared that young people had many concerns that crossed generations, such as the affordability of public housing, cost of raising a family and employment opportunities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We must be careful not to pigeonhole young people's issues into a handful of areas and only seek to engage them on those.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That would be a big turn-off and a disservice to our young.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Besides not restricting the areas for youth participation, we must also ask what sort of participation would convince our young people of a direct role in governance and policy-making.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There is some indication that the many conversations, so far conducted, have led to conversation fatigue and scepticism.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Cynicism about talking and consultations is understandable, as these are simply input which will eventually either be incorporated or thrown out by decision-makers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Of course, the empowerment of young Singaporeans need not and should not be a top-down affair.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Young citizens can and should seize the day and organise themselves around the causes they care about, adding to the richness of society through such ground-up initiatives.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the Government's latest response this year, the Minister basically said that those between 18 and 21 years old do not have the skillsets required to cast their votes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I wonder how many citizens agree with this assessment?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As I said in February, in the 1960s, the movement in the United States (US) to bring down the voting age to 18 years gained momentum when youths below 21 were drafted to fight in the Vietnam War.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The slogan ran: "Old enough to fight, old enough to vote!" Sir, let me conclude.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For Singapore to fully harness the energy of every citizen, we must foster a dynamic environment where ageist stereotypes, prejudice and discrimination are blown away.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is not something for the Government alone but requires marshalling the whole-of-society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Each of us needs to examine ourselves too, to see how we individually can contribute to this endeavour in our everyday interactions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If Singapore is to be built to last, we must, together, build a Singapore for all ages.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One avenue in which we can accomplish this is through expanding opportunities throughout life for all, regardless of individual backgrounds and circumstances.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Earlier this year, during the Budget Debate 2023, I spoke on right-sizing our syllabus and increasing affiliations between schools.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, I would like to elaborate more on that, for I feel it is in-sync with what Mdm President charted out last Monday.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On education, firstly, right-sizing our syllabus involves asking ourselves how do we truly want to prepare our young people for a different world they are growing up in.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The way our world has changed and keeps changing and – with the influx of knowledge and technology and AI – we cannot focus on getting the best test scores or merely having the most knowledge.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should not go down the route of an educational arms race.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One key way to stop this is to reduce the syllabus.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am not saying it is the only way, but making the syllabus less voluminous will reduce the reliance on tuition to play catch-up.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An educational arms race has incentivised a tuition culture.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And if we do not stop the race now, our students are going to end up hitting a brick wall.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must inject the joy of learning, instead of reliance on tuition to play catch-up on the syllabus.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An educational arms race has built-in a tuition culture, where students are caught between doing school homework and tuition homework such that they are possibly, busier on weekends than they are on weekdays.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This can lead to more individualised attention, a greater capacity to monitor each student's physical, mental and emotional well-being, and the ability to tailor to different learning speeds and to cater to different learning styles.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Instead of students having to go for tuition, smaller classes can help better pacing, so each student can learn and keep abreast of the subject within class time itself.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This can also allow students to have opportunities to speak out and participate more, which would be especially helpful for students who learn as they verbalise.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another focus is helping students with special educational needs in mainstream schools.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By reducing class sizes, teachers will have more capacity to assist with the educational experience of these students and to allow the space for interactions between all the students in the class under the teacher's supervision.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our teachers choose their profession because of the value they see in raising students to their full potential and derive much intrinsic joy from it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But the tendency for teachers to be overworked and burnt out is known, especially in the past few years where they have had to cope with many, many changes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our teachers go far beyond just the academics, as they often counsel students and help those struggling with mental health.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By taking on more teachers and reducing class sizes, we can build a better environment, both for students and teachers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That is, at least, in my humble view.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In right-sizing our syllabus and having an appropriate class size, we put in place the foundational stepping stones to inculcate in our young, the love of learning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Perhaps, in tweaking our syllabus, that may make way to craft more opportunities for students to visit museums and libraries and have more moments to play, which is essential for creativity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A recent topical concern is protecting our vulnerable citizens from scams.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, Sir, the other issue that deeply concerns me, as we progress as a nation, is the increasing prevalence of scams.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many of the residents I serve in the constituency, have come to me at the Meet-the-People Session (MPS) or shared with me during home visits, their distressing stories about how they have lost tens of thousands, if not, hundreds of thousands of dollars to scammers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Prevention involves both building an infrastructure of laws and harnessing technology to detect and dismantle criminal organisations as well as preparing our people, both young and old, to deal with this threat.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The scale of this threat cannot be under-estimated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The variety of scams – from investment scams to e-commerce scams – all focus on one thing: targeting a specific vulnerability of a targeted group.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The scammers are highly sophisticated in directing different scams to different age groups and taking advantage of cognitive biases to psychologically manipulate people into giving more details and transferring larger amounts of money.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, to tackle this, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) need to work with the Singaporean public, the banks and our partners from other countries.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, I believe we have to double down and raise a proper bulwark with our banking security systems.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the constituency I serve and when I meet with residents, I have seen physically, bank statements of residents with multiple outflows of monies, just under the transaction limit each time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have seen bank statements where this happens between 2.00 am and 8.00 am, multiple withdrawals under the limit.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And then, when they wake up, the poor residents are $70,000 poorer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This should raise alarm bells and in my view, prompt the bank to halt the transactions altogether until further verification is obtained, or at least contact the customer to ensure that these are legitimate withdrawals.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have also to consider the new safeguards we should put in place.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, e-wallets make transactions far quicker, but do they have the same safeguards in place?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is time that we consider what trade-offs we make between advancing "frictionless" transactions on the one hand and putting in place enough safeguards to protect our people.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must look at how we can mitigate the effect of the scam.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, I humbly think we also need to consider how we should put in place, better support and compensation for those who lose their life savings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often, the compensation offered by the bank is insufficient for them to retire on.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That would leave many of our seniors having to find more work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That may not be ideal at all, if the couple is already in retirement.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I really believe this is a group of people we must stand alongside.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: While there are always areas for improvement, we have done well with governmental efficiency and urban planning relative to other countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: However, back then, I said that we have not done as well in fostering strong non-state actors and institutions to balance a strong state.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And I would add that we have not done as well in fostering a strong sense of participation in our democracy; a sense that we can speak out and, if needed, disagree with the dominant narrative, with our views actually having a chance to make a difference.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: An article by Tan and Preece in the Asian Journal of Comparative Politics in December last year reads, and I quote, "We find that mechanisms of diagonal accountability related to media and civil society have declined.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Countries that succeed in drawing strong participation in democracy will be more successful in fostering a confident populace, a people who deeply feel that this is my country, my home – a place where my voice counts for something, a place that I will sacrifice to defend.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We all want Singapore to be a country where everyone feels that they have a chance at realising their full potential and giving life to their dreams.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A place where tomorrow can be better than today for ourselves and, even more so, for our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Not a place where many cannot even envisage a better tomorrow; not a place where economic pressure and ever-intensifying competition from school to workplace lead to ever greater stratification in living conditions, social capital and social standing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The second part will address how we can build economic optimism, so as to create a virtuous cycle of economic dynamism.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The third part will suggest "a Singapore model" that can be a beacon for the region and also a bulwark against attempts by great powers to suborn or divide us.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: President Halimah's speech called for "an active citizenry" and "a passionate civil society".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: She also spoke of the importance of avoiding political polarisation and gridlock, having trust between "our political leadership and people" and keeping political discourse respectful and rational.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But as I reflected on this, I found that my unease was captured in a public comment from former media editor and academic Bertha Henson.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I will quote an excerpt here: "I am always bemused when I hear politicians warning Singaporeans against such 'polarisation'.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We do not have a two-party system yet nor a civil society which will take to the streets.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Yet, we hear about divisive politics as though we are teetering on the edge of an abyss…I don't think we should be guarding against 'divisive politics' but rather 'mono-politics': that there is only one narrative, one view and it must necessarily be the right or the best perspective – unless you don't trust me.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That is too tall an order for any citizen to submit to." Let us unpack and interrogate some of these assumptions in what I term "the dominant narrative".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think we should and I hope all hon Members want that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And if we take that ideal seriously, we should never treat differences of opinion as necessarily equivalent to polarisation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Polarisation happens only if some groups of people oppose others for the sake of opposing and not in a reasonable, fair-minded way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Polarisation happens only if vindictiveness and tribalism trump thoughtfulness and basic human decency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: No pun intended in the use of the verb "trump", by the way.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One can disagree with respect, courtesy and decency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It seems that everyone, nowadays, welcomes that well-worn phrase "robust debate".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But we do sometimes hear in this House that the other side has not explained the trade-offs properly and, therefore, was being dishonest in some sense.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Were those trade-offs denied, hidden or glossed over?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think in our political discourse and even in our debates in this House, we should strive to treat Members' views and other parties' views fairly and accept when there is a philosophical or ideological difference, call it what you will, rather than being too quick to label the other side as "disingenuous".

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such labels can affect the tone of discourse in the wider society, if alternative ideas become demonised or labelled uncharitably.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Rather than chip away at trust in the Opposition with such labels, the Government should focus on explaining why it disagrees with the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, on the need to keep political discourse rational, I do not think anyone would disagree with this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: There is a great deal of public opinion surveying done by the Government, some of it through opinion-sensing agencies, like Rysense, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Not all of this is made available for public scrutiny and debate.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, I come to the oft-repeated call for trust in Government.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I think trust in the independent institutions of the state is a very good thing, where it is warranted.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But should the public blindly trust the Government, as in the political leadership, regardless of whether relevant information has been shared; regardless of what the Government says or does?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That goes against the active citizenry which the President's speech referred to.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But surely, we do not want a citizenry that is active in deeds, but blind, apathetic or timid in thinking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such a citizenry may engage in the wrong deeds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And to trust the Government – does that mean that, since the Government and Opposition sometimes disagree and not, hopefully, irrationally, does that mean that it is right that the public distrust the Opposition?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should not strive for a political landscape where the public innately trusts the Government but innately distrusts the Opposition, or vice versa.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If any Member disagrees with this, please, I would love to hear your views later.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We should strive, rather, for a politically educated populace that accords trust based on facts and evidence from independent institutions that function as intended.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What can we do to strengthen everyone's confidence that we have an open society, where citizens can and should care, listen, understand and debate policies?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: How can we make everyone believe that there is a more level-playing field for ideas and not primarily one dominant narrative that you would do well not to challenge?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the interest of time, I will suggest just a few ideas to advance towards this goal which WP Members of Parliament (MPs) have expanded on in previous debates in this House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One, delink the People's Association from the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The current system creates a sense that state resources are invested in promoting the Government's thinking and the ruling party's politicians, which unlevels the playing field for politics and ideas in our nation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My hon friend, Aljunied MP, Mr Faisal Manap, will elaborate on this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Two, create an ombudsman with investigative capacity to strengthen confidence that the state and ruling party are accountable and cannot simply shut down a grievance that may be politically costly or for other reasons.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At the very least, a second unbiased opinion would be of value.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have argued for this at length previously, as have other WP MPs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Three, ensure that funding for civil society, the arts and so on is handled by independent committees who are not linked to the government of the day.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This would certainly help build the passionate civil society that President Halimah spoke of and counter any fears that civil society groups that advocate alternative policies to the Government may be penalised using state resources.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Four, since we do not have a Freedom of Information Act, we should publish every single public opinion poll and data collection effort conducted with state funds, redacted only for anything that has clear and strong commercial or national security sensitivities for better-informed debate amongst political parties, civil society groups and citizens.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Five, allow Opposition MPs to engage school students in their MP capacity, alongside ruling party MPs and Ministers, a subject I have raised in this House before.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need to mould the mental habits of our citizens from a young age to nurture independent, critical thinking.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Exposing them only to People's Action Party (PAP) politicians in schools and barring non-PAP ones in most student engagement contexts does not achieve this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Our future citizens need to be able to see both sides of a question, in a way that will inoculate them from the demagogues and foreign interference attempts of the future.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I now come to the second part of my speech on the optimism of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Right now, close to 50% of households live in 5-room HDB flats or more expensive homes, private homes and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: A little over 50% live in 4-, 3-, 2- or 1-room HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At the risk of oversimplification, those who live in less expensive homes may be the ones feeling the economic anxiety and pessimism that the Edelman survey measures.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: They may struggle to compete in the workplace or academia, especially if they did not receive the inherited advantages of wealth or social capital that President Halimah spoke of.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The elderly on fixed or no incomes, have to grapple with rising food prices.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Whereas others, the optimistic 36%, may feel that they can thrive in this very competitive society with high prices and expensive homes.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: At this point, I declare my interest as the Chairman of a Singapore company that undertakes market research and consulting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But the Edelman survey, plus a great deal of anecdotal experience from my conversations with Singaporeans in the Serangoon ward of Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC) and East Coast GRC previously, suggest that this anxiety is very real.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Many fear that the way food, house and other prices are rising, the way the job market is becoming more competitive, those with fewer advantages will truly struggle to build a tomorrow that is better than today.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, we should recall that real wage data may mask some things.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Real wages may appear to be rising but that may mask the fact that certain demographic groups may feel the pain of inflation more than others.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Also, within each income decile, there will be those who do less well than the median for that decile.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And lastly, the Edelman survey shows that whatever the real wage growth data suggests, the thinking of many Singaporeans about the future reflects a lack of confidence that they can thrive going forward.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This economic pessimism could be one reason for our globally low total fertility rate (TFR).

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the previous housing debate, I also cited academic evidence for a causal link between high home prices and low TFR in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If left to fester, such economic pessimism could lead to a brain drain as people leave for more liveable countries.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If that happens, that may tend to create an over-reliance on foreign manpower.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We need to address this economic pessimism fundamentally, not only through ad hoc measures, such as an additional grant here or an additional rebate there, helpful as that is.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: More far-reaching reforms are needed to make everyone believe that this society has their back.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The WP has called for many such reforms in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In the interest of time, I shall not expand on these, but I shall refer to them.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This is something the WP has championed for some time and I was intrigued by Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's reference to some form of unemployment support.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Three, seriously tackling the issue of poverty and breaking the poverty cycle.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have called for a war on poverty in this House.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My hon friend Assoc Prof Jamus Lim has also weighed in on this topic yesterday, as have other WP MPs over the years.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Five, revamping trades or vocational jobs to overhaul them for higher productivity, pay and conditions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I have spoken about this in the House several times.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I believe slowing down the growth of reserves is wholly justified at this stage of our nation's history, given the needs we have with an ageing population in a turbulent world and given the much larger size of the Reserves now versus gross domestic product (GDP), as they were in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: My WP colleagues and I have explained this repeatedly, on multiple platforms.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We must invest to ensure a confident current generation, lest our fertility go so low that there will be few people in the generations to come.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We offer alternative policies that differ substantively from the ideas of the PAP, for example, on slowing the Reserves growth to enhance liveability, social justice and social mobility and reducing BTO prices based on tweaks to the land valuation formula.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The alternatives we have championed in Parliament, in our manifesto, are too numerous for me to mention here.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We championed anti-discrimination legislation and redundancy insurance, policies that the PAP are now considering in some form.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister and the PAP know this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Not going for false but flashy soundbites that smear our opponents, that the media then viralise with huge headlines.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not want my children to grow up in a post-truth society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As I said in my maiden speech, we have got certain fundamentals right.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Let us fill in the other half with measures to enhance our active citizenry, civil society and engaged, rational politics.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: This thinking can extend to regional leadership in economic projects.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such projects can be designed to reflect Singaporean values of good corporate governance and efficiency, but also incorporating consultation and engagement with civil society and other stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for such projects could advance goals, like poverty alleviation, reflecting Singaporean values of egalitarianism and inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Singapore has positioned itself as a leader in economic openness, having the most free trade agreements (FTAs) in the region.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But one of our distant competitors is putting a twist on this approach.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The UAE's diplomacy focuses on playing a supporting role to Saudi Arabia, Egypt and so on, who have much bigger populations and armies, even as the UAE positions itself as the business gateway to the Arab World and Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: But the UAE has taken this a step further.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It invests in overseas assets with a very outsized investment in renewables.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: By comparison, Temasek-linked Sembcorp's 2025 target is 10 gigawatts; Keppel’s is seven gigawatts.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In comparison, Singapore has supported renewable energy companies' expansion into the region and internationally, but largely on a commercial, non-diplomatic basis.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Why green investments as the backbone of these regional leadership efforts?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Because green energy is cheap, lasting, critical and has the potential to make a far-reaching impact.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In 2018, I spoke in this House about the idea of Singapore leading a flagship project in the region on renewable energy or some such theme to serve multiple economic and diplomatic ends.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Such projects need not be primarily government-financed, but can raise financing in capital markets globally.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Leading and catalysing such a regional flagship project will help bolster—

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Leading and catalysing such a regional flagship project will help bolster Singapore's economy and also Singapore's soft power in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) region, a region which has a potentially important historical destiny, namely that of a bulwark and zone of buffering and balancing between the great powers of China and the West.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And what if Singapore demonstrates how its traditional bureaucratic efficiency can be combined with policies that ensure openness, accountability and democratic ownership among an active citizenry?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That could serve as a good example for this vital region that will inspire emulation and perhaps help form an ASEAN identity around such principles.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: At different ages, they have different rights and different responsibilities."

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Whether it is in education or employment, the Government has made positive and concerted efforts to promote meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As a labour MP, I have been lobbying in the past few years against discrimination and have been part of the efforts in the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness to uphold the principles of fair and merit-based employment in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On the education front, I can see the efforts at levelling the playing field and providing opportunities for all to maximise their full potential in the entire learning continuum from mainstream to adult education and continuing education and training both in and outside of employment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Yesterday, the WP through hon Member Gerald Giam proposed through-train schools for the first 10 years.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is not a new idea, as my fellow MOE Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) member and former Chair, hon Member Denise Phua, had suggested almost a decade ago and on different occasions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: MOE, during the Committee of Supply, had explained considerations to right-site our students according to their learning needs and the associated challenges of implementation that we must carefully consider.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There are also those who want to retain the PSLE and want to have a choice of the secondary school they want to enter at some interval.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Likewise, with SBB to be rolled out across all secondary schools in due course, it will allow students to discover and pursue their passions and interests while deepening their strengths and abilities and have a more structured and less painful process for learning.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We do not want an arms race or more stress due to examinations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We also do not want to cram children with even more content as character and values are equally, if not more, important.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am glad we have made significant changes to the education system and must continue to do so to improve.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I, therefore, agree and support what Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong mentioned in his speech yesterday on our refreshed meritocracy, which is a continuous one with learning opportunities, milestones, ladders at multiple junctures through this learning continuum.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It, therefore, holds true that it remains a treadmill journey and we need to constantly evolve and find new and innovative ways to imbue the love for learning in everyone; foster a lifelong learning culture and ensure our people stay ready, relevant and resilient – ready to do better, relevant to move forward in life and resilient to try again.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In my recent contribution to ETHOS, a publication of the Civil Service College, I reiterated the importance of adopting a mindset of lifelong learning to address the issue of skills mismatch.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: SkillsFuture, the national movement to provide Singaporeans with the opportunities to develop their fullest potential throughout life, regardless of their starting points, is Singapore's initiative towards inculcating that mindset and embedding it within our culture.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We have already seen how SkillsFuture has paid off for businesses.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These findings are promising and we certainly hope that all businesses will provide their workers that access to quality continuing education and training (CET) and upgrading opportunities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Labour Movement will continue its work in advocating that employers provide adequate training support for their workers so that they may tap on opportunities that arise in the new economy and ensure a just transition for all.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, I feel we can do more for the individual Singaporean in ensuring that this system, that supports lifelong learning, works for them too.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The vision to strengthen our SkillsFuture ecosystem, such that everyone is enabled to do significant skills reboot during their working lives, is one that I firmly believe in.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: What the entire SkillsFuture programme does is that it provides us access to a toolbox.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Call it a CET toolbox – a collection of educational courses and training programmes that are meant to support and equip us on this journey of lifelong learning, enabling us to accomplish skills mastery and even second-skilling ourselves.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Just like the SkillsFuture Credit, which arms every Singaporean citizen from the age of 25 with this toolbox.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, not all of them open this toolbox, much less use it.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Anecdotally, through my engagements with workers as well as with residents, this could be attributed to two reasons.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, there are just too many options for training programmes out there.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, there is a perceived lack of guarantee that undergoing training would result in tangible outcomes for the individual's career, in terms of wages and progression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Returning to my toolbox analogy, what this means is that: first, there are just too many tools in our toolbox, leading to confusion; and two, a lack of knowledge on how using a certain tool or a combination of tools would help us accomplish certain tasks, revealing a lack of clarity or information asymmetry.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The next question, then, is a straightforward one – how can we help Singaporeans navigate these tools, cut through the analysis paralysis, resolve the paradox of choice and have the confidence that the utilisation of these tools would empower them with the means to fix a leaky pipe, replace a light switch or assemble a table and become the version of the skilled tradesperson that they have always aspired to be?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In other words, how can we tighten the nuts and bolts of our SkillsFuture ecosystem to generate outcomes that will ultimately be beneficial for Singaporeans and their careers and, eventually, our economy?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our workforce is made up of workers of varied profiles and it is imperative that we adopt a more targeted lifelong learning strategy for different worker segments – to ensure that everyone has fair access to opportunities, a level playing field for jobs, while, at the same time, balancing companies' manpower needs in the immediate and longer-term, to achieve equitable outcomes.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We have skills frameworks and annual reports on skills in demand, which are very instructive and useful.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But I opine that a more individualised and speed to market approach is needed so that time and resources spent on training and skills upgrading lead to clear outcomes in terms of wages and career progression and ensure every worker stays employed and employable.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There is a way to enable this targeted lifelong learning strategy by tapping on the expertise of career coaches and counsellors.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Professional, industry-accredited career coaches and counsellors work with us to explore our strengths and weaknesses, build confidence and chart our career paths.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: They are invaluable help and support throughout our careers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For our young fresh graduates, mid-careerists in the throes of a mid-life or mid-career crisis and vulnerable segments, such as those who are not so young, as well as inmates and ex-offenders – having a career coach to mentor them, to help them navigate the journey of upskilling and retraining with them, can make a world of difference.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The advice and guidance rendered by the career coach would complement what SkillsFuture, in its existing form, already offers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It may even reduce or resolve the psychological barriers to training and ensure all Singaporeans that they have equal chances and opportunities at all stages to develop their skills.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Whether they are in the midst of a life transition, or just looking to upskill, Singaporeans can look towards SkillsFuture as providing the full suite of services that would support them in that journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Toolbox in hand, Singaporeans can be confident that there is a master tradesman by their side to guide them in the effective use of tools to achieve skills mastery.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Taking a longer-term view, the SkillsFuture initiative could then be what reduces the skills and jobs mismatch, thereby reducing under-employment and skills shortages.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It would maximise our intended structural outcomes in progressing the development of our people and economy, while ensuring that Singaporeans continue to have access to opportunities – regardless of their life stage – to help them find their true north and realise their full potential.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: On a final note, I have previously lobbied in this House on many occasions in the past decade, the possibility of monetary support for those unemployed to help them tide over the difficult period before finding and landing the next job.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The idea has been fleshed out in our joint NTUC-Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) Professionals, Managers and Executives in Singapore (PME) Taskforce Report recommendations and again during our recent #EveryWorkermatters conversations.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: All workers, including PMEs, especially those in their 40s and 50s, are visibly concerned and anxious over skills obsolescence and unemployment.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: I note that Mr Patrick Tay said that the 10-year through-train-school idea is not new.

speaker: Mr Gerald Giam Yean Song (Aljunied)
text: Ms Denise Phua proposed it more than a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: If I may give a quick response to the hon Member Gerald Giam, I think there are constraints and it was highlighted again in my speech.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: As of today, the teachers and staff already have very exacting requirements and demands on their time and resources.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: So, doing this will mean dedicating even more resources, and even stretching workers in this space and the entire education ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This requires serious consideration and, therefore, it is something we need to think carefully before we move on to the step.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: As to what it will take to create a pathway like this – the challenges – and to solve some of the root issues that the ground faces and will be having.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, the debate is not just to have or not to have – that is like a 10-year-old debate; whether to have or not to have – but really to go on to the next level.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Why it should happen or why should it not happen?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What constraints will come in if we choose that pathway?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I join the hon Member to express gratitude to the President for her Address.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have come a long way since gaining Independence and achieved what many would consider an economic miracle.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Trust in Government, as measured by Edelman, remains consistently high and we should not take that for granted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Our political maturity has also come of age with this Parliament having its first Leader of the Opposition appointed by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: However, all of us need to acknowledge that Singapore is at a point of inflexion.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We have had a declining birthrate since 2017.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And like many of the advanced economies, we are in the middle of a silver tsunami.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singaporeans are faced with a dilemma of accepting this reality and creating a welcoming culture of integrating our foreign guest workers into our communities, or, allowing the continued tight labour situation to (a) negatively impact our service quality and the Singapore brand; (b) cause the burnout of our workforce due to their having to double-up for the shortage of labour; and (c) limiting our companies' growth opportunities, just to name a few.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I salute the 14,000 Singaporeans from civil society and businesses who have stepped forward to co-create with the Government in re-imagining what success for Singapore 2.0 could look like.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I attended a couple of the sessions myself and I could feel the love by so many of our Singaporeans for our country.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Most heartening for me to know is – the affirmation that Singaporeans wish to hold intact the core values that we cherish, as Singaporeans, that is: fairness, inclusivity, mutual support and the desire to give back to society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In her Address, Mdm President spoke about the need for a broader and more open meritocracy that will work well for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The Collins dictionary defines meritocracy as a society or social system in which people get status or rewards because of what they achieve, rather than because of their wealth or social status.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, the idea behind meritocracy is that the most talented and hardworking individuals should be given opportunities to succeed, regardless of their background or social class or their gender.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Many positive outcomes of meritocracy have been realised: (a) top of the list is social mobility and many amongst us can stand to be counted as beneficiaries; (b) another positive outcome is that meritocracy promotes a more efficient and effective workforce as individuals are rewarded for their achievements and their hard work; and (c) meritocracy is largely seen as a fair system, thus promoting justice and equality.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: That said, there are also pitfalls to meritocracy.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Meritocracy assumes equal access to all opportunities by everyone.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And this is not always the case since those who come from disadvantaged backgrounds may not have the same resources or access and that can limit their chances of success.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Two, meritocracy can be limited by how we define merit.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore's case, merit has been closely associated with paper qualifications and, hence, the phenomenon of the "paper chase".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The narrow definition of merit to paper qualifications does not consider other qualities which, in fact, are competencies needed for the 21st century workforce and these qualities include, emotional quotient, creativity, ability to communicate with influence or even craftsmanship and other non-traditional skills.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Three, meritocracy can also create social division as those who are successful may attribute their success as solely due to their own merit, rather than recognising the role of their family, the larger environment and society that has enabled and empowered them to be successful.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This individualism mindset will, over time, erode the values of our society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Responding to Mdm President's call to action for a rethink of the approach to education and to work, so as to avoid the pitfalls of meritocracy, as it is today, I would like to start the dialogue along these two aspects and offer some "food for thought" along the way.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: First, let us re-imagine meritocracy in education and I will raise three themes.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: First and foremost, we need to go back to basics and remind everyone in the system of the following – embracing the dignity of the child and igniting in every child the joy of learning.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: It needs to be central in any education system and believed in by all stakeholders – parents, educators and teachers, principals, policy-makers and society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore does a reasonably good job in this regard and our educators deserve a big kudos for all they do for our children.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How we were able to keep our children in school throughout most part of COVID-19 with teachers having to pivot to provide hybrid-learning, is a case in point.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The child is certainly central to our educators in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Next, I am heartened to see that, increasingly so, more attention and resources are being given to children with special needs.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For youths whose circumstances are challenged, the Government is enabling more social services agencies to provide the appropriate care from preventive to developmental to rehabilitative.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And community initiatives, like Yellow Ribbon, to give youths who have made bad choices in their lives a second chance, is to be applauded.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: These initiatives will go a long way to narrow unequal access to resources and, in doing so, facilitate social mobility.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Three, the biggest challenge lies in changing mindsets.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Meritocracy inevitably drives individual achievements and that is how the individualism mindset gets ingrained.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: To break the individualism mindset, a few things need to be reset.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: First, expectations need to be reset for both the teachers, the principals, the school system and the parents: from focusing on grades to emphasising the dignity of the child; developing in the child the joy of learning and; inculcating in the child the values of fairness, inclusivity, mutual support and the desire to give back to society.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I submit to you that the adults need to walk-the-talk and role model the way forward for the students.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, dialogue and alignment amongst the stakeholders would necessarily be the first step.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Two, teach our students that "we are all in this together".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For this, perhaps, we can take a page from the late Nelson Mandela, and I quote, "In Africa, there is a concept known as 'ubuntu' – the profound sense that we are human only through the humanity of others; that if we are to accomplish anything in this world, it will in equal measure be due to the work and achievement of others." Ubuntu is the philosophy of "I am, because we are".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said yesterday, let our language be "more of us and we, and less of I and me".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The next step is to review the rewards system across the board.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Are the students rewarded based on academic achievements primarily or behaviours of their values in action?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How are parents engaged in the process to fulfil the common purpose of educating their child?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Are students encouraged to share their knowledge and their skills with classmates who may need help?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot ask the educators to deliver one thing, but measure and pay them on something else.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Likewise, for the students, how will their behaviours be rewarded, both in terms of the way they are graded as well as the way they will qualify for admission to higher levels of education?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And so, I come to the next point.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Specifically, admission criteria for students to progress can afford a rethink.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How do we reward team spirit and team behaviour and perhaps, penalise negative individualistic behaviours when crafting admission criteria?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: While we do want to develop our students to their best potential and have them be the Edusave Awards for Achievement, Good LEadership and Service (EAGLES) and soar, we ought to take a lesson from nature as even eagles in the sky fly in formation and take turns to be at the head of the "V".

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This formation helps them to fly longer distances.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, MOE and the schools and the parents might take this lesson on board and rethink the criteria used for rewarding students' EAGLES.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I have heard stories of how smart students attain the Singapore Government's prestigious scholarships only to break bond and worse still, the intention to do that was already there even at the point of application.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Breaking bond is a crime, as you rob a fellow Singaporean from the opportunity to access the education and the experience that the scholarship provides.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, there may be some scholarships which are in recognition of one's achievements.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: For such scholarships, perhaps, the Government can consider not imposing a bond but, instead, other forms of paying it forward.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This will spread out the talent to our local industry and, at the same time, these smartest of the smartest of Singaporeans will have a better understanding of issues on the ground and be better policymakers when they return to the Public Service.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Six, teachers play a significant role in all of this.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How can we help teachers by having them do less administrative work, so they have more student encounters?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How can we help to unburden their stress and keep their mental wellness in glowing condition?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: A kind word, a thank you, a please, a smile from the students and from parents would mean so much.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: And I would like to add that teacher-student interactions play a big part in educating the child.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Seven, it takes a village to raise a child.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike the past, our students today face constant disruptions.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: What they have learnt in the first 25 years will need to be constantly upskilled and reskilled to stay relevant to the industry and the workplace.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore's SkillsFuture is a brilliant and strategic vision.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Its implementation will go a long way toward changing the view of meritocracy earned at point of graduation, to meritocracy earned over a lifetime.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, let us re-imagine meritocracy in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Just as MOE has developed multiple pathways for success, there should be multiple pathways for success in the industry.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to focus my attention on the 60% of each year's cohort of students who attend the Institute of Education (ITE) and/or polytechnics.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The industry has a big part to play to help themselves as this is the pipeline of their workforce.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, the polytechnics and ITE have stepped up engagement with industry and in many instances, imbedded industry into the curriculum.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: This is very important to ensure that the students are skills-ready and job-ready when they leave the system.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: MOE's Work-Study Programme has been designed to facilitate such a pathway.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore Polytechnic's Industry Now Curriculum has imbedded such elements.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The target group should be the polytechnic and ITE students who are unlikely to take the university route right after attaining their diplomas.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: In Singapore, I said earlier, most employers still hire and pay by qualifications and not by skills and value.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I would advocate once again that SGUnited Jobs and Skills may be leveraged to target certain jobs which we want to have more Singaporeans in the roles but whose compensation package is currently not appealing for the Singaporeans to be excited to step in and companies need to be weaned off supposedly cheaper foreign labour.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: The target jobs ought to be aligned with MTI's Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) so that the support and incentives can be more targeted.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: MTI's Accelerated Pathways for Technicians and Assistant Engineers grant to support manufacturing companies in training and hiring ITE graduates for critical technical roles is a good case in point.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Between the Public Service, the Temasek-linked and Government-linked companies, they hire a sizeable percentage of the Singaporean workforce.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope that they can lead the way from all the points that I have mentioned and start now.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Many of our SMEs do not have the same access to capital, tools, networks and leadership.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: How can we incentivise our MNCs and large local enterprises (LLEs) to bring along our SMEs who are the vulnerable community in the business world in their value chain and, in so doing, intervene to avoid the pitfall of meritocracy which SMEs may be disadvantaged?

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: Government procurement, if open to SMEs directly or via the value chain, will certainly help minimise the pitfalls of meritocracy as well.

speaker: Ms Janet Ang (Nominated Member)
text: I am confident that as One Singapore, we can make every tomorrow better than today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The President's Address points to the urgent need to refresh our social compact.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This includes, helping Singaporeans with more job support, strengthening the social safety nets, broadening the definition of meritocracy and promoting a strong sense of shared identity, where every Singaporean feels that they have a stake in our country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are noble aspirations which the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) strongly supports.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, to refresh or to redefine our social compact, PSP thinks that we need to, first, rethink fundamentally, some of the more important policies on jobs, public housing, education and work; and ultimately, what it means to be Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP has vigorously debated the Government on some of these issues, especially jobs and public housing, in the past three years.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ms Hazel Poa and I had demonstrated what PSP, as a responsible Opposition party, will do to allow the voices of Singaporeans be heard.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have proposed serious alternative policies, as a responsible Opposition party does.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But regrettably, the Government does not generally seem to be prepared to consider our proposals seriously.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister's message yesterday confirms that one more time.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Based on our debates with the Ministers, we believe that the policy changes advanced by the Government are inadequate to address the problems on hand.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, the job security of Singaporeans and the surging HDB prices.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Notwithstanding that, PSP is committed to work with the Government and all political parties as one Singapore team to empower our people, renew our social compact and secure a brighter future for ourselves and our children.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: From my very first speech as a Non-Constituency Member of Parliament (NCMP) in this Parliament, I have raised the concerns of Singaporeans who believe that the current socioeconomic policies are not working for them.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many Singaporeans are very concerned that the benefits of job growth and economic growth are mainly accruing to the foreign workforce in Singapore rather than Singaporean workers, even though our workers are well-educated, well-skilled and hardworking.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We raised the widespread anxiety experienced by Singaporeans, regarding their jobs and livelihoods, during the debate on our foreign talent policy in September 2021.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regrettably, during that debate, instead of answering our questions directly and allowing the debate to focus on the more substantial issues, the Government tried to paint the PSP as a xenophobic, nativist and even racist political party.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The PSP has always maintained that for Singapore to achieve greater economic success, we will always need the right foreign talent to complement a Singaporean core.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, when the quality, number and concentration of Work Pass holders affect the job security of Singaporeans, we must speak out.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unlike the Americans in New York or the Chinese in Shanghai, our countrymen have nowhere else to go if they cannot afford the cost of living or are displaced from their professionals, managers, executives and technician jobs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no hinterland for these Singaporeans to retreat to.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They will have to leave Singapore and go to another country.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must treasure our citizens and cannot let this happen.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is why, over the last three years, I have continued to ask so many questions and focused so many of my speeches on our foreign manpower policy, the wage and employment situation of Singaporeans and workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These are rational and constructive policy alternatives to level the playing field for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: They are not meant to close our doors to foreign talents or target any nationality or race.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
