text: It is important for our domestic capability resilience to nurture and build local expertise in as many sectors as possible.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Presently, car dealers bid for the COEs regardless of whether there are clients buying cars from them or not.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They can keep and hog the COEs for months and trade and sell these COEs to other car dealers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic was a crisis of our generation but also a test from which Singapore emerged more united and our trust in each other strengthened.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But we must not take this for granted.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking ahead, our operating environment is increasingly complex.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Pressures in and outside of Singapore continue to mount and these can threaten to tear us apart.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Game-changing technologies, rising cost of living, shift in social values and heightened international contestation are some of the key forces pulling us in different directions.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Therefore, even as we strive for progress and push for excellence, we must ensure that Singapore remains united.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our policies must remove barriers and minimise gaps, our Parliament must focus on building up trust, not tearing down and our society must be more inclusive and compassionate.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: President Halimah spoke of broadening meritocracy and making sure that it continues to work well for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is no better alternative to meritocracy, but we need to temper it so that it is more compassionate and more relevant to today's context.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: My take is that for those among us who can and want to excel, we ought not to limit them and should wish them well.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For those who want to but cannot because of financial circumstances, then we must intervene more strongly to support and move them along.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: It is not just about giving equal opportunities but to direct more resources to help the abled but underprivileged.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: One thing precious about Singapore is that despite our different jobs and roles in the economy, we still see ourselves as Singaporeans of similar standing and similar in other areas too, for example, in our taste for hawker foods. "Towkays" and workers can all turn up at the same coffee shop to queue for "bak chor mee" or "roti prata" and share a table to eat thereafter.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: There is no expectation that one should be deferential or give way to another.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The expectation is that they will be treated all the same.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Meritocracy can lead to differences in economic outcomes, but these should not lead to differences in social treatment.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our system must give all our people equal rights and opportunities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: All of us must affirm our egalitarianism in both spirit and practice.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Yesterday, Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong spoke of creating Singapore to become a full-fledged learning society, from cradle to grave.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Disruptions brought about by technological revolutions have been a constant feature throughout history and the pace is gathering.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Great Reshuffle also means that jobs and skills needed are changing and will continue to change.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And specific to this industry, seven out of the 10 top skills are considered new.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: These new skills, include new programming languages; but also softer skills, such as stakeholder management and strategic partnerships.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Clearly, we cannot expect to learn the universe in school, but we can acquire the basics from which we continue to build.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our education should focus on inculcating a sense of curiosity in our young, so that they will always be intrinsically motivated to seek out new knowledge and skills.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over the years, changes have been made to the system, but we could do more to foster a culture of curiosity.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, could we focus less on standard answers but more on imagination and creative solutioning?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Indeed, our education system has done away from PSLE T-score and replaced streaming with banding – these are encouraging moves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But what about students who are inventors and storytellers or who have topics of interest not found in the textbooks?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: How can we recognise and reward them more formally?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Can there be an "independent study" subject that allows the student to choose a topic of interest to deep-dive into and be given a grade that is just as important as an English or mathematics subject, so that we move towards learning that is more versatile, more blue-skies thinking and hopefully, less need for tuition, which is often cited as a costly endeavour that widens the gap?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As pointed out, learning does not stop after graduating from the mainstream education system.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In future, as industries continue to be disrupted by new technologies, we can expect to change tracks many times in our working lives.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Mature workers starting afresh in radically new industries several times, within a lifetime, will become a norm and it would no longer be something to feel embarrassed about.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: To support this, adult learning should then focus less on long, structured courses with expensive certificates, but shorter and more targeted ones to build practical skills that can be readily deployed at work.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And could we recognise these credentials by recording them as part of our national digital identity, creating a personal digital resume for each Singaporean?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Public Service can, perhaps, take the lead in formally recognising these short courses taken by officers.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Second, a mastering technology and not be mastered by technology.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: A key development driving the next wave of disruption is artificial intelligence (AI).

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But what is scarier is that the stiff competition to lead in the field of AI could mean a willingness to overlook ethical considerations and other consequences.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: For example, ChatGPT caught the world's attention in recent times.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We are all impressed by its almost-human capabilities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But has the company OpenAI really thought through the long-term social implications of ChatGPT before releasing it?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Media reports would suggest that it had not.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Consider ChaosGPT, which is the autonomous implementation of ChatGPT that is touted as, "empowering GPT with Internet and memory to destroy humanity".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: While ChaosGPT has yet to work out how to really destroy mankind, but, by its autonomous nature, it will keep going until it achieves the goal it is given.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And with each iteration of technological advancement, one can be sure that ChaosGPT will also get better.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Surely, OpenAI could not have invented ChatGPT to destroy ourselves.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Even if there was a tinge of hesitation back then, it is now too late to pull back, because the launch of ChatGPT triggered a frenzy amongst tech giants, like Google and Baidu, rushing to release their own versions of generative AI.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: When technology confers power, an arm's race begins.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Some questions arising from this are: while people are still struggling, in trying their best to keep up digitally, would we have inadvertently moved the goal post so much that we widened the gap between the digital know and know-nots?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And between those who have access to powerful technology and those who have not.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What happens if enterprises increasingly feel that it is okay to ignore ethics, to be irresponsible and just do whatever to make money?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: What happens if fakes get proliferated and it becomes too difficult to discern what is real and what is not?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Given enough time, nothing is impossible with technology.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: But we, as humans, must collectively exercise the will to draw a line in the sand and be clear about what technology must never replace or do.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must embrace technology to better lives, but we must master it and not be mastered by it.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Third, on foreign investments and talents in Singapore, value-adding beyond the money.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should continue to welcome high quality and committed foreign talents and enterprises to Singapore, to supplement our Singaporean Core.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The Global Investor Programme has been one way of welcoming investments to Singapore, bringing along invaluable industrial capabilities and availing job opportunities to Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: By explicitly requiring them to take part in these activities, we create opportunities for meaningful interactions and, thereby, breaking down pre-conceived opinions and promote better mutual understanding.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Having chosen Singapore as a destination, I am sure these distinguished business leaders will be happy to support good causes here.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Fourth, on meaningful ageing so that every day is worth looking forward to.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Over the years, Singapore has done tremendous work to create the conditions for our seniors to age in place.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Looking ahead, we must continue to pay special attention to our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: As family sizes shrink, we can expect more seniors living alone for longer.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we must work to keep them socialised and keep them healthy, even as we continue to emphasise family values and prioritising family support.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Our policies and programmes will also have to be designed with future seniors in mind.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In my opinion, learning is a great way to stimulate minds and build confidence.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Is it not exhilarating to defy age stereotypes and know that "I still got it"?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: In essence, seniors should not be "waiting to die".

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This would reflect a certain grief over losing mental and physical capacities.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We must work hard to deliver a different, better future for our seniors.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Ageing need not be a countdown to life.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Entering the silver years can be a new beginning – where there is life, people, new dreams and new adventures worth looking forward to every day.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I believe that we should not be obsessed with economic competition or figures, but we must also not despise growth and progress.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Because of our economic achievements, even the most vulnerable member of our society can access world-class education and healthcare, supported by bursaries and the 3Ms – namely MediSave, MediShield Life and MediFund.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And because we have a strong Reserve, we have the fiscal capability to surmount the pandemic and the quiet confidence to face the unknown.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, we must excel in whatever we do, but for those who have moved further ahead, remember to look out for and help others who are still struggling.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This is the more tempered and more compassionate meritocracy that we desire.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: We should aim for everyone to be one mass, not stretched thin and far apart and move ahead together.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: I think this is more powerful as an engine for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: And therefore, I hope, as we reopen the Parliament, as we continue to chart the way forward for Singapore, we will continue to do so with Singapore in mind and to build a stronger nation for generations to come.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It garnered significant attention from the media and public, the alumni and parents.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Some applauded the move saying that it would bring about a more diverse student population, which is a view I wholeheartedly agree with.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: You see, I am of an age in which many of my friends and colleagues are planning for the primary school admission of their children.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Many of them come from very humble backgrounds, working hard to get to where they are today.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: They were able to do so due to our strong emphasis in meritocracy, and it speaks towards the success of our education system.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For those with a more comfortable financial situation, these parents will naturally seek to pass on these advantages to their children.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, the quest to do so has turned the provision of education and learning into something akin to a competitive arms race.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: My child is just shy of one year old.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, I, too, feel the pressure when my peers talk about selecting preschools, whether to choose Mindchamps or Odyssey versus the preschool right under the block.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Or what kind of enrichment classes should they send their child to – from Heguru to Kumon, speech and drama classes, art class, swimming class or coding class?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: I hear of and know several parents who have moved to a location near a primary school of their choice, often paying a premium to do so.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Some have resorted to renting houses near these schools.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: All very real things that parents have done to provide what is best for their children.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: But what about those who are not able to afford these opportunities?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: When pursuing the ideals of meritocracy, not everybody starts on a level playing field.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Will they get left further and further behind?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This ties in with the first key priority in Mdm President's Address, which is how the Government will expand opportunities throughout life for all, regardless of individual backgrounds and circumstances.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is something I feel most strongly about.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: And this is what I will focus my speech on.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In theory, a meritocratic society means that a person earns their success through their talent and hard work.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Aspirational but, in some ways, also an illusion.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: As illustrated, a child with a more privileged family background and financial situation may be scaffolded in ways that may allow them to achieve success more easily.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Education may be a social leveller, but access to education may not be equal.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to touch on the intense competition among parents to gain a Primary 1 place for their child.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The Primary 1 registration system essentially aims to address many different goals and does strive to ensure diversity in the student cohort.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: My concern though, is that for certain more popular schools, more privileged families may have more advantage for the different phases.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: For example, a family may move to a location to have an edge in terms of proximity.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Parents working to make ends meet may also be unlikely to be able to spare the amount of time needed to fulfil the volunteering hours needed to qualify for Phase 2B.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Alumni places in prestigious schools in affluent neighbourhoods may also contribute to the risk that certain schools may become more exclusive with a more homogenous, higher socio-economic status student population.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: This is why I believe ACS Primary's move to Tengah is a forward-looking one.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: The move appears to have struck a chord among its alumni and has raised uncomfortable discussions on what we have to do as a society to achieve inclusivity and diversity.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: But it is a step in the right direction.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Can I dare hope that this move also emboldens the boards of other popular primary schools, particularly those in certain affluent neighbourhoods, to do the same?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: At the height of the pandemic, we saw how the nation depended on the essential workers – our nurses, delivery drivers and cleaners – to carry on, even as the rest of the nation was safely sequestered at home.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: An ongoing study by Assoc Prof Irene Ng of NUS' Social Work Department found that, those with university degrees earned more than twice those of ITE qualifications and secondary or lower education.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: It is not enough to speak of an appreciation and respect for the nature of such work.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: In doing so, it sends a strong message to Singaporeans that skilled work is important and slowly shifts the social value placed on such work, creating a more inclusive and equitable society.

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: A recent article in The Straits Times had asked: how would you respond if your graduate daughter dated a plumber?

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: Let us hope that with this, the answer will increasingly be "no problem".

speaker: Dr Shahira Abdullah (Nominated Member)
text: We must send a message to our youths as well, that their value does not lie in academic qualifications alone but in their other strengths as well and that when they have achieved success themselves, they too have a role to build the next generation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I also thank their many suggestions, on how we can make SkillsFuture more impactful and effective for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Wong spoke on a new approach to skills yesterday, one that requires a fresh commitment to making continuous learning, upskilling and reskilling, a way of life.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will work with industry partners and training providers to offer courses to meet different training needs, encourage employers to support the development of their workers and recognise the skills the workers have acquired and, of course, support individuals to take ownership of their lifelong learning journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Mr Patrick Tay's analogy of a CET Toolbox is an apt one to describe the opportunities but also the challenges that adult learners face.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There are three key things that are needed for the toolbox to work well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: First, the toolbox must have a wide range of tools to cater to different adult learners with very different training needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some require skills top-up for new tasks or roles that their jobs require.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For these learners, short courses, like what Ms Tin Pei Ling suggested would suffice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To cater to such learners, the IHLs are offering modular upgrading.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG has also launched SkillsFuture series courses that are short courses designed to address skills needs in high-growth emerging areas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Others required more substantive skills reboot by pursuing a full qualification especially if they have left former education a long time ago or they are switching to a new sector or new job role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Next, I agree with Mr Patrick Tay that people need to open the toolbox and know how to use it.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: With a toolbox of diverse tools, we acknowledge that navigation can be an issue for some.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG is enhancing the MySkillsFuture portal to improve user experience and provide personalised course recommendation based on individual's careers and skills needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Third, I agree that tools must be able to get the job done.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This speaks to our efforts to ensure that the courses are relevant to the industry and are of high quality; and the employers recognise the skills that their employees have acquired.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: SSG has reviewed the course fee funding framework to ensure that SSG's highest tier of subsidies are channelled towards courses that deliver the strongest employment outcomes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These changes will be implemented progressively to allow our IHLs and training providers to adjust their offerings.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers must also play their part to recognise the skills that their workers have acquired through training, place them in appropriate jobs and remunerate them appropriately.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: To support employers in doing so, SSG is working with the trade associations and chambers and professional bodies to recognise skills attained through courses or on-the-job training in selected sectors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: However, we are mindful of the global economic uncertainties and how this may affect jobs here.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the same time, many businesses, especially SMEs, have told us about the acute shortage of labour.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Singapore Business Federation (SBF) has asked us to allow businesses to ease foreign worker measures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ms Janet Ang, just a while ago, also said that the shortage of labour here can cause burnout of our local workforce and limit our companies' growth opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We thank Mr Leong Mun Wai for his suggestions, many of which had been raised and debated at length in the past two years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At this year's Committee of Supply, MOM outlined the strategies and measures to help Singaporeans seize opportunities in the economy and be empowered to take on the good jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We will walk with Singaporeans every step of the way through new initiatives, such as Career Health and Careers Finder.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But MOM cannot do this on our own.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We seek everyone's understanding that we need partnership with the industry, employers and the unions on this journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I have met many parents in my work at MOE and, also, as an MP.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Most desire to be good parents and want the best for their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But parents may not always know what is required, as every child is unique and constantly growing up.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I will touch on the support for parents by three groups: fellow parents, employers and the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It is important to have a strong ecosystem of support for parents to make parenting a fulfilling journey.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I believe children are more likely to grow up resilient and confident if parents guide and support them well.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: First, on the support for parents, by parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Almost all MOE schools have Parent Support Groups (PSGs) today.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: While the main objective of PSGs is to enable partnership between the school and parents to strengthen support for our students, they have also become a source of support for parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Many of our PSGs are led by parent volunteers with experience in parenting and who are willing to serve as resource and peer supporters to fellow parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some of the parents continue to serve as PSG leaders after their children have graduated from school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I encourage parents to contribute or participate in the activities planned by the PSGs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: There is much that PSGs can learn from one another too.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: MOE has set up the PSG support circles, which are communities for PSGs to come together to support fellow parents in nurturing resilient and confident children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some of the common interest topics that they have chosen to cover, thus far, include cyber wellness, mental well-being of children and forging stronger parent-child relationships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These parent-led initiatives seek to equip fellow parents in detecting signs of distress in children, learn where they can get help from and how parents and teachers can work together to support the development of children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: An example is the "Let Us Chat" Programme, that seeks to strengthen parent capabilities in building good relationships with their children to enhance their children's mental well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This PSG programme has been shared with at least 30 schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It focuses on understanding ways to build children's self-confidence, self-awareness and self-regulation, encouraging an attitude of lifelong learning instead of an over-emphasis on grades and understanding the underlying causes of children's behaviour through productive parent-child conversations and relationships.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Indeed, there is much more parents can achieve by learning together with fellow parents.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For parents who are working, having a workplace with supportive bosses and colleagues can make a lot of difference.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It is understandable for parents with young children to need some time off occasionally to bring their child to the doctor, look after a child who has fallen ill or simply to cheer their child on who is receiving a prize or performing in school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For employees with genuine needs, we have to find practical solutions for them to continue to meet their responsibilities at work and at home.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Over the years, the Government has progressively enhanced leave provisions for childcare, infant care, maternity leave and paternity leave.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: These are definitely useful and well-appreciated by parents with young children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I remember my maternity leave was eight weeks when I had my first child 20 years ago.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: When I had my second child, maternity leave was 12 weeks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: By the time I had my third child, maternity leave was increased to 16 weeks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: So, I really see, in my own personal journey, progression in Government policies supporting families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Today, a working couple has altogether up to 22 weeks of leave in their baby's first year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: That is half a year of parental leave to bond and care for their newborn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is helpful for most working couples, but may not be enough for those who have not found viable childcare arrangements and those who have greater caregiving needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: I encourage employers to create workplaces that are supportive of employees with children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers that value their employees' well-being could benefit from stronger talent attraction and staff retention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Employers who would like to find out more of what they can do, may refer to the Tripartite Standard on Work-Life Harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The Tripartite Standard lays out a set of recommended employment practices that recognises the varying priorities of employees at different stages of their lives and also how employers can support them in managing both work responsibilities and personal aspirations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The practices in the Tripartite Standard include providing at least two enhanced leave benefits, such as extended childcare leave; and putting in place employee support schemes, such as annual family days, for employees to enjoy extra time-out with their families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We also have the Tripartite Standard on FWAs, which sets out best practices for employers to provide FWAs, be it flexi-place, flexi-time or flexi-workload.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: More companies are offering FWAs now than before the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This allows parents to better manage their work and family responsibilities concurrently.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: While employers have the prerogative to accept or reject an FWA request, they must have valid reasons for their decision.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: At the same time, employees should be reasonable in their requests and use FWAs responsibly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some FWAs may have resource implications for the company, which employers understandably need to consider when assessing the request.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: For FWAs to work for both employers and employees, adjustments may also have to be made to businesses and human resource practices, possibly also to the way work is configured, to allow for the flexibilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: In turn, I am confident that employers will reap the benefits of a more engaged and motivated workforce.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Ultimately, successful implementation of FWAs requires trust between employer and employees as well as among colleagues at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Besides an understanding boss, a supportive workplace culture is important to enable working parents to achieve better work-life harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: This is especially helpful for vulnerable segments in our community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Many of these initiatives are led by non-government organisations and grassroots volunteers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We should encourage more of these ground-up initiatives and coordinate their efforts to achieve the best possible outcomes for the families being supported.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: The year 2022 was the Year of SG Families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: We want to build a Singapore that is made for families.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: My wish is that Singapore will be one of the best places to raise children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: It is about what each of us can do to support fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: But these steps alone may not be enough.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: As the saying goes, it takes a village to raise a child.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some families are blessed to have the help of grandparents and extended family in taking care of children at home while the parents are at work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Some families have alternative childcare support from domestic helpers, friendly neighbours and childcare centres in the neighbourhood.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education and Manpower (Ms Gan Siow Huang)
text: Fellow parents, employers, colleagues and the community can play a part as well to make parenting a more joyful and fulfilling journey for all.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The events of the last three years highlight the important role Government leadership plays in unifying people and providing a clear direction forward for a nation to work towards.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Not only must leaders be competent, they must also demonstrate in the things they do and say that they have the nation's and the people's best interests at heart.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Only by working together can the people and the Government overcome the challenges in their path.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Leaders need to understand the big picture, balancing, sometimes, conflicting interests and ensuring that the pursuit of short-term goals do not compromise our long-term prospects.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin): Leaders need to understand the big picture and balance, sometimes, conflicting interests to ensure that the pursuit of short-term goals do not compromise our long-term prospects.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Government has implemented quite comprehensive policies and measures, but under certain circumstances, those who need help may not receive assistance for all kinds of reasons.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We need to identify suitable community leaders, volunteers or private sector helping hands to close the gap in the last mile to ensure that they receive assistance.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In English): One example I know of was that of a family in distress.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The head of this family was the eldest of a group of siblings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The eldest daughter was trying very hard to be independent and cope on her own, while tapping on various assistance schemes.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: A staff at an organisation providing help was able to earn her trust and managed to persuade her to accept certain changes in the care arrangements for her siblings.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Without this particular staff, in spite of the many available assistance schemes, the family would not be able to benefit from them.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We certainly need to nurture and strengthen our social and neighbourhood connectedness to enable the desired mutual help to happen.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Of course, the essential ingredient here is trust.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Government leaders have to earn the trust of our people so that in times of emergency and crisis, people will trust that they are doing the right thing for the good of the community and country.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Leaders also have to be very mindful of how they act and what they say.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The impact of even very simple gestures and words can be significant on the lives of the people they interact with.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: President Halimah graced the opening ceremony of the Dyslexia Association of Singapore Henderson Learning Centre in March last year.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ardyani's education therapist, Ms Miranda, had shared with the centre manager, Mr Bala, that since then, she had noticed that Ardyani has become a little bit more cheerful and confident, participating a little more during lessons and also talking a little bit more to her classmates.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ardyani's mother also noticed that her daughter is less shy in engaging others.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Ardyani herself shared that she felt very much encouraged by the President's kind words and gestures during their interaction.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Leaders should realise that the impact of such small gestures in inspiring others, be it to encourage someone or to provide some form of support, can really go a long way.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are many leaders amongst us – be it in the Government, private sector, social service sector or among community leaders.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I certainly hope and urge all our leaders to continue to stay close to the ground and to our people, reaching out, touching lives and building more trust day by day.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, I will focus my speech on the topic of ageing, specifically, the concept of productive longevity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have made significant progress to support successful ageing in Singapore in the preceding half term of the Government.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We raised the retirement age to help seniors stay active and engaged in society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our Central Provident Fund schemes were updated to better cater to the changing needs of the ageing population.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We have strengthened our healthcare system through Healthier SG by focusing on preventive care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We are also scaling up healthcare and long-term care facilities in the community to better support our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But there is still much more to be done.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Being a country with one of the highest life expectancies in the world, but also one having the lowest birth rates, we face a double whammy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This rapid expansion of our ageing population means that the productive engagement of our seniors is no longer optional.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must encourage our seniors to engage in gainful activities that will not only benefit themselves, but also their families, communities and society as a whole.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I will speak on three general areas – work, contribution and care for others – three areas which I believe are critical elements for productive longevity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Steve Jobs once said, "Your work is going to fill a large part of your life and the only way to be truly satisfied is to do what you believe is great work.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: And the only way to do great work is to love what you do." Wise words, indeed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can continue loving what we do even as we grow old.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must, thereby, support our seniors to work longer – for those who want to, are healthy enough and still have the passion to do so.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The relevant initiatives in this year's Budget are a step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is heartening to note that our senior employability rate is healthy, compared to the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Correspondingly, we should focus on creating quality jobs for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This enables them to utilise their depth of knowledge and experience obtained over a lifetime.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The health benefits associated with ongoing mental engagement are numerous.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Moreover, mentoring and job-sharing allow seniors to pass on their skills to younger and less experienced employees.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That said, it is important to recognise that many older workers desire part-time work with flexible options which allow them to spend time on leisure and with their families.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These concepts are relatively new to our workforce.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As such, there may be resistance and scepticism from employers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mdm Deputy Speaker, is the concept of giving.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must actively encourage our seniors to volunteer and share their skills with others.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Silver years can be a time for renewal where individuals can explore new passions and interests, engage in meaningful activities and continue to contribute back to society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The numerous benefits of volunteering for seniors include better self-rated health, higher life satisfaction and prevention of cognitive decline over time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Organisations, like RSVP Singapore, are excellent partners in growing senior volunteerism.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, we should assess our current volunteerism framework and determine how we can increase volunteerism rates.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How do we compare globally with other countries on this front?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are there specific targets that we have set ourselves in this area?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Besides, it would also be helpful to consider other demographic factors, such as income level, gender, race and religion, to ensure that volunteering opportunities are inclusive and varied.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mdm Deputy Speaker, we should enable care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This includes providing informal caregivers with more support and professionalising caregiving as a career to meet the rising demand for caregiving needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The role of a caregiver is a challenging one that requires significant physical and emotional effort.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: With our demographic shifts, we are also now seeing a greater number of seniors caring for other seniors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In my Yio Chu Kang estate, I have a 70-plus-year-old daughter caring for a 90-plus-year-old mother.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Regrettably, we often see the bulk of caregiving responsibilities being shouldered by a single individual – typically a wife, mother or daughter.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There remains a significant gender disparity in caregiving, with women assuming a disproportionate amount of the workload.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we take steps to encourage men to participate more in caregiving?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Achieving this will require us to challenge the societal norms and gendered attitudes that place greater emphasis on men building careers and less on caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Nonetheless, it is pertinent to evaluate the effectiveness of these programmes.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What is the current take-up rate and how beneficial do participants find these courses?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Additionally, we need to increase awareness about the availability of these courses and ensure that the accessibility and scheduling meet the demand.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can the Government provide additional support in this area?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Expanding caregiver support is critical, as Singapore's population ages and more people require informal caregiving.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There have also been continued attempts to encourage FWAs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is also good that we are recognising that caregivers themselves, too, need self-care to prevent burnout.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As the demand for caregiving services continues to grow, we should recognise caregiving as a viable career choice.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Professionalising caregiving may attract more people to the profession and improve the quality of care provided.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Presently, caregiving is often associated with tasks, like medical escorting, personal care and housekeeping.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: On the contrary, caregiving extends beyond these roles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: There are opportunities for specialisation and leadership, including caregiver trainers, managers, schedulers and care assessment professionals, just to name a few.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As part of long-term planning, we should also consider formal education to provide a solid foundation for professional caregiving and certification.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For instance, many community colleges and healthcare agencies in the US offer courses to obtain home care certification.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Highly skilled caregivers have more opportunities to service clients, especially those with specific needs, such as dementia or physical challenges.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How can we fully embrace the opportunities that comes with living longer?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I have shared in my speech that one way is to embrace productive longevity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is to be empowered to lead our lives the way we want to – to work, contribute and care for others.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To do so, we must also reframe our concept of ageing: first, it is not about when, but now.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I circle back to what I said earlier in my speech, an often-quoted statistic, that by 2030, one in four Singaporeans will be aged 65 and above.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we must remember that ageing continues, as we speak.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Currently, almost one in five Singaporeans are aged 65 and above.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I certainly see it in my estate in Yio Chu Kang.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Over the past three years, I have seen how our residents have aged.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: More seniors are moving around in the neighbourhood with wheelchairs and walking aids.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, it is about opportunities, not about liabilities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Productive ageing requires a shift in our thinking from a paradigm centred on ageing as being problematic, to one which views seniors as resources – assets that can continue to contribute to society in various ways.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about opportunities for growth and contribution, rather than casting the aged as a liability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A simple shift on using more inclusive terms, such as "we" and "us", in place of "they" and "them", helps all of us to remember that we are all ageing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Personally, I sometimes do get comments from my residents that I look young.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But I remind myself that the operative word is "look" and that we will all grow old one day and be forced to reckon with our own mortality.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We will all need to come to terms and embrace the experience of ageing.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding, most will agree that to leverage productive longevity, we will need to embrace our silver years – to work, to contribute and to care and by acknowledging that ageing is not about when, but now.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about opportunities, not about liabilities, and it is not about them, but about us.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Only then, can we turn the good life into a great one.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin): I do not think anyone would object to the fact that more support should be given to our disadvantaged groups and lower-income earners to improve their lives and incomes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The key, though, is how we should do it more effectively and more sustainably.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Just blindly subsidising people might leave them idle and run the risk of consuming the whole savings?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the saying goes, "It is better to teach someone to fish, rather than to give him a fish." A fish can relieve your hunger pangs in the short term, but not for too long.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If you want to have fish throughout your lifetime, you must learn how to fish.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Teach a man to fish and you feed him for a lifetime.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, there is a need for the Government to continue to invest heavily in education, SkillsFuture, reskill and upskill training.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Workfare Income Supplement scheme, Progressive Wage Credit Scheme and Special Employment Credit and so on and so forth are equally important.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whatever more to do or to be done, we should continue to leverage and enhance on our existing schemes.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree with the President that in an increasingly troubled world, we must stay united and strengthen our bond as one united people.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are not only facing an aged population; we are also facing a declining fertility rate.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the average education level of our population has increased over the same period and so has the average income.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, would the Ministry be able to advise if the current old-age support ratio is acceptable, in view of the rise in the average Singaporean's income and the continued investment in education and lifelong learning and training for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We may also need to consider if we should let each generation self-finance their needs in old age, for example, using their life contributions to the nation to avoid burdening our children and grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At the same time, to survive and stay competitive, Singapore must remain open.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But there is a limit to how many foreigners or new citizens any country can absorb before the sense of shared national identity is affected.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must maintain our Singaporean Core and, at the very least, prevent our TFR from declining further.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I certainly hope that it is partly due to 2022 being the year of the tiger in the lunar calendar, which usually sees fewer births among the Chinese and not another indication of a shrinking future generation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I welcome the commitment made by the Prime Minister's Office in the addendum to extend more help to parents caring for infants.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We, as a nation, must continue to try to do more to boost marriage and parenthood.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The proportion of singles in the age group below 50 years has increased and, more significantly, the increase is highest among those below age 35 – the age group which is most conducive for having children.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We understand that people generally prefer to meet members of the opposite sex in so-called "natural settings", even though, for many, their networks and social circles are limited.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, we should review how we can improve on facilitating social interactions for our potential couples.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, I think it would be helpful to review and get feedback on the activities and events organised by the Social Development Network (SDN).

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What kind of activities and events do the young find attractive and relevant in today's context?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, do the participants get to learn or experience something meaningful, even if they do not meet someone special?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If that is the case, SDN will be able to attract more participants, enlarging the pool and increasing the chances that singles will meet other interesting singles there, as SDN should also be able to offer a value-add, which is to provide the assurance that all participants are screened and they are who they claim to be.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Ministry of National Development (MND) is making the effort to ramp up BTOs for all applicants, especially for first-timer families.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It has many supportive policies which I commend, but I would like to make a request for future flats to be built bigger, like the older flats built in the 1980s and 1990s.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A sense of greater available space is more encouraging for families to have a second or third child.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many families with young children depend on migrant domestic workers and nannies to help out with caregiving.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the standards of their service can vary widely.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there any way for MOM to set up a training, assessment and accreditation scheme, which parents can use to inform them of the capabilities of the maids or nannies they are considering to hire?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a shortage of infant care, childcare and kindergarten teachers or centres in certain areas.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For parents, it is important for their children to be enrolled in centres near their homes to minimise travelling for the kids.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have to continue our effort to minimise the social divide in our society.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Values which divide high- and low-income groups should be discouraged, and harmonious social integration needs to be strengthened.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: There is a need for employers to establish policies to nurture a harmonious and caring work culture in our workplaces.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A good leader in the company is not only measured by tangible results.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I support the determination of our Government to refresh our social compact and broaden meritocracy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our efforts to build an egalitarian society where everyone will be treated equally with dignity and respect must continue.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: At the same time, we must reaffirm Singapore as an open society, expand our economic space and stay connected to global growth opportunities for Singapore to stay relevant and provide a bright future for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is against this backdrop that I would like to speak about family offices in their role in contributing to Singapore's development.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I declare my interest as the chief executive officer of the Wealth Management Institute (WMI).

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: WMI is the host of the Global-Asia Family Office Circle, a network platform that provides a trusted environment for the family office ecosystem to convene as a community to learn about best practices in family office governance, as well as opportunities in Singapore and Asia in areas, such as innovation, sustainability, co-investments and philanthropy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The number of wealthy individuals and family offices in Singapore continues to grow, which is a testament to Singapore's strength as a hub wealth and asset management.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There has been much interest about the arrival of family offices in Singapore recently.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: From my experience, they come from a diverse range of countries from around the world, including Greater China, South Asia, ASEAN, the Middle East, US and Europe.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many of them represent some of the most successful entrepreneurs and business owners across the globe, including notable investors, leaders in renewable energy, pioneers of world-changing technology platforms and leaders of Asia's largest family businesses.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These families do not just bring capital but also knowledge, networks, skills and talents as well.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: These are assets we can channel to support new innovation and enterprise, allowing businesses based in Singapore to benefit from mutual technological innovation and talent transfers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Some of these families also bring long track record of giving generously, sometimes stretching back across multiple generations.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They have built schools and hospitals, funded scientific advancements, supported conservation efforts and contributed generously to relief efforts, including disaster recovery and pandemic recovery.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Some are seeking safety and stability, whereas others are expanding to Singapore in search of attractive investment opportunities to support growth in Asia – and Southeast Asia, especially.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We are also seeing greater involvement of the next generation of family principals who are increasingly focused on areas, such as impact investment, venture capital and alternative Investments.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, recent reports of flashy and ostentatious behaviours are restricted to a minority.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We have seen strong growth in a short period of time.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This means that the industry is still nascent and many family offices are still in the initial stages of development.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Family offices typically go through three phases as they set up in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: First, they set up the governance, then investment; and finally, philanthropy and impact.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The first stage, governance, is about establishing an effective operational base and putting in place a governance framework under which the family office will operate.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How should they set up their legal and trust structures?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What systems should they put in place, from financial monitoring to cybersecurity?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What should their board and risk management processes be?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can they attract and hire the right talent in Singapore?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can they meet the evolving regulations in Singapore which have been introduced to raise the bar?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As they establish themselves, family offices contribute towards job creation – both directly and indirectly.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even though family offices are typically small in team size, they have to meet requirements on hiring, annual business spending and local investments.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The key impact of their set-up, in terms of job creation, will be driving the additional demand and job creation and professional services, such as wealth management, asset management, fund administration, trusts, legal, tax and consulting.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Investments are often the main purpose of the family office.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, before they deploy a large amount of capital or any amount of capital, family offices need to build a robust understanding of the investment landscape so that they can home in on areas of opportunity.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Fundamentally, they seek good financial returns and sound business models to invest in, and this often takes time to understand and evaluate the different investment options available.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Also, the market environment in recent years has been challenging.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They also need to find like-minded partners for co-investments.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many family offices tell us they prefer to co-invest with other families – but only with those that they know and trust.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: A newly-arrived family office will need to build up these trusted networks before they can co-invest effectively.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is also a need to help them become aware of the promising research and tech innovations that we have in Singapore from our startup communities and research institutes and where they can help commercialise and scale promising new ideas.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Family offices tell us they struggle to navigate the fragmented and fast-changing landscape.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They share that they need to work hard to understand who the credible players are and what the roles of different ecosystem actors are.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Newly set-up family offices need more help to connect the dots of the full spectrum of what Singapore has to offer.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We need to help orientate them towards the local ecosystem and curate a systematic introduction to the different areas within the innovation community.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many family offices actually have a stated objective to give back, in line with their family values.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: But conducting effective philanthropy is a thoughtful process going beyond chequebook giving.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The inspiration is often deeply personal and tied to the values of the family.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Based on these values, families will decide what their impact goals are and which causes to support, what assets they could contribute and how to leverage different giving structures.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Increasingly, wealthy families want to go beyond straightforward grant-making type philanthropy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They have contributed to important social services, public healthcare and education and cultivated a culture of giving that is central to Singapore's social compact.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Today, many among the new generation of wealth owners have a similar aspiration to contribute meaningfully to society.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, what is needed is greater effort to drive awareness and momentum to support both local and regional causes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We should also encourage sharing from family offices who are already major philanthropists, to provide aspirational examples for others.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Through this, we can make the most of this unique opportunity to shape this growth towards a more inclusive society for the benefit of all.

speaker: Mdm Deputy Speaker
text: Mr Murali Pillai, would you like to adjourn the debate?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Through the triumphs and tribulations, our forefathers have forged a nation not just through resilience but also unity.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The responsibility to bring Singapore forward now lies upon our shoulders.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We face challenges and opportunities like our forefathers, though of a different nature amid evolving ideologies and complexities.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The popular saying is that it is easier to grow an organisation but always harder to keep up its successes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: So, it is, all the more, that we must be alert not to succumb to complacency.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For me, the prorogation and our President’s Address provided valuable opportunities for introspection as a first-term Member of Parliament (MP); and today, I summarise my reflections in three key themes.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The first is the importance of an effective Parliament.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In an age of flux and dynamism, policy considerations are seldom linear and there may not be past blueprints and playbooks to rely on.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In most solutions, society is overall better off but there is often a cost where a segment may not benefit, and this is where different views expressed during a debate is important for the clarity and transparency of all.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In such situations where we articulate different perspectives, I would like to echo Mdm President’s message that our conversations must be constructive, respectful and responsible, so that we draw strength from our diversity.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: To uphold trust in the effectiveness of Parliament, we must conduct ourselves with integrity and civility, with truth and logic as the bedrock of what we say; so that at the end of the day, we galvanise our citizens towards a common direction.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Like Singapore’s progress, we cannot take the effectiveness of our Parliament for granted.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We should be careful not to follow the path of some parliaments in the world, where divisive politics and appealing rhetoric cloud genuine debates, such that they are not effective in making sound decisions and they confuse the people they serve.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In an effective Parliament, the responsibility also lies with all of us to be courageous in tackling difficult and potentially unpopular issues, and to make tough decisions for the benefit of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Looking back at the first session of this parliament, I believe this House has done well and demonstrated decisive leadership.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I had the opportunity to participate in many of these debates.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In the repeal of section 377A, we tackled this important topic even though we could have dealt with this further down the road.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Importantly, we did not push the responsibility to the Courts to decide what is good for our society.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In these examples and others, considerations and trade-offs were put forth openly, so we could debate these robustly and transparently.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As we look forward to the second session of the 14th Parliament, it is imperative that we continue to uphold the effectiveness, leadership and public confidence of this House.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Failure to recognise these “costs” defies the fundamental concept of scarcity in economics and could leave room for populist politics which will mislead and polarise our society.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: While we continue to cheer and enable every citizen to maximise their potential and lift their ambitions, the hard truth is that it is impractical for our Government to fulfil all desires.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Matching limited resources to meet ever-increasing and sometimes near-infinite expectations is an equation that cannot be solved by any government.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, this requires us to make choices and strike a balance for our policies to be sustainable.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: For example, in debating housing accessibility, we all fully agree with younger Singaporeans’ aspirations towards convenience and proximity to their parents' home.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is simply not possible for everyone to be availed a Housing and Development Board (HDB) flat in a mature estate as space in such areas are finite.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The key question will then be how to allocate them.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: And in terms of affordability, how should the Government balance between buyers desiring lower prices and sellers expecting higher valuations?

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The many calls for the Government to do more will mean that spending can easily increase beyond 20%.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is important for us to address transparently, how we are going to fund these increases without kicking the can down the road.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, the proposals are not viable to address funding shortfalls.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I said, at the GST Bill debate, that to spend more from our investment returns and to save less is an attractive but not a responsible approach.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Singapore’s Reserves serve as a strategic asset and insurance to support us during crises and provide us a long-term, recurring and growing annuity to fund our rising national expenditures.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Should we take this path, I worry that our children will be the ones to bear the costs of a much bigger fiscal burden to fund future expenditures.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The WP is entitled to a different view, and I respect that.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: However, they need to be honest about the full implications and costs of their proposals for current and future generations.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: We should guard against short-sighted policies that go against our values and principles of how we uphold fiscal prudence.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: If we do not manage this carefully, the trust in our fiscal stability, that we have painstakingly built over the years can be destroyed overnight.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In its manifesto and in this debate, the WP has put forward many proposals, all of which will require more spending.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In our debates, there will be some areas where we agree and some that we do not, like in the use of Reserves.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I am confident we will highlight our arguments and debate robustly about these issues.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It will then be for Singaporeans to judge which is the more responsible and better approach to take Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In the end, it is not a battle between political parties.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
