text: How successful we will be depends on how we approach these conundrums and trade-offs to make balanced policy choices for our society and for our society to see them as fair.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is challenging, but I can see that our Government is dedicated to doing its best; and better relative to many other countries including the ones where I lived in, which is why I chose to return to Singapore; in fact, it is exactly because our Government sensibly acknowledges costs and trade-offs that it is able to prioritise well and work hard so that our citizens benefit.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: A microcosm of this is reflected in my own constituency at Nee Soon Link, that has many new Housing and Development Board (HDB) Build-To-Order (BTO) precincts.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I have worked with many agencies to initiate and improve amenities, including launching a new bus service and building many new bus stops when none were earlier catered for.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: And I am thankful to my residents who had moved in earlier for exercising patience, as we appealed successfully to improve the frequency of bus services when more residents settled into the estate.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is from this perspective that I can attest to the dedication of our Government agencies towards serving our residents, demonstrating empathy and flexibility in calibrating public resources to meet needs on the ground, while ensuring value for money.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The final theme of my speech is how we all need to be hands on; for all of us, citizens to play our part.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In my maiden speech in this House, I spoke about how effective governance is not just about good policies but also about good execution.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Through the various Ministries’ addenda to the President’s Address, I am heartened to learn about the strong reaffirmation and refresh of their plans to take Singapore forward.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, while the Government can steer through sound policies, it is for our businesses, community partners, families and individuals to take their respective steps towards building a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: In overcoming the crisis of a generation, we have seen first-hand how a formidable force is built from everyone playing a role, as well as from the partnership and trust between the Government and its people.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It is also heartening to see that within our towering metropolis and residences, the kampung spirit of old is well and alive.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I encourage all of us to uphold this sense of personal and collective responsibility, as well as to continue to look beyond personal interests, so we contribute to building a caring and more resilient society where no one is left behind.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: The Forward Singapore exercise, aimed at renewing our social compact, encapsulates this ideal best.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: This social compact is an implicit agreement across Government, individuals, families, community and businesses on what kind of society we want to live in and what each of us are willing to give – and give up – for one another.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: It aptly circles back to recognising trade-offs and requires all of us to answer, given constraints, what we desire to build and what we are willing to do more together with the Government for a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I started today’s speech on how the responsibility to bring Singapore forward now rest upon our shoulders.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: As we forge ahead in the new normal with cautious optimism, we ask not for a lighter load, but for greater strength.

speaker: Mr Derrick Goh (Nee Soon)
text: I am convinced we can surmount the challenges and capture the opportunities that lie ahead if we come together as one Singapore because we are, Stronger Together!

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: She described trends that we have been concerned about for a few years now – growing obstacles to global trade and economic nationalism.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Both of these trends are expected to persist in the years to come and both of these trends are inflationary.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We have not seen food prices go up so quickly since 2008.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Last year, wage growth for those of us who are employed full-time outpaced inflation but only barely.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Working Singaporeans’ earnings power will be reduced again when the second GST hike kicks in in January 2024.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I find it ironic that in its latest monetary policy statement, it appears the MAS took pains to highlight that the higher inflation rates we have seen at the start of the year “reflected in part the increase in GST” and that “when the impact of the GST increase is excluded, core inflation would be even lower and closer to the historical average”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Government’s support measures are designed to ensure that Singaporeans “with greater means contribute their fair share of taxes”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But from an inter-generational equity perspective, you can see why so many younger Singaporeans feel anxious and uneasy about the future.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Some have even given up on the aspirations to raise a family here.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even some senior citizens I have met tell me that they worry most about how the higher cost of living impacts their children and feel compelled to carry on working, even though they may not wish to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As workers and business owners, we will strive to be more productive and more competitive, and hope that our wages can go up higher than inflation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But I also hope that the Government can avoid introducing more pressure into the system through an untimely GST hike, especially if wage growth remains uneven or weak.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Because when the cost of living – real or perceived – is too high, that hurts Singapore’s attractiveness as a liveable city, it weakens our younger ones' confidence to take risks and we become less competitive globally.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just last month, The Business Times reported that in a business sentiment survey conducted by the Singaporean-German Chamber of Industry and Commerce, almost half of German employers in Singapore polled, or 44%, said “psychological distress and lower work performance is visible among staff” due to the unpredictable housing situation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My second point is about income security for workers who may find themselves displaced if labour market conditions deteriorate.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Last week, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) warned that inflation is much stickier than anticipated even a few months ago and the chances of a “hard landing” for the global economy have risen sharply.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the Government has not updated its expectations for GDP growth of 0.5% to 2.5% in 2023, the risk of a recession is only getting higher.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Some of you would know that I work in the banking sector, for a bank which is the subject of an emergency takeover.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The recent turbulence at our firm has taken a very deep emotional toll on my friends and colleagues.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In Singapore, job security is especially vexing because there is no nationally defined social protection floor that our workers can stand on to feel secure.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There is also no law mandating retrenchment benefits in Singapore, which could be critical in ensuring displaced workers and their families have sufficient liquidity to meet basic living needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is especially pertinent during periods of recession and labour market weakness, where a longer time is needed to secure employment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I was therefore heartened to hear President Halimah say that the Government will study how it can extend support schemes similar to the COVID‐19 Recovery Grant beyond the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We should explore how the administrative arrangements for the COVID-19 Recovery grant can be adapted for a wider redundancy insurance scheme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Workers’ Party (WP) has consistently been pushing for a redundancy insurance scheme since 2011 and had also published a consultation paper on this back in 2016.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As our economy matures and as economic cycles become shorter and more unpredictable, many of us will have no choice but to make more frequent transitions between jobs and career paths, even when we are not financially prepared to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: By providing displaced workers with immediate income security, a redundancy insurance scheme can raise efficiency in the labour market and reduce underemployment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It will allow workers to take the time that is required to reskill and find a stronger job fit, instead of being pressured into choices that could hamper their longer-term career mobility, just so that they can pay the bills.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With intensifying risks to our economy and labour markets, I hope that legislation on redundancy insurance can be put in place as soon as possible, even if it is called something else like a targeted re-employment scheme.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Let us roll it out now before the next recession, when it will be needed.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: My third point is about a topic which is increasingly a key concern for many Singaporeans and that is housing – to which I wish to first declare my interest as an equity research analyst in a financial institution covering the real estate industry.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We have had an extensive debate in this House about this topic just two months ago and I will refrain from repeating much of the points which I have raised back then.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, as I have shared in my speech on the housing Motion debates, the root cause of much of our housing woes today relate to supply and the solution really is for the Government to take urgent and decisive steps to increase the availability of public housing and ensure that the housing needs of all Singaporeans are met.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, while President Halimah spoke of running up against more binding constraints in land, labour and carbon over the coming years, when it comes to having enough space for future generations, Prime Minister Lee gave us an emphatic assurance late last year that “Our problem is not finding the space to build enough flats, nor keeping homes affordable for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am thus comforted to read that Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong shared in a Budget roundtable discussion last month that the root of the problem is a supply issue.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, while I recognise Deputy Prime Minister Wong’s confidence in the Government’s ability to bring stability to the market again and perhaps this could eventually come when recession hits our shores, manifestations of the demand-supply imbalance in our housing market continue to persist in the meantime.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Over in the public housing rental market especially, The Straits Times reported last week that “overall, HDB rents shot up 27.7 per cent in February compared with a year earlier – a rate of increase not seen in 15 years”, with January too seeing a similarly pace of increase.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: During the Ministry of National Development (MND) Committee of Supply (COS) debates last month, I called on the Government to support Singaporeans who may need to rent in the open market to address their immediate housing needs, given soaring open market rentals.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At that point, Minister Desmond Lee shared that the Government will “keep an open mind and keep a close eye on the rental situation and will be prepared to take necessary measures in order to support Singaporeans”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I still hope that the Government will consider intervening in the market sooner than later, rather than continue monitoring the market, in order to preserve open market rental affordability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On that note, I am heartened to note that the MND recognises that we have more singles and caregivers in our society, and more young Singaporeans who aspire to live independently.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In particular, I am excited to read that the MND is working on developing more inclusive housing options especially for singles, seniors and those with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just as I have mentioned in my Adjournment Motion last year, I believe this is the right step to take for our public housing policies to be “inclusive” and to “reflect the diversity of our society”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our younger Singaporeans aspire to have a place of their own and this is a trend which I believe the Government would have been closely monitoring as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is why I have called on the Government to significantly increase the stock of rental flats across flat sizes, thereby creating a viable and expanded public rental scheme, with an emphasis on ensuring that our lower- to middle-income households’ housing needs are well looked after.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is also aptly captured in a recent Mothership series on housing, which documented couples who are affected by the delay in BTO flats but are not lucky enough to secure a flat under the Parenthood Provisional Housing Scheme (PPHS) and are faced with an option to either stay at their parents’ homes with no private space or pay an increasingly expensive rental lease.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is when most Singaporeans would have been in the workforce for a few years and have begun to lead more independent lives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This proposal would be a critical change, yet a continuation of the Government’s efforts over the years to expand HDB options for singles while still allowing HDB to give priority to providing for families.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, we believe lowering the threshold for owning HDB flats to 28 years would go a long way towards HDB’s stated aims for Singapore’s public housing to be “inclusive” and to “reflect the diversity of our society”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, even as we refresh our social compact on housing and reimagine a range of housing options for a more inclusive housing programme, the next chapter of our housing story still leaves one big question unanswered: what about the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS) and the end of the 99-year lease?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I am sure the Government would have been monitoring and studying this issue for a long time now and I was carefully scrutinising Mdm President’s speech and the MND addendum to the President’s Address for any mention of VERS and solutions to address the elephant in the room – the lease decay issue – but to no avail.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Is this an issue that the 4G leaders are prepared to address?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the housing Motion debates, my hon friend Assoc Prof Jamus Lim highlighted the fundamental tension between housing as a retirement asset and as a home.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Our current HDB and CPF policies may be a dangerous game of musical chairs: if one is able to offload one’s flat before its price collapses – as it must, eventually – then we can retire comfortably; but then, the one holding the bag is a fellow Singaporean who bought your resale because they needed the space for a growing family and could not afford to wait for a BTO.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The higher the climb, the harder the fall.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And it is not just the WP that is worried about this increasingly untenable link.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In a commentary published by The Straits Times earlier this month, Assoc Prof of law Eugene Tan spoke of the trap of ever-spiralling expectations in the housing market, which will be too much to bear for all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: He shared that “looking ahead, the reality of leases decay – as flats built in the 1960s and 1970s rundown their 99-year leases – will increasingly bite harder.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This sobering reality will have to be adjusted to as well even as older Singaporeans hope to leave their residential property to their children”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Senior Minister of State Sim Ann shared the same notion of having the Government coming in as the purchaser of last resort, although it remains to be seen how this can pan out in practice if VERS, as the name suggests, is voluntary and subject to voting by residents in the precinct.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But critically, I struggle to see how amid all of these concerns and the eventuality of the value of HDB flats reaching zero at the end of the 99-year lease, the PAP Government can honour its promise to all Singaporeans as shared by Prime Minister Lee last month, “that your HDB flat will be both a good home for you and your family, and a valuable nest egg for your retirement”.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I of course hope that what Prime Minister Lee shared can materialise.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But for the sake of the current and future generations of Singaporeans, it is imperative that we lay out our plans to achieve these increasingly untenable links between affordable housing and retirement adequacy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I would also like to know details of the Voluntary Early Redevelopment Scheme (VERS) and the Government’s plans to address the problem of decaying leases of 99-year leasehold HDB flats.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Currently, the provision of retrenchment benefits is not mandatory by law in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, this is critical in ensuring that jobless workers and their families have sufficient liquidity to meet basic living needs.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is especially important when there is an economic downturn and the job market is weakening, as workers may need a longer time to find employment during these periods.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Since 2011, the Workers’ Party has always advocated for the implementation of redundancy insurance and we hope that the Government will legislate this as soon as possible.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must plan for rainy days and be prepared for the next economic recession.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the issue of housing, I am glad that the Ministry of National Development (MND) is aware that there are many singles and caregivers as well as many young Singaporeans who desire to live on their own.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Even as we update our social compact on housing and offer new housing options, there is still a major unresolved issue in the next chapter of Singapore’s housing story.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With regards to the VERS and the problem of decaying 99-year leases, what are we doing to address these issues?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have looked into the President’s address and MND’s addenda in detail, hoping to find out the solution to the problem of lease decay but to no avail.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On the one hand, we need to ensure that flats remain affordable.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: (In English): In closing, I have one final reflection.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This concerns President Halimah's remarks that in so many societies, political parties aggravate rifts instead of bringing people together.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope it is clear to the House and Singaporeans from the positions that I and my fellow WP colleagues have put forth, that we speak always to advance the larger public interest.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It would be foolish and self destructive for us to do otherwise.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We are Singaporeans too and have just as much of a stake in the well-being of this country as the ruling party does.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: So, even though my colleagues and I do not enjoy the same access to information, networks and resources that some of our hon Members do, we continue to strive to make constructive contributions to the policy debates of this House.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Before I begin, I declare my interest as President of the Consumers Association of Singapore (CASE).

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The digitisation of almost every aspect of our lives has led to a new trend in consumer behaviour – and that is, convenience.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today's consumers have become accustomed to the instant gratification facilitated by technological advancements.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With a few clicks on their smartphones, consumers can order anything they want, from delivery of their favourite meals to buying groceries from an online market.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Companies that can offer the most convenient solutions are gaining traction among consumers, and this trend is likely to continue.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While e-commerce and online transactions have made life easier, they also carry significant risks and dangers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: As more transactions are being conducted over the Internet, the number of online frauds has also increased significantly over the years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My speech today will focus on the need to enhance our consumer protection laws for e-commerce, strengthen safeguards for digital payments, and regulate trending consumer credit schemes such as Buy Now Pay Later services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, let me start with the need to enhance our existing consumer protection laws for e-commerce.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: While the general position is that existing consumer protection laws are broad enough to cover online transactions, these were enacted at a time when consumer transactions were predominantly offline via brick-and-mortar stores.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our laws do not sufficiently address the distinction between online and offline transactions and correspondingly, the issues that are specific to online transactions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: First, we need to authenticate the sellers on online marketplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The duty of ensuring the legitimacy of sellers should be placed on the online marketplaces.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: By charging platform fees and commissions, online marketplaces are expected to ensure that the merchants listed on their platforms are genuine and legitimate.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Online marketplaces should vet, verify and authenticate the credentials of sellers before allowing them to list and sell products on their platforms.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Second, online marketplaces should ensure that there are mechanisms in place to protect consumers’ payments.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: One way to do this is to incorporate escrow into the transaction process.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This means that when a consumer makes a purchase, the payment to the seller is temporarily held by the platform for a period and only released to the seller when the consumer confirms that the item is delivered in good condition.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mandating escrow accounts would give consumers greater peace of mind when shopping online.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Third, we should extend our consumer protection laws to cover consumer-to-consumer transactions made through social media platforms.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, our consumer protection laws do not adequately cover sales transactions made between two individuals via a social media platform such as Facebook, Instagram or TikTok.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: To foster a safe and trusted online marketplace for consumers, CASE led an industry-wide effort in 2020 to develop Technical Reference 76, Singapore’s first national standards for e-commerce transactions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: CASE also introduced the Standard Dispute Management Framework for E-marketplaces in 2021 to guide e-marketplaces resolve consumer disputes equitably and efficiently.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Next, let me move on to the Government’s push for greater use of digital payment, which has undoubtedly also facilitated and fuelled the increasing popularity of online shopping.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Digital payment has risen sharply in recent years.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The convenience of being able to make payments without having to carry cash or visiting a bank is a significant advantage.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, I would like to highlight three risks associated with digital payments.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With digital transactions, there is a rise in data collection, processing, sharing and storage of personal information.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Hackers can steal this information, which could lead to identity theft, financial fraud or other forms of cyber crime.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Debit card fraud and phishing attacks are now a common occurrence, which could impact not only the individual but the entire banking system.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Digital payments rely heavily on technology and any system failure or technical glitch could result in significant problems.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Last month, DBS customers were unable to log in to the bank’s online banking platforms, including its PayLah! mobile wallet, for almost a day.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: DBS' digital banking services previously suffered a two-day disruption in November 2021.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Such incidences can create inconvenience and, in some cases, financial losses.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The rise of digital payments has provided an opportunity for scammers to create fake e-wallets, websites and mobile applications to perpetuate their fraudulent activities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Victims lost large sums of money when the scammers deceived them into sharing their digital banking credentials.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Cybersecurity should be a top priority, and financial institutions need to implement advanced safety measures to prevent data breaches, system failures and fraudulent activities.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: More needs to be done also to educate vulnerable consumers, such as our seniors and those who are not technologically savvy, to stay updated and cautious when using these services.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to a 2021 report by Mileu, close to a fifth of Singaporeans aged 16 and above have used a "Buy Now, Pay Later" service.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Such short-term financing services can appear enticing with their zero-interest deals, flexible payment options and convenience of access, but they come with a set of risks that can put unsuspecting customers in financial distress, especially for younger consumers below 21, as many of them do not yet have a stable income.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The first and most obvious risk is the accumulation of unforeseen fees and charges.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Customers who fail to pay the required instalments on time are slapped with hidden fees and added interest, pushing up the total balance and making it harder to pay off the debt. "Buy Now, Pay Later" schemes also typically do not conduct credit checks, hence there is no pre-determined limit to how much a customer can borrow.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This puts consumers at risk of overstretching their financial capabilities, leading to a spiral of debt.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Another risk comes from the psychological impact of these schemes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: With no immediate payment obligations, consumers may spend more than they would otherwise, as they feel less connected to the actual cost of purchases.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: This can lead to overspending and, in some cases, an addiction to online shopping.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I urge the Government to impose regulations to better protect vulnerable consumers, such as the young and those already in debt, from exploitation by these schemes.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: It has opened a new world of possibilities and opportunities, but also presents new risks and dangers to consumers, both young and old.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: We must therefore review and update our consumer protection laws accordingly.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Our laws must provide the same protection for consumers, regardless of whether we shop offline or online.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   During the President’s Address on Monday last week, Mdm Halimah touched on several issues related to the steps which we need to take to achieve happiness, prosperity and progress for our nation.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One of the things that caught my attention was about national politics.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Essentially, good politics is necessary to further advance Singapore’s progress, harmony and stability.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The opposite type of politics could spark polarisation and divisions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For my speech in this debate, I aim to share my own perspective on what would be considered as good politics.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The content of my speech is meant for all participants in national politics, especially members of this House, including myself, and it is meant for all of us to conduct some self-reflection or introspection.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In the words of a contemporary political phrase, “ownself check ownself”, in a positive manner.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: When we point a finger at someone else, we should be mindful that our other fingers that are pointing back at ourselves.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Among the factors that can produce good or healthy politics are firstly, having a level playing field; second, being able to agree to disagree; and thirdly, avoiding actions that cause fear among the public, or in English, “fear-mongering” especially during elections for the purpose of gaining support.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It is publicly known that Members of Parliament (MPs) who are not from the ruling party need to put in more effort at the grassroots level to meet the needs of our constituents.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Conversely, for a constituency won by the ruling party, the elected ruling party candidate is concurrently appointed as the Grassroots Advisor.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Apart from the usage of such places, the PA funds meant for the benefit of the constituents also could not be touched.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The manpower provided by full-time constituency managers and directors is invaluable.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This practice is not aligned with the phrase in our pledge which is to build a democratic society based on justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It certainly does not align with the values of justice and equality when the ruling party candidate who lost and was rejected by voters at the elections was appointed and recognised by the Government to hold the position of grassroots advisor while the non-ruling party representatives elected by the voters were set aside.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To illustrate the circumstances more clearly, I will give an example.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: To date, after almost 13 years constituting two and a half terms which I have served as the MP in Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC), I still hear comments from my residents during my house visits that the People's Action Party (PAP) seem to be organising more events than the Workers’ Party (WP).

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, when I ask for details of those events, it turns out that they were referring to events held at the community club as well as those organised by the RC.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They said so because they saw the PAP branch chairman, who is also the grassroots advisor, present at these events as the guest of honour or the event organiser.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In fact, some residents also said that their children received their Edusave awards from the PAP.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Undeniably, the funds utilised by the bodies under the purview of the PA are for the benefit of the residents in a given constituency.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, it is also undeniable that the existing system creates the impression and assumption that events organised by the PA are events organised by the PAP.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This proposal was also part of the WP manifesto in the previous General Election – ensuring the freedom of national institutions from party politics.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I understand that some efforts have been undertaken in this matter.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The question here is, in what capacity did this individual attend a ceremony which was jointly organised by the PA and the Ministry of Education (MOE)?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: What is the message that was meant to be conveyed?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: And why was the elected MP not invited?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Or at least, have both of them invited to this event.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Fundamentally and more importantly, where are the values of justice and equality?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Rather, what I want to raise is whether this is the proper practice in our efforts to build a democratic society based on justice and equality as inscribed in our national pledge?

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I now wish to touch on the factor of “agree to disagree”.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Staying respectful while navigating differences is important and fundamental in our efforts to preserve and further strengthen unity in society.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Differences of opinions and views are a fact of community life.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The approach that should be taken in managing and balancing such differences is the “agree to disagree” approach.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Failure to do so could lead to conflict and division.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Some of us supported the repeal while others did not.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On this issue, the MPs of the WP had discussed and could not find common ground for agreement on this issue, and thus moved to “agree to disagree”.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Although there were differences in this matter, we all agreed that we needed to embrace unity in diversity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In my perspective, what happened to the WP was a reflection of reality, in parallel to what was happening among Singaporeans on this issue, whereby society was divided into two sides – those who were supportive and those who were not.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Despite the differences in opinion and principle, these differences did not cause divisions that could have damaged our society because of the existence of tolerance, mutual respect and a willingness to agree to disagree when facing a situation with no mutual consensus.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is what is known as unity in diversity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Upholding these values will enable us, as a democratic society, to overcome “cancel culture”, which is a worrying practice because it could adversely impact our unity and lead to divisions.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Efforts to scare voters are unhealthy political practices that could lead to polarisation and division.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For example, once upon a time, fears were raised that if a political party other than the ruling party is elected and runs the town council, it will lead to bad management to the extent that garbage will pile up as high as a two-storey flat.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: It was also remarked that the prices of houses in constituencies held by political parties other than the ruling party will be adversely impacted and plunge.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These are among the political practices which are unhealthy and should be rejected.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The practice of fear mongering by anyone is irresponsible and goes against democratic values.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: If we are able to do that, it can also enhance the level of trust held by our citizens towards the national leadership system, which is another important factor mentioned by Mdm President on that occasion.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Overall, it will strengthen our efforts to build a democratic society based on justice and equality as spoken each time we recite our national pledge.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Rather, it is an invitation to all Members of this august Chamber, our elected leaders and to myself in particular, to engage in introspection and self-reflection with a view to improving what needs to be improved so as to achieve happiness, prosperity and progress for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, sir, there is a saying in Malay that goes “whoever eats the chilli will be the one to feel the spiciness”.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The first Parliament of our nation was convened in 1965 and in 58 years, those who came before us built Singapore into who she is today.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not lost on me that we are still a young nation, a little red dot with homes in the sky, willed into existence by the tenacity of our forefathers and carried by the resilience and harmony of our people today.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Statistics show that as a whole, people are living wealthier, healthier, safer and more informed lives than ever before.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But we are also facing new challenges that threaten our very existence, from climate change to social economic inequality, the rise of nationalism as the war rages on, reshaping our global order and threatening food security.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But despite the uncertainty and fragmentation, there are reasons to believe that humanity and that Singapore is capable of overcoming the challenges facing us.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a society, we are more than a sum of our parts and we can work together.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In her speech, President Halimah Yacob highlighted that we will continue to support the society where we care for and help one another, and pitch in to make a difference.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Indeed, it is our collective responsibility to shape our new social compact.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond providing support, the Government will also reinforce individual and family efforts and bring forth contributions including through committed businesses and a passionate civic society.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To ensure that Singapore thrives in another 58 years, we must create an environment where complex challenges are collectively owned and solved, and where each part of society is empowered to play to their strengths where we do not take what we have for granted.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: My speech today will centre around three points.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If there is anything I have absorbed as truth in the past two and a half years or so, is that the person I am, is made possible by the sacrifice and support of my loved ones, and the work that we are able to do on the ground is made possible by a team as well as residents who look out for each other and the many volunteers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have witnessed so many everyday miracles that defy the natural divisive forces that threaten to tear social fabric, in particular, during COVID-19 and social distancing.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: When people on the frontlines went above and beyond their duties; corporates who sent regular food packs to those in need; when a resident receiving welfare put aside some of the money she had received to order confinement food for a new mom, her neighbour, saying that is what she wanted to do with the money; and an uncle who walked to the market despite his weak legs because he wanted to cook a meal for the volunteer befrienders from our amazing Chengsan-Seletar X-teams who came to check on him every week without fail.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Zooming out to a societal and global level collective action is critical in tackling issues like climate change which pose an existential threat to our island state.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the President's speech, she highlighted Singapore's commitment to decisive action to reduce carbon emissions and take resolute steps towards meeting our net-zero commitments.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Individuals play a role in climate action, for example, through personal choices in consumption energy use and advocacy.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But personal sacrifices can never be the sole solution.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Systemic change requires large amounts of capital and mindset shifts which means states, institutions and companies have a duty to ignite this transformation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How do we encourage the different sectors with different primary objectives to work together?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On this I would like to declare my interests as Legal Council and Senior Project Leader in Tri Sector Associates, a social impact consultancy working on cross-sector social innovation.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Bridging this gap requires concerted and collective action and effective transition finance needs close partnership among the public, philanthropic, private and people sectors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While governments own the green agenda and can take good outcomes to scale, private and philanthropic investors play a crucial role in providing capacity building and concessional capital to new innovative ideas that may be untested.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At this point in history, in order to meet climate goals, we must nurture a collaborative environment that truly embraces co-creation, cultivate solutions that restores not extracts and tries new ways in order to ensure a habitable planet for generations to come.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A whole of nation approach is not just important for climate change but also for issues like mental health.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was heartened to hear the commitment to tackle loneliness and social isolation in Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's speech.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In their older years women are more likely to live alone than men.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As a Member of Parliament (MP) to a constituency with many older residents, it was sobering when I first came in to see many empty nests or single seniors.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I felt each elderly suicide that I knew of from the ground keenly.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In their golden years, why did things feel hopeless?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Is there anything we could have done better to offer a listening ear to have been what they needed at that point in time?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At each wake, I unearth that while some had strong support from family members who were devastated and questioning what they had missed, others had invisible health conditions or burdens, which felt too great to bear – especially if they were alone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Research has also shown that chronic social isolation increases the risk of mental health challenges like depression, anxiety and substance abuse, as well as chronic conditions such as high blood pressure.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Other advanced economies are grappling with this issue too.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am grateful that we are moving the needle and hope that we consider more support along the mental health spectrum, including considering the availability of insurance that does not discriminate against mental health conditions, lessening the load on Institute of Mental Health (IMH) as an acute hospital and offering more varied inclusive options of care for the community as well as for those who care for them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: A whole-of-nation approach is needed: peer support by friends, friendly neighbours by our people, responsible businesses to adapt and hire inclusively and targeted direction of resources by the Government.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We may not be able to save everyone but we must try.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Chengsan-Seletar, we are building on our efforts over the past two years to implement strategic plans for our seniors using a three-pronged approach, based on the theory of change, to increase the awareness of available resources and to remind our seniors they are not alone.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Early detection and screening, creating social support networks and making our elderly feel valued.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are training eyes and ears on the ground through partnerships among postmen and postwomen with SingPost, hawkers and trained psychological first-aid responders, running our 100x Seniors Club to encourage them to come out of their homes and targeting to launch Calm Corners in each of our residential zones to test out evidence-based programmes by ground-up initiatives.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through all this, I hope to remind our seniors that they are not alone and that they are valued.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Third, our youths would lead us into the future, by population, youths are approximately 25% of the residential population today, but 100% of our future.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Youths today are dealing with a more challenging landscape as they come of age, confronted with the climate crisis, fierce competition both in terms of placements for local Institutions of Higher Learning (IHLs) and the global talent pool for work.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, despite all these challenges, they are the ones who will lead Singapore into the brighter futures.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must invest enough in our youths to empower them to take us forward or face the consequences of them leaving for other pastures.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our youths are equal parts resourceful, creative and resilient and willing to put their hand up and be counted on.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, two National University of Singapore (NUS) students, Tim and Jen, who volunteer their time on the ground by joining a National Parks Board's (NParks) working group targeting human wildlife conflict, to interview residents, conduct overnight surveys and actively participated in an Otter Relocation Exercise throughout the night.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are facing new unexpected challenges, and I am grateful to youths such as them, who are willing to take ownership in finding workable solutions.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: But youths cannot do it alone, I have called many times for more space towards ensuring meaningful youth participation not just for quotas or at dialogues.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: If we want youth to show up, we must also trust them and make space at the table for youths to have a say and stake in their futures.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the co-chair of People's Action Party (PAP)'s MAB Muda, it has been my privilege to meet youths from all walks of life with a variety of interests.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For International Women's Day this year, two of our youth activists, Anatasha and Nadia interviewed everyday Malay/Muslim Singaporean women to give their stories, values and thoughts or voice via an interview series called "Dengar Suara Kita".

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They ran this independently and I am very impressed by their conviction to take quiet action on this matter close to their hearts.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   This Ramadan has been a meaningful one for our community.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For the first time since COVID-19, we witnessed our community coming together to break their fast and perform their prayers at the mosques with family and friends.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In the earlier part of my speech, I highlighted some of my concerns and suggestions relating to seniors and youths.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During a mass iftar recently in Ang Mo Kio, I teared up when a grandmother gently patted my face and told me she will pray for me to continue to have the strength to perform my duties.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of the elderly attendees like her faced mobility challenges and required assistance from a caregiver and needed to use personal mobility devices, wheelchairs or walking canes.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On youths in our community, I have confidence and faith in their capabilities.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is not only student leaders or scholars who are doing us proud, but everyday youths among us who are taking the time out to be active citizens.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For example, during this Ramadan, there were various ground-up efforts by informal volunteer networks of students like the IM Volunteers Network SG, faith groups and motorcycle enthusiasts, for example, Kazoku Riders, who spend time to make volunteering a part of their life.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must continue to find ways to support such groups.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition to us moving forward in a post-COVID-19 world, we must ensure that all walks of society are involved in building the future that they want.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As the Malay saying goes, "Climb the hill together, descend the valley together" – we must continue embodying this spirit so that each generation can achieve an equitable outcome.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As more people become involved in society, there will definitely be different views among them.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The PAP does not shy away from different views and does not say that we have a monopoly on ideas.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, I support the Motion.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.05 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.45 pm until 3.15 pm.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am grateful we have come through the pandemic well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: With minimal casualties, livelihoods intact and our people united.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We owe much to our healthcare and frontline workers’ steadfast efforts and sacrifices, and to Singaporeans for your trust and support.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am glad that we have smoothly transitioned to living with the virus.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Last month, this House took stock of what we did right and where we need to do better the next time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Now we must stay firmly focused on the challenges ahead.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: As a small country, our external environment has a huge impact on us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Thankfully, relations with our closest neighbours are stable and positive.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Airspace, military training, and extradition – these are three long-standing sensitive issues in our bilateral relationship, going back decades.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Airspace is vital for Singapore, and politically important to the Indonesians.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The FIR agreement provides both sides a workable way forward.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The DCA covers Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) training, including in traditional areas in the South China Sea.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is particularly important for our Air Force and Navy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The ET is something that Indonesia has long pressed for, but it was not straightforward to do because our legal systems are so different.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we had left these issues unresolved, they would have festered and quite likely one day turned rancorous.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This would have soured the entire relationship, which would have benefited neither side.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am very happy to have now settled these issues with President Jokowi.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We signed the agreements in Bintan a year ago.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: By putting these long-standing issues to rest, Indonesia and Singapore can move forward with greater confidence and trust and focus our energies on collaboration.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are working on promising new areas, like the digital economy, sustainability and renewable energy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We signed several memoranda of understanding (MOUs) on them when President Jokowi visited Singapore last month.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: With Malaysia, we also have a broad cooperation agenda.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It spans many different areas like trade, investments and connectivity.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At the same time, we have some significant bilateral issues to tackle, including Singapore’s development works at Pedra Branca, delimitation of maritime boundaries, water issues and airspace issues.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I hope to make progress on them with Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is important that both sides manage these issues well and not allow any single issue to dominate and disrupt our overall bilateral relationship.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I am glad that we are maintaining frequent exchanges at all levels with Malaysia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I hosted Prime Minister Anwar in January for his introductory visit, and we met again recently in Boao in Hainan Island and took our discussions further.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Also last month, at the invitation of His Majesty the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, President Halimah made a State Visit to Malaysia, where she was very warmly received.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The next big milestone is when we complete the drop-in span to join up both sides of the marine viaduct.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And I look forward to witnessing this with Prime Minister Anwar before too long.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, with our immediate neighbours – Indonesia and Malaysia – relations are stable and encouraging.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But further afield, the situation has turned much more troubling, even dangerous.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singaporeans need to realise the gravity of the external situation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are facing not just one storm, but several.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After more than a year, the war is deadlocked, with no good outcome in sight.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Neither side can win, nor can either afford to lose.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In fact, things have been at a stalemate since last November.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Ukrainians are understandably reluctant to stop fighting before they reclaim all of their territory, but this will be very difficult.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Russians are most unlikely to be defeated entirely despite heavy losses.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have a large population and can still conscript more troops and mobilise more resources.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is always a danger of the conflict escalating.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The US and NATO countries are supplying Ukraine with more and more sophisticated military equipment – like longer-range artillery, the Patriot air defence system and main battle tanks.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If the Ukrainians, using these Western-supplied weapons, make a breakthrough on the battlefield, we cannot predict how Russia may react.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What does this mean for the rest of the world?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even short of worst-case scenarios, the impact is bad.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The war continues to disrupt global energy, food and fertiliser supplies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are all feeling it in higher prices.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There are also significant implications on international relations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Relations between Russia and the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) countries, the US and Europe, have completely broken down and will not return to normal anytime soon.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For China, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has presented a difficult problem.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The US and Europeans want China to use its influence to get Russia to stop the invasion.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: China would prefer not to aggravate Europe and the US, by providing military support for Russia’s war in Ukraine.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But China is hard-pressed to condemn Russia’s invasion, or pressure Russia to stop fighting.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It shares a very long land border with Russia, and it has to consider its own substantial relations with Russia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, the war has made it difficult for China to improve relations with Europe, even though I think both sides would like to do so.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It has also complicated China’s already very troubled ties with the US.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Which brings me to the second big issue – which is US-China relations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When I visited China last month, this was on everyone’s minds.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Likewise, in all my recent meetings with US visitors.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Between the US and China, there is deep mutual suspicion and fundamental mistrust.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In America, the Democrats and Republicans disagree with each other on almost everything.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But they are united on one issue – China.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And it is not just the US government.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Negative perceptions are prevalent among the population too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Surveys in China similarly show that Chinese public perception of the US has deteriorated.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: More consequentially, China’s leaders have become convinced that the US is seeking to “contain, encircle and suppress” China, in the words of President Xi Jinping.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They believe that Washington wants to hold back China’s growth and weaken the Communist Party of China’s hold on power.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They say the East is rising and the West is declining, and they think the time has come for China to take its rightful place in the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore is good friends with China, and we are also old friends of Taiwan.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore rigorously upholds our “One China” policy and continues to support the peaceful development of cross-strait relations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: China considers Taiwan as the most important issue and the “One China” principle to be the reddest of its red lines.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But in the West, an alternative narrative is gaining currency – that the problem in cross-strait relations is a broader ideological issue of democracy versus autocracy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is even though most countries, including most Western countries, have officially adopted “One China” policies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All sides continue to make moves, responding to one another.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After Dr Tsai Ing-Wen met US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy during her recent stopover in the US, China launched three days of extensive military exercises all around Taiwan.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A CCTV report described them as "comprehensive and precise simulated attacks on the key targets in the island and surrounding waters".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The risks of a miscalculation or mishap are growing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even if the two powers avoid a direct conflict, which thankfully, I believe neither side wishes to see, enduring enmity and bad relations between them will be very costly for both and will mean big trouble for the rest of the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a very worrying outlook, but we still hope that relations between the US and China do not get worse, and that both sides can keep lines of communications open and with time, gradually repair their relationship on the basis of mutual trust and respect.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The third big issue is that the global multilateral trading system is under siege.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This has very serious implications, especially for small, open economies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For Singapore, a stable, well-functioning international trading system is vitally important.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We cannot survive other than as an open economy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We rely on the free flow of trade and investments across the world and a common set of rules that applies to all countries, no matter their size.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This has helped us greatly to compete against bigger countries, attract investments from around the world and to grow.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For the last few decades, there was a broad international consensus supporting globalisation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Countries were lowering tariff and non-tariff barriers, harmonising rules, seeking win-win economic cooperation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) economies talked about their vision of a Free Trade Area of the Asia Pacific (FTAAP).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even when countries clashed on political or security issues, they still continued to do business with each other.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And, from time to time, countries might violate the rules set by the World Trade Organization (WTO), but even then, the exceptions had to be justified and defended.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: All over the world, countries are prioritising domestic and national security considerations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Countries no longer talk about trade being win-win.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Too often, when countries quarrel, their bilateral trade becomes embroiled in these disputes.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It depends – if you need my imports more than me, I restrict my exports.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If it is the opposite, you will restrict your imports.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, sometimes it is high-tech items like semiconductor chips and sophisticated machinery.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Sometimes it is agricultural products like bananas, barley or wine.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They seek to inflict maximum political pain while blandly denying any hostile intent.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Countries trust others less and less to play by the rules.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Therefore, they are increasingly going their own way, and "on-shoring" or "friend-shoring" supply chains.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This then triggers a tit-for-tat response from the other side.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We are once again heading towards a world where protectionism is a default and trade rules are secondary, like what happened in the period between the First and Second World Wars.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The economic cost to the world will be very high.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Seven percent is the effect on goods and services not traded, but deglobalisation will also impact on the exchange of ideas and innovation, technology development and diffusion, as well as capital flows and cross-border financing – all of which to growth prosperity and human well-being.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: These are all vital for economic growth, especially for an open economy like ours.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A deep decoupling of the world economy would undo what has taken countries decades to collectively achieve.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The current global situation, both strategic and economic, is graver than we have experienced for a very long time.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore has survived difficult periods before – the Cold War between the US and the Soviet Union, and closer to home, the proxy fights in Vietnam and Cambodia; the Asian Financial Crisis and the Global Financial Crisis; public health crises like SARS and most recently, COVID-19.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In such a troubled environment, what can we do?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: First and foremost, we must remain one united people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have come through repeated challenges over the last six decades, because we worked together, took adversity in our stride and kept faith with one another.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We painstakingly created the harmonious multiracial and multi-religious society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We avoided the schisms and factions that have troubled other societies.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In recent years, we have tackled sensitive issues that could easily have caused deep rifts among our people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Last year, we repealed section 377A of the Penal Code while safeguarding the institution of marriage.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We handled these issues firmly and fairly, in a way that maintained mutual trust and understanding between different communities and kept ourselves together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You may think, "Nothing happened, so what was the fuss about?

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We should just have done it – and a long time ago".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But look what has happened elsewhere – opposing groups getting worked up, mobilising their followers, pitting citizens against each other and dividing society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This could easily have happened here too and it can still happen to us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many foreigners, especially our critics in the West, do not understand this about us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In Singapore, when faced with a divisive issue, our approach has always been to find a middle way, bridge the differences, strike compromises and heal divisions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Not grand posturing, not playing cultural or identity politics, not dividing and polarising people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our instinct always is to keep Singaporeans together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have to keep thinking and acting like this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Please do not take our harmony for granted.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is a very precious thing, very fragile.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must continuously work on it and build up our social cohesion and national strength.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The troubled external environment will create new stresses and strains in our society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: High inflation because of the Ukraine war will cause difficulties for many households, especially lower- and middle-income families.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Tensions between China and the US will expose our population to emotional pulls, commercial pressures and influence campaigns, from one side or the other, to take their point of view and support their cause.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The fracturing of the global trading system will mean slower, more uncertain growth and greater disruption to industries and jobs, businesses and workers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must not allow these pressures to divide Singaporeans along fault lines in our society, whether old or new, like the "haves" versus "have nots", the "liberals" versus "conservatives", the "locals" versus "foreigners", "new" versus "old" citizens and above all, differences between races and religions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In this new troubled world, it is all the more important for us to close ranks.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must do our best to see eye-to-eye on the fundamentals and try to appreciate each other's perspectives, even if we cannot always agree.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must not shy away from hard choices, but deal squarely with difficult issues based on facts and sound analysis.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Members have heard Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and other 4G Ministers outline the Forward Singapore agenda earlier.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will make sure meritocracy works for all.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will leave no one behind, as Singapore progresses.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will enhance safety nets against the uncertainties of life.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will fashion a common understanding and purpose that binds us together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is an ambitious agenda that will not be easy to realise even in good times.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In these turbulent times, it is all the more important that we get it done and get it right, so that we can stay united as one people, one Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But just being united will not be enough.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
