text: It is equally important that we have the go-getter spirit of self-reliance and enterprise, to create prosperity for our nation and achieve the best we can in a very troubled world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Long ago, in 1968, Singapore was heading into a major storm.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The British forces were here, they contributed about one-fifth of the economy and they were soon to withdraw from Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We faced the prospect of mass unemployment and economic collapse.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr S Rajaratnam had just become Minister of Labour and was girding Singaporeans for tough measures and hard times ahead.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Rajaratnam went on to say: "We in Parliament can, if we like, fool the people into believing that we can bring them prosperity without the tears and effort".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But he warned that if we did that, then "we would go the way of many independent countries – into bankruptcy and despair".

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Only in Singapore, we do not have an "escape hatch", the hinterland, that many other countries have.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This mindset of grit and self-reliance was crucial.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Now, once again, we are headed into difficult times.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Rajaratnam’s rallying call more than 50 years ago remains just as valid and critical for us today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I can hardly improve on the words that the drafter of our National Pledge used.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Again, we need “a sustained effort, a willingness to mobilise savings, a readiness to take risks, a propensity for innovation, a passionate vision of the future, a willingness to make the painful adjustments required by modernisation and, most important of all, a readiness on the part of the people as a whole to postpone immediate rewards for greater gains in the future”.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This formula has long worked for us and it will continue to do so.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is good reason to be confident that Singaporeans have not gone soft and forgotten these fundamentals.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Last June, I visited Rwanda for the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Africa is not the first place that comes to mind when Singaporeans think about venturing overseas.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But there, I met several young Singaporeans living and working in Rwanda.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: One was running a poultry farm supplying chickens to restaurants in Kigali, Rwanda’s capital.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Another was working with startups to raise financing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A third had started a distillery, brewing premium spirits; not just any hooch, but premium spirits.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I asked him what it was, he said it is special rum.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And he is hoping to make his rum brands as famous as single malt Scottish whiskeys.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And there were a few more, too, including some women, who dared to take the path less travelled, and struck out on their own in these less familiar lands.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Last week, at the reception after the Opening of Parliament, I met a student from National University of Singapore (NUS).

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He had spent a year in Silicon Valley on the NUS Overseas Colleges (NOC) programme and he found it exhilarating.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He picked up new skills, was inspired by the culture of innovation and the entrepreneurial spirit of the people he met.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He told me he intends to start his own business, together with a few of his NOC Silicon Valley classmates.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He does not know if his business will succeed, but he is prepared to take that leap of faith to start a business of his own.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And in my daily work, interacting with Ministers and their staff, I come across young officers who are passionate about their work, feel a sense of mission serving the nation and are keen to improve the lives of Singaporeans through their ideas and efforts.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many young Singaporeans think and act the same way.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Growing up in Singapore, they have benefited from a good education system, opportunities, exposure, and stimulation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have made the most of all this.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They know that nobody owes them a living.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They will work hard and blaze their own path forward.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Mr Rajaratnam would have been proud and delighted.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But we are not just asking Singaporeans to work harder as individuals.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have a strategy to make a living for our nation as a global city and an international hub.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It will be tough because globalisation is going the wrong way.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Countries with larger populations and bigger domestic markets are turning inwards.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But maybe, they can afford to do so.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must work hard to form good relations with other countries, big and small, and find ways to work with them.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even with wars, tensions, and protectionism in the world, countries still need to trade, there will still be opportunities and, therefore, we can still make a living.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Hence, Changi can still be one of the busiest and best airports in the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our Singapore port can still be a highly efficient and reliable transshipment hub, connected to other ports all over the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We can still be a financial centre, financing trade flows and infrastructure investments in the region and beyond.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our city can still be a magnet for talent and enterprise, a centre for technology and innovation, and a base for trusted services and advanced manufacturing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We just have to work harder and smarter than before.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: In a world of troubles, not every country will prosper, but Singapore will not perish.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Of course, we must make the right moves to continue thriving.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Staying open and connected means exposing ourselves to competition from the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We must be able to do things more competently and efficiently than our competitors to maintain our edge.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This means continually upgrading existing capabilities and building new ones, transforming and restructuring our economy to stay abreast of technologies and industries.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Take, for example, AI, a rapidly developing field.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: You have all heard of ChatGPT and maybe even have tried it out.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It did not write this speech for me yet, though it probably can already summarise it quite well.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But ChatGPT is just one AI application out of many.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: AI will affect jobs across all sectors, including white-collar jobs.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Some will be enhanced, others will be eliminated.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: At the same time, AI technology will create immense opportunities to improve productivity across the board.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To respond to AI and many more technologies to come, our businesses will need to adapt and transform, to develop new ways of operating and explore new markets.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our workers need to upskill and reskill to do the new jobs which will replace the old ones.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We need to complement our own talent with skilled professionals from all over the world who have the expertise and experience to help us make this transformation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: And we have to integrate these foreigners into our workplaces and communities so that they fit well into our society.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will feel tensions; we will experience disruptions.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We will have to manage the problems and deal with the trade-offs thoughtfully and sensibly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But we have some things going for us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Most importantly, we stand out, compared to competitors.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) recently ranked the business environment of countries for the next five years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Singapore has ranked top now for 15 years in a row.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Businesses, investors and talented individuals in the region and beyond show great interest in Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They want to come here, to bring in their talent, capital and investments.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: After COVID-19, every country wants to be able to make its own vaccines.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We have a strong base of biomedical activities, from R&D to manufacturing, and the prerequisites for building vaccine plants.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Other pharmas and other industries are keen on Singapore, too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They value the Singapore brand, they have a good view of Singapore, and that is how we can continue to create good jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Which brings me to my next point – we must uphold Singapore’s good reputation and standing in the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: When I meet foreign leaders and businesspeople, whether here or on my trips abroad, many express their admiration for Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They talk about having read Mr Lee Kuan Yew’s books; they tell me how they wish their countries could become like Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Many Singaporeans take this good reputation for granted.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They are glad to carry our red passport.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Overseas, they are proud to identify themselves as Singaporeans and not be mistaken as someone else.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But they do not realise how important this high standing we enjoy is to us, nor how astonishing it is for a small island state with no natural resources to enjoy this standing.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Based on our land size, Singapore is barely visible on the world map.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: By country population, we are hardly worth mentioning.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: China and India are each 250 times our population.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The US and Indonesia, more than 40 times.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Even compared with other major cities, by population size, we are not in the top 50 in the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: If we did not stand out from the rest, there would be no particular reason why other countries and investors should pay much attention to this little island and no particular reason why Singaporeans should enjoy a quality of life and a standard of living that we can be proud of and is among the highest in the world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is because of the strong international reputation that Singapore has built up over the years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: People know our people are of high quality, our workers are hardworking, skilled and reliable, our professionals are competent, honest and trustworthy.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We act based on principles, which we uphold consistently.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our leaders speak with the mandate and authority to deliver on what they say because they enjoy the support and confidence of the people.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our policies do not chop and change or get reversed from one election to another.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Thus, when Russia invaded Ukraine, we took a clear principled stand to oppose this flagrant violation of the UN Charter.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We did the same decades ago when the US invaded Grenada, and Vietnam invaded Cambodia.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Any part of the world, any power, any decade, same answer from Singapore, because that is where our enduring interests lie.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: People know that we make useful contributions on global issues.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: For example, the Director General now of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) – a UN outfit – is a Singaporean, Mr Daren Tang.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Senior Minister Tharman Shanmugaratnam is co-chairing the Global Commission on Water Governance, whose first report was discussed at the United Nations Water Conference held in New York last month.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our Ambassador for Oceans and Law of the Sea Issues, Ms Rena Lee, presided over negotiations under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) on Marine Biodiversity of Areas Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) – that means, on the high seas, belonging to nobody – and the negotiations had been going on for many years.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There are many other Singaporeans working in different fields all over the world also distinguishing themselves and enhancing our international reputation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Because of all these and more, confidence and trust in the Singapore brand has grown.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is a precious asset in an uncertain world.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: So, I ask all Singaporeans, through you, Mr Speaker, to uphold our country’s reputation, especially when you are overseas.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Make full use of the Singapore brand, but remember, never sully it.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Build on it, enhance it for future generations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: A high international reputation makes all the difference to Singapore.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: I have spoken about the importance of unity, a go-getting mindset and a good reputation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But the quality of a country's government and leaders matters too.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He said that ultimately, companies value good government, stable politics and a system that works.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: He said, "What I want is a place that I can trust.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This" – meaning Singapore – "is a country you can trust and which the world can trust." But there is no formula that can guarantee that our system will continue to work well for the long term.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Last year, when the Parliament debated the importance of honesty and integrity in public life, I spoke about the importance and the difficulty of maintaining the ideals and values of a country beyond its founding generations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Honesty and integrity are a crucial part of our success formula, but it goes beyond that.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It is equally essential and hard to keep the whole system working through the decades.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: People forget the values and experience of the founding generation.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Slowly, things can go awry and start to fall apart.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Nothing can magically prevent Singapore from going down this road.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: What we can do to give ourselves the best chance of staying on the right track is to make sure that our economy is sound, and our institutions are in place and strong.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our people have the skills and instincts to work hard, work together and earn a living for ourselves.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our leaders are capable, dedicated and trustworthy stewards worthy of their responsibility to Singapore, to this and future generations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: To ensure good leadership for the long term is an unending and demanding challenge for successive generations, but what I and my older colleagues can do and will make sure of, is to prepare a strong and capable next team to take over from us.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Then, the new leaders can take Singapore further forward and the country has the chance to produce and support new generations of leaders to come after them, who will be up to the job.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: During the pandemic, Singaporeans experienced firsthand the importance of strong political leadership.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But our response and the results would have been very different without political leaders who could set the direction, make the tough calls and rally the people together.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The Multi-Ministry Task Force (MTF) Ministers were in the hot seat, but the whole 4G team played a key role.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: It was a formative experience for the 4G ministers.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Handling the crisis, they got the measure of each other and gained confidence in each other's judgement and abilities.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: The 4G Ministers are increasingly responsible for the safety and well-being of the country.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They have a strong agenda to fulfil, domestically and internationally.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: But they cannot do it on their own.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They need the support of every Singaporean, including Members of this House, to see it through.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Show your support for a Government that works hard and works well for you.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Elect leaders whom you can trust to take us forward.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Give yourselves the best chance to keep our system working well for Singaporeans for many years to come.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is probably the tenth time I have told you this – if there is no other message you are taking away from this speech.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: There is much work to be done and to be done quickly.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Our forefathers worked hard to build up the Singapore that we have today.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They did not let themselves to be constrained by our small size or limited resources.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They were not powerful, but they fought hard to make our voice heard on the international stage.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: They were not well off, but they tightened their belts to create a better future for us – their descendants.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Against long odds, they determined to forge a prosperous nation and a united people, and they succeeded.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We, too, must embrace their can-do spirit and outsized ambition to be an extraordinary country – an exceptional place in the world, maintain our international reputation and build on our trusted Singapore brand of quality, reliability and efficiency, make full use of our strengths and turn opportunities into successes, stand up for what we believe in and uphold consistent principles to advance Singapore's long-term interests.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: This is the way for Singapore to be taken seriously and to count for more than our size.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: We may be a small island state, but we are not a small people and neither are our hearts nor our aspirations.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Let us think boldly, aim high and seek far.

speaker: The Prime Minister (Mr Lee Hsien Loong)
text: Let us work together, Government and people, to build a Singapore that we and our children will all be proud of.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Indeed, Singapore is at a new crossroad – an ageing population, rising costs and interest rates as well as greater global competition for business and talent force us to think about our future and our survival.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is imperative that Singaporeans trust and partner our 4G Government to combat these challenges, just like how we fought and overcame COVID-19 together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But as Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong mentioned a few days ago, beyond building infrastructure and hardware to future-proof Singapore, the future and welfare of Singapore is at the crux of it, the collective responsibility of all of us and not just the Government alone.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Today, I intend to share three things that resonated most with me from Mdm President's Address.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: First, our ageing population is now a reality.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I think Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and many others have highlighted this.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More and more Singaporeans aspire to live independently, which leaves more elderly couples living on their own.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am glad that Mdm President particularly highlighted enhancing retirement adequacy for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But our concerns must be over the remaining 30% and how far they are from reaching their BRS.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Further, this does not even include inactive CPF members or Singaporeans who sit outside the CPF system like non-working homemakers or self-employed persons (SEPs).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It may be useful to find out what is the MRSS' utilisation rate and most importantly, whether we need to do more to educate and encourage families to take advantage of such Government support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On SEPs, Senior Minister of State Koh said that MOM will continue to review if we need to go beyond encouraging SEPs to make voluntary contributions to their CPF accounts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Perhaps that exercise can include a study on the proportion of SEPs who can attain their respective BRS through their own voluntary CPF savings or private savings over the next few years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I also note that a fundamental review of our retirement adequacy policies is now underway under the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am looking forward to eventual definite timelines for that review as the changes to our demographics would entail rapid changes needed to our retirement adequacy policies at an early stage.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One area that continues to be important for Singaporeans is enhancing the flexibility of how and when CPF retirement monies can be paid out.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: New stresses are emerging and challenging the adequacy of the existing payout mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, I have mentioned this before, the 2% per annum increase of payouts under the escalating CPF LIFE plan may no longer gel with Singapore's long-term inflation projections, given the shifts in the global macroeconomy, supply chain and other factors.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Other areas I hope we can make changes will be on how we can more regularly and dynamically revise the methodology for applicable interest rates on the Ordinary, Special and MediSave Accounts in the upcoming quarterly reviews and adjusting the allocation ratios such that a greater percentage is allocated into the Special Account instead of the Ordinary and MediSave Accounts, to avoid increasing the financial burden on both employers and employees – the former of which I had raised in my Adjournment Motion on "Helping Singaporeans Navigate a High-interest Rate Environment" last year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In Malay):   The latest changes in cancer coverage under the Integrated Shield Plan will also change the way Singaporeans plan for their healthcare and insurance needs at old age.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: An elderly resident, who used to work as a horticulturalist and recently found out he had Stage 4 cancer, contacted me for help just a few days ago.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He is unable to work now, but fortunately he has received assistance through MediFund – which I think is an important source of help – but needs additional help to support his family and spouse.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He has no insurance coverage, and I can imagine that, with recent cancer coverage changes, more of such cases will face financial challenges.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is an important issue that I hope we can analyse and find comprehensive solutions in future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides sufficient funds, we must also ensure that our seniors enjoy a good quality of life and dignity during their retirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's call on the importance of “collective responsibility” is appropriate and timely.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To me, it is heartbreaking to read news about senior citizens who die alone at home without being noticed by anyone for weeks, months and even years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, although we build a more elderly-friendly building environment complete with special housing options and common space, we must supplement this hardware with people-centric policies.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The return of large-scale activities organised by community centres and organisations is very helpful.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But we also cannot ignore the less active senior citizens and those who are not physically active enough to go out and enjoy recreation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, I was heartened to hear Minister Desmond Lee and other Members of Parliament (MPs) mention the importance of cross-generation living.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But not all estates will have this opportunity because we are ageing quickly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This has always been a sensitive topic because, as an Asian community, it is considered “unfilial” to “leave” one’s parents in nursing homes or old folks homes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, as much as we want to ensure that we collectively support our seniors, there are still people who will need a place in nursing homes for the elderly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is useful to find out the subscription levels for existing nursing homes and how MOH projects the demand until 2030 and beyond as well as plan ahead for possible increased demand.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: (In English): Turning to my second topic, Mr Speaker, I share Mdm President’s view that the global competition for business will intensify.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The competition will not only be over business, but also over talent.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singaporean talent is sought after in many places in the world.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Recently, Mr Chew Shou Zi dominated the headlines as he testified before the US Congress as the CEO of TikTok.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have also heard that junior Singapore lawyers are today being drawn to relocate to work in London, New York and Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Such a legislation is pertinent in my view for a mature economy as middle-income Singaporeans are concerned over competition for jobs and opportunities at work in a future labour market that will be more contested.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I had, since my maiden speech in 2015 and several Adjournment Motions, pushed for anti-discrimination laws that carry penalties, given my concerns about a more complex labour market going forward, so I really, really look forward to the final report on the tripartite committee on workplace fairness and the eventual legislation that will ensue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But one other key thrust to help us compete and retain talent will be building a more people-friendly and connected city.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As Mdm President highlighted in her address, we must ensure our transport infrastructure and policies are refreshed from time to time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We are adapting to new commuting patterns after entering and emerging from three pandemic years.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our green ambitions will force us to pivot away from decades-old solutions towards new innovations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Even more can be done, for example, in the addendum by the Ministry of Transport (MOT), cycling was stated to “aid first and last mile connectivity to the major public transport nodes and key amenities”.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If this is the aim, we may need to complement our expansion of cycling paths with bike-sharing initiatives and with other enhancements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Those who own their own bicycles are unlikely to use their bicycle just to park it at the MRT station or bus interchanges near their house.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am conscious that private bike-sharing models have failed before and we may need Government involvement or intervention for bike-sharing to work.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Possibly, has any study been done on why operators like oBike, Ofo and Mobike ultimately called it quits?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Amid rising costs and interest rates in the past year, we are seeing more news that give us cause for concern over economic growth.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The collapse of Silicon Valley Bank in the US and Credit Suisse in Switzerland have sparked fears of a banking meltdown.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Amid the uncertain outlook, I am particularly heartened by Mdm President’s call to deepen Singaporeans’ sense of shared identity and responsibility towards each other – the collective responsibility that Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong mentioned on Monday too.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must remember to support one another and leave no one behind, especially as we are likely to face greater constraints in the future.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Costs and prices may go up a little further in light of growing constraints.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While we continue to explore innovative and creative approaches to manage our land, the fact is that land is scarce in Singapore and comes at a premium.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Being small and import-dependent, we are a price-taker, including when it comes to interest rates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is apt that Mdm President has called for us to better manage these growing constraints by being more adaptable and resourceful and, in so doing, compete stronger as a business and connectivity hub.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This must be our longer-term strategy, so that Singaporean workers get good jobs, become more productive and get rewarded for the higher value they bring.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the short term, we need to help Singaporeans navigate this new environment of rising costs and higher interest rates.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I will not repeat what I said during my Adjournment Motion in October last year, but I have some new observations to add.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Going forward, I hope the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS), the relevant Ministries – and the Chamber, possibly – will discuss this, and we will have studied credit card default trends or data by age group and beyond the Total Debt Servicing Ratio (TDSR) limits, whether we need to additionally regulate such leverage assumed by Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If not, then whether more upstream work can be done with our youths and our younger population.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, more couples will need to be dual income in order to meet their increasing liabilities.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides infantcare facilities, it is important to ensure that there are other new care options that MSF is studying to meet different preferences and needs.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The final point, Mr Speaker, I would like to touch on is housing affordability.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In this segment, I am talking about cost of living and rising cost, so I had to look at various reports and pieces.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In particular, I came across a report that was co-authored by hon Member Louis Chua and his team on that issue.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was trying to weigh in some of the points that were found in that report.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As an economist, I am actually more attuned towards more statistical and economic reports that bear strong statistical and data support.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I tried to balance it with what many WP MPs have suggested – that housing is unaffordable for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Leader of the Opposition too, had echoed sentiments, calling for the Government to intensify efforts in making public housing more affordable and accessible.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I was surprised when I came across this report as I was trying to prepare this speech on the issue about housing affordability and cost of living.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More recently, I was looking at the issue and found that this report in January, where WP MP, Mr Louis Chua, put up a considered, professional view in a report which was carried in the media, saying that housing in Singapore is affordable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is what he and his team of property analysts said.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Also, he anticipated that, I quote: "the global housing slump will deepen in 2023"; yet he expects the converse in Singapore, with a modest price growth of 3% to 5%.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Despite broadly higher rates, his scenario analysis suggests affordability continues to be healthy for the average household, given wage growth momentum amid a tight labour market.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And then, on page 13 of his report, he and his co-authors went on to say this: contrary to the private property market, he finds a "more favourable and resilient situation in the public housing market, i.e., HDB".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is largely attributed to the rise in average income in relation to the price of a flat.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: He consistently estimated a mortgage servicing ratio (MSR) that stayed comfortably below 30% bestowing upon households the freedom to still take up other loans.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, he is inclined to believe that HDB markets should continue to remain resilient, supported by healthy household balance sheets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And on the regional front, on page 26 of his report, he then assessed Singapore and our ASEAN region, and said this, I quote: "From a regional perspective", he notes that "affordability continues to be healthy in Singapore where residential price increases have lagged behind that of our household income growth over the last decade.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whereas the converse is true for neighbouring ASEAN countries.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Higher relative affordability for the general population of Singapore adds to relative stability and resilience, amid a rising environment globally." So, as a trained central bank economist before, I was somewhat attuned to the property report that Mr Louis Chua and his co-authors highlighted, which is somewhat in line and supported by data as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I was wondering if that is actually indeed Mr Louis Chua's professional opinion in January 2023.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I try to reconcile, as I tried to prepare my speech, it seems odd that he and the WP said something else in Parliament in the February housing Motion.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, I just wanted to highlight that story, as the story goes as I prepare my speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, that is my third point, Mr Speaker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: (In Mandarin):   Thank you, Mr Speaker, for allowing me to join the debate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The first issue raised by President Halimah Yaacob in her Address was that of the global situation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: How Singapore can stand firm in a turbulent world is a major challenge that the Government and Singaporeans must jointly face.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is commonly said in diplomatic circles that “foreign policy begins at home”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In other words, it is much easier to conduct foreign policy successfully when a country’s citizens share a common understanding of national interests.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is why it is also part of the Ministry of Foreign Affair's (MFA) role to attend community or school campus dialogues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The most commonly asked questions in recent years are: how does Singapore maintain good bilateral relations with the US and China at the same time?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: How should we continue to maintain this balance?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Observers and analysts of global developments, media commentators, and Singaporeans who care about current affairs are all likely to have views on this topic.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Take Prime Minister Lee’s recent Official Visit to China for instance.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: A friend remarked happily to me that the visit was excellent, because he felt that Singapore has been looking rather pro-US of late.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Maintaining a balance between the US and China appears to have become a yardstick by which Singaporeans and non-Singaporeans alike measure the success of our foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It is akin to a panel of judges assessing a gymnast’s performance on the balance beam.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Based on this yardstick, if Singapore’s leaders made remarks that appear to favour one side, then balance must be promptly restored by saying or doing something that pleases the other side – to demonstrate ‘impartiality’ like holding a bowl of water in equilibrium.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Some might think of our foreign policy in terms of not taking sides, keeping our head down and maintaining neutrality in all matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Does Singapore’s foreign policy boil down to a balancing act?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I wish to make three points: first, our foreign policy is driven by our principles, not a quest for balance; second, the space available to Singapore depends not on our ability to perform a balancing act, but whether any basis for cooperation remains between major powers and third, Singapore will do its utmost to broaden the basis of international cooperation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As a small country lacking in natural resources and highly dependent on free trade, we need a peaceful and secure external environment, transparent and effective international law and a stable global order, and an efficient, well-regulated and globalised market economy system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore depends on these factors for our survival, autonomy and prosperity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These are the core principles that shape our foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: How does the perception of balance come about?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In a highly harmonious world, where all bilateral relations are equally good, no one country would stand out for having particularly balanced or imbalanced relations with others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: However, in a highly fractious world, it would be hard to maintain equally strong ties with countries belonging to different camps.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Serious differences have emerged between China and the US, yet Singapore continues to maintain strong bilateral relations with both sides.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This creates the perception of a so-called “balancing act”.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But Singapore-China and Singapore-US relations were not built on the basis of Singapore unilaterally maintaining a balancing act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Rather, these bilateral relations reflect decades of substantive, win-win collaboration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have longstanding and friendly relations with China.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Over the past decades, we have witnessed profound and rapid changes in China alongside its development.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Through its pursuit of market-based economic development, China has made great strides in uplifting the lives of its 1.4 billion citizens.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We believe that China’s peaceful rise and growing economy will be an important engine of growth for the Asia Pacific and the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore has supported China’s continued reform and opening up and participated in China’s development journey over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our three government-to-government projects have supported China’s economic development through various phases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Suzhou Industrial Park (SIP) was established in the 1990s during China’s rapid industrialisation; the Sino-Singapore Tianjin Eco-City (SSTEC) was launched in 2008 in concert with China’s focus on sustainability; and the China-Singapore (Chongqing) Demonstration Initiative on Strategic Connectivity (CCI) started in 2015 to grow China’s linkages with the world, resulting in the establishment of the CCI-New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Trade and investment with China have brought tangible benefits for its many economic partners, including Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We are one of the largest investors in China, who is our top trading partner in goods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our eight Provincial Business Councils across China have brought about mutually beneficial opportunities for our peoples and businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: When Singapore-China relations are discussed, many would also think of the role played by the ethnic Chinese community in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Indeed, the fact that Singapore has an ethnic Chinese majority population means that most Singaporeans would be able to trace their ancestry to somewhere in China, usually the southern coastal provinces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Moreover, with Singapore’s bilingual education policy, many Singaporeans of Chinese descent would be able to use the Chinese language to some degree, even though English is our working language.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The sense of familiarity and ease makes it more convenient for ethnic Chinese Singaporeans to communicate and work with partners from China.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Without a doubt, people-to-people ties spanning culture, kinship and language help enrich Singapore-China relations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But to interpret Singapore-China relations from the cultural perspective may result in a skewed view or misunderstandings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Those who are not equipped with a deep understanding of Singapore might find it hard to hoist in this point.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singaporeans are citizens of an independent country, but may also identify culturally with being ethnically Chinese, Malay, Indian or others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: National identity and cultural identity are two different matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At the same time, we seek to shape a highly unified national identity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It would be inaccurate to project Singapore’s position in international affairs based on what one observes of Singapore’s Chinese community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In an editorial published in Lianhe Zaobao early this year, veteran editor Mr Lim Jim Koon discussed how the newspaper has been assumed to take sides in geopolitical terms on various occasions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In an example he raised, Lianhe Zaobao’s website was identified as pro-China by a foreign news organisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If a reputable overseas news organisation could espouse such a subjective view of Lianhe Zaobao, we can only imagine what those who do not know us well would think of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Historian Prof Wang Gungwu’s recent speech on “What does it mean to be ethnically Chinese in Singapore?” has created some buzz.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Tracing the development of the Chinese community in Singapore over several centuries, Prof Wang made clear that the definition of ethnic Chinese in Singapore is a complex and indeed convoluted issue.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As Prof Wang pointed out, Singapore is an independent sovereign nation state, a global city, situated at the heart and centre of Southeast Asia and under the umbrella of ASEAN.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The following was put in particularly succinct terms by Prof Wang, who said : “…Singapore had started out with an extraordinary principle, not known in any nation I know of, one that recognised everyone born here as equal, and that the plural society would be the basis of a new nation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As far as I know, every other nation began by saying that whoever was the majority would determine the fundamentals of nationhood… Singapore is the only one I know of in which it was the other way round; the majority accepted that they live in a plural society, in a neighbourhood in which they are a minority.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: They accepted that they had to treat everybody as equal and that the plural society was the foundation of Singapore’s nationhood.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It was an extraordinary way to start the nation-building process.” Prof Wang’s expert analysis on the extraordinary choice made by Singapore in pursuit of national identity would be of great value to anyone seeking to understand Singapore better.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Hence, Singapore’s foreign policy must stand for the interests of all citizens, including Chinese Singaporeans, Malay Singaporeans, Indian Singaporeans, Eurasian Singaporeans and so forth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These are reflected in our pursuit of a safe and secure external environment, a stable global order, and a globalised market economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: China’s embarkation on reform and opening up has created a broad basis of collaboration between Singapore and China.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Hence, we have been able to build excellent bilateral relations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore-US relations are similarly excellent, and established on the basis of the principles shaping our foreign policy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The US played a vital role in underwriting the world order that emerged after the Second World War.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It paved the way for stability and prosperity in Asia by championing an open, integrated, and rules-based global order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: By providing a security umbrella for the region, the US has enabled regional countries to trade and grow peacefully.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: American companies invested extensively in Asia, including Singapore, bringing capital, technology, and ideas, and contributing to the vibrancy of the region.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The US continues to be a force for economic vitality and greater engagement will bring about benefits for the entire region.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The US is also our third-largest trading partner in goods.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: US companies are well-regarded in Singapore for their innovation, business practices and commitment to growing talent.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our leaders have maintained good relations with their US counterparts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The Prime Minister visited the US twice last year while several Cabinet Ministers have visited the US in the past year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have also hosted visits by key members of the Biden Administration and Members of Congress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our security and defence ties with the US go back many decades.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The IPEF will strengthen the US’ regional economic engagement, and is in line with our interests for promoting an open, inclusive, and rules-based world order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore hopes that the IPEF would bring about more tangible economic benefits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: US-Singapore cooperation is also expanding into new frontiers like cybersecurity, digital economy, sustainable development, and even space.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These areas of cooperation reflect the breadth and depth of our bilateral relationship.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: As with the Singapore-China relationship, it is not hard to see how the grounds for Singapore-US cooperation is inseparable from our principled pursuit of regional peace and security, a stable international order, and win-win economic collaboration through trade and investment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This approach is not limited to how we have built up our ties with China and with the US.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We pursue our interests by strengthening and deepening our ties with all countries including the superpowers, middle powers, and our neighbours in the region.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At this point in time, our relations with all countries are very good.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We seek to make friends and keep friends, but above all, we must maintain our standing as an honest broker.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This concept stems from our obligations as a free port, but is also how Singapore seeks to create value for our partners in international affairs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This means doing what we say and saying what we do; not just telling others what they want to hear; and not saying different things to different parties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: At times and on certain issues, we have to be prepared to take a stand and even say “no” to a superpower on the basis of our own national interest.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We do so carefully, after careful analysis of the principles at stake.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We have not been afraid to take a position and make known our views, even where we disagree or what we do displeases others.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Cooperation can also co-exist with differences in values and ideology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The global market and trade in goods and services is one of the broadest mechanisms of cross-border cooperation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: International law is equally important, providing a peaceful avenue for resolving differences and disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There has never been full agreement on all global issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: But differences do not and should not necessarily translate into conflict.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: With a rules-based international order, international cooperation is made possible, with conditions for all countries to trade, do business, and compete peacefully.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Ultimately, these mechanisms depend on trust and respect between the world’s major players.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In theory, global supply chains reflect comparative advantages enjoyed by various economies and promote the rational allocation of resources.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Consumer welfare throughout the world depends on the division of labour between numerous businesses spread over different economies, particularly at a time of rapid innovation in complex technology products.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In a world without mutual trust, national security considerations will fuel suspicions between economies, impacting cross-border division of labour.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This is especially true of dual-use goods, software, and technology.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Hence, international controversies surrounding 5G network equipment, the production of semiconductor chips, and even specific mobile apps have arisen.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: These controversies are extremely difficult to resolve without mutual trust.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: This could cause global supply chains, once tightly integrated, to unravel, to the detriment of all.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It becomes harder for all parties to maintain confidence in multilateralism and globalisation, while nativist sentiments overshadow economic imperatives.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: If major powers treat each other with suspicion, misunderstandings and prejudices will only deepen, and the international order will inevitably be shaken.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The erosion of the foundations of international cooperation would have grave consequences for regional peace and security, a stable international order and economic collaboration – all critical for Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: There will be significant missed opportunities to prosper jointly, and to tackle global problems.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: No amount of balancing would help in such a scenario.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: It would be rather passive to focus on lying low and avoid taking sides.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We want to see the global situation improve and will make efforts towards this.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We will do our part by taking concrete steps to broaden the basis for international cooperation wherever possible.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: In our region of Southeast Asia, Singapore is committed to building an ASEAN-centred regional architecture.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Beyond ASEAN, Singapore has championed and contributed to the rules-based multilateral system, which is key to effective governance of the global commons.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Our success in facilitating the conclusion of these landmark agreements reflects the trust that the international community has in Singapore to play the role of an honest broker, especially at a time when geopolitical rivalries are intensifying.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: We take climate change very seriously as it is an existential issue for a low-lying island like Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: On the economic front, we continue to uphold a free, open and rules-based multilateral trading system as embodied by the World Trade Organization (WTO).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: Singapore participates and takes on leadership roles in these platforms to foster common ground on which countries big and small can work together; to encourage the restoration of strategic trust; and to fortify multilateralism as the way forward to address new challenges and opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: While there are limits to what we can do as a small country, we must act on our conviction on multilateralism and our needs for peace and security and economic development, and do our utmost to broaden the basis for international cooperation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: The effectiveness of a country’s foreign policy rests on the understanding and support it receives from its people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Foreign Affairs and National Development (Ms Sim Ann)
text: I hope that what I have shared would help Singaporeans who care about international affairs gain more insight into what we hope to achieve with diplomacy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Just a quick clarification for the Member Mr Saktiandi Supaat on the comments that he made just now.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I just wanted to ask through you, basically, to put into context.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And similarly, the number of BTO launches has been lower than what it was, say, 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And so, if you look at the demand and supply picture, I think that was consistent in what I have talked about in the last two months.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we look at the affordability that was —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Chua, it is a clarification, not to repeat what you had said earlier.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think if you want to, highlight the seeming discrepancy between what was in the report and what you have said.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: So, essentially, in terms of the report, the private property prices continuing to rise may be seen as a healthy investment opportunity to some.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: But from our national interests, I wonder if Mr Saktiandi would agree that, especially as an economist, if you have house prices not conforming to, in a way, economic norms, whereby with rising interest rates, house prices typically should fall but yet, they continue to be very firm.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis
text: Would that not be a concern from a national interest standpoint versus an investment decision standpoint?

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, I do not think he heard the clarification.

speaker: The Leader of the House (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Perhaps he can respond to Mr Louis Chua later when he comes back.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Before commencing my speech in proper, I would first like to declare that I am a practising lawyer.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The COVID-19 period has taught us that just as businesses must have the business continuity plans, families should create their emergency preparedness plans to deal with unforeseen circumstances, such as losing a financial pillar in the family due to sudden death or terminal illness.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But one group which we should pay particular attention to in this aspect is our seniors.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As shared recently by Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong at the book launch of "Singapore Ageing: Some Issues and Challenges Ahead", our Singapore population is not just ageing, but ageing rapidly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Apart from investing in the appropriate infrastructures in public housing and healthcare, I have shared on several occasions with this House that in my opinion, helping Singaporeans enjoy their golden years with greater peace of mind begins with comprehensive estate planning.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This entails the making of Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) nomination to appoint your desired donee, so that: one, he or she can manage your assets, welfare and affairs, should you become mentally incapacitated one day; two, making of CPF nominations, to make sure that your desired beneficiaries need not wait too long to receive the financial aid which you have left behind through your CPF savings; and thirdly, making of wills, to ensure that your final wishes pertaining to your legacy are respected.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Comprehensive estate planning brings about benefits, not just for your own personal interests, but more particularly, for your loved ones as well, in terms of convenience and saving in costs and time.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Proper planning will eliminate the need to deal with tedious paperwork, while grieving over the sudden unfortunate loss of a loved one at the same time.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Over the years, the Government has worked with relevant agencies and community partners, stepping up its efforts to increase Singaporeans' awareness in this aspect.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For almost a decade, Community Development Councils (CDCs) have been partnering with law society's Pro Bono SG to conduct law awareness weeks to educate residents on basic legal knowledge through legal talks conducted across the five districts at various community centres (CCs) and residents' committee centres (RCs).

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The talks tailored for those who are not legally trained, are easily digestible and ensure that attendees are equipped with basic legal knowledge, which will come in useful in times of need.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This is, in fact, the fifth extension since its first extension in 2016, as an effort to encourage more Singaporeans to plan ahead and apply for an LPA.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But despite these efforts, the take-up rates of Singaporeans making comprehensive estate planning remain less than the majority.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: I had the opportunity to speak to several seniors during one of the recent law awareness talks organised by our Woodgrove PAP Branch, where our young PAP volunteers who are legally trained, took the opportunity to explain the importance of doing an LPA and walk residents through the process of registering for it.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: One shared with me that she can understand the importance of doing an LPA, but she hoped that she can sit on this issue for as long as possible, and that "touch wood", she will never need to rely on it.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Another couple whom I have spoken to shared that they will not want to trouble their working children to sign the papers as they are all very busy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While I respect their opinions on the matter, it may be that they are simply kicking the can down the road.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Just as what Minister Masagos has shared in his speech yesterday, I concurred that Government policies should be deemed as enablers.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As policymakers, there is a need for us to be proactive because we know we need to identify issues early before they snowball into larger issues for Singaporeans in need.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As such, I think that perhaps the real way to resolve the problem that the seniors and their families may face subsequently, is not to just encourage them to do an LPA now, but to look at how their immediate next-of-kin can assume the responsibility and power to manage their affairs more quickly, without the need to go through a stringent deputyship Court application, should the day come when one becomes mentally incapacitated before an LPA has been made.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Notwithstanding, while the FJC has now offered a simplified deputyship application, the process is still viewed as cumbersome and costly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Moreover, consent of immediate family members and relevant persons will need to be sought.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In such instances, these requirements often cause more dispute among family members.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Siblings or distant relatives of the bedridden patient may feel that the applicants, such as the spouse of the patient, should not be the appointed deputy.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This cumbersome procedure may not eventually even lead to a desired outcome, as sometimes, the patient might have passed away halfway through the application.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have to find ways to lighten their burdens and worries, especially when they have to deal with onerous legal procedures.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: (In English): In closing, Mr Speaker, I wish to quote an abstract of a speech by Minister Mentor Lee Kuan Yew at one of the National Day Celebration Dinners which he attended in 2009. "We have done well for the last 50 years since 1959.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We overcame many difficulties in the early years from 1961 to 1965.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: After we achieved the steady growth in the mid-1970s, we met setbacks.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We overcame them because, together as a people, we faced our difficulties squarely and worked together to resolve them.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Had we evaded the problems, hoping that they would go away, we would have failed.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore is likely to do well in the next five to 10 years.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We can reach a new level of development, but difficulties will crop up and we must always face them squarely, work together and resolve them."
