Fast forward to today, nearly 14 years since the late Minister Mentor made his speech, we went through his departure, the COVID-19 pandemic and many economic and geopolitical uncertainties, but I am glad and heartened that we have overcome these challenges and will continue to overcome future challenges with the leadership of the People's Action Party (PAP) Government who do not evade problems ahead but face them squarely, working hand in hand with fellow Singaporeans to resolve them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Before I touch on my two points, I would like to respond to Mr Faisal Manap's speech earlier.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   In his speech, he said that one of the characteristics of good democracy is that we must be able to agree to disagree.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I agree with that, and I respect that because among the PAP Members of Parliament (MPs), there are also differences in opinions with one another.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: On the issue of the repeal of section 377A and strengthening the definition of family, each Workers’ Party (WP) member took a different position based on the principle of “agreeing to disagree”.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The debate on section 377A was a very sensitive one.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A leader’s responsibility is not just about opening up space for disagreement.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We are also responsible for uniting people with different opinions, move forward and not become divided.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is not just about them expressing different opinions.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Therefore, although I agree with what he said about “agree to disagree”, that is simply half of the truth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: After debating, we make the best decision to enable everyone to move forward.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Not to become divided but to stay united.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Nonetheless, the most glaring point is not about an incomplete principle.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In his speech, I did not hear him highlight an equally important principle in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is the principle of integrity and honesty – honesty to the Parliament, to the people and to the nation.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): I would like to come back to my speech and touch on my two points.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Allow me to elaborate on my first point, which I have shared in previous speeches.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore faces challenges in maintaining global competitiveness due to geopolitical uncertainties, such as the ongoing war in Ukraine and the rivalry between the US and China, which can impact global trade and economic growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Major powers prioritising their own advantage instead of promoting interdependence and multilateralism also pose a challenge to Singapore's position in the global economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The high labour cost in Singapore and high inflation globally have increased the cost of doing business.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, the tight labour market has made it challenging for businesses to attract and retain talent, posing a significant challenge for many industries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These challenges, along with existing cost pressures, make it more expensive for businesses to operate in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Furthermore, the US and other countries are offering aggressive tax breaks and subsidies to attract investments and revitalising their domestic manufacturing, which poses competition for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To remain globally competitive, Singapore must reposition itself and find new opportunities amid economic headwinds.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This requires being nimble and agile, responding quickly to new challenges and seeking new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Staying united and working together is key, with the Government nudging businesses in the right direction but not fostering a sense of dependency.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses must be willing to pivot and transform, workers must upskill and retrain, and unions must work together to seek opportunities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the era of disruptive innovation with artificial intelligence (AI), Industry 4.0, and new business models, stakeholders must focus on working together to maximise opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They should focus on improving productivity, attaining new capabilities and driving best value instead of depressing wages to remain competitive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses and workers must work together to remain agile.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Businesses must invest in developing talent and skills, unlocking new areas of growth.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Wage growth must be accompanied by productivity growth, otherwise, it will just increase the cost of doing business, leading to less competitive businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There will be times that despite productivity improvements, we must be being prepared to pivot, change business models or exit non-competitive businesses.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To avoid structural unemployment due to skills mismatch, workers must also be comfortable and confident to retrain seamlessly into growing industries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To navigate the economic headwinds, Singapore needs to stay united and work together between the Government, business, unions and workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The tripartite partnership between the Ministry, the unions and employers is unique and must be leveraged.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is thus essential to strengthen the tripartite alliance to avoid the breakdown of trust and disastrous consequences seen in other countries.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have shown much care and compassion to each other, acting as concerned citizens helping one another in the face of incredible adversity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should not let this deepened unity dissipate with the decreased threat of the pandemic and instead, we should harness to expand opportunities for all citizens at every significant stage of life.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To ensure equity, we need to mitigate the negative impact of meritocracy by prioritising the distribution of need, where the less well-off gets added resource and support to help them.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We must also re-evaluate how we value skills and qualities beyond academic achievements, such that those more skilled with their hands or who are empathetic and employed in community service are also equally rewarded.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Providing multiple pathways to success will be key to fulfilling every citizen's potential and moving away from an education arms race.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Let us value pursuits beyond paper qualifications and ease the pressure and stress on our young.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have started on a journey of creating equal opportunities long ago and though there is much more that we can do, we have made significant progress in gender equality.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to do more to support these individuals and ensure that they have access to opportunities to fully participate in society and contribute to the economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our seniors, persons with disabilities and special needs workers still face an uphill task in finding meaningful employment and opportunities to contribute to the economy.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have heard much anecdotal evidence – stories shared by our residents – that the opportunity a senior felt that they have was in the conservancy or cleaning industry, which requires long hours on their feet and physical work, is to their disadvantage.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This could possibly be due to several limiting factors such as literacy and digital literacy among our current senior workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, our next generation of seniors in the next 10 years will be more literate and more digitally capable.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to prepare them for future reemployment.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we then design jobs and leverage on remote working so that our future senior workers will have even more opportunities?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Similarly, how do we redesign jobs and leverage on remote and flexible work arrangements so that we can provide opportunities for persons with disabilities, caregivers and back-to-work mothers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Malay):   The COVID-19 experience has taught us the importance of staying united, believing in one another regardless of differences and working together as a community to overcome challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Over the past two years, at M3@Pasir Ris-Punggol, our volunteers have conducted many programmes such as Get-Together at Pasir Ris-Punggol where more than 1,000 families participated in a children's games festival, and among others, held the KelasMatematika programme to help preschool children by developing their basic mathematical skills.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Each month, the M3@Pasir Ris-Punggol volunteers also distributed care packs to underprivileged families.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They also conducted a Back-To-School programme where around 160 children from underprivileged families have been given bags, stationery and joined Mathematics classes and the Mendaki Tuition Scheme.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: M3@Pasir Ris-Punggol also held a Learning Journey series to encourage youths to explore careers in the engineering and 3D-printing industries, as well as the #HashTech hackathon, where students had the opportunity to enhance digital and cybersecurity skills from tech professionals.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These programmes were implemented with the support of volunteers, agencies like Majilis Ugama Islam Singapore (MUIS), Malay Activity Executive Committees Councils (MESRA) and Mendaki, as well as industry partners.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our social compact is about society understanding how we communicate and support each other.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It reflects our values where it is not only about self-interest but also about the interests of the community.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I urge individuals who have made it to give back to the community so that we can further uplift our community especially those less fortunate.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, Sir, the past three years have taught us the importance of staying united, trusting one another regardless of differences, and working together as a society to overcome challenges, no matter how hard it can be.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have seen how in other countries issues can be divisive and societies fall apart with deep divides that will take generations to mend.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have learnt that by staying united, trusting one another, we are able to overcome challenges and emerge strongly as a more closely-knit society having gone through adversity together.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our shared understanding of how we relate to and support one another will be critical in shaping our future.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While we shape our social compact, it is important to avoid creating a culture of dependence on the Government and, instead, we work collaboratively as we tackle the challenges ahead.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Since the launch of the first Masterplan in 2007, we have made good progress in areas, such as early intervention, education, our built environment, public transport, assistive technology and societal norms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But clearly, however, more needs to be done.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: After the launch of EMP2030, two task forces looking into “alternative employment models” and “independent community living” were set up.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Be that as it may, I am dedicating my speech today to persons with disabilities, to speak about some of the challenges they still face today, to keep disability-inclusion on the agenda of Singapore society and suggest how we can do better, collectively.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For the central ideas I am going to mention in this speech, I owe a vote of thanks to a few individuals, namely, Karthik, Kelvin, Sze Wee and Judy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We often speak of persons with disabilities as though it were one homogeneous population made up of individuals with similar needs and common challenges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Let us take a moment to try to imagine what our world might be like if we were autistic, visually impaired or if we had lost the function of our limbs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: The onset of disability can be congenital, traumatic – as in the case of traffic accidents – or progressive, as in muscular dystrophy, to describe just a few possible trajectories.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Consequently, service provision in the disability sector demands a keen eye for detail, as diversity is the order of the day.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: How disability-inclusive a society is can be defined by how well we understand and appreciate the diverse nature of the disability sector and, by extension, how our policies and programmes are designed to cater for the multitude of needs and challenges across disability types and spectra.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: First is the adoption of a case management approach.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In the course of their lives, a person with disabilities will interact with support services across different domains, including education, healthcare, employment and social support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: A young child with disability typically receives a diagnosis in our hospitals, is referred for services in the early intervention centres and may go on to mainstream or special schools.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In his or her adult life, he or she may receive services from employment support programmes, day activity centres or residential homes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Depending on specific healthcare needs, he or she may concurrently receive healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: To ensure that persons with disabilities can access the support they need in a seamless manner, transition coordination is paramount.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This can be achieved with an effective case coordinator or manager.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: So, in this case, a case manager is needed for this group to continue to support the young adult with disability and his family members.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For example, the case manager could (a) help navigate the various agencies and systems these young adults are interacting with because of their multiple health, behavioural, employment and/or social care needs; (b) support them to access the necessary support services and grants based on their needs; and (c) connect them and their caregivers to others in the community and enable their meaningful participation and prevent social isolation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Second, we need to recognise that the condition of a person with disabilities does not remain static throughout his or her lifetime.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: In addition to strengthening case management for persons with disabilities in the post-18 space, we should also adopt a more continual and holistic approach towards assessing and understanding their specific support needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We cannot solely assess their needs at specific, pre-determined milestones, such as when they graduate from school.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Instead, we must review their support needs throughout their lives, as these needs will change from the time they finish school through their adult and, finally, senior years.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For example, a person with disabilities’ health condition and level of functioning may change as they age, requiring a different intensity of medical support and personal care services; their work support needs may change, too, as they transit to different types of jobs across their career; or their social and emotional support needs may change as caregivers age and family circumstances evolve with time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We should empower disability service providers, case managers and befrienders to adopt a more person-centric approach, one where they listen to the person with disabilities and their family members, understand their changing needs and support them in navigating the various services they may need to enable them to live independently and continue participating in the life of their home, workplace and community.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We should also consider how we can provide more integrated support for PwDs across the health and social sectors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: For example, some PwDs need a whole range of home-based services, such as therapy to maintain their physical and mental well-being, personal care services to assist with activities of daily living, such as showering, and befriending and social activities to reduce social isolation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Today, some of these services are provided by healthcare providers, whilst others are provided by social service agencies.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Persons with disabilities and their families must navigate a complex web of multiple service providers across different domains.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: We should simplify this system to provide more coordinated, holistic home-based services for those who need them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Similarly, we should also consider how disability services such as Day Activity Centres and Adult Disability Homes can better meet both the social and health needs of the persons with disabilities they serve simultaneously, such as by providing nursing or therapy services in these centres based on clients’ needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: This would improve the support for adults with physical or multiple disabilities who experience mobility issues and may find it challenging to travel to other facilities just for healthcare services.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Applying the same logic of strengthening the social-health integration, we could also consider how our financial assistance schemes can be more integrated for adults with disabilities, especially across the health and social sectors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: Of course, we must study this in detail and ensure that any such move is financially sustainable.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: But I raise this as an example of how we should consider more integrated social-health support for persons with disabilities and their families, approaching policies from a more person-centric lens.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Minister for Social and Family Development (Mr Eric Chua)
text: There is broad acknowledgement among them that we have come a long way since the first Enabling Masterplan in 2007.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Indeed, it is affordable because of the Government policies.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, do you want to respond?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Speaker, I just want to reiterate again, same points.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But as the saying goes, "Courage is what it takes to stand up and speak; courage is also what it takes to sit down and listen".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And so, in the past eight years, I have also listened.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have listened to painful stories of injustice, discrimination, stigma and hurt.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have shared these stories in this House because we should not be a nation focused only on hardware.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As important is the software and the heartware that I spoke about in my maiden speech in this House.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Those are the things that make, as President Halimah said in her speech, a Singapore "where we care for and help one another, and pitch in to make a difference to our community".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the past eight years, I have also seen so much positive change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen how the impossible can be made possible when the Government and civil society work hand in hand. "Nothing is impossible, miracles take time".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That was what was drilled into me during my NSF days and indeed, nothing is impossible if we do not give up and if we persist.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor recently commended me for my persistence and so I shall persist.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this second session of the 14th Parliament, I will continue to speak up from my heart about issues that matter.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will continue to speak up for a more equal and just society where heartware matters.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I will also continue to speak up for giving our people the most valuable thing of all – time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Every Budget, this House debates how our Government should spend its money to support Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Every Budget, I have stressed that we cannot just give money; we also need to give time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my Budget speeches in the past three years, I have spoken up for teachers, social workers and most recently, nurses.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They build the heartware of this nation by helping others.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But they need time to help themselves too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I spoke up about how we can provide more support to them so that they can help others better.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But not only do our teachers, social workers and nurses need more time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Surveys after surveys show that we are one of the most overworked cities in the world, one of the most fatigued countries, one of the most stressful cities, and one of the worst when it comes to work-life balance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do believe it is time for us to seriously rethink our policies when it comes to work-life balance; time for a reset.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know I sound like a broken record again but these are important things that will help countless people.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: President Halimah spoke about wanting a society that values and supports families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us give people the time to spend with their loved ones for a start.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I recognise that the Government is looking into work-life harmony and balance.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know we have the Tripartite Standards on Work-Life Harmony and we will soon have the Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Before COVID-19, many of us in this House fought hard for legislating the right to flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We were told that we could not legislate this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It took a pandemic to show that work from home is possible.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We aggressively shared how work from home benefits everyone – employers, employees and the whole of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It benefited our transport system, healthcare system and even addressed gender equality.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The right to work from home benefited so many people, including one mother who messaged me last week saying: "Flexibility to work from home has been so crucial in terms of being able to send my daughter to school, given that I commute from Canberra to Jurong Island and don't own a car like many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, work from home allows me to work out during lunch hour without sacrificing time with my child and elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Without this, I would definitely be neglecting my health in favour of family time and chores.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I genuinely believe work from home enables a happier society and will facilitate Singapore's move towards being the sort of family-oriented, health-conscious society we want to be.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is especially crucial given the ageing population we expect, and the increasing burden on the working generation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is not just about having time to support children and elderly parents for appointments or events but having time to form foundational emotional bonds to build strong families across generations".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: That really sums up the importance of the right to work from home and I could not have said it better.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We made great progress during the pandemic when it came to working from home.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We repealed the work from home legislation and plan to only introduce guidelines on flexible work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, it is strange that the penalty under the guidelines for not providing FWAs would be to curtail a company's Work Pass privileges.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If you do not give your employees FWAs, you cannot hire foreigners.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am not asking that we make work from home compulsory.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Employers can still require employees to be in the office for specific business-related reasons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will truly help in the work-life harmony we are all fighting for.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We know through many surveys that people want this right.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should listen to the calls and provide this to help reduce the stress and fatigue in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have spoken up about this many times in this House.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How many of us sitting here would want only seven days of annual leave?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many other countries in this region provide a higher minimum number of annual leave including Malaysia, Bangladesh, Japan, Myanmar, East Timor, Sri Lanka, Laos, Mongolia, South Korea, Qatar, Yemen, Iran, Kuwait and Indonesia and many more.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many of these countries not only have more days of annual leave, they also have a higher number of paid public holidays.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Last week, one netizen shared with me: "I'm honestly shocked that seven days is the minimum annual leave we have.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have 15 days from an MNC and that's the least I've ever had.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While we don't have to be as generous as European countries, really seven is embarrassing for a developed country that seeks to allow for its citizens to find some semblance of balance outside of work, for a more sustainable workforce if we need to be pragmatic." I do understand that we need to balance this carefully against what businesses can sustain.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we have an overworked workforce and we need to sustain our workforce too.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our people will always work hard to top global rankings in all industries.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But let us make sure we do not top the ranking of the being most overworked city in the world.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As President Halimah said, "We want every person to be treated equally with dignity and respect." And "we want to reaffirm the core values that we hold dear as Singaporeans – fairness and inclusivity." As we work hard to ensure a less stressful environment for workers, we also need to make it less stressful for women, for breastfeeding mothers and single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I repeat my calls to make sure our policies are inclusive for them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my speech on the Motion of thanks to the President in 2020, I called for more inclusive workplaces for women.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad we are making good progress on this by having workplace discrimination laws.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have two further suggestions on how we should further tackle discrimination and be more inclusive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In my Adjournment Motion for breastfeeding mothers, I described the shame and discrimination they face at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These mothers are only trying to feed their children, but they are shamed and discriminated against by their co-workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: A nurse who had recently returned to work after her maternity leave shared with me last week that her managers asked her three times on separate occasions to pump in the toilet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When she mentioned that it is not hygienic or sanitary, she was shocked to have them reply saying that other mothers have been pumping in the toilet "all these while".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She was appalled by the lack of empathy, understanding and even the sense of basic hygiene.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should ensure that the proposed workplace discrimination law will cover the discrimination breastfeeding mothers face at work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: President Halimah spoke about how "no one should feel left behind".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As we work hard to ensure that we strengthen protections against workplace discrimination, the Government should take the lead and ensure that our own policies do not result in any discrimination and that single unwed parents do not feel left behind.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For single unwed parents, we know our policies do discriminate and we really should change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After many decades of discrimination in our housing policies against single unwed parents, I am glad they now have fair access to public housing.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In 2019, I shared the story of Ema, a single unwed mother.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ema came to see me to appeal for a rental flat.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: She brought with her a letter from her baby's doctor stating: "As she – the baby – is currently staying in a shelter, she is frequently in contact with other residents who are unwell and hence predisposed to recurrent infection.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, it will be greatly appreciated if her application for the HDB rental flat can be expedited." Ema told me that she was not asking for sympathy and was simply looking for a roof over her head and her baby's head.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I appealed to the Housing and Development Board (HDB) to allow her to rent a flat and I am glad the appeal was successful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: HDB replied that: "We are pleased to inform you that we have obtained special approval for you to rent a 1-room flat with your daughter on compassionate grounds." Since I shared her story, Ema has been living in a rental flat with her daughter who has grown to be a happy, bubbly and, most importantly, healthy child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I raised that we are stigmatising single unweds and their children when we tell them that they can only get a roof over their heads through special approvals on compassionate grounds.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that HDB has since updated its website to make clear that single unwed parents can approach HDB for assistance with their rental housing applications.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just last month, a HDB officer told me how HDB is actually not the Housing and Development Board but actually the “好心” Board or, translated into English, the "Good-Hearted Board".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have seen HDB officers with big hearts, like Bee Lan and Jeffrey from the HDB Yishun Branch, and Zing, who heads HDB's Rental Housing Department.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I was recently asked in this House whether I want more single unwed parents.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Imagine being a single unwed parent or a child of a single unwed parent, watching the debate at home and hearing those words.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Imagine a child wondering whether Mummy is wrong for being a single unwed parent.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Speaker, in a couple of years, or 843 days, Singapore will celebrate her 60th, our Diamond Jubilee.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is easy to say from where we stand that we have achieved, but we should not forget the difficult journey and the tough decisions taken to be where we are today.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Many from our Pioneer and Merdeka generations, the generation of our parents and our grandparents did not have the same opportunities we have today.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At that time, infrastructure was basic, resources were limited and many of that generation made deliberate sacrifices to give up their education early to work, not because they were uninterested.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They sacrificed their progression so that a brother or a sister had the money to go to school and enough money for food, to survive.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They did so, so that their brothers and sisters could have a better life despite their own detriment.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Two volunteers recollected an incident when they responded to a community distress call recently.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: An elderly lady in her 80s had a suspected cardiac event and needed CPR.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: They did their best to keep her ventilated and the AED was ready.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The ambulance soon arrived and she was taken to hospital.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As the two volunteers spoke to the granddaughter, they could not help but notice that the elderly lady's home was full of family photographs.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: On the wall were the photographs of many of her grandchildren who were university graduates in their graduation garbs – a proud legacy for the family.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Her children did well and her grandchildren did even better.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In Singapore, in two generations, the entire family was uplifted.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This elderly lady is the epitome and paragon of that generation that enabled us, with much certainty, for us to celebrate our Diamond Jubilee.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: The world today faces a myriad of challenges unprecedented in scale and complexity.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We now face increasing geopolitical tensions, the challenge of climate change and rising global economic uncertainties ahead.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Domestically, our ageing population is one of our gravest concerns.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To put it into context, our boomer generation had an annual birth of about 60,000.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: And because of this ageing population, we must be mindful of our future economic survival and competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We will need to accelerate our pace of innovation and technology, drive growth and create new industries.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Our institutions must continue to evolve and remain relevant and trusted.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must maintain our skills and capabilities, connectivity and modern infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must remain open to trade and investment and maintain our strength and ambition through a strong entrepreneurship culture.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Singapore has faced several existential challenges since Independence with much fewer resources.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Since then, we have progressed from strength to strength in a continuous journey of nation-building.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: As we look ahead, we must build a clear vision for our future and imagine what our country and our society would look like.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How should we Singaporeans work together to overcome the challenges of today and work towards our future?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Most certainly, in our minds, this vision must be inspiring, ambitious and achievable.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How do we empower, steward, equip, care, build and unite for our future?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: At its core, it is about building a strong national identity and promoting social cohesion among citizens.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It requires the active participation of individuals and communities at all levels of society, from Government leaders, industries, voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs), grassroots organisations and every citizen.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: All of us Singaporeans can contribute to nation-building.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This includes being an active and engaged citizen, participating in community events and initiatives, volunteering and providing resources to help others and supporting policies and programmes that promote the common good.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How can we help one another take the next step forward through mentoring, volunteering, helping a colleague improve, training junior staff, caring for a neighbour, helping an industry partner become more competitive or partnering a local competitor to win larger overseas projects?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: How can we collectively push our nation forward?

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: We must work together and empower one another.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: This means setting aside our differences and working towards a shared vision for a better future for all citizens.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It also means investing in education, innovation and infrastructure to create a strong and competitive economy that can provide opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It starts with us – individuals and then families, communities and then inspiring others to do more.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Every Singaporean plays a vital role in nation-building.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To our seniors, we want our seniors to be able to live longer and healthier lives, one that is filled with meaningful social interaction, where our seniors can continue to be relevant and, to the best of their abilities, continue to contribute to society and the community.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Many of them are experienced and have much to give back.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Above all, we want them to be valued members throughout life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: It is a precious and worthy intangible achievement, probably moving from lifelong learning to lifelong teaching.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: But fear not, for you are not alone.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: There is strength in our Singapore collective and our community.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: In unison, like a tug of war, we will drag, we will push, we will pull, with a full heart and full effort and, collectively, we will help one another achieve a full and meaningful life.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: To Singaporeans and Team Singapore, we strive for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Yes, a rising tide can lift all boats, but remember that we are all on the same ship, whatever the tide.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: If the waves are relentless, we must be able to submerge and explore below the choppy waves.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Where there is no water and we have run aground, we must hover and fly.

speaker: Mr Shawn Huang Wei Zhong (Jurong)
text: Let us all work together to build our nation and home for future generations.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: She emphasised the importance of inclusiveness, the need for a refreshed social compact and, regardless of our different backgrounds, the support for one another in our next phase of nationhood.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To be inclusive, the Government must consider the needs of different groups of Singaporeans in their policies and implementation of social programmes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Policies related to housing, caregiving and taxation are causing a divide that favours married Singaporeans more than singles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This policy bias has created growing dissatisfaction among singles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Given the change in lifestyle priorities, singlehood has scaled up to around 30% of Singapore’s population.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Broadly speaking, for every Singaporean couple, there is a Singaporean single.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This percentage will continue to be more prevalent.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The proportion of singles in the age groups below 50 years old has increased and the rise is higher among those below 35.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: An inclusive society like Singapore should not allow any group, let alone such a significant group, to feel left out in contrast to their married siblings, friends or colleagues simply because of their marital status.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Like married individuals, singles work and contribute at workplaces, in communities and take care of their families.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They must not be left to feel disengaged, disappointed or even disenchanted.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If we do not look into taking better care of this group of Singaporeans, they may well decide to work overseas or even migrate altogether once after their parents pass away.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope that as a society, we can better appreciate Singaporeans who choose to remain single.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singles contribute to society and they should be provided equal support from the Government and the community.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They, too, will need help to cope with the challenges that are more particularly felt by being single.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There are three pertinent aspects that we should highlight, namely, caregiving for parents, ageing with support and advance care planning.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: At a certain old age, regular visits to the doctors, frequent hospitalisation or taking care of health conditions that require 24/7 care, such as advanced dementia, is inevitable.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With our rapidly greying population, longer life expectancies and smaller families, caregiving duties for elderly parents typically land on singles.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Most singles will stay with their parents if their siblings are married with kids.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This is seen as the right thing to do.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There are even some who decide to remain single so that they can be caregivers and take care of their ailing parents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These caregiving responsibilities require substantial time off work.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Often, the health conditions of both parents may deteriorate at the same time, doubling the caregiving load.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Not all employees in Singapore get extra leave to care for their parents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some companies may provide a few days of caregiving leave but this will not suffice if the elderly parent suffers from chronic illnesses.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Often times, the caregiver will have to use their annual leave or even apply for unpaid leave to care for their parents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The lower-income groups will tend to face more challenges because most are unable to afford additional resources such as domestic help.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Should the caregiver be an unmarried sole breadwinner, he or she will have to continue working while attending to the ailing parents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Having time off for medical appointments and caregiving leave for ailing parents is much needed for singles who are also primary caregivers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Malay):   Not all workers in Singapore get additional leave to look after their parents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Companies in Singapore are required to provide maternity leave, paternity leave, childcare leave and unpaid infant care leave but not family leave, parental care leave or eldercare leave.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Some companies may give a few days of caregiving leave but this is not enough if the elderly parents of the workers suffer from chronic diseases.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Usually, the caregivers have no choice but to use their annual leave or apply for no-pay leave to take care of their elderly parents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The lower-income group will face more challenges as most of them cannot afford additional resources such as domestic help.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If the caregiver is the sole breadwinner who is still single, he or she must continue to work while taking care of his or her frail parents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Having leave for medical appointments and leave to take care of elderly parents who are unwell will be a boon for unmarried caregivers who are also the primary caregivers.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: This benefit will likewise apply to married individuals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Most singles end up living alone upon retirement and after their parents pass on.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Divorced and widowed individuals may also live on their own.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There will be more and more seniors staying alone.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: HDB has embarked on assisted living facilities in December 2020, such as the pilot Community Care Apartments in Bukit Batok.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It is only 32 square metres and will not solve the concerns of the singles as many seniors will still eventually end up staying alone after their spouses pass on.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We could consider developing spaces for three to four singles living together comfortably.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: These could be leased apartments catered for senior citizens who live alone.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To make it work, single seniors could have the option to sell their own properties and invest in such a retirement co-living space.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must provide the support for these single seniors to age well and allow them to enjoy their time together with their flat mates.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They could be playing mahjong games, growing plants, cooking or whatever.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: To add, the co-living flat mates can also help to look out for one another, especially during medical emergencies and request for assistance in a timely manner.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The lease could include basic service package comprising cleaning, cooking, marketing and emergency response services.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Services could be outsourced to private senior care operators.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: That way, a group of singles can have the option to stay together and take care of one another in their golden years.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Other than securing a roof over their head, singles may also be concerned about securing their finances.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In particular, the elderly are more likely to be vulnerable and exploited by scammers and other criminals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They may be preyed upon their confusion due to new technology.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We do not have to reinvent the wheel.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: In fact, we can tap on current infrastructure, such as the CPF and accredited insurance companies, which are members of the Policy Owners' Protection Scheme under the Singapore Deposit Insurance Corporation.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: With economies of scale, the trust arrangement fees can be kept quite low.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In Mandarin):   During the final phase in life, many singles may be concerned that they do not have people whom they trust to assist them in preparing for their final days.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: For instance, they may need help with their Lasting Power of Attorney (LPA) for decisions to be made should they lose their mental capacity.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: They would also need guidance and advice to lodge their medical care preferences through an Advance Care Planning (ACP) session as well as Advance Medical Directive at recognised healthcare institutions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: End of life discussions pertaining to tube-feeding and Voluntarily Stop Eating and Drinking (VSED) may be made in advance with qualified medical practitioners and counsellors.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Many may require assistance to review their CPF nominations and draw up or review their wills.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: If these singles do not have children, they can contribute their assets to benefit the community after they have passed on.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: (In English): Social programmes are essential to create community ties and to keep our singles deeply rooted to Singapore.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Singapore has to be a place that is attractive, accessible and affordable for our seniors, so that they can live their final years comfortably.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Involvement in community work will help singles feel more connected; friends, family and neighbours give them a purpose to stay on and contribute to their homeland.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: I hope the Ministry of Community, Culture and Youth (MCCY) can work with the PA and VWOs to attract more singles to participate in community work.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: There are many programmes that are designed to engage families with young children, but singles may feel they do not fit in and are not keen to be a part of such programmes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We must review our social policies to ensure that singles are not left out.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: While we encourage people to get married and have more children, pro-family and single-supportive policies need not be mutually exclusive.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Whether you are single or married, we are all part of a Singapore family.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We do what we can to take care of our siblings and elderly parents.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: We would not want our well-resourced singles who do not have close relatives anymore, retiring in countries like Australia, New Zealand or Canada.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Let us make everyone feel more included and rooted, with an equal stake in Singapore’s future.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In my maiden parliamentary speech, I spoke about engendering and ensuring the collective and holistic well-being and happiness of our people.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This remains a key thrust of my efforts as a Member of Parliament (MP).

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I thus resonate with the important points made by Mdm President in the Opening of Parliament for the second half of this Government term.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we continue to transit from the COVID-19 pandemic, with a purposeful and comprehensive legislative agenda ahead, I would like to speak on three "M"s that are close to my heart.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Not the usual three "M"s debated in this House, but important three "M"s that I will champion to further contribute to building a better Singapore for all.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through the new Jalan Kayu Community Health Club opened in February, our grassroots leaders partner our regional Central Health system, anchored by Tan Tock Seng Hospital, and the general practitioner (GP) clinics in the neighbourhood to increase health screening awareness and disease management knowledge among our residents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Through the corporate social responsibility (CSR) sponsorship of smart watches, we empower our residents to know and monitor their health better.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we are starting with physical health and common chronic conditions like high blood pressure, high cholesterol and high blood sugar in line with the national Healthier SG roll-out in the next few months, we will also be looking out for the mental health and wellness of our residents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Slightly more than one life a day and one too many lives lost.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We need to equip more parents with the basic mental health knowledge and skills to help their children and youths when they are going through mental distress beyond normal levels.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In super-ageing societies, such as Japan and South Korea, increasing age is associated with increasing depressive symptoms, largely due to poor physical health status and lack of extended family networks.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With our fast-ageing population and increase in seniors living alone or only with another senior, we too must be alert to these issues.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While early efforts like the National Mental Health Blueprint in 2006, the Community Mental Health Masterplan in 2012 and most recently, the Interagency Taskforce on Mental Health and Well-being in 2021, have all worked towards expanding psychiatric programs and shifting towards more community-based care to increase accessibility to mental health support, the most recent spike in mental health concerns during the COVID-19 pandemic indicated further transformation required in the delivery of mental health services and support, especially for our young and old at the early risk or onset stages of mental health struggles.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Walking into a GP clinic is way less intimidating than walking into a psychiatric section of a hospital for most parents, children, youths, young adults and seniors.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most GPs have the basic training but as common mental illnesses, such as depression and anxiety, are more complex to treat than coughs and cold, many GPs need refresher training, specialists’ peer consultation, teaming with counsellors and higher subsidies for the longer consultations usually needed.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Two, by enabling simple-to-use, clinical evidence-based and privacy preserving technology to augment prescription of medicines by GPs and specialists.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Innovations like Cognitive Behavioural Therapy Based AI chatbots, to provide lower cost counselling, has been progressing worldwide.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More can be done to insert these tools to the medical-social team for integrated care of medicine and counselling at a lower cost for patients.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: And three, by empowering more in the community, including parents, students and grassroots volunteers, with mental health first-aid skills.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I will be piloting “Be a Samaritan (BAS) Programme” by SOS in my constituency soon.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is a two-part programme with a one-hour e-learning and a two-hour physical role-playing workshop, which will teach participants the basic skills to be first responders to those facing mental crisis, suicide ideation, or affected by suicide.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that more support can be provided to proliferate such skills in the community, like the way we have been training grassroots leaders in Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation (CPR) or Automated External Defibrillator (AED).

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I agree with Mdm President that Singapore must not allow advantages and privileges to become entrenched and persist over generations in a small group.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To broaden and make more open the idea of meritocracy, it will require conscious efforts from the whole of society, not just the Government.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Young people today continue to have high aspirations and expectations.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: According to IPS’ “Future of Work Singaporeans Want” survey conducted in October 2022, young people are more likely to value growth, learning and career advancement to job security.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In another survey published by TODAY Online in 2022, it was found that although fresh graduates are landing in full-time jobs with higher median salaries and better-than-expected starting pay, those between 21 and 34 expressed lower upward mobility compared to older respondents.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is intertwined with the global macro-economic challenges and competitive realities that our young Singaporeans face.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that corporate and business leaders can do more in mentoring our young people.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Among the many lessons I learned, one that stood out for me was how their older people were willing to mentor all younger ones.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was told that this has been their survival instinct through the generations, so that as many of their people can continue to succeed as possible despite the Jewish Diaspora and traumatic persecutions their people experienced through history, like the Holocaust in World War II.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are a small nation where our people are our most precious asset.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have our collective memory, formed in our fight for independence and national hood, shaped by threats and opportunities of larger countries and regional powers around us, often outnumbered in size, but not in the will to survive and thrive.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Singapore business sector can proliferate a stronger culture of mentoring.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Personally, I enjoy mentoring and will be formally or informally mentoring several younger people between five and 25 years younger than me in a year.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I learned about the Australian Business and Community Network or ABCN for short recently at the inaugural Singapore Volunteer Management Conference.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The CEOs know that education is crucial for lifting young Australians out of disadvantage and partner almost 200 schools to empower students through a structured mentoring by volunteers at all levels from companies in the network.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope to see such collaborative mentoring model replicated and scaled by the business community in Singapore too.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, on the tough but rewarding role that I most value, being a mother.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have never regarded having children as a duty but a joy.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Whether by natural delivery or by adoption, parenting teaches us many things in life beyond self.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there remains a gap in Singapore for young people who aspire to be married to do so, and for young couples desiring children to have them.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: During my Budget speech earlier this year, I recommended for more upstream and local resources to enable social interactions among our young people.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I was involved in a REACH-Friendzone Conversations @Me event in my constituency recently.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While it is certainly not a dating platform, the interactions and sharing were most authentic among the participants, majority of whom are 26 to 30 years old.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many said they could come after a long day work, because the get-together was near their homes.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am a firm believer that an authentic friendship is the foundation of any enduring relationships, sometimes leading to marriage like for me.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This event would have been a one-off if not for a kind sponsorship I personally obtained to plan more sessions in the months ahead.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government would consider empowering MPs with more funding support to regularise such thoughtful local social interactions opportunities for our young people in our constituencies.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For sandwiched dual-income families, caregiving of both elderly parents and young children can add to further burden.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As such, besides financial incentives, I hope that the Government will continue to press in on the tripartite approach, to implement more physio-social support and flexible work arrangements for more employees in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even in positions like frontline service staff and intense workplaces like in the healthcare, legal and financial sectors, where flexible working arrangements seem difficult today, I think bolder human resource policies, including employing slightly above establishments to cater for peaks and surges must be trialed to manage work stress, especially for our younger couples.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, I would like to thank the President for the speech which she delivered on behalf of the Government.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope to raise three suggestions here to contribute to a better Singapore.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: First, in view of our high-stress society and an aging population, I hope the Government can speed up the delivery options for treatment and support of mental illnesses.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Currently, psychiatric illnesses are primarily treated by psychiatrists or psychologists in hospital psychiatric wards.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I believe that mobilising neighbourhood GPs as the first line of care defence for mental health is a good strategy.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I hope that the Government can provide more subsidies and training to GPs with regards to the treatment of mental illnesses, so that they can play a greater role.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I believe that companies and business leaders can play a greater role in mentoring young Singaporeans and further promote a mentoring culture.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, on the issue of encouraging our young people to marry and young couples to have children, besides the financial incentives that are important, I hope the Government can press on in the tripartite approach in providing greater support and more flexible work arrangements for more employees.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I would like to end with a message of unity.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As Singaporeans, we possess the spirit of kindness, drive, and hope.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As we start the second session of this Parliament, may we stay united, combining our national will and grit with good stewardship of the hard-earned resources availed to us, to create a better future for ourselves and for our future generations to come.

speaker: Ms Ng Ling Ling (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I support the Motion.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In an increasingly multi-polar world, I hope that we will, at the same time sharpen our skills and ability to maintain unity in diversity; whether this is the diversity of different backgrounds, cultures, abilities, or even political views and allegiances.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is not a foreign concept in fields such as management and relationship counselling, that disagreement – done respectfully – can be turned into an opportunity to strengthen bonds and build a stronger team.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And it is my hope that we can sharpen our skills and ability to do this Singapore and to lead by example here in this House.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, greater inclusivity and respect between diverse individuals and groups has to go beyond lip service – the multiple cross-Ministry and cross-agency task forces, national conversations and consultation exercises set up to look into this matter are only one step in the work to be done for us as a nation to move towards greater inclusivity and accommodation for all.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The principle and embrace of our diversity must form the backbone and core of our systems in all areas, whether they be the education system, our built environment, or the workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I recall from my growing up years the oft-repeated refrain that our people in Singapore are our only – and greatest – resource and it is this that I will focus my speech on today.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: To strengthen inclusivity amongst our people, I believe these groups of workers need further attention – our invisible workers who undertake the unpaid labour that forms the backbone of our families and society and our blue collar workers, including migrant workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Some of these points have been made time and again in this House, but they bear repeating, because we have a ways to go when it comes to moving the needle in a meaningful way.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would make such work more visible, better valued and ultimately, allows us to concretely measure the magnitude of the work undertaken and also the success – or not – of our policies in supporting our unpaid workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And while it is important to get the economics right, we must also ensure that holistic support coming from the entire surrounding ecosystem is in place, from ensuring that flexible work arrangements and meaningful accommodations are accessible to individuals who have to juggle additional caring responsibilities on top of their paid work.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As brought up by many in this House, legislation in the forms of right-to-request or even anti-discrimination legislation have an important role to play in bringing this about.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And even when such schemes are implemented, we must also continue to remove internalised barriers that prevent our caregivers from leaning in to take advantage of these schemes and accommodations, and make them feel that they should not have to hesitate to use them for fear of being perceived by their employers to be less valuable as a colleague who does not have the same domestic responsibilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving to our blue collar and migrant workers, we appear to be forgetting many key issues that captured our attention during the pandemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The work that they do may historically have been lower wage and lower status, but without them, where would we be today?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Met Service recently released their report on the urban heat island effect being pronounced in Singapore and I hope that this would underscore the urgency in tackling issues relating to heat inequality.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to do our best to alleviate discomfort for workers as well as ensure that workplaces – particularly outdoor workplaces – are safe.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Many of us on both sides of the aisle have also spoken about the topic of worker safety, following the number of workplace related deaths and injuries in recent years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While it is likely that casualty rates could fall this year as the pressures of worker shortages and COVID-delays ease, we must reflect deeply on tackling the structural issues that contribute to unsafe working environments for our workers.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is a positive step that the Government has continued to take a tough stance through our criminal justice system against safety violations, but I cannot help but note that these responses only take place after the casualty occurs.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I therefore reiterate the calls made by my colleague, the Member for Aljunied Group Representation Constituency (GRC) Mr Leon Perera at this year's COS to reduce the imbalance between migrant workers and employers with a view to improve safety standards and ultimately protect lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And for migrant workers in particular, it sometimes seems that there is a dignity deficit in the way we treat them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: These are people who literally build our country.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Recent episodes relating to the way we address the most basic needs of our workers – from inadequate nutrition to poor food handling practices such as lunches left out by the road side exposed to pests and the elements, to the debate over whether standards for new foreign worker dormitories are enough – show that we still have far to go in treating these essential workers with dignity and respect.
