speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This also extends to the way we handle their transportation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Just last month, I was driving down the expressway with my five-year old, when he suddenly blurted out, "Why are there so many workers riding on the back of that lorry over there?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Why do we have to buckle our seat belts and use car seats to keep us safe, when those workers are sitting like that?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Is their safety not important?" I had no answers for him and would like to reiterate calls that I made during the debate on the amendment to the Road Traffic Act in 2021 to ban the ferrying of workers in this manner.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I note that Members in this House have been asking about the possibility of using buses to ferry workers all the way back to at least 2010 – 13 years ago.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: There is dignity in ensuring high safety standards for all.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I hope that we can be bold and commit to a timeline for this to happen.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Beyond broad calls for better inclusivity, I would like to hone in on a specific piece of upcoming legislation: anti-discrimination legislation for the workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In Mdm President's speech, she reiterated the importance of ensuring a broader and more open meritocracy that works well for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I believe that anti-discrimination legislation is a key tool in achieving this goal.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The workplace fairness law was announced by the Prime Minister during the 2021 National Day Rally and we are glad that this is in line with the WP's 2020 manifesto's proposal that we enact legislation to take this step to join the majority of countries that legislate against discrimination at the workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this regard, I noted that the interim report was published earlier this year by the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness and would like to share some thoughts on its contents.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is glaring in the wake of last year's repeal of section 377A of the Penal Code and our Prime Minister's acknowledgement that members of the LGBTQ community are our "colleagues, our brothers and sisters, or some of our children".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Second, the interim report does not contain a definition of discrimination and it is unclear whether or not, indirect discrimination will be covered within its ambit.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This was noted by the law firm Baker McKenzie, who also published commentary stating that in jurisdictions such as Australia and Hong Kong, both direct and indirect discrimination is unlawful.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For those unfamiliar with the concepts, "direct discrimination" refers to intentional discrimination against an individual, while "indirect discrimination" refers to a situation where a person is disadvantaged by a requirement that applies equally to all persons, but has the effect of creating disadvantage against a particular group of people because of a particular characteristic; an example of which would be a ban on headwear at the workplace for all, but has the effect of disproportionately affecting Muslim women or Sikh men more than other groups.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Clarity in the new legislation is important for both employers and employees.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Upcoming legislation should make clear that all forms of discrimination will not be tolerated in Singapore and prohibit all types of discrimination.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is important, considering that the Milieu survey found that the most common form of discrimination is indirect discrimination.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would also fulfil our international law obligations as a state party to the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Reasonable accommodations are adjustments at the workplace that are afforded to a person with protected characteristics to assist them in enjoying equal employment opportunities.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This issue is especially important to the disability community, which continues to face issues of severe unemployment and under-employment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Reasonable accommodations, such as the provision of screen readers or an accessible office environment, are important for disabled people to contribute meaningfully to our economy.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They are also important for other groups, such as breastfeeding mothers, who may require a lactation space in the office, Muslims who require time off to go for Friday prayers and carers who may need flexible work arrangements.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should also make the process of trying to enforce these laws as simple and user-friendly for workers who may not have the time or energy to go through a lengthy or complicated process to seek recourse.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Currently, the process that a worker must go through before reaching the Employment Claims Tribunal (ECT) can seem complicated and daunting to someone who is not familiar with the law.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Tripartite Committee should consider how the system may be simplified and streamlined.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One way is to empower workers to decide whether they wish to attempt mediation or go directly to the ECT, instead of requiring mandatory mediation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Forcing parties to mediate may be counterproductive in some situations and could also re-traumatise workers who have had particularly bad experiences at their workplace.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Additionally, the upcoming workplace fairness legislation is but a first step towards a more diverse and equal Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It does not address the important principle that discrimination cannot be tolerated in every aspect of life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am sure that many of us have heard troubling accounts about discrimination in schools, in the housing rental market, in healthcare and beyond.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The role of the law is indispensable in sending a clear signal that discrimination is not tolerated in Singapore and I hope that we can consider our part in enacting a comprehensive anti-discrimination law to ensure that nobody in Singapore has to feel like they are not equal to or less than others.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is true that a healthy, good relationship is always built on a bedrock of trust and that the maintenance of this trust is a constant work-in-progress and it shifts and flexes with the effluxion of time.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The Government often quotes the high levels of trust our people have in Government and public institutions as being key to our success as a nation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And it is true that we have largely avoided the deep political divide that is believed to have contributed to phenomena like the partisan response to mask mandates and vaccine roll-outs in countries like the US, and that this greatly benefited us in our whole-of-nation fight against the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Yet, what this narrative often neglects is that for any healthy, resilient relationship to properly function, trust has to be present in both directions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: During COVID-19, I saw the best in people, not just when we trusted the institutions in their new mandates, but when members of the institutions trusted in people to do the right thing, be it residents who stayed home even when no one was watching, or residents who checked in and bought food for their vulnerable neighbours who had to isolate.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Maybe not always, but very often they do.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Apart from expecting and demanding that our people continue to trust in public institutions and leaders, we also need to find ways to repay that trust, to be able to show that we can trust our people.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Which makes it an appropriate time to ask the question: after all these generations of nation-building, do we trust our people?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And how can we move to building systems and networks where we can reap maximum benefits for the greater good of our nation that are built on strong mutual trust?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: One concrete way in which we can start to display and build the trust we have in our people is to look at the information that we make available to all.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should start finding ways to trust our people to be able to maturely and responsibly handle more information, rather than assume the worst of them.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, greater knowledge and transparency on the Budget process let our people understand the sometimes-difficult trade-offs that policymakers have to make and to get buy-in on why we have to push ahead with certain unpopular policies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Indeed, a 2016 paper by Hollie Russon Gilman found that more information leads to collaborative decision-making which, in turn, improves processes and delivery of services, as communities work towards sustainable development and engaged civic innovation – which I cannot help but note is the ostensible goal of the Forward Singapore exercise.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On reservations expressed about the costs of enacting such laws, or concerns that civil servants may start trying to take truncated notes as ways to get around freedom of information requests, I hope we have more faith in the integrity and the professionalism of our civil servants and to entrust that they will find means and harness technology to make the administration of such requests more efficient and less costly.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, as noted in a 2019 article in the Harvard Business Review, when trust is given, you empower the recipient and, in doing so, you develop team members to become stronger contributors and this leads to further empowerment of leaders.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, I would like to address the important topic of empowering our seniors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Importantly, our seniors have the capacity to contribute to our communities and lead purposeful lives.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Education levels over the years have increased, and these differing archetypes also mean that seniors have different expectations and capacities in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Newer cohorts of seniors, who are more educated and healthier due to advanced healthcare, will feel they have more to contribute to our society.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my speech, I will further discuss how we can further support older men, such that they have a solid support system after retirement, the importance of creating more opportunities for seniors with interests to contribute back to society, civic engagement with seniors and the necessity of inclusive workplace policies.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Statistics have shown that men are more likely to experience loneliness in old age compared to women.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This phenomenon can be attributed to various factors, including societal norms and expectations around masculinity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Men may have been socialised to be more independent and self-reliant, which can result in fewer social connections and support systems as they age.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, traditional gender roles may have limited men's opportunity for socialisation outside of the work and family roles, leading to fewer social connections in later life.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a result, older men face increased risks of loneliness and its associated negative impacts on physical and mental health.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important to recognise and address the unique challenges that men may face in terms of loneliness in old age and to promote strategies and interventions that support healthy social connections and well-being in this group of the population.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In other words, men living alone with weak social networks were reported to have higher depressive symptom scores, compared to those with strong social networks outside the family.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is an interesting idea I chanced upon: Men's Sheds.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They refer to any community-based, non-profit, non-commercial organisation that is accessible to all men and whose primary activity is the provision of a safe and friendly environment.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A major objective is to advance the well-being and health of their male members.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are community spaces designed for men to connect, converse and create, and have become one of the most widespread and effective tools in addressing health and well-being, especially for older men, in many countries, including the UK and Australia.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Men's Sheds provide a supportive environment for men to engage in a diverse range of activities, from technical skills like furniture-making and woodwork, to simply grabbing coffee and talking.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This movement originated in Australia around the 1980s as a way to improve the health and well-being of older men, recognising that men may be more reluctant to talk about their emotions and seek help due to societal expectations of toxic masculinity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Men's Sheds are often run by the men who use them, in a bottom-up approach, which can elicit stronger feelings of fulfilment and achievement.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the UK, many Men's Sheds are run by grassroots organisations, such as Age UK, while in Australia, there are management committees responsible for creating a safe and welcoming environment for men to work on community projects of their choice.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Men's Sheds provide an important avenue for older men to combat isolation, loneliness and depression and to regain a sense of value and productivity in their communities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A 2021 study on the impact of Men's Sheds provided a model that showed many different and interlinked ways in which Shed activities can positively impact the behaviours and attitudes of Shed users, in the areas of increased health seeking behaviours, improved perspectives on personal and management of health and improved ability to manage and overcome physical and mental illness and recovery among men.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The model also demonstrated some of the less obvious ways in which activities can have positive health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, men may attend a Shed simply to engage in practical activities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, this may lead to unexpected improvements in their ability to cope with adversity by finding a social network that they could experience support and understanding from.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These findings are significant from a policy standpoint because they suggest that initiatives like Men's Sheds, while not directly delivering a health service, can contribute to engaging men in health improvement practices and increase their health knowledge, thereby strengthening the case to push for such initiatives.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Similar to Men's Sheds, Senior Activity Centres (SACs) in Singapore's context function as centres to provide support for seniors through various programmes, activities and outreach.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can see that membership rates at this centre are fairly even, while participation rates are skewed, with more women taking part.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Possible reasons shared by our staff are that some male members are still the breadwinners of their family and they do not have the time for such activities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Male members may also be more closed-off and do not wish to be engaged at all.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Activities, such as craft sessions and Zumba, are generally held in many centres but may not be appealing to the male members.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, activities, such as drone flying and carpentry which are more attractive to men, are hard to come by due to space and cost constraints.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The need for dedicated Men Sheds and activities, hence, becomes even more important to engage men.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, can the Government work together with operators of SACs to better understand the factors that result in men being less likely to frequent SACs?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such data will be helpful in enhancing the current slew of programmes offered in SACs to better cater to the needs and preferences of older men.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This information is also important to ascertain if current SACs possess the capacity to support older men or if dedicated facilities for men, as in the case of Men's Sheds, are necessary.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moreover, if the data eventually reveals that present programmes in SACs can be tweaked to better encompass the needs of older men, can the Government consider implementing a consolidated framework across SACs that streamlines key objectives, approaches and outcomes for older men?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I would also like to call on the People's Association (PA) to look into providing more programmes to encourage grassroots participation among older men.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At present, PA, through the Women's Integration Network Council, manages a network of Women's Executive Committees (WECs).

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: WECs run a range of programmes to meet the needs of women from different backgrounds, ranging from health matters, parenting, managing work-life balance, financial literacy and employability.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: WECs also help to form interest groups for women to interact with one another over shared interests and volunteering opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can PA consider similar approaches for men that, in particular, focus on providing more tools and programmes to better meet the needs of older men?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Abas bin Jaffar is one such inspiring resident in Zhenghua.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: His first job was in a shipping company, where he worked from 1976 to 1989 as a pattern-maker and excelled in the role so much so that he received the NTUC Model Worker Award in 1984.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Later, he became a hawkerpreneur for 30 years from 1989 to 2019 at various locations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He then joined the PAP Community Foundation (PCF) Sparkletots as a part-time cook in 2019 and, from 2022, now works full-time as their chef-in-residence.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Throughout the shift in his career paths, he has found tremendous fulfilment and enjoyment in his various professions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Cooking allows him to be creative and he loves experimenting with new flavours and techniques.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Moreover, the joy of seeing young children at PCF Sparkletots enjoying his dishes is incredibly rewarding.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Overall, this third wave of his career has been a perfect fit and he looks forward to providing nutritious meals to our children for many years to come.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This made me reflect on the untapped potential that other seniors have, and how we must utilise it, such that they can contribute to society in whatever ways they find meaningful.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Many studies have shown that the way to longevity and health is the constant stimulation of the mind through social relationships like work and continuous learning.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One, social relationships that you can gain from continually working and staying connected and, the other, continuous learning.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is very important moving forward as our population ages and our senior workers continue to form an ever-increasing share of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Enabling companies to provide inclusive workplace policies continues to be crucial in addressing age discrimination in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Employers can take steps to integrate older adults into the workforce by offering informal and formal "second or third wave of career pathways" that allow older adults to re-enter or remain in the workforce.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While these policies enable companies to provide inclusive workplace policies and prevent age-related discrimination in the workplace, I believe that initiatives can go beyond just a senior's employment longevity.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Like younger workers, our senior workers are also required to keep up with the ever-changing workforce and economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Are there any concrete training programmes identified in these JTMs that would benefit seniors and ensure they continue to stay relevant in the workforce?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Apart from formal work for our seniors, there can be more opportunities for seniors with interests to contribute back to society as a way to feel purposeful in their golden years.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such opportunities could be in the area of volunteerism.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today, it is heartening to see many volunteering programmes that bring together young volunteers and seniors to engage in activities to build intergenerational bond.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, the YOLDEN programme helmed by Youth Corps Singapore brings together our young and senior individuals through activities like the senior befriending programme.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What if there could be volunteering programmes where our seniors are instead the volunteers and our young ones are being engaged in activities?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the same intention but different execution, it could create a sense of fulfilment amongst our seniors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: During my Meet-the-People session at Zhenghua, I am often heartened to witness the robustness of our senior volunteers in registration for our residents and even assisting with the administrative matters that involve the use of digital gadgets.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Often, our young volunteers and I draw on our senior volunteers' language and dialect abilities to assist in engaging residents in need.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Watching how our young and seniors serving collaboratively at the People's Action Party (PAP) Zhenghua Branch, is one of my greatest joy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, this is one of the actionable ways to address ageism.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By providing opportunities to serve collaboratively, we break down corrosive stigmas.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important that we continue to be innovative in engaging our seniors, be it through employment or other forms of active ageing that is purposeful and fulfilling.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another important aspect would include civic engagement with our seniors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Civic participation involves the active involvement of seniors in collective decision-making processes, ranging from sharing of information to participating in public consultations and community ideation.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Research shows that seniors who engage in civic participation tend to feel more invested and valued in their community, fostering a sense of belonging and meaning in life.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mechanisms used to engage seniors in community decisions also have a social component, facilitating the formation of new social ties and strengthening neighbourhood social capital.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, there are barriers to civic engagement among seniors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Barriers such as ageism and mobility challenges can make it difficult for seniors to access places where decision-making takes place.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, age-related declines and impairments in physical and mental functioning may pose challenges to seniors' participation in civic activities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This in turn creates a positive virtuous cycle that ensures our seniors are valued, included and actively contribute to our communities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The ForwardSG exercise is an excellent opportunity to do so.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Our seniors have the capacity to contribute and we must, we must, purposefully engage them.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Like Mr Abas bin Jaffar who is experiencing a third wave and numerous senior volunteers at the PAP Zhenghua Branch, many more can contribute.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must energise them and provide pathways to do so.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By doing so, we will effectively respond to the President's address that "we want a Singapore where everyone belongs and every citizen has the chance to achieve his or her fullest potential".

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, this is relevant to our seniors as well as they have the potential to give back multi-fold to society in many aspects.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There is something sacred about the Parliamentary process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: And in Singapore, in this House, we take great effort to honour this process and preserve the sanctity of Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This House is often a place of disagreement, but we strive to debate with decorum.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We all seek attention so that the views of our constituents and the people we serve are heard, but we have to do so tastefully and without theatrics.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: And beyond just talking about issues, we have to take action.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In particular, the Government has to translate the debate, to the policies and execute them, to address issues and make lives better for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Whilst there may be a general understanding by the public that Parliament is an important place where issues of significance are debated and laws of the land are made, there may not be full appreciation of the rigour and decorum that members have to abide by and the work it takes to bring forth meaningful debates.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The words uttered in this house are not merely our thoughts alone but represent the voices of the Singapore community we serve.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: All Members of this House have a responsibility to seek out feedback, listen, discern, prepare and convey the views constructively.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For many of us, this entails hours of block visits, going through residents' appeals, dialogues, meetings and research.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Parliament is not the only channel for us to raise issues and nudge for change, but it is certainly a significant platform.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I have seen what transpires in other Parliaments and I am glad we do things differently here.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I believe in the Singapore way of doing things.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: An approach that is substantive, data-driven, pragmatic, forward-looking and constructive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We learn and imbibe furiously lessons from the developments and advancements in other countries, but we always acknowledge and adjust to our local context, often cautious and calibrated so as not to dismantle all that we have built.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We should continue to take this approach as we discuss the refresh of our social compact.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In the book "What We Owe Each Other", Minouche Shafik said and I quote, "The way a society is structured has profound consequences for the lives of those living in it and the architecture of opportunity they face.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It determines not just their material conditions but also their well-being, relationships and life prospects." Minoushe explains that the structure of society is determined by institutions such as its political and legal systems, the economy, the way in which family and community life are organised.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She believes the social contract – the norms and rules the society has agreed to, is the most important determinant of the kinds of lives we lead.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The impact of the structure of society on an individual's development and well-being cannot be underestimated.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am a woman, from a minority community, born to parents who were not highly educated and who had modest income.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In some other part of the world, my circumstances would have set me back and denied me of many opportunities – education, opportunities at work, a chance to speak in Parliament.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Honestly, often, I find that because I am from a minority community and a woman, I am given many opportunities as there are institutions, establishments and people who seek to embrace diversity and support those who do not start with much.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am not oblivious to the fact that some may not have the same experience as me.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: And therefore, as many in this House have espoused, we must ensure access to opportunities for social mobility are available to all.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am heartened by the different efforts by the Government over the years to build the architecture of opportunity.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One effort is in developing early childhood education.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We know that early childhood experiences can impact the child's trajectory in life.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We make early childhood education affordable and support parents who need help.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: It is an upstream programme supporting pregnant mothers and children from low-income families aged zero to six.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am very glad the programme has been scaled up to benefit more children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Another area I am particularly excited about is in mentoring.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We all know the virtues of mentoring – in particular, to help open world views, exposing young people to new sectors they would otherwise not know exist.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Through the National Youth Council and the YouthCorp, there have been many programmes supporting youth development.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There are also now specific efforts in the mentoring space.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: While the Government can help provide structures for key areas, there will never be enough resources to go around and we need stakeholders to step up to fill in the gaps.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: President Halimah spoke about the strengthening of collective responsibility.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Indeed, as a society, we need to internalise the important role we play individually and collectively to build the society we want to see.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In the course of my work serving in Bukit Batok East, I have seen residents, people in the community doing just that.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One of my residents, became a temporary caregiver to her neighbour who fell ill and became immobile.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She would bathe her, feed her and care for her daily till she regained strength.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: She did that completely out of goodwill and her compassion is inspiring.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am also inspired and grateful to a group of business owners, elderly gentlemen who have consistently donated to my food pack programmes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: They hardly speak English and I can barely string a sentence in Mandarin but we would meet every once in a while for an update on the programme and I would make a request for continued support for donations.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am grateful to my volunteer Mr Desmond Sim for always coordinating this and also always donating towards the cause.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I am referring to building the capability and skills of volunteers and nurturing a healthy culture of social responsibility and sense of community in all aspects of our lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I will focus on the workplace as an example.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: More and more now, we will be relying on volunteers to help execute national programmes, for example for the ComLink efforts, or in mentoring programmes, or for M3.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The volunteers today need to be skilled because they have higher order roles.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We would also want our volunteers to grow, take ownership, develop strategies, leverage on technology and think about better ways of doing things.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I therefore think it is important to make an investment in capability building.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In Malay):   M3 is the Malay-Muslim community's effort to uplift lives, in particular, of those from low-income families.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Volunteers form the backbone of all the M3 efforts that we have carried out.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On this occasion, I would like to thank all who have contributed to this noble cause.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: A lot have been done with the past three to four years, but a lot more has to be worked on.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In particular, I feel we need to think of our community's strategy as we discuss collective responsibility.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I know many of us care about the wellbeing of our community and have our own ideas on how to carry out certain programmes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: But I would like to call on volunteers to pause and reflect on the effectiveness of the effort carried out.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We should also move towards long-term programmes which can truly help the families or youth that are targeted, to change their lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: For example, instead of giving food donations once a year, could we see how we could continue to connect with the family or be a mentor to the young child in the family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Because consistent efforts, when done in a rigorous manner, may be more effective.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I hope we can continue to improve our efforts in helping families who face challenging circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: (In English): The other area we should look at is in building a culture of collective responsibility and a sense of community in all aspects of our lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The workplace is where we spend a large part of our lives.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: What we do at work has an impact on the organisation we work for as well as the larger community and the economy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The work and work culture also have an impact on our well-being.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We want workers to feel excited about their roles, take ownership in what they do.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: This can only happen if they feel valued and treated with respect, where their strengths are nurtured and where they can thrive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: There was a Lianhe Zaobao article by Mr Liu Jiakeng which commented on the “I’m just an employee” attitude.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: He recounted his personal experience with a shared car-renting service.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: In summary, he was concerned with the rather robotic responses he received which reflected a lack of initiative and a lack of a sense of responsibility.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: He feels it is troubling if many young people have this attitude.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: On the other hand, I have had conversations with some young people who shared why they feel uninspired or are just doing the bare minimum at work because they feel they are just numbers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: One of them shared about how a recent mass lay-off and the way the company treated the staff made her not want to give so much of herself in her new workplace for fear of being burnt again.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Another person, whose company also had a mass lay-off, but was not laid off himself, also had similar sentiments.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I have also heard about those who would very much like to upskill but are not given the time and opportunity to do so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I urge employers to take more effort in doing so, as there are clear benefits that arise from investing in goodwill with your employees.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I hope as more employers become more conscious of their roles and take real steps to create a healthy workplace culture, we will see a more dedicated workforce that is energised and committed to ride the wave of challenges that will come.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: Our society has matured, where, in general, our basic needs have been met.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We now need to nurture the soul of our society.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: The President’s Address to this House on the direction of the Government in the second half of our term has come at an important juncture of our history, as we are maturing as a nation, as we transit to living with COVID-19 and as we seek to navigate the challenges in this troubled world.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: We face an important challenge of rallying everyone to a common vision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Health and Minister for Law (Ms Rahayu Mahzam)
text: I hope people are encouraged by the passion shown by Members of this House and respond to the call to step up and walk this journey together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Most youths I talk to understand and appreciate their importance to society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Nevertheless, Forward SG gives us the chance to listen to our youths, to understand their hopes and dreams so that we can revitalise our social contract.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Since Forward Singapore began, I have spoken to a number of youths from 16 to 35 years old in groups and in person.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They broadly understand and support our social compact, believing that Singapore can help them to reach their goals.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, as circumstances change, we may need to finetune our policies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I have identified two groups of Singaporean youths who may need more support from the society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of them grew up in rental or 3-room flats, usually in the sandwich class.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These youths face financial pressures from the moment they receive their first paycheck.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They must often care for their parents, a responsibility that can be especially difficult if somebody falls ill.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When it comes down to settling down, while housing is affordable, saving for a downpayment for them can be a challenge.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: These youths also feel overwhelmed when compared to their more accomplished peers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They may not have the same breadth of experience in education or co-curricular activities (CCA) because they spent most of their youth doing part-time work.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They also lack access to social capital when faced with life's obstacles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is, as I said, not a very big group of Singaporeans, perhaps maybe 10% of all youths.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of them are tested by COVID-19; they are hardworking, realistic and resilient.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But we have been dropped to the floor and rolled over by life.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We may not have grown up into durians but, hey, we are still standing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We understand that the world is complex and disruption is the new norm.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But we do not know much beyond what we read online.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We wish that there were knowledgeable people in different walks of life and different industries who care about us, who can guide us in our career path.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We do not seek shortcuts; we just want help to reach our fullest potential as soon as possible.” For this group of Singaporean youths, we can do more to support their aspirations in three ways.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As they are still young, they are likely to be able to afford higher monthly instalments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: For poor families living in rental flats, HDB has consistently leaned forward and exercised considerable and, I might say, admirable discretion to help them buy the homes through programmes, such as Fresh Start.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: So, I hope that, in the same vein, HDB can provide more support to this small group of Singaporean youths to finance their flats, so that they have the cash flow to pay for basic renovations and to settle down.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: My volunteers at Kebun Baru plan to partner volunteers and social enterprises in two ways.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: One, we observed that youths spend a vast amount of their time online and have a limited social circle, which comprises mainly of friends from school.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They hunger for friends in real life but, frankly, they do not know where to start in befriending more people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Kebun Baru would like to partner groups like Friendzone to spark friendships among youths in our neighborhood.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Two, we have many capable residents who love to mentor the youths in career and life.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We will partner The Astronaut Collective to guide our youths to help them match their passion with their careers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: There are many such efforts where the people sector partner together to help our youths.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I hope that the Government can also incentivise such projects and social enterprises, for there is much work that must be done.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This will disproportionately help youths from disadvantaged backgrounds, given the fact that they face more challenges and possess less social capital.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our youths today need greater skill in navigating very different economic lives compared to generations before.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A lot of their decisions, such as balancing needs vs wants, must be made through a lens of financial prudence.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Financial literacy is an important thing to teach.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Second is meditation, which is taught in a secular way in some school systems in the world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We are living in an age where our youths are overloaded with information.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With artificial intelligence (AI), knowledge is practically free.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: What is needed in this brave new world is wisdom to apply the relevant knowledge and information, and it is difficult to be wise unless a person is emotionally balanced.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: And mediation is a powerful way for one to centre one’s mind.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We can and we must teach our youths this.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They are not overly concerned about their careers due to their educational success and their resources.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They possess social capital to navigate through adulthood but face a bigger financial burden in purchasing a home compared to a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Their good salaries and career progressions make them ineligible for a new Build-To-Order (BTO) and not all parents can assist them with the purchase of a resale flat or private condo.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Fearing prices will only increase, they often buy houses before they are financially prepared.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This means that if applicants have an unexpected career progression and a pay jump, it can be accommodated if it is not excessive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I have met more and more young, successful couples who are considering taking a backseat temporarily because of this potential cliff effect.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They are worried that if they take on this promotion, they will have more pay and they will miss out on HDB and they might be pushed to buy condominiums which are more expensive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: I understand that beyond the current approach, such as much higher Additional Buyer's Stamp Duty (ABSD), there are no easy answers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Over the past few decades, past two decades in particular, we have built an inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We have taken major steps in the last decade to raise wages, particularly for low-wage workers and seniors.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We have boosted our social safety net and made strides in environmental protection and, now, more than 50% of our Budget is for social spending.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Fortunately, Singaporeans are willing to make the trade-offs in terms of higher cost of living and taxation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: However, let us not assume that our youths will automatically sign off to pay for this fair and just society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It may be a surprising thing to say, as there is a strong national consensus on this today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But we only need to look at many developed countries, developed democracies, to know that this is not a given.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of their citizens today are now questioning the generous social compact and debt that they have inherited.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When I speak to our youths, I realised that many of them are more pessimistic about the world, at least compared to my generation at their age.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This is even as our society has now a lot more resources to care and nurture them, compared to my generation.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many of them do actually worry about bread-and-butter issues and how to keep their aspirations and passion in the face of reality.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: But if we look the world through their lenses, it is possible to understand why.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: When I was their age, Singapore and the world were brimming with optimism.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We were celebrating the end of history, and we were at the cusp of the Asia Pacific century amidst balanced and positive US-China relations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Then, technology and the Internet brought a seemingly endless promise.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Social media has yet to accentuate the perception of reality or hobbled democracies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Climate change was not even a thing and everybody read the newspapers, especially the Straits Times.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Now if you open the social media feed of our youths today, you will see a vastly different world.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: They may not be able to fully articulate the uncertainty of the unprecedented times but they certainly feel it.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Building a fair and inclusive Singapore is, to me, a crowning achievement for this generation of elected leaders in this House.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The consensus, I strongly believe, cuts across party lines, and I believe more Members, all Members in this House, believe that, on this issue, we are on the right side of history.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Therefore, through Forward Singapore, let us make an extra effort to make sure that the youths are firmly rooted on this fair and inclusive Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: With that, I stand in support of the Motion.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is just in case I have one paragraph left and the time runs out.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Every generation needs to confront their unique challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For this generation, it has to grapple with climate change, geopolitical tensions and uncertainties the Prime Minister talked about yesterday, rapid technological advancements that can disrupt jobs and industries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think the biggest social transformation for this generation will be ageing, which is the topic of my speech today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ageing is unlike other elements of health – it is human condition which we can neither prevent nor cure.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: France took 115 years to transit from "ageing" to "aged", and it became "aged" in 1980.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Sweden took 85 years and then became "aged" in 1975.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The US took 69 years to become "aged" in 2013.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We took 19 years and became "aged" in 2017.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, we are one of the fastest ageing countries in the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many countries, such as Japan, South Korea, Germany and UK are already where we will be in 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The impact of being a "super-aged" society is profound.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, it causes population dispersion as young people gravitate to cities to seek better jobs and opportunities, leaving rural areas old and depopulated.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is projected that by 2040, close to 900 municipalities, which is nearly half of Japan's total, could disappear.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To counter this demographic polarisation, Japan is taking some aggressive measures.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They are giving cash incentives to young people to say, "Move out of the cities, come back to the rural areas".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Second impact: when people get older, the way they consume, they save, they learn and the way they work change.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: China has confronted this issue for some years already, but it came to further prominence when China reported a fall in their population by 850,000 in 2022.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, that is the first time China's population shrank in the last 60 years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Notwithstanding, with a large population, China is in no danger of running out of workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It still has eight million or more graduates every year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the demographic shift has probably prompted China to rethink its economic development path, away from growth in labour intensive, export-driven industries, to higher quality, higher productivity activities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Third, ageing has cast a big question mark over the sustainability of social welfare systems.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many pension systems around the world are becoming no longer viable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because there are more and more older people drawing from the central pension pool, and fewer and fewer young people contributing into it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The country has enacted new laws only recently to raise its official retirement age, and hence also its pension age, from 62 to 64 – just two years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But that alone has led to massive public protests.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The UK National Health Service is facing a crushing patient load.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is described as facing the "scissors of doom": one blade represents patient load and disease prevalence and that is going up; the other blade represents resources and manpower and that is going down.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In Singapore, we have been thinking about the problem of ageing for a long time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We first started thinking about changes to the retirement and CPF system with the Howe Yoon Chong Committee 40 years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government set up the Committee on Ageing Issues almost 20 years ago and formalised it into the Ministerial Committee on Ageing in 2007.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So far, the Ministerial Committee has coordinated and launched two comprehensive action plans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If you are wondering, the Minister for Health is the Minister-in-charge of the Ministerial Committee.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because of this strong foundation, we are in a position to cushion the impact of ageing and perhaps even reap dividends from it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If we continue pressing on along this journey we started, we will have a bright, dynamic, vibrant and happy future.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: While Singapore will inexorably become a "super-aged" country, it can also remain a superb country.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: My speech will cover five key areas of impact.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Together, they are the enablers for Singaporeans to live a meaningful and happy life, whatever their age.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We fortunately do not face the challenge of population dispersion like Japan.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We do not have many rural areas – the furthest is Lim Chu Kang, maybe.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We also have a significant advantage in that 80% of our population live in public housing and HDB can play an active central planning and development role in ensuring inclusive communities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A few years ago, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua hosted me for a constituency visit to Queenstown.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is one of our oldest towns, with more than 20% of its population aged 65 and older.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, Queenstown at that time is almost a "super-aged" town – 1%-point short.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But Queenstown is like a time machine that gives us a glimpse of what the future will look like in every town in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By 2030, most towns in Singapore will be like Queenstown, in terms of the residents' age profile.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last week, I made another visit to Queenstown.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I can see that the place is transforming.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is now labelled a Health District, an initiative that I launched with Minister Desmond Lee some time ago.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a Health District, many agencies came together to implement various initiatives to improve the health and well-being of Queenstown residents.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This includes integrated planning, evidence-based design of the living space, and then many community initiatives, including physical activities, befriending programmes and healthcare services, to support seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What left the deepest impression on me was HDB's effort in planning ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To ensure inter-generational mixing, HDB is redeveloping the old areas, launching new BTO projects to inject a younger population into the town.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A BTO project now occupies what used to be the former Queenstown town centre.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Stallholders from the former Commonwealth Drive Food Centre have moved into a new two-storey Margaret Drive hawker centre located in the development.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I was told that the chicken rice stall is still there; it is preserved.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another BTO project integrates a block of Community Care Apartments for Seniors and is strategically located next to the soon-to-be redeveloped Alexandra Hospital.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As we redevelop and rejuvenate older towns, we continue to encourage inter-generational mixing in younger towns, such as Sembawang – my constituency.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: HDB has incorporated a range of flat types, including studio and 2-room Flexi apartments, into new BTO developments in places like Sembawang, and they cater to singles and seniors, and as a result, we have a more inclusive town.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have the Proximity Housing Grant, priority schemes for parents and children to live with or near each other, and larger 3-Gen flats which further encourage inter-generational mixing in all our housing estates.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At the neighbourhood level, the physical environment is becoming more friendly and liveable to all ages, all over Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Wherever possible, Active Ageing Centres, three-generational playgrounds and childcare centres are located side by side.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Such facilities are a mainstay now in HDB estates.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There are visibly more congregation and rest points, exercise parks, lifts at pedestrian overhead bridges to allow barrier-free access and roads redesigned to slow down traffic through implementation of more Green Man+ and Silver Zones.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When I was growing up, living in HDB estates, I could see the traffic circles disappearing, replaced by traffic lights junctions because they are more efficient in carrying heavier traffic.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Now, at this age, I am seeing the junctions being replaced by traffic circles again in order to slow down traffic, to cater to a more senior population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It has been a massive effort and HDB is now moving on to select newer flats built in the following 10 years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, you can see that our living environment is bending its form to suit today's society's shape.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All these are deliberate efforts to help us prepare for an older society.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second area is that we need to adapt our economy to an ageing population.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The most imminent impact is on the labour force.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The growth rate of our resident labour force has already slowed down.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the fact is that we still managed to continue to grow the workforce, despite the onset of ageing in the past two decades.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One, more Singaporeans are able to stay economically active for longer.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We should continue to support the aspirations of older workers to continue working and contributing.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have also been gradually raising the retirement and re-employment ages, from 60 and 65 in the past, to now 63 and 68.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Ministry of Manpower (MOM) aims to raise them to 65 and 70 by 2030.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think it is worth noting here that raising our retirement and re-employment ages does not affect the retirement savings that people have built up in their CPF accounts, and it is unlike in France and many other developed Western countries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, the main impact of raising these ages is that workers are protected from being dismissed due to their age by their employers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Workers can choose to retire early should they want to.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Hence, raising the retirement age in Singapore is an unmitigated good to workers.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Employers must certainly do their part, for instance, through job redesign and reskilling, and learn to benefit from tapping the silver workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Two, and equally important is female participation in the labour force.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With universal education and greater opportunities, labour force participation rate for women increased from about 51% to 63% over the last 20 years.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This House debated the White Paper on Women's Development last year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our work to ensure equal opportunities between men and women must continue, so that our wives and daughters can fulfil their full potential.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Workforce Singapore has launched the herCareer initiative to support women to come back to work.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: By 2024, we will give this a further push by introducing the Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangements.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Three, we complemented our local workforce with foreign workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The quality of the Singapore workforce is world-class, but there are just not enough Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, in many labour-intensive industries, we will continue to need foreign manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some of these, like construction, are sectors which locals are less likely to join.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Others, like healthcare, need more manpower to take care of more seniors.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will need more foreign manpower to complement the local core, which will remain the majority.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For Employment Passes, MOM will continue to calibrate its policies, to bolster our local talent pool with an international pool.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Complementarity Assessment Framework (COMPASS) evaluation system is more sophisticated, sensitive to both economic needs and the social impact of foreign manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Four, our economy will continue to upgrade and evolve, to rely more on brain than brawn, to enable machines, computers and AI to augment the ability of the human worker and indeed, drive growth through productivity improvements.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: That is why we are driving research and development through the National Research Foundation, implementing Industry Transformation Maps (ITMs) and growing high technology and high value sectors, such as biomedical, financial services and information technology (IT).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Governments around the world have two common manpower worries.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are concerned that technology will replace human workers and then, if that happens and on a large scale, there will be too many workers and too few jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are also concerned about the imminent shortage of manpower due to an ageing population and so there will be too few workers and too many jobs unfilled.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, instead of losing sleep over contradictory worries, one perhaps may be the solution for the other.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The confluence of both major trends, AI and technology and ageing, can be an opportunity to elevate our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But education, training and a personal responsibility to evolve our attitude towards our career with age, that will be key to unlocking this potential and this possibility.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is already a super-aged society, as more than 20% of its population is 65 and above.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Yet, pre-COVID-19, it had been growing at around 2%-4% a year.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Singapore will become older, but we can remain economically dynamic and vibrant, as long as we continue to remake our economy and prepare our people for it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many pension systems were designed when life expectancy was much shorter, between 50 and 70 years old.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Now, with people getting older and fertility rate falling, pension systems have become unsustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Some governments have had to borrow to plug the funding gap.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The accumulated national debt is then passed to the next generation to shoulder.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
