text: In Singapore, we are fortunate to have the Central Provident Fund (CPF) system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For many Western developed countries, the starting point is "defined benefits".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This means there is a national pension pot.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Everyone pays into the same big pot while you are working and after retirement, every retiree dips into the pot to draw their defined pension benefits.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The starting point of our CPF system is "defined contribution", where workers save up in their personal accounts, employers and the Government contribute into the accounts too, and workers draw down from their own personal accounts when they retire, until the funds run out.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With the CPF system, we avoided the major problems faced by pension systems around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The CPF system, however, is not without its challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One challenge is that life expectancy differs from person to person.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When they retire, CPF LIFE uses risk pooling to provide a steady stream of monthly payouts for as long as they live.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The scheme was further enhanced two years ago.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: MOM will continue to look at ways and means to improve retirement adequacy of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The fourth area is to reform the healthcare system, what I feel is probably the most important.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Like pension systems, most health systems in the world are designed when life expectancy was much lower.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These systems focused on hospital care, which is the most costly part of the whole healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But so long as the population is young, the system works fine.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But as life expectancy rose, so did the disease burden.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is like you have been training very hard for a sprint and then, you realise your race is a marathon.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The situation is also like an overflowing kitchen sink.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can keep mopping and soaking up the water on the floor, but the work is endless and the effort increasingly trying.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At some point, we need to figure out how to turn down the tap.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In healthcare, this means slowing down the onset of severe diseases and making people healthier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If this cannot be done, the sheer disease burden driven by ageing will overload the healthcare system.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Healthier SG delivers preventive care by building up primary care, family physicians in community and polyclinics and it becomes the foundational layer of healthcare.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But at this level, family physicians in primary care, they cannot work alone.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For the minority of more serious cases, they need to escalate the care upwards, to secondary and tertiary care in our hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But then, for the great majority of less serious cases or even healthy residents, they need to devolve the care downwards to community and family care.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The communities we live in, the families we hold dear to, are places that create and sustain health.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is about having a good family environment, hygienic living conditions, nutritious food, education for children, good employment opportunities and public amenities like parks, libraries and sports facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And where health interventions are needed, they are more social than medical and often verge on common sense – sleep well, eat well, have rewarding relationships, exercise, do not smoke, undergo periodic health screening and vaccinations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: However, it is the common-sensical easy things that always get put off because there are no immediate consequences and therefore, they fall prey to inertia.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Community support can help us overcome those inertia.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In particular, with community support, there are great opportunities for seniors to age healthily in communities.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I am glad that quite a number of Members has spoken about this.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It will be a continuation of Healthier SG and as a national programme as ambitious and extensive as Healthier SG.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Forward Singapore has been described as a refresh of our social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A social compact is usually understood as an unwritten contract between the individual and the state, the responsibility of the individual to contribute to the larger good and the obligation of the state to provide assurances and opportunities to its citizens.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, under Healthier SG, how does this concept apply?

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But then, beyond the relationship between individual and the state, the community is at the core of the healthcare social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: There is also the significant factor of good governance.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Preparing for ageing, be it in the areas of urban planning, economic development, retirement adequacy or healthcare reforms, requires anticipatory policy-making, which is the hallmark of the Singapore Government.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have made preparations for an aged society in these areas well ahead of time.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have had more than a decade of head start before the problem caught up with us.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I described how the pension systems in the Western developed countries are contributing to significant national debts, which burden future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, inherent in the pension crisis is the Government's inability to look after both the current and future generations of their people.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We consciously avoided those problems and, in fact, have built up a national nest-egg in our reserves.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are drawing income from it and want our future generations to continue to benefit from it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai alleged that the Progressive Singapore Party (PSP)'s concerns and questions were often dismissed by the People's Action Party (PAP) Government and there were occasions where the PSP was painted as, I quote, "xenophobic, nativist and racist".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The Government has always acknowledged the concerns raised by various Members of the House, including by the PSP Members.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This includes Singaporeans' anxieties about jobs and competition in a globalised and fast-changing economy, affordability and accessibility of HDB flats and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And it is raised by all Members of the House, regardless of their party.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And we are working hard to adjust policies and make deliberate efforts to address these issues.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I hope Mr Leong Mun Wai will also acknowledge the serious concern we have in the way he raises and debates issues.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I was personally involved in a couple of these issues.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This House would recall that we had a debate on Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA), our Free Trade Agreement (FTA) with India.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Running up to the debate, there was much demonising of CECA, that it allowed unfettered entry of Indian nationals into Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The discourse took on a worrying racial undertone.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As a former FTA negotiator, I asked to deliver a Ministerial Statement in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I acknowledged the concern amongst Singaporeans on jobs and livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I explained to the House how an FTA works – in particular, the chapter on movement of natural persons – and how CECA preserves our right to immigration policies and setting work pass conditions for foreign nationals who want to work in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I also had a fairly long exchange with Mr Leong.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But when Mr Leong filed a Motion on foreign talent policy in September 2021, two months later after the Ministerial Statement debate, he continued to refer to CECA as a cause for widespread anxiety among Singaporeans on jobs and livelihoods and did little to reduce the raw emotions and misimpressions on CECA that had been stoked.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was as if my Ministerial Statement and explanation in July 2021 did not take place.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I recall during that Motion debate, he eventually conceded that some people would think that his statements on CECA had racial undertones, against the Indian community.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In January 2022, Mr Leong made an allegation that teachers in Ministry of Education (MOE) were treating vaccinated and non-vaccinated students differently.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I was Multi-Ministry Taskforce (MTF) chair and I got quite worried whether our vaccine-differentiated safe-management measures (SMMs) had somehow inadvertently been imposed on young children.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Because this was a serious allegation, Minister Chan Chun Sing stood up and asked for details.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Leong then clarified that his information source was a Telegram chat and there were no details.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: All of us, including Mr Leong and the Progress Singapore Party (PSP), and everyone in the House, we know that race issues can be played up, especially in multi-racial Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can debate, we can spar, but we should not pit one group against another, over and over again, always looking to tear at the seams of our society and if we keep doing that, it will sow disunity and divide our society.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In multi-racial, diverse Singapore, our harmony is hard earned.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In fact, let us be very careful to preserve it.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Leon Perera had asserted that the Government tries to push a single "dominant narrative", without regard to the alternatives raised by the Workers' Party (WP).

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: If not, we would not be having such extensive debates on so many issues in this House and hearing out each other.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Further, every political party will have its own dominant narrative based on its manifesto, based on its values.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is part and parcel of political contestation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Many Members, including WP Members of Parliament, have raised many ideas in this House.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We welcome them and where appropriate, we take those ideas in while formulating or reviewing our policies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And where we have a different view, we will explain why.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I would say that many of the ideas raised in the House, including by the WP, are not fundamentally at odds with existing policies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: They build upon the policies that we already have and make them better, cover more areas.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Sometimes they are shades of the same policy and we need not exaggerate their differences.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the case of preventive healthcare or carbon tax, WP's proposals are actually similar to the Government's policies.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Very often, WP, as Opposition, wants more of what is already being done.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, here is one difference between our two Parties.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do not think it is a major one and it is again part and parcel of political contestation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But a fundamental difference arises when it comes to WP's ideas for the Budget.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, an alternate budget without the GST simply cannot work and is not a viable alternative.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You cannot give up a major source of revenue and yet want to spend more in so many areas.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The PAP Government will not agree to it and this is a fundamental difference too because it has to do with our beliefs and our values.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We debated this issue in the Budget Debate last year and Deputy Prime Minister Wong had explained the Government's position.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Our view is that the reserves belong to all generations of Singaporeans, current and future, even though they are not born, they cannot vote and their voices have yet to be heard.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As responsible stewards, we will nevertheless safeguard their welfare and interests.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The half-half apportionment is a formula that is simple, is fair, and I think, is wise.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is very tempting, even seductive, to say let us shift half-half to 60-40.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we debated and enshrined the fiscal rules in our Constitution not that long ago.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We should not at the first sign of need, push for changes in the rules, just to take the easy way out.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We should hold on to the equal apportionment principle for as long as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is good stewardship and it is the PAP's position and that is why there is a fundamental difference here.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But previous generations had their unique challenges too, be it the plague, the industrial revolution, the World Wars, unravelling of the global monetary system, threat of nuclear holocaust, Cold War.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Specific to Singapore, this and earlier generations had to weather the threat of communism, racial riots, becoming an independent nation, severe recessions, COVID-19 and we overcame them all.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is the overcoming and not the problems and challenges, that defines a generation.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I had earlier said that ageing is a part of the human condition.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: As someone who is one Zodiac cycle away from becoming an "aged", and as the Health Minister, I consider ageing a stage of life to be greeted like an old friend and certainly not a pathology.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: A recent New York Times article caught my eye, reported that the reality of the state of happiness in Finland is actually more complex.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The report went on to say this, "the happiest people in the world aren’t that happy…more like content." It went on to say that there is a way of life in Finland called "sisu", which roughly translates to "grim determination in the face of hardship" that apparently brings you happiness.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: You can understand how "sisu" came about, given Finland's harsh climate living conditions and a strong sense of insecurity due to a long common border with a big and historically unfriendly neighbour, Russia.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When you have such a long yet inaccurate English description struggling to translate a specific concept, you know this must be some kind of unique characteristic embedded in the DNA of a particular people and in this case the Finns.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I do not think we want to say "kiasu".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One may be advanced in age, but still feel young and even if the body feels old, the heart remains young.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I think the key to happiness is having a tea break.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Sorry to stand in the way of the break.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I just wanted to thank the Minister for his responses to my speech and I just have two points of clarification.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: One is, I think, the Minister did refer to the fact that we have different views on the NIR ceiling, so I just like to ask Minister if he would acknowledge or agree that there is philosophic difference, but it is not a difference that we have not explained.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: We have, when we put out our proposals, talked about where the financing is going to come from.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Assoc Prof Jamus Lim and another WP Member of Parliament have explained and put forward proposals for financing and different ideas that we put across and the Minister referred to one of them which is raising the NIR ceiling.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, would he acknowledge that, that has been done as opposed to not being done?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And would he also acknowledge, in the same vein as some of the things that he said that we do put forward concrete ideas and the PAP may disagree with some of those ideas and we can debate them and agree to disagree, but they are alternatives and I mentioned some of those alternatives that we have put forward in the past in my speech.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: That is the first one and the second one is really on the point about future generations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I would ask Minister if he would agree that it is a balancing exercise because if conditions become too difficult, if liveability becomes damaged too much for the current generation, that would affect our fertility and there may be fewer people in the future generations to enjoy the benefits that the reserves and other things are meant to provide.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: So, would the Minister acknowledge that there is also some balancing that needs to be done on that front.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If I may, Speaker, there is a Hokkien song, "Jit Lang Jit Pua, Kam Qing Buay Suah" (一人一半，感情不散).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you divide things in half, you preserve the relationship, you preserve the peace.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And the song did not go "Jit Lang Luck Chup Bak Xian, Jit Lang Sze Chup Bak Xian, Kam Qing Buay Suah" (一人60%，一人40%，感情不散).

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: No, it does not say you have 60%, you have 40%, you preserve the peace.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is – I do not know if Members remember when we were young – we learnt the story of the fox dividing the meat amongst two parties and the fox deliberately tear it 60-40.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The one who gets the 40% of the meat protested to say the other piece is bigger.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, the fox took a bite of the 60%, he deliberately took a bigger bite and then the situation got reversed.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The other one who got a smaller piece said that the other piece is bigger and so the fox kept taking bites, until in the end you have nothing left.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I remember that lesson, not because it is an interesting story – because at a formative age, that was to me a lesson in values.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We do not want to change it too easily.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: On Mr Leon Perera's first point, as I said in my speech, yes, there have been many ideas raised by the WP, as well as other Members.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But on GST and the Budget, I still do not know – and this could be due to my ignorance because I am not in finance – I still do not know if the WP supports the GST system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And in your alternate budget, whether you are contemplating not having the GST system, because I do recall WP has always been against the GST system.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if that is the case, I would say that that your alternative does not make sense.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is not a viable nor serious alternative because without that source of revenue, it is not possible to do more.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But if your position is: you accept the GST system, but stay at 7%, and not go to 9%, then I think I may have a different view; and I will explain.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: As I was saying, I propose to take a break now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, our position, as explained in the debates relating to the GST —

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That was the position that we have conveyed and debated in this House from those debates from 2018.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I was there as well until the current time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In your proposal, amongst other things, it is to shift the NIRC – which, as we explained, I think we have a fundamental disagreement on that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But may I say this, Speaker, that we can debate the issues, we can point out where are the shades of differences, where are the areas where the PAP Government says, "we do this" and the WP Opposition says, "let us do a bit more"; and where are the areas with fundamental differences.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In the end, for this whole system to work, for this House to be a constructive Chamber for debate, for us to serve the people well, we have also to decide between us, that we have to uphold good politics.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: What is it that the people really want?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: From the ruling party's point of view, we say "Singapore is a vulnerable small place, we will have significant challenges.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need a strong, competent Government – clean, with integrity and able to deliver the goods; and we will have checks and balances, but we need the agility and the strength, in order to serve Singapore well.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: For the Opposition in WP, you will tell the people, "You need a checker against the ruling party.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There should be checks and balances." What is best for Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I say the answer to many Singaporeans is probably both.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They want a strong, competent Government, but they also believe that power cannot be absolute.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And so, it is our duty, if we want to serve the people well, to make sure we have good politics between us.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If I may just offer my view – for the ruling party, it means being able to recruit good people, with strong integrity, strong Government, competent.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In particular, we need to be able to listen to people more, empathise, understand pain points and be able to address them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And where we have to implement policies that are not so popular, that will even cause a bit of pain, but for the long-term good of the people, we need to explain sincerely, honestly, why we need to do this.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to put in place institutions, systems, checks and balances within our system; it is part and parcel of institution building.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Then, for the Opposition, the main thing you need to do is to present alternatives, so that people have a basis of decision, have a basis to compare.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And, in doing so, first, you got to do homework, put forward proposals that are credible.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: There is so much data out there, there should be no excuses that there is not enough data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In any case, if you need specific data, you can always submit a written question to ask for specific data.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then, when there are sensitive issues, like section 377A, take a stand and not hedge.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Because it is important to take a clear stand, so that the people have a measure of what the party truly stands for.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Third, when it comes to alternate proposals, take principled, consistent approaches, have consistent considerations.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It cannot be that in 2015, you proposed zero population growth for foreigners; and then, when there are not enough workers – now what?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It cannot be that in 2019, the housing paper said cut back and do not build too many houses, but now that we are short, you say build more and the contexts are different.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, you need consistency in your considerations in your policy proposals.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then, applied to all political parties, we need to ensure our leaders and our representatives carry ourselves well, so that people know that we are people of integrity and honesty.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: That we have a heart for the people, we are doing this for the people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And then, there will be moments of truths.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: When bad things happen, members misbehave or something illegal gets uncovered within the party, how we handle them.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: They give people a deep evaluation of what is the core of this political party.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, this is what I feel all of us need to do, to ensure there is good politics that serve the people.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: A lot of words are said to each other, it is part and parcel of political contestation.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But in many ways, we are also working together.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: At a time when the political landscape of Singapore is evolving, the people want a good, strong Government, but yet they want checks and balances in the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Every election, they are thinking through what is the equilibrium?

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We are contesting, but we are also working together to find the equilibrium for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I share what I think we need to do to uphold good politics, because then, we will serve the people well.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will just respond on one point that Minister Ong raised earlier and leave my colleague Mr Leong to give a fuller response when he is back in Parliament.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And that is the point about targeting a particular race.

speaker: Ms Hazel Poa (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I just want to clarify that we are not targeting any particular race.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We have always acknowledged the angst and the anxiety of Singaporeans on many issues, but we will see.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Let us see how the debate moves on from henceforth.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I just want to remind Mr Leong, and also, Ms Hazel Poa, how we raise issues matters a great deal.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Many of us Members of Parliament, we tend to the ground in our constituencies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Sometimes, disputes between two units with occupants of different ethnicity.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: So, you can have problems like noise, or your flower pots along my corridor.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: You can approach it based on what the problem is – find a way to remove the flower pots.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Or you can approach it with a certain racial undertone, the same problem, but different ways of approaching, different ways of describing it; and the latter can create sworn enemies out of neighbours.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: In Chinese, there is a saying: "人言可畏" – words can be very scary.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: We need to preserve the harmony that is so hard-fought and hard-earned.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Just very briefly to respond to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, I thank the Minister of acknowledging that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just want to make a few points very quickly in response.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: One is that, he talked about the role of the Opposition as offering alternative ideas.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: A few of us spoke about alternative ideas – just in the course of this debate and also previous debates.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I want to point out that we have offered differentiated policy proposals.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: In some cases, the Government has moved closer to the proposals we have made in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It is not that we have not explained it; it is not that we have hidden the trade-offs; it is not that we have no explanation for how to finance that gap.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That is going to happen only in, I think, about 12 years' time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, it was not a call for an immediate cut or any kind of cut in BTO construction at the time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I think I have explained this multiple times, but I just thought that, clearly, I need to just explain it one last time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I will also explain my side of the story one last time.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: As I mentioned, substantively, what matters to Singaporeans is that they want to see what is the difference in policies between the two parties.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And, as I summarised just now, there are a lot of policies on which we are actually on the same page.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I mentioned carbon tax, I mentioned preventive care, and there are others which are really shades of the same policies.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But as the Opposition, you will always ask the Government to do a bit more.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: It is your job to do so and it is our job to think about it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: But there are additional suggestions and MOM will think about it.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I talked about healthcare, that we got primary care; above that, we have secondary and tertiary care; below that, we have community care.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: I think just debating policy differences is just "primary care".

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: If you want a full-fledged good political system that serves people, we got to go beyond that.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: The ruling party needs to do what is required – listening to people, explaining things well, including difficult policies, keeping yourself clean and honest, always think of the long term, correct mistakes, if it commits mistakes and constantly refresh itself.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And for the Opposition party, do its homework, do not say "no data" as an excuse.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Take a stand, even on sensitive issues, such as section 377A.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: Take a principled, consistent approach to your policies and explain how benefits are to be paid for.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And for all of us, carry ourselves well, ensure we are parties of integrity, honesty.

speaker: Mr Ong Ye Kung
text: And if anything goes wrong, handle it well, so that the people know where we stand.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: And on that note, we need not "sisu" anymore.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the chair at 4.05 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.45 pm until 4.05 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This has been a clear theme throughout our development as a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Since Independence, we have looked beyond our immediate needs, taken a long-term perspective to plan for Singapore's growth, and incorporated environmental stewardship in our development.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When our forefathers planted trees, it was to create shade for the future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The trees our forefathers planted continue to provide us shade today, creating lush green spaces where we can rest and recharge.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Another example is our efforts to clean up our waterways.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When our forefathers cleaned up the Singapore river, it did not just solve the immediate problems of public hygiene and public health, but also transformed the Singapore river over decades.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Today, the river channels into the Marina Reservoir, providing clean water for our daily needs.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is now a distinctive icon of our bustling city.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Like tree planting and waterway clean-ups, our efforts in environmental stewardship are made possible through the dedication of many generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As President Halimah Yacob said in her Opening Address last week, and I quote, "We are here today only because of what previous generations of Singaporeans did." Times may have changed, but we need to preserve our forefathers' values of putting before self, the interests of the family, the community and the country; of self-sacrifice; and of hard work and determination in the face of adversity.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we respond to a changing world and its new demands, we will need to find ways to steward Singapore towards a new and more sustainable future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: There is a growing awareness that mankind's current reliance on fossil fuels is no longer sustainable.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Humanity needs a fundamental change in the way we power our economy, our way of life.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: There is a need for us to adapt and prepare for a future that is warmer, with more unpredictable weather and their full consequences.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have also realised that our pursuit for convenience through the linear "use and throw" consumption model will have to change.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To keep Singapore going and sustainable for future generations, we must adjust how we live as a society and how we grow our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: How can we achieve economic and social development, while protecting the environment that gives us life?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: How can we account and be accountable for our environmental externalities?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: How do we change our societal norms and behaviours to live more sustainably?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: What does it take to prepare ourselves to be a more environmentally sustainable and resilient country, so that we can have a better Singapore for tomorrow?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Many Members, such as Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Sharael Taha, Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Shawn Huang have reminded this House that sustainability remains one of the integral issues during our time.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Don Wee spoke about positioning small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) to capture green economy opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Leon Perera spoke about renewable energy and the investment opportunities it brings to the region.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And Ms Nadia Samdin called for collective action to support the sustainability agenda.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong spoke about how we have to adjust our social compact, not just among ourselves, but between this generation and future generations to come.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We need to re-examine and reaffirm our social compact at three levels.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, the social compact between "me" and others.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: How do I, as an individual, relate to other individuals?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: What is my obligation and responsibility towards others around me?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Second, the social compact between "my group" and other groups.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Every one of us is part of a group or several groups in the society.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We may be part of a for-profit business, a public sector agency, an organisation in the people sector or a special interest group.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In our social compact, what are the respective roles of our group vis-à-vis others?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: How should we come together to address the complex challenges of today and advance our common interests?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Third, the social compact between "my generation" and other generations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: What should my generation do and more importantly, set aside for the future ones?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: What can we afford to let our future generations do and decide for themselves?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: What are the common values that thread and weave across multiple generations of Singaporeans, binding us together and making us stronger as One People?

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our choices and actions impact not just ourselves, but others around us.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Take our hawker centres, our community dining rooms where people from all walks of life go for their daily favourite local fare.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our hawker centres are microcosms of our everyday relationships.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They reflect the societal norms and accepted behaviour across all segments of society.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As diners, when we return our crockery and clear our tables after our meals, we are being considerate to other diners who use those tables after us.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When we bin our used tissue after a meal properly, we reduce the risk of infecting our fellow patrons, our cleaners and our stall holders.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As diners, we cherish and support our hawkers who serve up delicious, yet affordable food tirelessly.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We want our hawkers to have a better living, to have a standard of living that progresses with the rests of us and we are prepared to pay more for their hard work over time.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must also be prepared to pay more for cleaning services over time so that our cleaners can also enjoy higher wages and a better living.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This helps to keep our hawker heritage alive and encourages the next generation of hawkers to join the trade.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Simply said, our individual choices and actions matter.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Not only do they directly impact those around us, but collectively, they shape our norms, our cultures and determine the collective tone of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must normalise good habits and exhibit sustainable behaviour.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We owe it not just to our environment, but also to one another to keep our shared home clean, green and safe.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The social impact between my group and others.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our efforts are not only confined to what we do as individuals, but also when we contribute in our capacities as members of groups and organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I have touched on dining in hawker centres and let me move along the food chain and look at the retail of foods.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: At the heart of a sustainable Singapore is all of us being more resource efficient.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We need to move away from our use-and-throw culture.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The buy-use-throw consumption model is a convenient one.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: However, it also puts a tremendous amount of stress on our resources, both in having to produce more and having to throw away more.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The shift to a more sustainable consumption model requires all groups in the society to play a part.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Consumers bring reusable bags when grocery shopping and recycle the packaging of goods where possible.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and schools help spread the message and educate the public in using alternative packaging for bagging garbage in the households.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Businesses redesign their processes to reduce the resources we use to produce and the waste that we dispose.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, to reduce packaging waste, businesses use the right materials to increase the rate of recycling, use the right design to make recycling easier and reduce the amount of packaging materials used.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Industry organises the collection and treatment of recyclables and help shape consumer behaviour by making environmental costs more visible.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Closing our waste loop is challenging but achievable.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: There are costs involved and it requires change of habit across all parties.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But as we reduce our draw on earth's resources, we use this common mission to form new partnerships and discover creative solutions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: CRUST Group is a food tech start-up that works with other companies to turn surplus food ingredients, like bread and fruit peels, into beers and sodas.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: CRUST group has partnered bakeries, hotels and supermarkets to upcycle their surplus ingredients and create new unique products, which can bring in additional revenue while reducing their own food waste.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They also generate compost to replenish and nurture the community garden and landscape.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These initiatives show how our social compact is shifting in the right direction.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Groups pool together resources and expertise to collectively address complex issues.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are encouraged by such efforts and will continue to find ways and means to further catalyse such partnerships.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The inter-generational social compact — the social compact between "my generation" and other generations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I started my speech by paying tribute to the work of our forefathers and stressed that we must do the same and pay it forward.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While the full impact of climate change may not hit us now, it is clear that we need to make the investments now to secure a brighter future for our next generation.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The inter-generational social compact is clearly illustrated in our approach to coastal protection.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Sea level rise emerging from climate change is an existential threat to Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Without effective adaptation measures, rising sea levels, storm surges and extreme high tides could result in transient sea levels rising up to five metres.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will pose great risks to our community, our infrastructure and our livelihoods.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The work to strengthen Singapore's flood resilience against sea level rise is a multi-generational one.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It will take long-term investments in adaptation solutions and the capabilities needed to bring these solutions to fruition.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These investments will need to start today and from today's generation if we are to successfully meet this long-term future challenge.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Most of this will be spent on coastal barriers, both nature-based and man-made, and drainage infrastructure to protect Singapore against sea level rise.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have yet to determine the specific solutions that we will put in place, for each segment of our coastlines.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have started the site-specific studies, starting with the stretch from the city to the East Coast.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: What we know is that this requires steady investments over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The solutions will take time to put in place and we need to put the pieces together in good time, ahead of the rising tides.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These are the ways we see the inter-generational social compact, in how the current generation does it part for future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We currently import more than 90% of our food needs.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have ample supply and we have access to a rich variety of foods from all over the world.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is about buying insurance against systemic food supply disruption, so that future generations are in a better place with food security.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This initiative, at its core, is a commitment to future generations.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It will require sustained contributions from the private, people and public sectors and for all parties to stay the course.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will invest, now, in infrastructure works such as land preparation, coastal protection, power and water supply and waste management facilities.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Farmers take bold steps to increase the productivity of the farms through investing in technology.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They are not starting from scratch; several are second or third generation farmers who inherit the experience and wisdom of their forefathers.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Green Harvest is one such farm that has combined farming expertise with technology.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As a joint venture between Kok Fah Technology Farm and Teambuild Construction Group, Green Harvest brings together their collective expertise in agriculture and construction to break new grounds.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They have constructed Southeast Asia's largest hydroponics glass greenhouse, which uses high-tech automation to grow vegetables efficiently and productively without the use of pesticides.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The farm has started production since July 2022 and I have already seen some of their produce on our retail shelves.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As our local food supply ramps up, consumers and industry buyers also step forward to provide the demand that our farms need to be commercially viable.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When we buy local, we are supporting our local farms and F&B businesses that use local produce.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are co-investing in our food resilience for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is a symbiotic relationship – the local farmers give our F&B industry and consumers certainty in supply and quality; and reduce the vagaries caused by extreme weather events.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The supermarkets and F&B buyers in turn give our local farmers certainty in demand, thus reducing their business and financial risks.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Local produce may cost more but they are more reliable and fresh, attributes that are valuable to consumers and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By building up our local food production today, we are gaining food security for tomorrow.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our current generation must make the long-term investments in capability-building.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Through research and development, we sow the seeds for a broad spectrum of innovation and technological solutions that will allow us to thrive in a more uncertain world.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By pursuing innovations in sustainable novel foods, or planning and building long-term for coastal protection, or investing in energy-efficient water treatment technologies, we ensure that Singapore can remain resilient to climate change into the future.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By pioneering the deployment of low-carbon energy in support of our net zero ambitions, we lay the foundations for building a green economy in a carbon-constrained world.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By deepening our understanding of climate science and its regional impacts, we discover new opportunities for international collaboration.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: By collectively changing our consumption and living habits, we reduce our footprint on the environment and support sustainable businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We recognise that we are caretakers and stewards of a country that will endure beyond us.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our forefathers showed what could be done in our early years of independence.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As we face the new challenges ahead, let us continue to translate our convictions into actions.

speaker: The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When we work together, as we have in the past, we can create a sustainable Singapore in the decades to come.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Meritocracy has been a central topic in the first two days of this debate, so, as one of the few speakers remaining, I thought it is perhaps fitting that I round back to this topic.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But rather than talk about what more, or what else, the State can, or should, do with regard to our meritocracy – be it more intensive redistribution, wage restructuring or reforms to our education system – I would like to focus instead on what else each of us, citizens, can and should do for our meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And each of us – all of us – can and should do much more.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because in Singapore, I believe that meritocracy represents both a privilege and a responsibility of being Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Meritocracy represents both a privilege and a responsibility of being Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, meritocracy remains the best basic organising principle for our society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think no one in this House will quibble with this point.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: There is broad agreement within this House but I think it is worthwhile to also highlight the point for society at large, for Singaporeans at large.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And the point is that we do have a consensus in Singapore, that we will use "merit" as the basic principle to determine who is sorted to which station in life, at which stage in life, across our life courses.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This consensus may have been more tacit than explicit but it exists.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is a robust consensus and it is also useful to bring this consensus to the fore from time to time and remind ourselves clearly of its existence – that meritocracy remains the best basic organising principle to keep the Singapore Story going.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But in order for this meritocracy to work, we must also allow meritocracy to operate fully and be fully expressed in our society.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We cannot and should not put an artificial lid on meritocracy.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This means, in the simplest terms, allowing the best, the most "meritorious" amongst us to run as far and as fast and soar as high as they can.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Instead, they will be supported and cheered on by the system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is the privilege that our framework of meritocracy in Singapore provides to Singaporeans; that every person can look forward to run and fly and chase rainbows and fulfil his or her full individual potential within the framework of meritocracy that we have.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is not a half-hearted meritocracy because we as a society have committed to allowing it full expression and it is one privilege of being Singaporean – to be able to operate and flourish within this framework.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: They are two sides of the same coin.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: A framework that allows each of us to run far and fast and chase rainbows will also lead inevitably to some amongst us who cannot keep up, who need a lot more help to keep up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, it becomes our responsibility, our personal responsibility, each citizen's responsibility, that while we enjoy the privilege accorded by our framework of meritocracy, we also each do our part to make sure that no one falls too far behind nor falls permanently behind.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Each of us has a responsibility to reach back, pull others along and help everyone to keep up.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is in our collective interest to do so, but I think, more fundamentally, it is also our basic responsibility as Singaporeans, our basic responsibility to one another and to society at large to do so.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Now, if I may put it another way.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Decades ago, when we started out as an improbable nation, meritocracy defined Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Instead, ability, industry, merit; these would make the measure of a man or woman in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And these would also make a society, our society based on justice and equality.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And so, on this basis, our improbable nation got everyone onto an escalator, the escalator of progress and prosperity.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It also means opening up a whole range of pathways, a whole range of escalators, not one but multiple escalators that Singaporeans can get onto, all escalators going up, progressing in tandem.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And this work continues today, as Deputy Prime Minister Wong has laid out in his speech on Monday.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Much more remains to be done to make our meritocracy ever broader and more inclusive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But I see a third lap, a third chapter, in the evolution of our framework of meritocracy going forward.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this third lap of our meritocracy, we can make sure that no one is left by the sidelines of the multiple escalators that we have, unable or unwilling to get onto one.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It would take each of us to care, to step off the escalator from time to time to get those of us by the sidelines onto the multitude of escalators, onto some escalator, so that all of us can move up together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I call this third lap of our meritocracy a generative meritocracy, not just broader and more inclusive, but generative.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Generative because I believe it will set forth a new wave of active citizenry in which all of us recognise and embrace our basic responsibility to keep meritocracy going and take action.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This will be active citizenry at its best.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And generative because the difference that we can make through this movement is not only to help others, but as Minister Chan Chun Sing has put it in his speech in this debate, we can enable others to thrive.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: We have an opportunity to apply ourselves to enable others to do well for themselves.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And finally, I believe it is generative because instead of a meritocracy in which some winners take all, together, we can create a meritocracy in which all are winners.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And this is not just a hope that can be left to the state, the Government to make happen.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It will take all of us to make it happen.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Embracing our responsibility, active citizenry at its best.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And in my mind, this will be a wonderful manifestation too of what Deputy Prime Minister Wong has described as our "renewed commitment to one another in the path ahead".

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I hope we can find application of this renewed commitment specifically in our meritocracy, make our meritocracy a key plank of this renewed commitment to one another and make our meritocracy a generative one that keeps going because of all of us, because of our collective efforts to one another.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Well, for one, I hope we can do much more to come forward as mentors to these children.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Mentors, on a sustained basis, committed to the long haul.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Mentors, who start by meeting the child where he or she is, mentors who accept before attempting to fix.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I hope many of us can come forward to be such mentors, be role models and just be there for children born to lesser means.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this way, we can help them to keep up in a generative meritocracy, help them to get onto the multiple escalators, enable them to thrive and do well for themselves.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: This is a precious thing in Singapore and we have got to cherish it and keep growing it.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: First, we need to do more to celebrate our traditions, embrace our traditions, preserve and sustain them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think it means, among other things, that ethnic, cultural and religious organisations all need to look at renewal, drawing in younger Singaporeans and being deliberate about succession.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Because things can be easily appropriated in this day and age, sensationalised, amplified and once the genie is out of the bottle, sometimes damage done cannot be undone.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: So let us all be extra conscious and extra deliberate.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Perhaps only in Singapore do we have, just this month alone, folks observing the ancestral festival of Qing Ming, in fact, some groups observe this for up to 10 days beyond the actual day, and at the same time, we have Jewish friends this month celebrating Passover, friends celebrating Puthandu or the Tamil New Year and we have Christian friends concluding their observance of 40 days of Lent while Muslim friends were getting into the thick of their observance of Ramadan.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And of course, in a couple of days, our Muslim friends will be celebrating Hari Raya Puasa.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: All in the same month, only in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: It is a beautiful harmony and long may we, all of us, commit ourselves to keep this going.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   In this debate, meritocracy in Singapore has been a topic of particular interest, and the Government has also laid out ways to improve the system.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In other words, the social consensus of not setting a ceiling for meritocracy means individuals need to have the awareness and sense of responsibility to help those at the bottom.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this way, meritocracy will no longer be based on competition and distribution.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Instead, it will be based on mutual assistance and benefits, as well as a win-win mindset, with a vision to create a new meritocratic system as one united people.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Therefore, I hope that as the Government works to improve the meritocratic system, every Singaporean will better understand their individual social responsibility, and take on this responsibility more proactively, by actively helping Singaporeans lagging behind in the system and lend a helping hand to those at the bottom.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I think this is critical for all Singaporeans to move forward together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Meritocracy is one of our core values in nation-building and governance, while another core value is multiculturalism.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In the social media era today, good things are seldom propagated, but bad things are particularly viral.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Hence, I hope that we will be more prudent and exercise greater caution when we speak and act, to think carefully before we speak or react, in order to protect our precious multiculturalism.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, I have spoken about meritocracy and multiculturalism and the role each of us can play to keep these going.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: Meritocracy and multiculturalism are core values in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: In this debate, we have heard polls being cited, polls indicating that Singaporeans lack confidence, lack optimism in our future.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: But the bottom line is I think, I believe that we can all be confident of our future, together.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And chief amongst these reasons is our collective core values, like meritocracy and multiculturalism.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: And these same core values, if we remind ourselves of them, stay alive to them, refresh them as it may require to meet needs of the hour and draw optimism from them.

speaker: Mr Xie Yao Quan (Jurong)
text: I believe these same core values, our "sisu" will drive us forward and help us forge ahead, confidently, as one Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Three years ago, I delivered my maiden speech in Parliament in the throes of the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I ended my speech describing a scene in JRR Tolkein’s Lord of the Rings trilogy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The wizard Gandalf was mentoring the young hobbit Frodo Baggins.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Frodo wished that the terrible events that had befallen the world need not have happened in his time.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To that, Gandalf responded, "All we have to decide is what to do with the time that is given us".

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I also shared that "years from now, in this very House, our future generations will judge us by how we have met that moment".

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have done much with the time given to us during the pandemic and have since met that moment by most accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Collectively, we steered Singapore through the proverbial “crisis of our generation”, just as Frodo and his team did at the end of the story.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Today, I will focus on our young Frodos – our youths, since Members have already spoken about other segments of society this week.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I will share how our youths have indeed met that moment together with us and how they can continue to serve, shape and lead our country even as that moment passes and another moment approaches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Every week, I meet with youths in my capacities as Deputy Chair of the National Youth Council (NYC), Advisor to Young PAP and many youth organisations, also in businesses, schools, unions, the interfaith community and the community.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Ms Nadin Samdin raised the importance of ensuring meaningful youth participation, not just for quotas or at dialogues.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, please allow me to share with this House and our fellow Singaporeans, how our youths are taking action and how we are continuing to enable them to shape, serve and lead in our social and economic spheres.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We have youths carrying the torch lit by our founding leaders to strengthen racial and religious harmony.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Last month, at Masjid Khalid, I met with 75 Harmony Champions, mostly youth leaders from the ground-up organisation, Roses of Peace, to discuss how to continually refresh our interfaith work on the ground.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In my local Harmony Circle, we just welcomed 39 new volunteers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: There are many youths, many women and many members from diverse backgrounds, including the digital savvy team at Masjid Al-Falah, led by the young Ustaz Khairul Anwar who is my Harmony Circle Vice Chair, and our secretary Lily Lim, an outstanding young Singaporean undergraduate of Iranian roots.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I have always cautioned that if we take our eyes off this important work, we will not have the foundations upon which to build our society and our economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It is imperative that our youths continue to carry this torch.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We also have youths who care deeply about our people's mental well-being and they have followed-up with action.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In my Moulmein-Cairnhill (MOCA) Division, my Youth Network is working with our Neighbourhood Committee to build our local Mental Well-Being Circle.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We also have youths who care deeply about migrant workers living among us and who are helping to build Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Youths like Rachel Divashini from the Alliance of Guest Workers Outreach (AGWO), Benjamin Kuan from HealthServe and Wesley Lim from It’s Raining Raincoats (IRR) are working with us on the ground to care for, recognise and create space for our migrant worker friends.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In my MOCA constituency, youths like Alister, Aaron, Andy and Qi Wei set up OMG for Our Migrant Guests, to bring our residents and migrant workers together to celebrate festivals and recognise their work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: They are partnering with the voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) I mentioned earlier in this meaningful and important work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Youths like Woo Qiyun, Samantha Thian and Tan Shi-Zhou are leading the way in this regard.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In MOCA, one of our most successful initiatives is "Our Green MOCA", where youths are involved in activities such as greening our Cambridge Neighbourhood, Green Hackathons, Climate Conversations and even led a mural painting project at Our Green Hub.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Last year, our young Green MOCA Young Ambassadors also connected DBS with ACS Junior on their sustainability game outreach to raise awareness about food waste, e-waste and conservation locally.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, our youths care about and are taking action on the issues I just highlighted.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
