text: But we are also keenly aware that bread and butter issues, social mobility and progress and opportunities are top of mind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Ms Sylvia and Mr Henry Kwek spoke out on these issues in their speeches.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: There are many ways that we are collectively addressing this.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: For example, we are partnering with our youths as they lead ground-up initiatives and efforts to equalise opportunities, through initiatives like mentoring.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Youths like Kelley Wong at Young Women’s Leadership Connection, Clarence Ching at Access Singapore, Hafiz Kasman at Kinobi and Mock Yi Jun at Advisory, are driving our Mentoring SG movement, ensuring that youths have access to mentors and opportunities to learn, grow and thrive in their areas of interest.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The Astra Collective which Mr Henry Kwek's Kebun Baru team is partnering is a member of Mentoring SG and we are supporting their work and helping them to expand their reach into communities like Kebun Baru.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Mr Xie Yao Quan's calls for mentors is thus also pertinent and relevant.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is an important upstream effort to prepare our youths for the fast-changing world and economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So, please do join Mentoring SG which is a key initiative under our Forward SG Movement.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Beyond mentoring as a way to equalise opportunities and guide our youths, another key way to tackle social mobility and bread and butter issues is to create jobs and career opportunities for them, ensure also that they have the skills to take on these opportunities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Allow me to share how we have created these opportunities and examples of youths who have turned up, seized them and are distinguishing themselves in their careers and shaping our economy in their own unique ways.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: When I left the private sector to join the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) back in 2020, I was asked to help look after our tourism sector, which was hardest hit by the pandemic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: During the depths of the crisis, I met weekly with many of our tourism workers, gathering feedback on how best to support them and help the sector recover.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: At this month’s Tourism Industry Conference, I shared about a young SHATEC trainee I met during the downturn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: She told me she was picking up skills at SHATEC during the downturn to "catch the wind" for when tourism recovers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Another young Singaporean in the tourism sector is Matthew Yong who is now Assistant Chief Culturist in Capella Hotel Sydney.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: During COVID-19, Matthew decided to upgrade his skills, believing correctly that the hotel sector will thrive and boom post-COVID.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: They took the down time to upskill and many like them are trailblazing new ideas to build a more sustainable tourism sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I have also met youths who are seizing opportunities in emerging sectors that we are growing, like tech, cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing, robotics and agri-food tech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I serve as Advisor to Cyber Youth Singapore (CYS), led by Ben Chua and his team.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: CYS prepares youths, including those studying in Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs) and polytechnics, to acquire cybersecurity skills and secure internships and jobs in the cybersecurity sector which we are growing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I meet them regularly to help shape their programme and direction.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Leading up to their Cyber Youth Summit in June, I had a fruitful exchange with student leader Marcus Tan and his fellow students at ITE College Central last month to share about opportunities in the cybersecurity space.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our youths are tech-savvy and passionate about shaping our digital future and are in good stead with leaders like Ben and Marcus taking the charge.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our youths are also taking on new and exciting jobs in the emerging advanced manufacturing space that we are nurturing.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: When I visited companies like the semiconductor manufacturer Micron and biotech firm Amgen, I met young employees using Augmented Reality (AR) and robots to produce innovative products for the semiconductor and biopharma markets respectively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We will continue to support them through our various SkillsFuture offerings, trade associations and unions to prepare them to take on these jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are also preparing our youths for a future of automation and robotics, a theme I shared at our MTI Committee of Supply (COS) in February.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: At the Sixth Anniversary of the National Robotics Programme (NRP) at Singapore University of Technology and Design (SUTD), I met youths from Victoria School and Raffles Girls’ School who were deeply involved in the design, programming and deployment of reconfigurable robots.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We will continue to support the use of robots in high-tech manufacturing and create futuristic jobs for our people through our work at MTI and the National Robotics Programme (NRP).

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Another area we are literally growing is agri-food tech.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Last week, I inaugurated the launch of a new agri-genomic farm by Singrow, an agri-food tech startup that develops and grows the world’s first climate-resilient strawberries.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: While there, I met many youths from National University of Singapore (NUS) and our polytechnics, including Janice Tong who is studying Biomedical Sciences in Singapore Polytechnic.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: They were using AI and Machine Learning to improve crop yield.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Janice is a smart and confident young lady.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I also regularly visit our startups regularly to get feedback about our StartupSG and other Enterprise Singapore schemes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I was at Block 79 recently to engage startup founders and ecosystem players and attended the NUS Entrepreneurship Society’s University Conference (UNICON), its flagship student-led entrepreneurship and tech conference that features many promising startups.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Through my engagements with this industry, I have met many young startup founders looking to break ground, including Alexandra Zhang from Factorem, a precision engineering startup manufacturing 3D printed parts for larger firms using AI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Startups, like Factorem, are making strides and we are supporting them to realise their potential.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: While doing so, we are also continuing to help our young business owners navigate the various schemes and grants we have available and find one that is suitable for them, in order to address the challenges that businesses might have in identifying schemes that meet their needs, as Member Mr Don Wee raised.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And financial institutions and fintech companies are looking to hire our students across universities and polytechnics.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Next week, I will be at Ngee Ann Polytechnic for the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Institute of Banking and Finance's Growing Timber series, where we will plan how to grow opportunities for our youths in the sector and help them take on these jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I will share more details at the event and look forward to meeting our youths, including many who have made their mark in the sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I first joined the financial sector as a youth 13 years ago in Boston and New York, and then moved to Hong Kong, and then back home in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I have seen many of my former batch mates in the financial sector now leading their organisations or building new companies.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We will grow our timber in the financial sector and our youths will benefit from this work.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Many have been leading and taking action on social issues crucial for our nation-building and preparing for, seizing and even creating job opportunities to secure their future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And our youths have indeed met the COVID-19 moment with us and have accomplished much since.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But as Prime Minister Lee cautioned yesterday, there are many storms ahead of us, with geopolitical challenges and new risks and opportunities to contempt with, such as artificial generative intelligence and climate change.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our youths will need to navigate these waters and we will, of course, brave these storms together with them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I have always responded with two words "turn up".

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: At this point, please allow me to speak directly to our youths and unpack what I mean by "turn up".

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Much has been said this week about ChatGPT and the mainstreaming of Artificial Intelligence (AI).

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: A Financial Times article by Ian Hogarth cautioned against the perils of opportunities of "God-like AI" and Stanford University, the State of AI report, explored issues around Artificial Generative Intelligence or AGI.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: How then should you, as youths, navigate the future?

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It cannot strengthen mental well-being or mentor a new generation.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Rather, you must turn up, gather physically, attend one another's festivals/events, learn about one another's beliefs and backgrounds, meet face-to-face, hold someone's hand and guide them and journey with them through life by being present.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Be human in the coming age of "Gold-like AI".

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our collective handling of the COVID-19 pandemic has further strengthened Singapore's global reputation and appeal.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To reap the benefits of these investments, our workers, our people and you, our youths, must be prepared to take on these jobs, create new ones within our growing ecosystem and build value for themselves, for society and for others.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It has often been said that no one owes Singapore a living.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I have worked in the private sector most of my career.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I have learnt that we need to create value, show value and share value to be relevant in the market.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We do not have the markets and opportunities bigger countries have.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But you can tap on the many schemes and programmes we have designed for you.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Use what you have learnt through our educations system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Use our economic schemes to help your enterprises grow and succeed.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Take on internships, apply for jobs and excel in them.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We need to be prepared, remain exceptional and strengthen our raison d'etre.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We did not come this far just to sit on our hands.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: While we continue to create value and stay relevant, we also need to be mindful about recent global trends, like quiet quitting and lying flat, which will slow us down and set us back.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The world and its challenges will not be kind.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: You must be courageous, diligent, determined to keep innovating and pushing barriers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I agree with Mr Shawn Hwang that our youths must have determination, ambition, passion, centred on a strong set of values, strong set of identity, strong set of culture, youths with a "go-getting spirit" that Mr S Rajaratnam described that Prime Minister Lee quoted yesterday, youths who will not just run the race but stay the course, rise to the occasion and meet the many moments that will come your way.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: But the battle and adventure was Frodo's and Frodo's alone.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: So too his decisions, the outcomes of his decisions and the lessons he had to learn.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Gandalf gave Frodo the platform to learn, grow and thrive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And at the climatic end of the story, Frodo and team played a decisive role.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To try, to create, to innovate, to fail, to learn, to try again.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: They are full of ideas, passion and energy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Recently, I hosted three Forward Singapore exercises with youths, living and working abroad.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: It reminded me of the nine years I spent abroad as a youth living overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: These youths are exploring the world, connecting with people, making their mark.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: They remind me of my friends and cohort of youths who were overseas.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Some in my cohort had gone on to fund companies, lead global firms, making their respective differences in the social and public sectors to which they had been called.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: As I spoke with these youths, we exchanged ideas of the Singapore we hope to shape.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: After the session, I have received a few LinkedIn messages from the youths.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I am now trying to figure who is Smeagol or Gollum in this whole narrative.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Certainly, it is not Miss Rachel Ong, who will be next.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In her speech, the President outlined key priorities for Singapore for the remainder of this term of Government – one being the need to expand opportunities throughout life for all, an inclusive meritocracy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This right and necessary work for Singapore's next growth phase lies not only with our Government.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The President's speech is indeed a clarion call for a closer and more intentional partnership between our people, public and private resources.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To ensure Singapore becomes a more inclusive meritocracy for our persons with disabilities, or PwDs, and their caregivers, I believe the active participation of the non-SMEs in inclusive employment is critical.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: They include Uniqlo, Cushman and Wakefield, Shangri-La Hotel, UOB, NLB as well as others who have tapped into Workforce Singapore's Open Door Programme to support employment of PwDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But the impetus for non-SMEs to build a more inclusive workforce cannot be rooted in social responsibility alone.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: There must be a clear understanding of the tangible competitive advantages PwDs bring to the workplace, even after factoring in adjustment costs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Accenture rightly coined this, "The Disability Inclusion Advantage".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The first advantage is that inclusive workplaces lead to higher work productivity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Last week, I had the opportunity to spend some time at SPD Contact Centre, a partnership between SPD and startup firm Octopus8.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Octopus8 is a business process outsourcing and software firm with an intentionally inclusive workforce.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: What I found interesting was that Mr Lawrence Luan, founder of Octopus8, did not start this work with the intention of being a social enterprise.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In fact, he had not heard of the term "social enterprise" until much later.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Prior to starting Octopus8, Lawrence worked in a multinational company (MNC) serving clients in business process services.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Lawrence was asked how he decided on this uncommon workforce profile from a solely business perspective.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: He shared that at his previous work in the MNC, he saw how PwDs in his workplace provided fellow colleagues a different perspective of life.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Lawrence shared that when his colleagues learnt of how a PwD staff took painstaking years to learn to speak, fellow colleagues were themselves convicted for using the ability to speak on grumbles and complaints.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: When another PwD staff would take over two hours to commute to the office each way, the rest then saw the privilege of work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The lived realities of PwD colleagues continue to inspire greater productivity and grit in daily work done by non-disabled individuals.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This, in addition to the fact that a well-placed PwD can well perform or even better than the average non-disabled staff.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In the course of his consulting work, Lawrence also observes that when an organisation includes PwDs as part of their workforce, it often leads to a review and simplification of their business processes.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The outcome is also corroborated by SG Enable's commissioned study published last year.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The second advantage is that PwDs foster innovation and problem-solving skills.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Reena Rajas-vari was my very close friend and colleague of eight years before she passed away last year, to cancer.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I share her story because she lived a most remarkable life despite turning blind at a prime age of 28.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: After taking years to grieve the sudden loss of sight, Reena regained purpose and committed to creative ways to unlearn and relearn how to go about the daily tasks and be independent again.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: An athlete by nature, she took up sound-tennis while going on regular hikes and mountain climbing.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Her love for fashion gave her impetus to create her own system to coordinate her clothes, shoes and jewellery despite not being able to see.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: On the work front, no one could inspire and facilitate corporate programmes on resilience and innovation as effectively as Reena did.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Her creative problem-solving skills and tenacity shared in training workshops, went on to inspire our corporate clients to do the same.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: When someone wakes up thinking about how to do mundane things differently, that is innovation on display, a skillset.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If companies would take time to uncover these innate and valuable skillsets in PwDs, place them in positions to thrive, I have no doubt that we will find some of the best gems in our local talent pool.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Far from being anecdotal, the business case for an inclusive workforce is backed by a 4-year research conducted by Accenture on 140 companies.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Appropriating the “Disability Inclusion Advantage” fully requires both PwDs and enterprises to take risks and be open to making adjustments.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: First, willing to redesign jobs and leverage technology.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A young man with cerebral palsy had come to interview for a data-entry job as that had been his training.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, during the role assessment, it was evident he was unable to perform the task efficiently.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But this young man had a noticeably sharp mind and engaged well in conversations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As such, the recruiter encouraged him to give Digital Marketing a try.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Though he had not been offered any other position apart from data entry, he decided to take on the opportunity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This young man discovered his niche and progressed at work because his employer cared enough to take the time to identify his talent, redesigned the role to maximise his genius.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Our enterprises need to be willing to invest in their PwD talent.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The good news is with technological advancement, some of the tasks that once hindered PwDs from taking on job roles can now be automated.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Work that once required onsite presence can now be done remotely by PWDs with mobility issues.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: We need only take the first step to give our PwDs an opportunity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The training support accessible to each PwD in their earlier years, differs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Placement officers in companies or social service organisations may need to work more collaboratively with PwDs or their caregivers to further uncover skills that may have been overlooked due to early training bias, as in the case of the young man with cerebral palsy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I hope our Enabling Masterplan will continue to build Singapore’s capabilities to identify and train PWDs in skill sets that amplify their abilities and self-confidence.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As our nation moves towards a digital economy, technological advancements can work to the advantage of our PwDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For example, Profileprint is a Singapore tech startup located in Enabling Village that uses AI to perform accurate food grading without the need to taste, see or touch it.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Such job roles open employment opportunities for both PWDs and non-disabled.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I am encouraged to see that tech startups not designed as social enterprises, are choosing to leverage technology to engage PwDs in meaningful work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I hope that we will see more startups like Octopus8 and ProfilePrint who proactively consider PwDs as a viable part of their workforce.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Meanwhile, as non-small and medium enterprises also digitise and upgrade their work processes, they could also proactively explore how more PwDs can be integrated into their workforce.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Supervisors must also be trained to manage staff in a diverse workplace.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If management is perceived as overly empathetic to PwDs or does not correct staff for poor performance, it negatively impacts workplace culture for both PwDs and non-disabled staff.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: At the same time, it is vital that non-disabled staff are properly oriented to the value of inclusion and her application at work.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Without proper onboarding of all staff, PwDs may still feel excluded or discriminated against.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I shared at the recent COS that some of our PwDs do not participate in work because they may not be aware of or do not believe that there are jobs or workplaces that can accommodate their disability.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: SG-Enable and their partner NGOs have done a tremendous amount of work in engaging the disabled community.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Corporations with established inclusive workplace practices can also collaborate with schools and grassroots organisations; to run community outreach programmes to share how PwDs are engaged in their workplaces.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I hope that the lived examples of how PwDs are empowered to do meaningful work in their organisations can inspire PwDs and their families towards a greater hope and future.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I note with interest the multinational corporation (MNC) Lawrence Luan had worked with.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This caused his former firm to be more open to hire PwDs across business divisions.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Government project tenders can be a great lever to encourage suppliers to participate in Singapore’s inclusive workplace agenda.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In addition to such “set-aside” clauses for tenders, our Government could consider a preferred purchase programme for suppliers with the Enabling Mark.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I have spoken extensively about what enterprises can do for our PwDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Many of the adjustments shared can also be applied to support the caregivers of severely disabled PwDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I quote Baroness Minouche Shafik, Director of London School of Economics and Political Science, and former Deputy Managing Director of the IMF: “Harnessing everyone’s talents is not an issue of fairness; it is also good for the economy.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: A new social contract is not about higher taxes, more redistribution, and a bigger welfare state.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is about fundamentally reordering and equalizing how opportunity and security are distributed across society.” We have an opportunity here in Singapore, to once again be at the forefront of what makes good sense economically and what is also good for our collective citizenry.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: There need not be a trade-off if we fundamentally structure intentionally the inclusion of PwDs and their caregivers into our workforce.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As may be recalled, the hon Member Mr Perera mentioned, in relation to the Goods and Services Tax (GST), that the Workers' Party (WP) accepted the GST at 7% and conveyed this in 2018.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My interest is that I actually spoke about the WP's position from 1993 when the GST Bill was being introduced all the way to date, and I checked the Hansard.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: So, I would like to seek clarification from the hon Member as to when and where this position of the WP was articulated.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Pillai makes reference to positions that were articulated by the WP in the 1990s.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I do not know whether it is fair to bring up positions that were taken in the 1990s and have a debate about that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: And if there is anyone or if there is any evidence or reference that the Member can make, for anyone in the WP making that specific call, then we would be glad to discuss that.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Just on a point of elucidation, GST was not being increased for the first time in 2018.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: It was actually being increased progressively from 3% to 4% to 5%.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And if that is the case, then I think we have a happy situation because the gulf or the gap between the WP and the PAP is now narrowed from 9% to now 2%.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: So, that is, indeed, the position and that would be borne out if you go back to those debates from 2018 until now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I would again remind the Member, with respect, that if we are to bring up policy positions that had been taken decades ago and table them for debate, then I think the policies of the PAP from decades ago should also be put here and tabled for debate as well.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But I do not think that that would be constructive because everyone evolves their position as conditions evolve.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And I think for us in the WP, and it may be the same for the PAP, whenever we have to make a decision on whether to take a position on a policy, you look at all the options that are there on the table and you decide what is in the best interest of the country, what is rational, what is fact-based, and you take a position at that point in time on that particular issue.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: But I thank the Member for his comments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And maybe, Your Honour, if I could clarify, my interest in relation to raising the position of the WP from the 1990s is, with respect, not unfair because what we need is clarity on where the WP – and, for that reason, any party – stands on important issues.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, if it, indeed, had evolved, then it will be incumbent on any party to then make that position very clear, so that the public understands where the parties are on these important issues.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The President of the Singapore Vehicle Traders Association, Mr Neo Tiam Ting, told The Straits Times that the companies that are supplying cars for ride-hailing services are a key driver behind the demand for COEs in recent years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Be that as it may, as prices spiral out of reach for many Singaporeans who aspire or need to buy a car for different reasons, can we not do more to review how we can ensure that businesses, whether ride-hailing companies, car-leasing companies or car dealers, do not push up the COE premiums at the peril of private buyers who need to buy a car for various reasons.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Such reasons can include using their vehicles for work purposes, taking care of their families with young children, taking care of elderly family members or handicapped family members.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For some of these people, operating a PHC from a ride-hailing company or using Grab or taxis may somehow not be a suitable substitute.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Can we also see to it that COEs for commercial vehicles are not subject to similar pressures?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The rising COEs for this Cat C have contributed to rising business costs and present further challenges for our smaller businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And added business costs also contribute to the increase in cost of living for everyone.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the past week, when we have been talking about combating stratification and building social compact amidst rising costs of living and rising property prices, we should be wary of the possible social effects of spiralling COE prices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, President Halimah stated in her address that we have committed to decisive action to reduce carbon emissions and are taking resolute steps towards meeting our net-zero commitments.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Minister also said that we will review financial incentives to encourage the adoption of electric cars and monitor related developments in other vehicle segments, such as motorcycles and goods vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To date, the pricing of electric vehicles (EVs) is still relatively unattractive, compared to internal combustible engine (ICE) vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I agree that the Government should further review to see how we are better able to encourage and incentivise more people to switch to EVs and reducing the number of new ICE vehicles on the road.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: One importer reported encountering problems with the homologation and/or registration for EVs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It was also reported that EV models with dual electric motors require proper documentation from manufacturers that confirm their power rating, and this makes it tougher for parallel importers to register these cars for road use as, unlike authorised dealers, they do not have direct contact with the car makers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Another importer stated that EV options are quite limited for parallel importers and they hope for, I quote, "better support in terms of clarity on importing rules".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the Government can look into the concerns of these parallel importers to clarify and review the rules and documentary requirements for EV sales and registrations, which may be more disadvantageous to parallel importers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More importantly, I hope the Government can provide more assistance to parallel importers to encourage them to focus on getting higher volumes of EV sales as opposed to ICE vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In my Budget debate speech in February this year, I expressed my concern that it remains unclear how soon certain logistics fleets, including but not limited to light goods vehicles, will be switching to EVs entirely and I said that a number of prominent logistics companies have not yet had any plans, or have not announced any plans for EV conversion or some have preliminary plans for only limited initial conversion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Indeed, I have brought up my concerns for the green transition in last-mile logistics and asking for our plans for conversion of goods and logistics vehicles variously in the Committee of Supply (COS) debate in 2022 with the Minister for Sustainability and the Environment and during the debate for the EV Charging Bill in November 2022.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the MOT COS debate last month, I also asked whether the Government will actively engage logistics companies directly on their plans to convert to EVs and to speed up the process.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More recently, we read that, in the United States (US), Schneider has delivered its first short-haul logistics EV trucks while Tesla has also delivered EV trucks to PepsiCo.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope MOT will have a dedicated roadmap on the conversion of the logistics and goods vehicle fleet operating in Singapore in the next few years and will work closely together with logistics companies on such a roadmap.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the Government will have a plan to handle this large group of foreign ICE vehicles coming into Singapore and travelling all over Singapore every day, even if this may take even more time, given that they are foreign vehicles.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Yes, we may need the goods and supplies these goods vehicles bring in every day, but it will be good to know that the Government has a plan in respect of these vehicles, even if it may involve foreign government or agencies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I support these plans and I hope we can achieve the targets ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In the course of my professional work over the years, I had to use harbour launches to board vessels lying in nearby anchorages and I hope the familiar smell of the engine fuel of the old harbour launches will be a thing of the past.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: In fact, I can remember in the past, I would have to pick one of the many harbour launches lying alongside Clifford Pier, effectively like water taxis and the piercing smell of the fumes.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The oil major, a major part of our oil and gas industry, is intending to transit from fossil fuels to cut emissions and meet global low carbon energy needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I acknowledge that this is part of a wider global trend in a transition towards low carbon fuels and undoubtedly, will affect Singapore in some ways.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I hope the Government will provide updates on our efforts in attracting more businesses in areas, such as biofuel refining or sustainable aviation fuel production or storage for such fuels, as well as updates on carbon capture and sequestration at petrochemical plants.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: And finally, I hope the Government will continue to update the House on the just transition in manpower for our workers working in Shell and other companies in the petrochemical sector, what we are doing to retain and retrain workers in this sector as the sector transforms within Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A significant part of the information contained in the addenda to the President's Address has been made known previously even before Parliament was prorogued.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP Members of Parliament (MPs) have therefore raised issues that remain at the top of the public mind, such as Housing and Development Board (HDB) matters, the cost of living issues that affect seniors and the young, and matters of fairness and inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For my part, I will cover three broad points.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, I will speak about foreigners in Singapore and restate my call to the Government to ensure that our foreign talent policies translate to tangible benefits for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Third, I will address the Deputy Prime Minister's remarks on the WP as an opposition that seeks to chip away at the people's trust in Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will also address the Deputy Prime Minister's questions to the WP concerning the GST and list several policy proposals made by the WP, which have been adopted by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: WP MPs know from our engagement with the public that a unique Singapore identity – proud and distinctive – has formed but continues to evolve.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Insofar as a new social compact is concerned, Singaporeans seek a fairer, more inclusive and more caring society.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Government recognises this, and my colleagues have signposted areas where these objectives can be operationalised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With respect to tangible benefits for Singaporeans, the WP has made that specific point repeatedly and we continue to see it as an important requirement to ensure society remains welcoming of foreigners.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The publication of outcome-based indicators of Government policies would be useful tools in ensuring continued public support, or at least, understanding of the Government's foreign talent policies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Providing evidence of how foreign talent policies help Singaporeans in concrete ways will help prevent xenophobia, something we must always guard against.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, it is useful for me to restate the point the WP made on the Parliamentary debate on free trade agreements and the India-Singapore Comprehensive Economic Cooperation Agreement (CECA) in September 2021, a point that Minister Ong Ye Kung brought up yesterday.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As that debate proved, getting the PAP Government to reveal information on the number of intra-corporate transferees (ICTs) from India that worked in Singapore upon the introduction of CECA was like squeezing blood out of a stone.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Parliamentary Questions had been filed by the WP on the issue from 2016, but forthright answers were not forthcoming.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the meantime, pressures and tensions on the ground built up as a small number of Singaporeans became emotionally charged about CECA, using it as an adjective and in very uncharitable and downright racist ways.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP sought information, answers to which could have shed light and reduced heat before things reached a boiling point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Unlike as suggested by Minister Ong yesterday, sometimes filing a Parliamentary Question does not guarantee receiving an adequate and substantive answer from the PAP Government, from which alternatives can germinate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are already murmurings of discontent that are led by emotional perspectives, created by facts such as the mass buying spree of properties in single developments by foreigners.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If the Government does not step in early and fill the information vacuum on how outcomes for Singapore and Singaporeans are enhanced, this subject may turn ugly too and it would be important for the Government to be on top of this.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In future, the PAP must not see calls for information as a Trojan horse for ulterior motives or a red herring.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When there are requests for detailed figures, the PAP must not turn defensive in response to the Parliamentary Opposition of the day playing its role checking the Government of the day.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In moving this Motion, MP Mr Murali Pillai stated that we must recognise that the nature of the electorate is changing and today, a new generation is emerging – standing taller and brighter than the ones before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: He also said, and I quote, "People's psyche will change and as they do, the Government must change to a degree and at a speed unprecedented." Likewise, the interventions of the Opposition in this House, the questions it asks and the proposals it advances must reflect this new psyche.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Going forward, the 4G PAP Leadership cannot be dismissive, or breezily use national security or sensitivity, as reasons for withholding information without good reason.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the point of the Prime Minister's Office's Strategy Group's addendum covering better integration of newcomers into society, I had proposed an English requirement for PRs and citizenship applications in last month's COS debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Prior to the release of the survey result, in some limited quarters, the proposal for an English requirement was incorrectly understood as a divisive one, with the implicit point being that mother tongue languages would somehow be compromised or that an English requirement was actually a test for "Singaporeaness".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But these criticisms missed the key point of the proposal, which was focused on integration.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am gratified that the demographically representative survey respondents did not miss the point.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The wide support for an English requirement, as shown by the survey, can perhaps be traced to the historical use of English in Singapore, as established by the Pioneer Generation of PAP leaders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the 2012 publication, Singapore's Bilingual Journey, the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew said, and I quote, "When Singapore celebrated its 21st National Day on the 9th of August 1986, it also celebrated a different sort of milestone.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It was the first-time emcees of the event used English to lead the audience, where before they had to use three languages – Mandarin, Malay and Tamil.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Where before the different races in Singapore were like different tanks of fish in an aquarium together before your eyes but segregated from one another, now they have a common language linking them together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They still retained their mother tongues whether Chinese, Malay or Tamil?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But a common knowledge of English enabled them to share together the joys of the occasion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I was a proud man that day." On the occasion of the 100th year of his birth, this year, those words of the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew are timely.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: English would be a functional language with which to access the knowledge of the world and a tool for survival.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The mother tongue is the cultural language used to transmit the culture's traditional values.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More than three decades since his words in 1986, Singaporeans understand that immigration is necessary to top up our population but they also instinctively appreciate the importance of a lingua franca for better integration with newcomers and the signal it sends of Singapore as a multiracial and multicultural nation not just in form, but in substance.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, no one should be surprised at advocacy for our lingua franca, namely English, to bind Singaporeans together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At the same time, however, we must never sever our cultural roots.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: All of us must remain proud and celebrate our individual cultures, including our mother tongues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would suggest that an English requirement for foreign spouses can be one of the criteria for fast-tracking these applicants.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the Government has openly stated, our immigration policy and immigration intake are calibrated to preserve the racial balance and by extension, an English requirement would not favour one racial group over another just because applicants in one racial group already use English and the other does not.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In effect, for foreign spouses, the English requirement would serve as a plus one criteria or bonus criteria.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It would nudge and better align immigration policy with our bilingualism policy, which is a fundamental aspect of the Singapore system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the record, this WP proposal does not contradict any of the eight principles of Singapore's bilingualism policy established by the late Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For a young nation, this is a positive force.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is wholly consistent with the values professed by the Government's agenda that seeks, and I quote, "a deepening of Singaporeans' sense of shared identity and mutual responsibility towards one another".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Government can explore the best ways to reinforce the importance of English as a common language in our daily life, as it makes a big difference to the lived experience of many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The signalling effect on the centrality of our multiracial and multicultural society is immense.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I did not expect the Deputy Prime Minister to use his speech on the President's Address to attack and accuse the WP of advancing opportunistic or populist ideas to chip away, bit by bit, the trust in Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The PAP shifted its position yesterday in the course of the debate, when Minister Ong Ye Kung conceded that the WP have brought up many good ideas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But both Ministers were consistent in calling for the Opposition to present an alternative agenda and even an alternative Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will deal with this point in the course of my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If chipping away at trust in the Government was our real agenda, we would not see the Minister for National Development acknowledging the WP point highlighting the inherent inequity of the HDB taxpayer subsidies as currently applied between mature and non-mature Build-To-Order (BTO) flats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a most unfair charge levelled at the WP which, in reality, chips away at the integrity of our Parliamentary democracy as an important platform for the exposition and contestation of ideas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, we welcome the PAP taking up WP points because the real beneficiaries are not the WP	or the PAP – but the people of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Number one, verifying educational qualifications of Employment Pass (EP) holders.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our 2020 General Election manifesto, we called for the introduction of EP credentials assessment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We said that all EP and S Pass job applicants with university degrees and diplomas should be subject to mandatory educational credentials assessments, with cost to be borne by the applicant.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our 2020 and 2015 General Election manifestos, we called for the live, unedited broadcasts of Parliamentary Sittings.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From 4 January 2021, Singaporeans were able to view livestreamed sessions of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Aljunied Group Representation Constituency MP Gerald Giam called for a national renewable hydrogen strategy in Parliament in January 2022 during the Motion on a low carbon society and again during Budget 2020.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On 25 October the same year, the Energy Market Authority announced that Singapore was launching a national hydrogen strategy to accelerate the transition to net-zero emissions and to strengthen energy security.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Number four, equalised maternity leave of 16 weeks for single unwed mothers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our 2011 and 2015 General Election manifestos, we called for equitable support for single parents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our 2011 manifesto, we stated that while having children outside of marriage should continue to be discouraged in our society, children born to single parents should not be denied the benefits that children of married parents receive.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The children are innocent parties and should not start life being disadvantaged.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We said that single parents should receive the same parenthood benefit packages as married parents.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our 2015 manifesto, we reiterate our call to grant single and wed mothers the full 16 weeks of paid maternity leave.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, we argue that single mothers should be made eligible for both the Working Mother's Child Relief as well as the Foreign Domestic Worker Levy relief.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Excluding single mothers from these schemes unnecessarily penalises vulnerable children and single mothers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We added that the Government should extend the same help to single fathers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Number five, BTO priority and forfeiture for non-selection.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our 2015 General Election manifesto, we called for the "three-tries BTO".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We proposed that first-timer BTO applicants on the fiancé-fiancée scheme be given priority up to their third try in selecting a flat, so as to minimise the waiting time for couples to buy a flat and plan for starting a family.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We called for the priority to be forfeited if the first-timer BTO applicants were invited to select a flat in any one of their previous tries but did not book a flat.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From the August 2023 BTO exercise, first timers who fail to choose a flat once will be deemed second timers for a year in the computer ballot.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second timers who accumulate one non-selection count, down from the current two counts, will have to wait one year before they can apply for flat again.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Number six, impose a charge for the use of plastic bags.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our 2020 General Election manifesto on curbing the use of plastics, we called for the introduction of a single-use plastic charge, phased in over five years to encourage a reduction in plastic waste while looking for alternatives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is what we said: the value of the charge would need to be sufficiently high to change behaviours but remains sensitive to the needs of lower socioeconomic groups and PwDs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We called for a nationwide public education campaign to raise awareness of the effects of single-use plastics and other more sustainable alternatives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Number seven, one family paired to one general practitioner (GP).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our 2015 General Election manifesto seven years ago, the WP called for the family doctor pairing scheme.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We argue that pairing families with GPs would encourage patients to remain with one family doctor who would be more familiar with their background and medical history.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would facilitate earlier detection of illnesses, provide more accurate diagnosis, reduce duplication of treatment and improve coordination with other care providers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We proposed all resident families be paired with a GP near their home and that Singaporeans could be given the option to change their assigned GP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In October 2022, this House debated the Healthier SG White Paper, which among other things put forward the Government's proposal for one family physician and one health plan for everyone.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Under the plan, each resident chooses the family doctor or clinic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Flexibility will be provided for residents to change their enrolled doctor if they need to do so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In our 2015 General Election manifesto seven years ago again, the WP called for the fair regulation of mandatory FWAs, where companies should be obliged to cater for a work-life friendly environment for workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We suggested that employees who work for a company with more than 20 employees for more than six months should be allowed to make requests for FWAs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Employers could refuse the request on reasonable business grounds but must discuss the options available with the employee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The discussion must be duly documented, and employees may appeal the refusal if there is a dispute on the grounds for refusing a request.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We also called for tax breaks and enhanced work-life grants to be made widely available to help companies accommodate the FWAs relevant to their respective industries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are of course proposals that were long advanced by the WP MPs, for example, on criminal legal aid which was strenuously rejected by the PAP.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, on criminal legal aid, the PAP's long-standing position was that it could not accept the taxpayer simultaneously funding both the prosecution and criminal defence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But they shifted positions, and criminal legal aid finally became a reality in the last session of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: When the WP raised the matter of anti-discrimination laws and redundancy insurance, the PAP similarly offered many reasons why it could not be done then or were unmoved and not persuaded, only to shift its position later and take up the suggestion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One specific point which the Deputy Prime Minister reopened in this debate was the GST and the WP's approach to it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is rather strange because the debate over the last few years has been about the GST hike and not the GST per se.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even so, as the Deputy Prime Minister spoke on Monday, I wondered why the Deputy Prime Minister would want to raise the GST question at this debate because those questions ought to have come during the Budget debate.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Had the question on the WP position on the GST per se been asked then, the answer would have been obvious.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP policy positions cannot be immutable and have to evolve with the political realities of the time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We may not have supported the GST when it was first introduced decades ago, but we recognise it as part of the system.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But accepting the GST as it stands does not mean accepting every GST hike put forward by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP went into the last General Election opposing the hike in the GST.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We did not ask for the removal of the GST completely since the GST has been an endemic feature about tax system for many years now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At least from the time I entered this House, the WP's position concerned the necessity of GST hikes because the GST hurts the poor and middle class the hardest.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singaporeans are also acutely aware that a 1% increase in GST this year does not mean that the prices of goods and services will only rise by 1%.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As we all know, for the men and women on the street the rise can be compounded many times, especially for basic things.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Even with the Government's newly enhanced permanent GST Voucher (GSTV) scheme in 2022 by the Ministry of Finance's (MOF's) own reckoning, for low-income households who do not have elderly members, the GSTV scheme will offset about half of their total GST expenses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am aware that in February this year, the GSTV cash component of the GSTV scheme was increased by up to $350.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, I have not been able to find an MOF statement that sets out in parallel how much this increase will offset the total GST expenses for a low-income family without elderly members.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That is what we must be expected to do in this House, rather than just accept whatever the PAP says.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister does not want	the WP to relitigate the alternative ideas we raised to make up the GST hike by saying that the sums do not add up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe when he says this, he means the sums do not add up if you want to remove the GST completely.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the Deputy Prime Minister would be acutely aware that this House was never debating the total removal of the GST in the last session of the Parliament, nor have we been doing so as long as the Deputy Prime Minister has been in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If our agenda was rank opportunism or populism, as suggested by the Deputy Prime Minister, the people will reject our brand of politics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But many Singaporeans do not want the cause of the Opposition in Singapore to fail and instinctively recognise the importance of a rational, responsible and respectable political Opposition in this House.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For that reason, the public expectations of the outcomes in General Elections are not necessarily in synchrony with Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence Wong's point that every election from now will be about who forms the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What the Deputy Prime Minister is true in a theoretical sense.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The elections are about who forms the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But as the PAP itself likes to tout, Singapore is unique.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The political reality in the Singaporean context – a combination of the first-past-the-post system, the size and footprint of Opposition parties, certain grassroots organisations' manned by PAP apparatchiks and an Electoral Boundaries Review Committee that comes under the Prime Minister's Office, amongst other factors – all these reveal that the real prospect for a change of government during General Elections today, conceals the advantage of the PAP's incumbency far more than the Deputy Prime Minister cares to let Singaporeans in on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister has asked us to be honest about our plans, policies and intentions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the heady dreams of displacing the PAP and forming the Government, the reality is the WP is a small party and we have a long way to go.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I said this in 2018 in a speech to WP's members, which is publicly available under the "Key Speeches" section of the Office of the Leader of the Opposition website and this was reported by the mainstream media.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Why the significance of this figure of one-third and why is it important?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Should any political party with more than two-thirds of the seats in this House decide to change the Constitution arbitrarily, there is nothing that can be done to stop them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, the PAP does not just have a two-third majority, it has a supermajority of more than 75% of the seats.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If we exclude Nominated MPs who cannot vote on constitutional changes, the total denominator is 93 elected MPs and two Non-Constituency MPs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: That brings the PAP's supermajority at close to 90% today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We are not playing "masak masak" when we make changes to the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These are serious matters that involve the lives of Singaporeans to a very acute degree.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The PAP can even change the entire Constitution at one go, with 20 MPs to spare.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On 21 March this year, just last month – in fact, exactly one month ago – the Parliament passed amendments to the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some of the changes included amendments to Article 9, that sought to ensure that laws relating to the misuse of drugs that authorise the arrest and detention of any person for treatment and rehabilitation, remain valid under the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A separate change involved the introduction of a legal mechanism to reduce the balance of the Contingencies Fund so as to maintain discipline in how the Government manages its finances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If all the WP MPs had not been present in the House at the time of the vote, the Constitution could not have been amended as sought by the PAP as only 60 PAP MPs were present.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I want to emphasise that the WP's intention is not to block all the changes to the Constitution proposed by a PAP Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If constitutional amendments are in the interest of our people. we will support them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But if we assessed that the proposed changes to the Constitution are detrimental to Singapore and Singaporeans, we will speak against them and vote against them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Voting against Constitutional amendments is not something that PAP MPs will be able to do if their party whip is not lifted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They can talk all they like in this House and go to the ends of the earth claiming to make a principled stand, but they cannot vote other than how the PAP leadership dictates.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We do not seek a revolution that includes a change of government at this stage of Singapore's political development.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Based on my reading, this view is consistent with the general public's sentiment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the PAP should not rest on its laurels because this can change, and it is because of that question that has been asked before – what if a rogue government sprang from the bosom of the PAP?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The PAP knows that as long as the WP is not in government, it will never have the full breadth of considerations and access to detail the PAP is privy to – Cabinet briefings and papers, access to hundreds of classified public surveys and, of course, the intellectual and operational engine of the Civil Service.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the Deputy Prime Minister demands that we come up with a serious alternative agenda and an alternative budget at this stage, knowing that there is a more than likely chance that we will inevitably fall short on details, owing to obvious information asymmetries.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And come election time, the PAP can tell the public that no serious alternatives have been presented.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But where we have alternative ideas, we have advanced them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We will continue to do so, in spite of the political realities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We have been open with Singaporeans and nailed our flag to the mast in the course of campaigning for the people's votes to put us in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our manifestos have not been an amalgamation of broad statements of purpose and glossy pictures, but specific proposals with a view to better the lives of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At its core, Mr Speaker, respectfully, what the Deputy Prime Minister has to appreciate is that the public expectations of the WP in Parliament as elected MPs differ from the PAP's expectations from the WP – and rightly so.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For many Singaporeans, the key operative consideration in making their vote count goes far beyond and transcends just a change of government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: There are real political questions the voters have to consider, which they are acutely aware of.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, PAP MP Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim has said in the course of this debate, "Iron sharpens iron.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The rigours of debates and contestation of ideas on issues that are important to Singaporeans can help all of us formulate new ways forward for Singapore." He could not have put it better.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: At some point, in the name of inclusivity and a united Singapore in the face of grave external challenges, I hope the PAP can rise above political partisanship and acknowledge the political contribution of the WP towards the betterment of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP's approach involves an acceptance that the political reality in Singapore is the overwhelming dominance of the PAP today.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Part of that PAP's supremacy comes from the performance of the PAP in delivering what citizens want, especially in the early decades of Singapore's self-rule, then Independence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Part of that dominance has also come from hardball political tactics that also hosted policies with collateral purposes that suppressed the growth of an Opposition, such as politicising ostensibly community-focused organisations such as the People's Association (PA), which does the bidding of even unelected advisors.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is the appropriate response to such dominance?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Some believe, perhaps naively, that it is best to work within the system, to change things from within the establishment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If you make it to one of a handful of top positions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But even the late President Ong Teng Cheong, who was very close to the top of PAP politics as the then-Deputy Prime Minister and seemingly right at the top of our political hierarchy as the then-President, could not get the information he wanted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How much less realistic then for those lower down the establishment's pecking order to achieve substantive goals for change?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The alternative in responding to PAP's dominance is to appeal directly to the people – by contesting in elections and leaving it to the voters and having faith in their judgement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is the path that the WP, its MPs, members and volunteers have chosen.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the direction the WP must take while in Parliament is to worthy of the votes that have put us in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Just as the Government is essentially continuing its last term and also the previous session of Parliament, so are we.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We will continue to raise alternative proposals within the limits of our resources and the information we have or is made available.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We will be glad to see the PAP implement policies we have suggested, whether they say that those ideas were already in their pipeline or whether they merely adopt them without attribution.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But most critically, no matter the challenge or obstacle, the Opposition must be focused and continue to endeavour, work for and defend the interests of Singaporeans and Singapore, as equal and fellow Singaporeans, together in the same boat, rowing in the same direction, be it in or out of this House.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In his speech, he said that asking the MOM to release statistics is like drawing blood from a stone.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And, of course, the rest of it is available in the Hansard.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is also published in The Straits Times as well.
