speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I think the point to highlight to everyone, every Member of the House and particularly in response to the Member's statement is that many of the questions that were asked – both by the WP as well as by the Progress Singapore Party (PSP) – were not just on the numbers pertaining to ICTs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Indeed, the Member has also put the questions together on the breakdown of whether the jobs went to Singapore Citizens (SCs) who were born in Singapore or who were naturalised Singaporeans, amongst other types of confidential information that was not readily released.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Notwithstanding that, in the interest of addressing the issue in Parliament, to the best extent that is possible, our MOM officials came up to put the statistics up required by MPs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I hope that we can have this social compact – and let us make no mistakes about it that the vitriol and the raw emotions at that particular point in time, I hope was really something that we should all try to avoid.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And I hope that they were not due to other factors outside of what the questions were intended to be.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And I hope that they were not due to deliberate efforts to frustrate our social compact.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To the Member's point about the confidential information that could have been released earlier, I believe that it cannot be the reason for the ugly xenophobia, the racial undertones surrounding CECA.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower and Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I think that is the point that I would like to clarify.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Before I go into the nub of the matter as raised by the hon Minister for Manpower, in terms of the xenophobic elements which the Minister raised, we are at ad idem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We do not want our compact to be disrupted and overturned because of these reasons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, to that extent, we are on the same page.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But let me just share with the Minister that when I referred to the ICTs, Minister would recall in the debate that Minister refers to, that the Parliamentary Questions were asked well before the answers that he gave in Parliament in July.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And the point I am making was I could not understand why it was difficult to provide the information in 2016, but then when things are descending into an abyss, the numbers start coming out.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I made this point in the course of that debate and this was then Minister Ong Ye Kung's reply.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I made the same point and there is no real difference in the point that I am making now.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And this is what he said in my response to releasing information earlier: "I take to heart what the Leader of the Opposition has said that, with information, we can quell such falsehoods much earlier.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Some data is classified secret, confidential and so on.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, we are not at liberty to always disclose them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First and foremost, given the low number of ICTs and, as the Leader of the Opposition has persistently said that these are matters of national interest, it appears that in every single debate that we have, every single issue has now been put up as national interest.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am glad that he acknowledges and shares my point about having this common social compact.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I hope that in terms of, perhaps, prioritising some of these questions and having a more precise and surgical differentiated way of asking these questions could be one way of making it a lot easier.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I was not intending to speak but the Leader of the Opposition mentioned my name a few times.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What the Leader of the Opposition said in his speech, I think it was a similar point that he made in the July 2021 debate, which was that if only MOM released the number early, you could have quelled all the xenophobia.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And my answer in July 2021, I think it is the same answer today.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We take to heart the feedback that the Member gave.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, it is not something that Ministry officials will readily say, "Let us release it for Parliament".

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the situation became like that, CECA became a big issue with a lot of raw emotions and it got debated here.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And so, we take the Member's point, however it is not that straightforward a matter but nevertheless.

speaker: The Minister for Health (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think what Minister Tan See Leng is also trying to say is that after all this, let us not blame this whole debate and raw emotions around CECA on MOM because they never released ICT data.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But because Minister Ong mentioned yesterday in the context of presenting alternative budgets, alternative agendas, he said, "just file a question, you'll get a written answer".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Because the answer that was given in 2016 – and again, I stand corrected if my memory fails me – was not that the reason we are not releasing the ICT data was because there could be commercial sensitivities and so forth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In fact, there was no reason given at all, if I am not wrong.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It was "We don't release this figure, period".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, again, I think the question really comes back down to thinking carefully about whether that information truly is going to be problematic and what is in our interests, given Singapore's situation, given how some of these agreements can be problematic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I have to add, again, I am going back six years.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I remember the question of CECA did not just drop from the sky in 2015, 2016, 2017, around that period.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Factually, the Government website also had to come out and clarify some of these issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, in that context, I am not blaming MOM or pointing the finger at MOM, but making a larger meta point about how important it can be for information to be released and to take a different attitude towards it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: He has a different view on the way I have characterised some of the proposals made by the Opposition.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: That is his view and I accept that.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I think we may well have to agree to disagree.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But I made this broader point about how our democracy will evolve because I do worry when I look at how democracies elsewhere have evolved.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Look at the great democracies of the world, democracies far bigger, far more developed than us and look at where they are now – how their societies have become divided and polarised, how their systems have become stuck in gridlock.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: It is not as though their people are unloyal to their countries, not at all.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But how is it that these countries have become so dysfunctional where politics is concerned?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And what makes us so sure that Singapore is immuned and we somehow can avoid such a fate happening in Singapore, down the road?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I think there are lessons for us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: And the lessons are, if you look at many of these countries, populism has taken root and populism has damaged greatly their societies; divided and polarised their people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Populism is politics that suppresses the truth, shades the truth, gets into post-truth, distorts the facts for political advantage.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, from the Government's point of view, our stand is very clear.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: We make sure and we uphold honesty and integrity in policymaking.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Conversely, if the Opposition were to propose ideas and policies that we feel are populist, we, likewise, will highlight them and highlight our concerns, rightfully so.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I hope that is our common understanding of how we can take Singapore's politics and democracy forward.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Pritam Singh said that Singaporeans believe in the cause of the Opposition and does not want the cause of the Opposition to falter and fade away.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: I believe there is a role for the Opposition to play in our politics, in our democracy and it is a very important role to campaign for the WP's ideas and proposals to hold the elected Government to account and to offer serious alternatives to the Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: Mr Singh says it takes time and that they are not ready to form the next Government.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: You take one step at a time, one-third.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: But in politics, things can happen very quickly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: So, I am glad Mr Singh is mindful that there is an important role for the Opposition to play and I think he should start thinking about how he and the WP can, indeed, perhaps, not sit on that side of the aisle, but on this side of the aisle in the future, down the road.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Lawrence Wong)
text: What sort of agenda you would offer Singaporeans and what you would do if you were to form the Government?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I do not think there is any difficulty for me or my colleagues to agree to that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And I think that coming back to the Prime Minister's speech, which I think a lot more Singaporeans should listen to, we know the future is not exactly smooth.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: There are a lot of unpredictable factors that we have to contend with and, in the course of debate in this House, we will be going back and forth at each other's proposals and ideas.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But having said that, I accept the Deputy Prime Minister's concerns of our democracy and, certainly, the WP, and I hope the Opposition in general, will be mindful going forward and work towards the betterment of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, I would like to thank, first of all, the 4G leaders led by the Deputy Prime Minister, to have initiated this very frank discussion as to how our democracy is maturing and also what and how should be the way we work in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Unfortunately, I had been observing the proceedings at home for the last few days because of my family's medical problems; and I also thank Speaker for being so indulgent in allowing me to have my absence.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First of all, I would like to say that the PSP is also very in agreement and supportive of the view that in a maturing democracy, we need both a responsive Government and also an Opposition that can put up alternative policies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, I think what we have discussed so far in the debate is that there are two areas that we hope the Government would realise.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: One is, from the point of view of the PSP in the course of all my debates with the Government is: one, data is really not enough; two, which is quite obvious over the last few years from my experience in this Parliament, is the attitude of the Government towards the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And that point stands out very strongly, especially recently when the Deputy Prime Minister made the point that Opposition parties have not put up serious alternative agenda or policies.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, just to clarify, are you asking some clarifications?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, on the issue of data, can I ask the Manpower Minister, Dr Tan See Leng, that I was the one who initiated the job debate in 2021, and the purpose of initiating that debate is to really determine whether Singaporeans, overall, have been affected by the foreign talent policy or not.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But until today, would the Minister agree that we do not have enough data to conclude, with certainty, that Singaporeans have not been displaced from the job market?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In 2021, we raised this point that the Minister has claimed — I raise this point again that the Minister had raised the data that in the 15 years from 2005 to 2020, 380,000 professionals, managers and executives (PMEs) jobs had been created for locals, which also include the PRs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But then we took the data and we looked at it, and then we asked, but this includes all the PRs in the definition of locals, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, during the same 15-year period, we have 650,000 new —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if I may ask, what is the clarification you are specifically asking for?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, so, the Minister has not provided enough data to prove conclusively that Singaporeans have not been displaced from the market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Perhaps the Member may not understand my overarching English, maybe the proficiency of my English.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is precisely my point earlier on to Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: When you want to go and dive into the data between whether that SC is born here or born elsewhere and then become naturalised, or how many generations, I think those kinds — no, no, I am not conflating it, Leader of the Opposition.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am just saying, using it as an example to say that this is the type of data we do not release.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope that he does not conflate the entire discussions together.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Just for the record, I need to state this for the record because the WP never made a request for information on people born in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I just want to be very careful about that, because that gets us into very dangerous territory.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, this is not meant to be a debate on that particular issue.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In that case, can we sort of agree to disagree here, that the Minister thinks that it is because the data is so sensitive, we cannot get to the bottom —

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I was providing a point of clarification to Mr Pritam Singh's speech.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope that we can keep it as that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Speaker, I do not understand what is the meaning of that.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister Tan See Leng, Mr Leong does not understand you.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Perhaps if he would like a separate debate, he can file another Parliamentary Question on the issue of jobs statistics.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But, Speaker, just now I raised a clarification, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, now, I ask for another clarification, that is okay, right?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In that case, can I clarify that we agree to disagree?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The Minister said that we cannot get into the breakdown of those numbers because he does not want to differentiate Singaporeans, naturalised Singaporeans, locals, PRs, all that.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: And, as a result, we cannot get to the bottom of whether Singaporeans have been displaced or not.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, if I may, I think Minister Tan responded by explaining as to the employment situation in Singapore, as to how employment is being created.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, I think that was his response to your query about the displacement and so on.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: So, if you have further clarifications, please proceed.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Yes, Speaker, but I would also like to make the point that the unemployment data and the overall employment figures sometimes can hide some of the other relevant information about what are the changes in the job market.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At the start of this Parliament term, I delivered my maiden speech titled "The Nation that Learns the Fastest".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I spoke then about what I felt was needed for Singapore to thrive in a rapidly changing world: the importance of lifelong learning; the need for companies to take responsibility for their employees' learning; the need for companies to give more Singaporeans a chance and to look beyond paper qualifications; the need for stronger anti-discrimination protection; the need for each of us as leaders to go beyond telling people to be better, faster; work harder to providing emotional support, networks and social capital; and the need for companies to be better corporate citizens and proactively address critical social issues in order to earn the social licence to operate.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, it is with the greatest humility that I express my appreciation to the Government for the significant moves that have been made in the past two and a half years on each of these, and the significant moves that will be made in the next two and a half years, some of which have been announced in the past weeks and days, and some that are yet to come but were foreshadowed in the ForwardSG conversations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I do not claim to be the first to bring forth any of these ideas.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is no such thing as a monopoly of ideas, but if my analysis and the voices of my residents and other Singaporeans that I have surfaced have had even a small impact on their thinking, I think the past two and a half years would have been well spent.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: On the announcements, there are a few areas where I would offer a slightly more nuanced view.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Take, for example, the idea of supporting workers to take time off to train.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The reality is, many companies, especially small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), find it challenging to give "time off" to train and this is exacerbated by the experience that some SME owners have shared with me – that their employees do not seem to bring something useful back to the business after going for training, so, it is almost like sending them on a holiday.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is not good for employees either – the forgetting curve I referred to in my maiden speech tells us that they will quickly forget what they have learnt.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We have to push both, not separately, but together.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: An even more joined-up approach among the economic, workforce development and skills development agencies, would be incredibly useful.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But generally, the policy questions being considered and positions being taken address a lot of the preoccupations on my mind two and a half years ago.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, this could be a rather short speech, if the environment around us had not changed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But in that same two and a half years, some things have changed or accelerated, significantly and suddenly.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Prime Minister Lee and other Members have talked about the different storms and opportunities that preoccupy us today.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I wish to speak today on one of these things that has become a preoccupation on my mind and that of many business leaders, that is, the rapid advancement of AI, precipitated by the explosion of interest in generative AI (GenAI).

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Suddenly, in the words of Andrei Karpathy, one of the founders of OpenAI, "English is the hottest new programming language" and anyone could access ChatGPT to generate the most likely output to any query and take advantage of its key distinguishing feature – the ability to generate new realistic content – text, image or video.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In effect, GenAI has democratised AI – and when democratisation happens, revolution is usually swift to follow.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Much as the launch of the first Web Browser MOSAIC in 1993 democratised the Internet and triggered the Internet revolution, ChatGPT and other GenAI technologies are triggering the AI revolution and will transform all industries and societies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The possibilities opened up by GenAI are well documented.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The hon Member Dr Tan Wu Meng, and others have referenced some of these in their speeches this week.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: GenAI enables greater productivity and the turbocharging of innovation to solve unsolved problems in business, but also in education, in healthcare and in other areas that are going to help a lot of people.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But there are also a lot of risks and worries about GenAI and rightly so.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Anyone who has used ChatGPT will know that the model can generate nonsense output.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are also real issues of output that is not factual or bias, due to bias in real world data.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Businesses engaging in AI are grappling with the risk of data leaks, copyright infringement and uncontrollable shadow AI in their organisations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Companies and societies worry about socioeconomic displacement, the potential of job losses at an unprecedented scale, including of "knowledge workers" – marketers, lawyers, accountants, architects, developers, engineers, analysts, and, yes, even management consultants.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: No less worrying is the risk of ever more sophisticated phishing, deepfakes and fraud at the hands of bad people – cybercrime has never been easier! – the potential impact on security and defence, and the very institution of democracy itself.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Then, there is the fact that a few companies control a large share of the technology, tech that is now moving from open source to proprietary ownership by companies with a for-profit motive, leading to an AI arms race among companies and countries, for bigger and better algorithms, data, computing power and talent.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If you thought Bitcoin's energy consumption was bad, well, an OpenAI study showed that the energy cost of training an AI algorithm is increasing at an exponential rate, which if it is continues, by 2027, in just four years, the largest model's cost will surpass the gross domestic product of the US.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Then, we have the speculative doomsday scenarios, where machines attain human level intelligence or artificial general intelligence (AGI), and take over the world, destroying humanity in the process.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Speculative or not, so great is the worry, that the Future Life Institute put out a call for a six-month pause, or moratorium, on training AI models more powerful than OpenAI's GPT-4 model, and some very smart people have signed this proposal.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In reality, we are further away from AGI than the recent hype may suggest.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As Yann Le Cun of META put it, we humans are very language oriented. "We think when something is fluent, it's also intelligent, but it's not true".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And I think that resonates with many of us.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I will not go into the merits of the moratorium proposal – others much deeper in this field than me have opined on this, but as a believer in progress through knowledge, the idea seems unfruitful and impractical.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For me, the real question is not whether machines can attain human intelligence, or even when that might happen, but rather: how do we, as a country, best prepare for the eventual future and have a voice in influencing how it all develops to protect and advance our interests.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The time has come for governments to recognise that we are at a precipice and that they must act to determine the position they want to hold with respect to AI, the impact on their people and the required adaptations and the policies they must make going forward, to ensure the effective and ethical development and deployment of AI and GenAI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But if we are standing at the precipice of an AI revolution, do we need to revisit the ambition, scope and pace of our national AI strategy and our AI policies, to avoid being left behind in the arms race, and to create more value for the world and for ourselves?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Today, I want to focus on two potential areas to double down on: one, building an AI and GenAI-ready people; and two, leading the way in promoting better and safer AI and GenAI development and deployment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This AI revolution will have a massive impact on people and jobs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are four things we need to do.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Anticipate how jobs will change in a GenAI world.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Instead of creating content or code or preparing or processing documents, people will be supervising first drafts by AI while focusing more on strategic thinking, building customer relationships and developing more complex campaigns using AI tools.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is not new – we are used by now to technology disruption.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But what is going to be different is the scale and speed at which this will happen.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, reskilling and re-employment, at scale, at speed, alongside managing the impact on people's professional identity and self-esteem, is going to be a serious challenge.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And we will need to face up to the possibility, the probability that some will be left behind and this will require a new tilt towards redistribution.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is timely today, but think about what might be needed 10 years from now.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to anticipate this and time the shifts appropriately.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In making these shifts, I hope we will remember that AI itself could be part of the solution, removing some traditional trade-offs.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For example, AI can help in personalised reskilling at scale.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We could also look at using AI in social services to provide tailored social and re-employment support at scale – rather than compromising someone that tolerated it for the sake of ease of implementation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: All this will require public trust in AI and Public Officer's proper adoption of AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Develop talent for the range of AI roles required – data scientists, but also designers, engineers, ethicists and so on.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Remember it is possible that AI will create as many jobs as it displaces.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: AI talent will be needed in business, academia and public service.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Attract the global talent with the new skillsets for the new jobs that AI will create.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I think we do not have to explain that.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Engage Singaporeans to not fear this AI revolution, but to embrace it and this is a massive change management effort.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I once received an email from a resident.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He observed the challenges and stress that people have adapting to technology, and asked, why does Singapore have to move so fast to adopt the latest technology?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Why are we so obsessed with becoming a Smart Nation?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Why can we not make the choice to stick to low technology or non-technology approaches on some things to make life easier for our people?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to make people understand it is not a matter of choice.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The AI revolution will not wait for us.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But we need to assure people that humans are not going anywhere – humans are needed to deploy AI effectively and ethically.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We need to inspire people – it is not all about avoiding displacement – there are all these very exciting opportunities that a general purpose technology like GenAI allows the young and not so young, to find application in all facets of the economy, of life, that can create value for a lot of people and help a lot of people and that should be empowering.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And we need to monitor the pulse of our people and make interventions along the way.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Second, leading the way in promoting better and safer AI development and deployment.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As Minister Ong said, responsible stewardship is a hallmark of our policymaking.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: AI governance and ethics is already a key pillar of the National AI strategy.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Earlier in the day, Senior Minister of State Janil had talked about AI Verify and some of the tools that we have already developed by Infocomm Media Development Authority and Personal Data Protection Commission.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But the many ethical and legal concerns that people have about AI point to the fact that research in AI governance and ethics has lagged other aspects like compute power.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are big questions yet unsolved on issues like liability in the event of harm or bias, like data protection, privacy protection.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How to prevent ChatGPT from becoming a tool for spreading misinformation and bias?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As we move towards to AGI, how to ensure that AI systems behave in ways that are aligned to human values will be critical to advancing the progress of AI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, regulation of AI is gathering momentum globally.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Prominent among these is the European Union (EU) AI Act, the first broad regulatory framework on AI, unveiled in 2021.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But the rapid advances in GenAI show how difficult it is for regulations to keep up, with EU lawmakers struggling to reach consensus as to how to deal with them in the Act.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore, the Model Governance Framework lays out principles, but not penalties.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It seeks to build public trust and understanding and to balance innovation and protection.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There is no AI-specific regulation, but deployment of AI requires consideration of other existing regulations.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I think this approach is pragmatic, but some have wondered if it is too top down and does not do enough to ensure that responsibility cascades down the organisation.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And others have asked if more regulatory power is needed given our status as a global financial and technological hub.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, how could Singapore be of value to the world in this regard?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Global standards are needed but difficult in a world where the global governance order is collapsing and on an issue that is so ideologically charged.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: As a colleague commented: "Singapore's middle ground between the East and West is uniquely interesting.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The US or Western logic of absolute freedom of expression is hitting the limit of fake news at scale with GenAI.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Chinese over control is hitting the limit of tech progress".

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: He continued "I find policy making in Singapore much more nuanced when approaching those questions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: So, for me, it brings legitimacy."  His comments raise an interesting question as to the role Singapore could play in leading a global effort.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Whether we strengthen ethical guidelines or put more teeth with regulations and legal protections is something to be evaluated against the trade-offs between innovation and protection.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But there can be more regrets in increasing understanding.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: How can we increase understanding and align others to work together to manage our common concerns?

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Forums with technology providers, civil society and governments help.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Could the approach taken in dealing with online falsehoods and Protection from Online Falsehoods and Manipulation Regulations be something to consider – rigorous public hearings and a national debate to study the risks and issues and recommend strategies to deal with them?

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: At the address for the Opening of the second session of the 14th Parliament last week, Mdm President spoke on the geopolitical and economic challenges we face on the horizon and the need to refresh our social compact.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: She also set out the Government's agenda for the next half term of the 14th Parliament.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These core values may appear intuitive to most Singaporeans in the context of the present day.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is almost like an unwritten code that forms part of the psyche of being a Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And yet, we sometimes forget that these core values underpinning our social compact is not an inherent trait nor did it happen by chance.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is the result of hard work, deliberate effort and, dare I say, a lot of gumption and guts by our founding leaders in their efforts to build and forge social cohesion and unity among a diverse group of disparate migrant communities who have come to Singapore in search of a better future.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It was just after Independence – four months, in fact.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Then-Prime Minister Lee was brutally frank and honest about the immense challenges that Singapore was facing post-Independence, but he also made it crystal clear the direction and values upon which Singapore was to be built upon moving forward.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: A part of his speech I thought summarised our social compact very well.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: He said, "Anyway, the end result was that we were kicked out of Malaysia after two years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And I say that we make it succeed – from here.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Provided you are loyal, you belong, you intend to make this place tick.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I say you are a partner with me in this enterprise.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: And slowly, over the years, something is going to happen." Sir, that something did happen.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In 1976, I started studying at Serangoon Gardens Secondary School as a 13-year-old, a stone's throw from the same Serangoon Gardens Circus the speech was made a mere 11 years earlier.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I was the middle child of three boys to a pair of Chinese language teachers living in the promised low-cost housing, attending the same school with my Malay, Indian and other Chinese schoolmates from varying socio-economic backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Looking back, Sir, it is an absolute privilege to have lived through the earlier years where we worked towards this social compact together as a nation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As Mr Lee Kuan Yew also shared in his speech, the other path, which was arguably an easier and more popular route by other countries of the time, was communalism, where one appeals to one's race, one's language, one's religion, oftentimes that of the majority.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But we were determined, together with our successive leaders, to hold on and continue to build upon the core values of a multiracial, multicultural society that leverages diversity as a strength towards creating a shared sense of belonging and identity.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In so doing, we have also allowed different communities to be free to preserve and promote their cultural heritage and to practice customs and beliefs while always being mindful of the rights and sensibilities of others.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We were diverse but united in our belief that we are here to build a nation that every single one of us, regardless of race, language or religion, had a stake in.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Being unique took many years of hard work and consistency in nation-building and I will be the first to say that while we have come a long way, we are far from the finished article.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, this is likely to be a continuing work in progress for as long as we believe that this is the social compact we want for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There are some who point to instances which suggest the polarisation of Singapore's society along socioeconomic status, race and nationality.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: There have also been vocal discussions on many social issues involving these topics.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These topics that relate closely to our social compact.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I had also raised these issues at the COS debates for the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY) in the last two years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It can also prompt a deeper reflection about our values and what it means to be Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: From another perspective, if we were instead a nation of one race, one language and one religion, then such discussions would surely end in a tragic outcome, as shown elsewhere around the world.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Being able to constructively discuss such sensitive matters freely speaks volumes on how far we have come since Independence.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We exhibit concern over these matters because they are vitally important to us.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: We take collective action because it goes to the very core values of the social compact that we have so painstakingly built over the years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: It is therefore with much anticipation that I look forward to our Government's efforts and agenda in refreshing our social compact.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: They made some comments about PA that I disagree with completely.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Leon Perera and Mr Faisal Manap are quite wrong.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: PA and its members are here to serve fellow Singaporeans and not to advance the interest of any political party.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, there are very strict rules on PA's activities, its roles and its objectives.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Leon Perera and Mr Faisal Manap's statements do not do justice to the contributions of many thousands of grassroots leaders, staff and volunteers in our PA community.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: These people come forward to serve the community and fellow residents and build a better Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: He only asked to be involved in some small selected part of the work of the grassroots advisor.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: He has asked to only do the nice things – hand out awards, take photographs, congratulate families.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: As a grassroots advisor, I am glad to be able to be with the families and share their joy and pride.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: But these are the results of Government programmes and Government policies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Prime Minister spoke about the grave geopolitical and economic outlook and how we must stay united, be go-getting and uphold our good standing in the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Members have offered perspectives and suggestions across a range of issues and concerns.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I will not attempt to sum up, which will not do justice to the range and quality of ideas that have been raised in this House but allow me to commend Members on two counts – first, for identifying difficult issues early, putting forward ideas and solutions to address them and highlighting the trade-offs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Second, that even in proposing changes, many Members abide by certain fundamentals precious to Singapore, such as fairness, multiracialism and our approach of tripartism.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is what ForwardSG is about – building on strong foundations and at the same time, having the courage to do things differently from before if needed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is befitting that this debate is taking place in the year that we commemorate the 100th birth anniversary of Mr Lee Kuan Yew.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some 30 years ago, I was at a meeting where Mr Lee asked a successful American venture capitalist why he had asked Mr Lee to meet with him.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The American replied that Mr Lee was the "ultimate entrepreneur".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: While he, the venture capitalist, helped build successful companies, Mr Lee built a new nation – two remarkable lifelong learners learning from each other.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, the newly independent Singapore was akin to a startup – figuring out our economic strategy, attracting companies to invest, building up our workers' capabilities while ensuring national cohesion and security.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He had a team of capable comrades like Dr Goh Keng Swee, Mr S Rajaratnam, Encik Othman Wok and many more.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Together, they laid a strong foundation for Singapore to take off.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The best way for us to remember Mr Lee and our founding fathers is to learn from and build on this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Indeed, this is what Deputy Prime Minister Lawrence and the 4G team are doing – to refresh our social compact and bring Singapore forward.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Like Mr Lee and the founding fathers, the 4G team must win the trust of Singaporeans by setting out a clear plan to secure a better future for all.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our plans must address Singaporeans' aspirations and concerns, given today's context of an ageing population, greater economic disruption, a worrisome international environment and differences in starting points.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is why the ForwardSG agenda sets out the shifts we need to make to refresh our social compact.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This unity and clear sense of purpose is crucial if we are to continue to secure our place in the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As the President said in her address, we must "take the world as it is, and not what we wish it to be".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over the years, our policies and hard work have earned Singapore and Singaporeans a good reputation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The next lap will see new challenges as geopolitics become more unsettling, technology and innovation disrupt jobs more rapidly and our constraints of land, labour and carbon become tighter, but I am optimistic that we can, once again, turn challenges into opportunities and secure a bright future for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Within our short history, we have managed to survive and thrive through even more difficult circumstances.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: A key lesson is that to continue to succeed, we must stay relevant and useful to the world while deepening our social cohesion and national unity.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As we look forward towards the future, allow me to touch on three things we need to get right, in addition to the many that many of you have suggested.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Second, we must develop every Singaporean to their fullest potential and empower each one to thrive and succeed.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Third, we must remain open as an economy, as a society and as a people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Some may ask whether we should move beyond economic growth to focus on other pressing domestic issues, such as caring for our seniors and uplifting those with disadvantages.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: After all, we are almost at full employment and the constant call to upgrade and reskill can be tiresome.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Throughout our history, growth has never been for growth's sake.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Growth is critical for giving us the means to build a better Singapore and better lives for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Growth allows our people to access good jobs, fulfil their aspirations and raise their families.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It generates the resources for our nation to fund needs and priorities, such as supporting families, caring for our seniors and uplifting those with disadvantages.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Thinking longer term, growth coupled with prudence has enabled us to build a buffer to weather many storms.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our national reserves were created through the surpluses generated by strong economic growth.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our founding fathers and successive governments were disciplined about saving for a rainy day.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Within my career, I have experienced many of such rainy days – the Asian Financial Crisis, the dot.com bubble, the Global Financial Crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic, which plunged us into one of the worst recessions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We supported our workers and companies through these crises and retained their capabilities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am grateful, as a citizen, that we could do this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Without strong growth and the discipline of setting aside resources to provide a buffer against the unexpected, Singapore and Singaporeans would have been worse off.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, let us resolve to not just think about the next election, but to think long-term, about the future of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This will slow down the rate of accumulating reserves, leaving future generations with less resources.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Sustaining growth and creating good jobs for our people will become harder in the years ahead.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Besides getting our fiscal and monetary policies right, we must address structural changes that are sweeping across the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: First, scientific and technological innovation will reshape every sector of the economy even more rapidly than before.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Today, robots can enable factories to operate round-the-clock.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In fact, I myself have seen several dark factories, where it is not even lighted up, because the robots were all doing the job and they did not need lights.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And an AI can spot disease on x-rays as accurately as a human radiologist.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ms Mariam Jaafar spoke about the impact of AI earlier.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: New sectors like the digital economy and renewables, biotech and a whole range of others are advancing rapidly.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There is now a more dynamic corporate landscape of startups and smaller companies, pushing the frontiers with greater agility.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many traditional firms and workers will find this competition unsettling.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Competition not just from other countries or from foreigners, but from greater automation and AI.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Yet, these advances also offer the best hope for addressing global challenges like climate change and ageing populations, from extending healthy longevity, to new low carbon technology that can bring us closer towards a net-zero world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must learn to harness the best of science, technology and innovation, while supporting our workers and companies to ride these advances and blunting the sharp edges that they bring.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The shift towards national security considerations and industrial policy will reverse the past three decades of globalisation and free trade.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore's small open economy, which has benefited from an open, multilateral framework, can be badly affected.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Third, ageing populations, especially in the developed world, will be a challenge for many governments.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ageing can significantly affect personal consumption, retirement adequacy, healthcare consumption and economic dynamism.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In many countries, the social compact is being strained as societies confront this crisis.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: More fundamentally, we need to grapple with the difficult but critical issue of talent and immigration, which I will speak more about later.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These three structural changes will transform the global economy.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To succeed, we must press on with efforts to transform our economy, with the Government, businesses and workers working closely together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We had made a good start seven years ago.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The ITMs mobilise companies and workers in every sector to prepare for the future.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Resilience to address shocks in the supply chains and sustainability to address carbon constraints.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: There is also a sharper focus on the future of jobs and skills, to better deploy technology and prepare for an ageing workforce.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I visited two companies which leveraged technology to redesign higher-value and better jobs for their older workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The founder explained to me that he trained a staff in his 60s to supervise the new automated system.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I should tell Mr Leong Mun Wai that the founder was a foreigner who has been working here for many years and the older worker was a Singaporean whom he cared about and said, "I'd better redesign the process to keep him employed".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This staff was very qualified to do this because he had gone through the difficult manual work before and if there was any breakdown in the system, he would happen to be the best person to be able to do that.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: He was thoughtful and caring enough to redesign the whole job and train him to do it.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Another company adopted the use of exoskeletons to enable their staff to lift objects safely.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The broader point is that job redesign can be empowering and inclusive, a point that Miss Rachel Ong mentioned yesterday about helping PwDs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Besides enabling older workers who wish to continue working to do so in a fulfilling and safe manner, it can enable differently-abled people to take on good jobs and fulfil their potential.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: With science and technology determining the next bound of growth and competitiveness, we must deepen Singapore's investments in research & development (R&D), and tighten the linkage between our R&D and industry transformation efforts.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In a more contested world, we should position Singapore as a Global Asia node of technology, innovation and enterprise.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This way, we can attract, create and capture value in Singapore, which will benefit not just ourselves, but the region and the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Over the years, we have invested in and grown our research, innovation and enterprise capabilities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We have strengthened our research capabilities in our universities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University are now ranked among the best in the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Besides anchoring multinational enterprises, we have also developed a lively startup ecosystem, connecting venture capital and private equity with innovative startups and companies.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In an age of contestation, we must build bridges, not walls.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Positioning Singapore as a Global Asia node is of strategic importance.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We seek to be a trusted partner with strong regulatory frameworks and rules, and connected to different parts of the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We can be the place that facilitates collaboration between like-minded partners and countries.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must continue to welcome the best researchers and scientists and entrepreneurs from around the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As several Nobel laureates who were in Singapore for the Global Young Scientists Summit earlier this year told their audience, "Science is global.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: By building bridges, we can stay relevant and useful to the world".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: So, I was glad to hear Mr Pritam Singh say earlier on that the WP is not xenophobic.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Ultimately, economic growth is about creating tangible benefits for all.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To do this, we must develop every Singaporean fully, and enable each to maximise his or her potential and seize opportunities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It reflects our investments and shifts, particularly in education, to support different pathways, skills and inclinations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And we plan to further widen the notion of meritocracy, as Minister Chan Chun Sing said earlier.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Through our education system, we prepare our young people to navigate shifts and seize opportunities with confidence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: One aspect is nurturing "Asia-capable" students who can operate and build connections in the region, which is a vast and growing market.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Bilingualism and the experience of growing up in a multiracial society bring advantages.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We nurture competencies like global awareness, cross-cultural literacy, communication and collaboration skills.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And we provide opportunities for overseas exposure throughout the schooling journey, from internships to immersion programmes.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These enable us to shape an outward orientation and acceptance of diversity from young.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We also prepare our young people to harness and complement technology, by building skills that machines and AI cannot yet deliver well.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: For example, creativity, empathy and building connections are areas where human endeavour remains superior, at least for now.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is why we focus on building socioemotional competencies and enable our students to put scientific principles into practice through the Applied Learning Programme.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Coupled with scholarships and study awards that span industries and sectors, our young people receive a continuum of support to build relevant competencies, pursue their passions and join the workforce with confidence.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But developing our people must go beyond the schooling years.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Success in a more disruptive world requires continuous reskilling throughout life.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This goes hand-in-hand with jobs transformation and business transformation that we mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It also complements ongoing efforts at the industry level to develop Singaporeans, including ongoing efforts by the Singapore Business Federation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And there is scope to partner companies to develop Singaporeans for regional and global leadership roles.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: What does success look like when we put the efforts to develop our economy and our people together?

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: In our universities and research institutes, we have top academics and scientists working alongside Singaporeans who studied in the best universities in the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This builds a strong ecosystem that attracts collaboration with the best researchers and universities.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our students benefit because they get to learn from top professors, interact with peers from all over the world and strengthen their cross-cultural skills.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Overseas, we are seeing enterprising Singaporeans and Singapore companies chasing opportunities and building new partnerships.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When I visited Ho Chi Minh City last year, I met a startup formed by a young Singaporean and his Vietnamese friend.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: They had studied together in Singapore, and the both of them gamely ventured forth, the Singaporean staying in Singapore to run the business operations, and the Vietnamese in Vietnam, running the IT operations.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These two examples illustrate the final point I would like to raise, that is, for Singapore to continue thriving, Government-led efforts to deepen collaboration, be it in free trade, investments or research, is not enough.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To reap the full benefit of these collaborations, Singapore and Singaporeans must remain not just open and connected, but relevant and useful.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: An open mindset and eagerness to venture beyond our shores enables Singaporeans to capture opportunities in the region and beyond.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must continually think about how Singapore and Singaporeans can be relevant and useful, and what special role we can play.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our value proposition is building connections across cultures and economies, and we must strengthen this.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is, in fact, core to our identity and values.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We chose to organise ourselves to ensure opportunities for all, regardless of race, language or religion.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Just a few minutes earlier, we heard from Mr Sitoh Yih Pin a very moving account of his personal experience as a young student.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It is an extraordinary principle, as the eminent historian Prof Wang Gungwu pointed out.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Singapore, Prof Wang said, is the only nation that he knows of where the majority accepted that they had to treat everyone as equal and that a plural society was the foundation of her nationhood.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This open-mindedness, coupled with our stable environment and strong governance, no doubt has resonance in today's more fractured and fractious world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many local companies are also internationalising and finding success overseas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our companies tap on their diverse workforce to navigate foreign markets.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This spirit of adventure and entrepreneurship in our people is commendable.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The value of being a Singaporean will rise if we remain dynamic, outward-looking and effective in building connections with people around the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must continue to encourage Singaporeans to venture out and to integrate the foreigners who are studying and working here, so that we can draw energy and capabilities from diverse sources.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The value of being a Singaporean will rise, if we remain dynamic, outward-looking and effective in building connections with people around the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We must continue to encourage Singaporeans to venture out and to integrate the foreigners who are studying and working here, so that we can draw energy and capabilities from diverse sources.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, we must recognise that when the old encounters the new, this could spark off both opportunities and friction.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: While we pursue opportunities, we must also address frictions.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Growing up in Singapore with fellow Singaporeans, we have developed a certain set of norms and behaviours.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: New citizens, PRs and work pass holders will likewise bring different sets of norms and behaviours.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: It may be uncomfortable experiencing these differences when we encounter newcomers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Mr S Rajaratnam, in the early days of nationhood, said that "being a Singaporean is not a matter of ancestry, it is a conviction and choice".

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Conviction and values remain fundamental when we consider newcomers who seek to be a part of Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: If there are those who share in our convictions and values, let us encourage them to contribute and invite them to grow Singapore together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many already are and we will further nurture the philanthropy ecosystem.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, having developed a set of norms and behaviours that is precious to us, we should set out these expectations and exhort newcomers seeking to sink roots in Singapore to adapt to these norms and behaviours.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: On the part of Singaporeans born and raised here, we must have the patience and empathy to help newcomers settle in and integrate better.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is how we can remain open yet cohesive as a society; open-minded yet proud of our Singapore identity; and successful as a nation and a people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: (In Mandarin):   Since our nation's independence, openness and diversity have been critical to Singapore's success.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Today, Singapore's ability to stand firm in a volatile world depends on how open-minded we are.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To create a bigger stage for Singapore, first, we need to fully develop local talents.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, we must continue to attract the best companies and the best talents.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Foreign talents and the local labour workforce complement each other.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When we attract high quality companies to set up shop here, we can create more jobs for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: But foreigners could also compete with local workers.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: When local workers could not secure job offers or lose out on promotions, they might feel unfairly treated.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: On the other hand, when some foreign workers and their family members do not fully assimilate into our society or do not adapt to our social norms, this could result in conflicts with Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government is also doing more to develop and train Singaporeans to enhance their competitiveness.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: At the same time, I would like to encourage foreign talents and new immigrants.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: As long as you are determined to make Singapore your home, put in effort to assimilate and contribute to our Singapore society and build a sense of belonging, you will be one of us.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Only then, can the Singapore society remain cohesive and our people united, with everyone working together for the prosperity and progress of our nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: An open and diverse Singapore society allows us to connect with the rest of the world.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Only when our society remains open and diverse, can Singapore continue to embody our values and shine internationally.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I started this speech with a story of a venture capitalist who described Mr Lee Kuan Yew as "the ultimate entrepreneur", for building a nation out of a colonial outpost.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Since our Independence, we have navigated major changes well and innovated in many areas.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This way, Singapore and Singaporeans will stay relevant and useful to the world, and stay united and successful.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 3.10 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 2.55 pm until 3.10 pm.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I have had several requests over the break to cut down on the speech.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I am also mindful of colleagues who are celebrating Hari Raya and I want to wish them in advance "Selamat Hari Raya".

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Members have spoken about how we can strengthen our policies and our socioeconomic infrastructure, in areas like education, employment and housing.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But equally critical and urgent is for us to be able to achieve all of this together, working in unity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: All of us, a people of different backgrounds and persuasions, a diversity of cultures, faiths and languages coming together to build consensus, create space and forge a compact that can see us thrive and which can also help us withstand the growing external threats on the horizon.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One shining example of how unity and cohesion have served us well was in how we tackled COVID-19 together, as a nation.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Prime Minister spoke about this on Wednesday.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our nation's collective sacrifices and efforts, with a high trust quotient for Government and institutions, saw us through COVID-19 and we came out stronger and more united after COVID-19 than we were before.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In fact, Singapore was ranked highest by quite a distance.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This has, in turn, led to other positive outcomes, with our unity being a key driver behind the confidence we have in our healthcare system, as well as in our economic outlook and recovery.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Working together, caring for one another, having trust in our institutions – these qualities have seen us through the crisis of a generation.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Compared to many other countries, some of which were deeply divided to begin with – they came out even more fractured after the experience.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is therefore vital for us that we continue to grow the reservoir of social capital that we have worked so hard on, over the years, to accumulate.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As various Members have noted in this House, we have long recognised the need for our country to be special, to forge a unique path as a multiracial and multi-religious society, to be one that celebrates our ethnic diversity as a strength, while having a shared sense of belonging and identity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Few societies around the world have succeeded in ensuring its citizens live harmoniously together, let alone one with as much diversity as Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I have no doubt that even as we have done well and we have.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our unity, our ability to stand together, will continuously be tested.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We were an unlikely nation to begin with and perhaps, we still are.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We must never lose sight of our roots.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 1965, we were forced out on our own.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At that time, we had a diverse population with a Chinese majority.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We were surrounded by much larger Muslim-majority countries around us.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
