text: And as Mr Sitoh Yih Pin so emotionally and eloquently shared earlier, those were the founding circumstances of our country.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And almost counter intuitively, our founding leaders chose the path of most resistance.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We chose to go against the grain and embraced multiculturalism and diverse ethnicities, to recognise and to uplift everyone to make our country a Singapore for all – not just for Chinese, Indians or Malays – and having a space for all religions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It was this bold step, born out of extremely difficult circumstances which became the original seed that has allowed our unique multicultural society to grow, to become more cohesive over the years and to flourish.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to draw strength from that unity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It makes us stronger and it certainly gives us a basis to move forward, and we are stronger than the sum of our parts for that unity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I would add that we did not just proclaim that we want to be a multicultural, multiracial society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We worked hard at it, we worked hard to make this happen, through our policies and through our institutions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have laws like the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act, which set out clear parameters to deter hate speech and other derogative comments on religious communities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And we do so because we want to ensure that every minority, whether in race or religion, will have the space and freedom to practise their religion and culture as much as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our electoral system guarantees minority representation in Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And by doing so, no political party can prevail by narrowly appealing to only one racial or religious segment of society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a policy that has ensured that for all of us, in our lived experience day-to-day, where we go, where we live, where we do our supermarketing, we will come across a diverse range of different ethnicities at our doorstep in our daily lives.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It helps us foster a strong relationship between our people and it shapes who we are and how we approach ethnicity and diversity in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Yet, even while we have made our diversity a pillar of strength, the uniqueness of Singapore, we must recognise that if we are not careful, it can very quickly become a point of vulnerability.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When a society is as diverse as we are, harmony is not the natural order of things.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And it is something that we must constantly work on, to jealously guard it and to be always fearful that it is taken away from us.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Around the world today, we see societies becoming more pluralistic; and as they do so, they also become more fractured.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As various Members in this House have said, it is exceptional that Singapore has so far bucked that trend.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This global trend of falling trust levels leads to deeper apprehension and suspicion.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The shared common space is reduced and divisive ideologies take hold.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are not just foreign concepts or phenomena; these are developments that affect us in Singapore here as well.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The increasing interconnectedness of the virtual world means that many concerns that were once distant and foreign to us, now have the same immediacy and resonance as much as local ones.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As Mr Seah Kian Peng has pointed out, it opens the door to foreign influences seeking to create divisions in our society, to target and to accentuate existing fault lines, or perhaps even create new ones by churning out increasing amounts of emotional, emotive, provocative media, with little or no basis in truth and we must assume that these foreign influences exist here, right here, on our shores.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we cannot be complacent and take our cherished unity for granted, and we cannot for a moment assume that we will be immune to this.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is why our ForwardSG exercise is so important.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is, of course, not a new agenda – national unity has been one of our foremost priorities for many years.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But aspirations change, challenges are different, they have shifted and the context in which we tackle these issues must also change.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And so, we must be alive to all these changes, be cognisant of them and work out what would be the new approach in this new compact, to tackle these issues.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, how do we create deeper personal, social bonds – particularly in a world that is so digitally connected?

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: How do we nurture what is common between us, while at the same time celebrating our individual diversity?

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: How do we stay united in the face of global headwinds?

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I have attended several ForwardSG dialogues, met a range of people from different backgrounds, exchanged many views – some of which I will share here.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And I must say that overall, I am very encouraged by what I have heard.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I have come away with a significantly renewed sense of optimism, that Singaporeans care deeply about that unity, they appreciate how fragile it is and they want to come forward and proactively play a part to contribute, to ensure that we do not lose that unity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is realised through these shared experiences, the various social and communal interactions that we may have and the spaces that we have to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I have been Minister at the MCCY for almost three years now.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I started almost three years ago when we were in the thick of COVID-19 – we could not come together, safe distancing measures meant that we had to keep people apart when our very mission was to bring people together.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But over the last half a year to a year or so, I have been fortunate to be, in my capacity, at the intersection of so many different touch points of our community, where people from a broad cross-section of society come together to pursue their passions.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Whether it is in sports or arts, heritage, culture, language, the youths, the grassroots network, or the various Chinese clans and associations that I meet on a regular basis.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: All of them come together at the different intersection points and all these sectors of our community represent tremendous opportunities for us to build our social capital and enhance our sense of cohesion and unity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are the platforms on which people can engage with one another, day to day, and through such interactions, begin to foster deeper relations and build trust and rapport.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But we can institutionally create the environment for people to come together to intermix across different fault lines, across different segments of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, let me share some thoughts on what MCCY has done and has in mind, to ensure that we continue to foster this deep sense of unity.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, Mr Murali Pillai, when he spoke and talked about sports as a tremendous opportunity for us to level the playing field.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng spoke about togetherness and, indeed, all of these are different ways of expressing that we need to have avenues for us to have social mixing between different segments of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On this note, I am very grateful for the good work that has been done by many ground-up organisations.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I have visited many of them, as I am sure many of my colleagues here have – whether it is the social service agencies or voluntary welfare organisations, clan associations, self-help groups and so on.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Through their own initiative and effort, people are brought together in a variety of ways.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, within churches, mosques and temples, and other places of worship.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These places of worship might serve a specific religious community, but they are completely agnostic when it comes to running programmes with a broader social reach and impact.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth and Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, the Al-Mawaddah mosque, Sengkang Methodist Church and Arulmigu Velmurugan Gnanamuneeswarar – and I hope I got that right.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I will have to work on my pronunciation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They work together constantly – and while I may get the names wrong – they all come from different faiths, but they come together to serve underprivileged residents in the vicinity, the neighbourhood in which they operate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Different faiths bound by a common social purpose.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I was recently at the Masjid Kampung Siglap for buka puasa, again, as I am sure many of my colleagues here were.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The mosque had invited groups from the surrounding temples and churches, and lay people in the estate to come and join them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And when I chatted with them, I found out that many of them had never seen the inside of a mosque, let alone experience buka puasa.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was a special occasion to be able to share that experience together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Young children who were seeing this for the first time, I am sure, would have been left with a better understanding of the Muslim faith and of the meaning of Muslim practices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And so, the next time they step into a mosque or the next time they engage with a friend who is from the Muslim faith, who is fasting, it no longer feels strange or unknown to them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This how we foster understanding and build unity, bit by bit, at a very micro-level, but coming together, stronger than the sum of our parts, as I said.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we want to go beyond just religious tolerance, to a better understanding and appreciation; and grow as a country to embrace differences in our multicultural and multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the local level, Harmony Circles provide the structures that foster friendships and build mutual respect in local networks.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These circles have served us well, over the years, to bring different stakeholders in our neighbourhoods, coming together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But to reach more and newer sections and, perhaps, younger segments of our community, MCCY will further support their efforts to digitise and expand their programme offerings so that we bring more people in to participate and get to know each other.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Going beyond that, to connect with one another through these traditions and share the understanding of these traditions, to deepen an understanding and inculcate the value of openness and appreciation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Another step that we are exploring is a joint initiative we will have with the Ministry of Education.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Students, as you know, are allocated to their schools based on their academic merit.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It allows students from different schools, different backgrounds to take part in their chosen CCAs, and helps them to come together outside of school to form friendships.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our students may attend different schools based on the academic curriculum offered, but these non-academic interactions need not be confined by the same terms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, outside of the subjects they study, they are more enriched when they engage with the wider social network, mix with and form friendships across different schools.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, as we build a better home for ourselves, staying united as a country also means being inclusive – having a space for all of us.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this debate, we have heard a lot about meritocracy and how we will uplift our workers, our families, our children to ensure equal opportunities for all and how, for certain groups, we will have to actively intervene and shape the environment so that there can be better opportunities for all.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At MCCY, there are also several ideas we are pursuing.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My colleague, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Eric Chua, spoke on Wednesday about enhancing the landscape for PwDs to alleviate the impediments that they face so they can come along together with us.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And beyond that, how we should open up opportunities for persons who are differently-abled and differently-interested to fulfil their passions and their potential.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For PwDs, one area we would like to spend a bit more time on is in sport.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To spur greater sport participation among PwDs, we have updated the Disability Sport Master Plan (DSMP) for this reason.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Indeed, as I am sure many Members who have had experience in this sector will attest to, sport can be a transformative tool, especially for PwDs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It allows them to acquire vital social and communication skills, develop confidence about themselves and feel no inferiority complex.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Through sport, PwDs are also able to reduce the social stigma associated with their disability and are empowered to realise their potential.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will develop pathways for aspiring para-athletes so that there are equal opportunities for talented Singaporeans, with ability or disability, to compete at the highest levels.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This includes growing the pool of coaches and better coaching individuals with disabilities by developing their own professional and technical expertise in disability sports.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have also introduced a range of programmes, including learn-to-play programmes and the annual Play Inclusive campaign.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Play Inclusive campaign is where students from both the Special Education and mainstream schools come together.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They train together and they compete together in unified sport competitions, for example, in goalball.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: By playing together on the same team, they bond because they understand one another far better.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our students who participate in these programmes say that these help to normalise what can otherwise sometimes be an awkward situation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It reduces the curious stares and the moments of being overly polite when someone does not quite appreciate the circumstances that they are in.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It also allows them to interact in a positive context and challenge assumptions about what they can or cannot do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: An inclusive society is also one where diverse skills and talents can be better appreciated and valued, and those with these talents have opportunities to develop and to advance.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have done much to open pathways in the arts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The School of the Arts, for example, has made it possible to have high quality specialised arts education from the age of 13 and the University of the Arts now allows us to culminate with a degree in the arts in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have invested in this to provide a comprehensive arts education so that those who see this as their strength and as their passion, there will be rich opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will continue to invest in building up our creative industry, to grow a flourishing and globally connected creative economy for the arts through new business models, development pathways and internationalisation opportunities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are unlocking these new opportunities with the next iteration of Our SG Arts Plan and Our SG Heritage Plan so that we do not just stop at providing added qualifications but also create an entire cultural ecosystem and value chain for those interested to embark on a career and fulfil their aspirations and their potential.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think this is central to our notion of unity.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have also stepped up our support for those who excel in sports by providing pathways through the High Performance Sports system and enabling our TeamSG athletes to perform at their very best.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Take Shanti Pereira, for instance, our national sprinter.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: She now trains full-time and competes overseas, all supported by the spexScholarship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Her decision, as Members would know, has paid off well, with her recent performances.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We expanded the support so that athletes with the potential can focus full-time on their sporting pursuits and do us proud in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Beyond supporting our top athletes, we will also enhance the accessibility of our programmes and facilities so that even more can participate in sports, perhaps not just for fitness but also socially, as a platform for bonding and mixing, as Mr Murali Pillai has suggested.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It needs to be refreshed to look beyond academic domains of schools and grades, where diverse skills and talents in non-academic domains such as the sports and arts are also recognised and everyone is given an opportunity to pursue their passion, hone their talents and do their best in their chosen field.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is why at MCCY, our work is focused on opening these different pathways in arts and sports, for instance, for us to celebrate and include those of different merits.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: After all, a significant proportion of Singaporeans throughout our history has not been able to speak English well, many of our parents and grandparents amongst them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: My own grandmother would not pass this test.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: She probably still would not pass this test today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But she continues to be a source of joy and value to the family in different ways, many of them intangible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If we had applied this test years ago, then someone like her may not have made it into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we have to think about that as well, as a consideration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That is why I urge this House, as we talk about this and think about this issue, let us not close our hearts to this, but to be open.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Pritam Singh said the key is in integration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think that is the point that I have been emphasising.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Is a single-point English test the best way of doing this?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Or perhaps that we look more broadly at the process of integration, which I believe is a long-term process.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: After all, our Constitution sets out the criteria.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: You have got to be in Singapore for a period of time as a resident.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This includes factors such as the length of stay, which I have mentioned, family ties to Singapore and whether the applicant has studied in a national school or done National Service, for example.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you look at Japan, South Korea or the United Kingdom, I think they have a language test requirement.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is likely to be because they have a single, more common, more unified operating language.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But that is unlike Singapore, which has four different official languages.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I would not say that English proficiency is not important – I think there is value in that – but let us not make it a single qualifying test or single-point assessment for citizenship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The ForwardSG exercise is about charting our way forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Youths are an important part of this journey.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To forge a viable compact, we must understand as well as support their dreams and aspirations in a completely different paradigm from when we were growing up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We must also give them a stake in Singapore's future and have a voice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Our young people today must come to terms with a myriad of complex world issues – challenges and constraints such as climate change, economic uncertainty, slowing social mobility, and they will be growing up in the context of the ageing population that Minister Ong has spoken about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For all of these, there are no easy or quick solutions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Yet, as my colleague Minister of State Alvin Tan and many other Members of this House have articulated, our youths are undaunted.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They have expressed a keen desire, on the contrary, to be a key part of the solution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In my own engagements with the youth, I have found them to be very much seized with the issues of today.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They know that the solutions that they can contribute will make an impact on their lives tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: After the President's Address last week, I came across an article in TODAY online.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Several youths were interviewed on how they wanted to be involved in nation-building.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some of them made comments and there were reactions which piqued my interest.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I arranged to meet with a few of them and several other youths to learn and hear first-hand for myself, what they were most concerned about, how they saw their role as future leaders and what more we could do to partner with them, to engage them, so that they can be part of that solution.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One point which came up was the desire for a more in-depth discourse.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They hoped for more details as to how their feedback and suggestions on policies, which were being considered by the Government, might result in some trade-offs that they had perhaps not thought about.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We agreed that instead of taking an adversarial approach to policy suggestions, we could perhaps engage on these trade-offs and share views on opportunity costs, develop a deeper understanding of these considerations that would be helpful to making policy suggestions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Youth panels will be for youths to develop policy recommendations together with the Government, with some differences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will be youth-led and will be resourced by agencies like the National Youth Council and perhaps the appropriate agency, depending on the domain.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They will work on a topic or a policy which resonates with the youths of today – something that is topical, that has traction, interest and a fair number of young people support a discussion on the topic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will share our policy considerations and trade-offs, exchange data points and most importantly, think with them on these questions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Against this backdrop, we will create space for our young people to take the lead in the deliberations and formulate suggestions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Through these panels, we want to engage our youths in meaningful and constructive discourse where they can also listen not just to us in the Government or the agencies, but also to the experience of other people in their position, appreciating that opinions may differ from their own and weighing competing priorities, looking at both the short term as well as having a longer lens perspective of these trade-offs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Together, they will develop policy considerations and present them to the Government.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In turn, these recommendations will be taken seriously.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will make a conscious effort to close the loop with them, whatever the outcomes might be.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those which merit further discussion, we will consider for them to be presented here, in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Those involved in giving views or preparing the recommendations can see the impact of the work that they do.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We are formulating this carefully and more details on these youth panels will be provided when ready.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Over the next few months, we will consult with youths on the panels and on the key policy issues that they wish to see under the youth panels.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We look forward to the active participation of our youths to shape the future of our country.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I have always been encouraged by the heart that they have in bringing Singapore forward through my interactions with them.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Earlier this month, President Halimah and I met our Youth Corps leaders at the commencement ceremony of the leaders' programme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: One of them, Lim Jia Yi, led a project called We+65.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you speak to Jia Yi, her sense of responsibility of her commitment to the community will shine through clearly.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: She is passionate about reaching out across generations to befriend seniors, even as she herself is currently a full-time medical student.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Busy as she is, she volunteers her time in many other charitable projects and events as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And while she is young, her leadership was apparent – to bring and convene her fellow youths together to rally them to support her cause.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: She is one of the many Singaporeans who continue to step forward, without being asked, to contribute their time and their treasure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And we will continue to work with people like Jia Yi, striving to be those granules of sand which connect us to the bigger blocks of our society and our institutions collectively make us stronger across generations, across racial and religious groups and across the diversity of our population.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: When I meet people like Jia Yi, I am reminded that, in fact, we are already different from so many others in the world, with what we have – diversity and harmony that has resulted from a system that structurally fosters equality, social mixing and integration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is what the wisdom of an earlier generation of leaders have given to us and has allowed us to build on a strong foundation to chase our dreams and fulfil our ambitions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, let us not throw out what has worked well for us over the years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Sometimes, you must look back to look forward.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And these are the elements, the fundamental building blocks that has made it work for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: To continually work at fostering harmony between diverse communities of different races and faiths, creating opportunities for people of all abilities, talents and interests to excel, powered by a culture of inclusion, care and volunteerism.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It was an evocative and inspiring exhibition; also, thought-provoking.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I left it, feeling a deep sense of pride.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If there is one lesson that I learnt from this exhibition, it is that as a nation, we do not have much.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And if we can continue to stand as one united people, as we declare in our national pledge, then I have no doubt that we will overcome these challenges with confidence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think that the Minister, in his characterisation, framed it as a sort of litmus test.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: In fact, I made it clear in my speech today that it was a nudge to align our immigration policy and our bilingual policy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And for individuals like foreign spouses who would have some difficulty, especially if English is not a common language that they use; or with respect to the Minister's family member who is now very old, for which a test may have been problematic a long time ago – the test is not in that context a veto factor.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The existing criteria would apply and it would be a consideration when an immigration decision is considered – that this person already has a common lingua franca that many Singaporeans actually share.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, I think the point was a little more nuanced than what the Minister enunciated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the second point is international students who are today foreigners; if they want to enter our primary school system, they already have to take a Cambridge English qualification test.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: So, it is not as if this is really a left-field suggestion or something which is too off the mark.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And to that end, I refer to the survey in my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I think the Minister would have seen it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: And in that context, I think it is a good time to include what MP Murali Pillai spoke about the psyche of the nation and how people's views change through generations and how important this is becoming as a consideration for some Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: But I do not want to lean too much into one survey alone.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am sure the Ministry may have a more global perspective of opinion.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am just suggesting that this is something which I felt was important for the Government to consider.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And perhaps, with your clarification, it now appears that we are not that far apart, because you did use the phrase "English test" when you first raised it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And so, when I heard your speech then and earlier today, a test is a test you either pass or fail.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And there must be consequences if you do not pass.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it was in that context that I said let us not use it as a single point consideration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I am glad we have clarified that and you are now saying that is one of several factors that we look at.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On the survey, I understand, and as I said, it is not an unimportant consideration and I accept that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think we all want to ensure that we can communicate with the people we see in Singapore, at least to a basic degree.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And I can see where that is coming from.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I can accept the sentiments conveyed in that survey.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is one survey, yes, but it does reflect sentiments in our society, and I think we must take heed of it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But the point about international students, I think, comes from a different perspective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: They are taking a qualifying test for a different reason.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: From my rough count, we heard 67 speeches in this debate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Just a short while ago, before the break, I left this Chamber to visit the loo.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: There, I bumped into an hon Member, who said to me, that he was really looking forward to seeing me deliver my wrap-up speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Pleased with his exuberance, I asked whether he was interested to get a sneak preview of what I intended to cover later.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He clarified that what he meant was that once I stand up to speak, it will be a cue for his family, who is seeing these proceedings "live", that the debate would shortly end.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: So, just like the hon Minister Edwin Tong who spoke before me, I get the drift.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This debate is significant because of the sheer breadth and depth of topics highlighted by hon Members for the Government's consideration.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I am not able to exhaustively set out all the topics, but I will mention a few of them.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: The topics covered included: ensuring that economic growth benefits Singaporeans from all backgrounds, strengthening the tripartite trust, developing our skilled tradesmen, the need to reskill middle-aged workers for them to remain employable and decisively tackle workplace discriminations.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: All these points persuasively put across by our hon Members from the Labour Movement, such as Minister of State Desmond Tan, Mr Desmond Choo, Ms Yeo Wan Ling, Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman and Mr Patrick Tay.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Concerns about our social compact, the need to strengthen help for the have-nots in our society – a point that several hon Members, including Mr Seah Kian Peng, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Leong Mun Wai, made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Ensuring better educational outcomes and prospects for children and youths from less privileged backgrounds – this was raised by, amongst others, the hon Members Mr Vikram Nair, Dr Wan Rizal, Dr Shahira Abdullah and Mr Henry Kwek.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Keeping a keen eye on and addressing the impact of cost of living and inflation on our people – a topic that, again, a number of hon Members spoke on, including Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Louis Chua.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Highlighting the potential threat of AI on our social trust and togetherness, and at the same time, the need to capture opportunities from this technological advancement – points that were eloquently put across by the hon Members Dr Tan Wu Meng and Ms Mariam Jaafar.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Ensuring that trust is a two-way relationship between our people and our Government, the need to promote active citizenry and retention of our core values as a society – points raised by the hon Members Ms Tin Pei Ling, Ms He Ting Ru, Mr Leon Perera and Mr Shawn Huang.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Moving away from credentialism and valuing skills and competencies instead – something that several hon Members spoke on, including Ms Janet Ang.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Looking out for the needs of the differently abled – a topic that the hon Members Mr Don Wee and Miss Rachel Ong touched on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Ensuring that our families remain the building blocks of our society, promoting marriages and parenthood, and at the same time, supporting these families as they become smaller and caregiving responsibilities increase – something that the hon Members including Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Gan Thiam Poh, spoke on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Providing our rapidly ageing society with a better support structure, tackling ageism and at the same time, empowering them to contribute to our community – points raised by the hon Members Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Ms Hany Soh and Mr Edward Chia.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Protecting our aged and vulnerable citizens from scams as we continue to digitalise our economy – a topic raised by amongst others, the hon Members Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Melvin Yong.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Providing more support to people with mental health issues – an important topic that was covered by the hon Members Ms Ng Ling Ling and Ms Nadia Samdin.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Opening up a whole range of pathways to ensure that our meritocratic society is more inclusive – a good number of hon MPs spoke about this, including Mr Xie Yao Quan.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Concerns about the environmental issues that our country faces were expressed by several Members, including Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Dennis Tan.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Concerns about the impact of unbridled asset acquisition in Singapore by the increasing numbers of wealthy individuals from overseas who set up family offices – a point made by the hon Leader of Opposition.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And finally, upholding public confidence in this House and ensuring good politics, strong leadership and good governance at all levels – areas that the hon Members Mr Derrick Goh, Ms Joan Pereira and Mr Faisal Manap touched on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is the point that Mr Sitoh Yih Pin emphatically made.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: He said that our values are and must continue to be hard coded in our psyche as a people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is what will allow us, as a nation and society, to continue to forge forward to secure a fair share of opportunities for our people to lead fulfilling and dignified lives.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Attainment of transformative competencies by our children in school – a suggestion of the hon Member Mr Darryl David.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Financial literacy programmes for our children – a suggestion raised by the hon Member Mr Gerald Giam.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Protection of whistle-blowers who report on discrimination and unfair employment practices – a suggestion by the hon Member Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Equipping community volunteers with mental health first aid skills – a suggestion by the hon Member Ms Ng Ling Ling.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Redesigning of the Progressive Wage Models to provide for more wage rungs to enable workers to climb more easily – a suggestion by Mr Raj Joshua Thomas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To evolve our charity policies so as to support emerging forms of giving by potential grant-makers – a suggestion by the hon Ms Foo Mee Har.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Tapping on our seniors to get them to volunteer and share their skills and experience with others – an idea raised by the hon Member Mr Yip Hon Weng.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Legislating the right to work from home – an idea of the hon Member Mr Louis Ng.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I appreciate that they feel strongly about their ideas and are convinced that it is for the larger good of our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I wish to point out that there are also numerous cases of suggestions made passionately by PAP backbenchers which also have not been taken up by the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In addition, for some of the ideas to be implemented, there is a need for progress to be made over time – a point that was eloquently put across by the hon Member Ms Denise Phua who had advocated the integrated 10-year education programme from Primary 1 to Secondary 4, almost 10 years ago.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Hence, I would not read too much into the Government's decision not to adopt all the suggestions made by hon Members.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In fact, if anything, it would be surprising if all the ideas have been accepted without exception.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: As the hon Leader of the Opposition stated in his speech just now, over the years, the Government did implement several policies that have been brought up by the WP.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: But of course, the Government, being accountable to this House, has a duty to set its position clearly on suggestions made in this House and articulate its reasons should it not take up the suggestions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In the same vein, for the purposes of establishing common ground which the President has identified in her address to be an important aspect of our work in this House, it would be good for hon Members from the Opposition parties to also entrench the policy of acknowledging, where appropriate, where they feel to be good ideas emanating from the Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This approach entrenches the shared goal of advancing the larger public interest even as we acknowledge that the political process naturally involves a level of contestation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: A great example of this happened just a few hours ago, when hon Member Mr Dennis Tan congratulated MOT and MPA for launching an electronic harbour launch recently, thereby reducing carbon dioxide emissions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: From the debate, it is noteworthy that there is broad agreement to the Government's plans, as articulated by the President, to secure our nation's future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: In my opening speech, I drew attention to the ambitious nature of these plans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I spent some time highlighting the broad spectrum of plans affecting everything, from defence to the economy to the environment, as well as the fact that a long-term view has to be taken to implement these plans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I, therefore, congratulate the Government for presenting these plans that have secured this broad agreement in this House.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: To an extent, this may be the easier part of the process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Collectively, we need to secure the all-important buy-in of fellow Singaporeans to make the plans work for the benefit of Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Whilst this is not an easy task, there is every reason to be confident, in my personal view.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This is where what the President stated in her address about moving forward with confidence becomes relevant.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: She said: "We are now in a much stronger position – better poised to overcome our vulnerabilities and armed with crucial resources to push forward with confidence, however stormy the weather.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: Our collective experiences have strengthened the mutual trust between Singaporeans and their confidence in our system of Government.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This virtuous circle relies on us partnering one another and working together to make the impossible, possible." I therefore call on all Members of this House, on both sides of the aisle, backbenchers and frontbenchers, to double down and work together to build happiness, prosperity and progress for our people.
